title: ‘The colander worked best!’ Guardian readers share their experience of the solar eclipse | Solar eclipses | The Guardian
description: Readers recall the breathtaking sight and community spirit of the rare celestial treat – and the handmade contraptions they saw it through
Author: Jane Clinton
Headline: Readers recall the breathtaking sight and community spirit of the rare celestial treat – and the handmade contraptions they saw it through
Content: Matt on the beach in Deal, Kent, where he and his wife, Becky, used a range of homemade viewing devices to watch the eclipse.Photograph: Matt/Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenMatt on the beach in Deal, Kent, where he and his wife, Becky, used a range of homemade viewing devices to watch the eclipse.Photograph: Matt/Guardian CommunitySolar eclipses‘The colander worked best!’ Guardian readers share their experience of the solar eclipseReaders recall the breathtaking sight and community spirit of the rare celestial treat – and the handmade contraptions they saw it throughJane ClintonandNicola SlawsonThu 13 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Wednesday evening, millions of people in Europewatched a rare solar eclipse. We asked some of them to share their photographs and experiences of this celestial treat.Here are some of their responses.‘A few minutes of glory’View image in fullscreenDeniz (in orange) with friends and two families.Photograph: Tom Harrup/Guardian communityA few minutes of glory with my husband’s welding visors in cloudy Loch Lubnaig.Deniz, 45, artist, Glasgow‘It was bizarre: dozens of people with cereal boxes and colanders on their heads’View image in fullscreenDavid’s picture of the eclipse on Hampstead Heath, London.Photograph: David/Guardian communityBizarre being on Hampstead Heath with dozens of people with cereal boxes and colanders on their heads as the light fades.David, 57, Hampstead, London‘It was amazing to see the sky change in front of me’View image in fullscreenAmelia said the solar eclipse was ‘a surreal experience’.Photograph: Amelia Thomas/Guardian communityI’m a keen photographer and enjoy capturing special moments and experiences through photos. I love being outdoors and photographing things that are unusual or memorable. Seeing the solar eclipse was such a surreal experience. I was really excited to witness it and capture the moment, especially as it’s not something you get to see every day. The atmosphere felt completely different as the eclipse happened, and it was amazing to see the sky change in front of me. I wanted to capture a photo that showed just how special and memorable the experience was.Amelia, 19, receptionist, Nuneaton, Warwickshire‘We thought that the colander worked best’View image in fullscreenMatt on the beach in Deal.Photograph: Matt/Guardian communityMy wife, Becky, and I watched the eclipse from Deal beach with a range of homemade viewing devices – we thought that the colander worked best!Matt,38,Eastry, Kent‘We were in awe’View image in fullscreen‘Some passengers got a bit choked up’ … The view from a ship in Iceland.Photograph: James/Guardian communityWe have travelled twice before this to witness an eclipse. Once in 2017 and once in 2024, both times it was too cloudy to properly see totality. This time, we travelled to Iceland and boarded a ship called World Navigator to find a clear spot. It was cloudy all day, but because of the work and talent of the captain and crew, and some very good luck, a large patch of clear sky opened up right before totality, with a few minutes to spare, and lasted long enough to witness the eclipse in all of its glory. We were really in awe, with some passengers getting a bit choked up. The pictures don’t nearly do it justice.James, 64, retired attorney, Sonoma County, California‘Such a cool, unifying event!’View image in fullscreenPeople out on a street in Islington, London.Photograph: Luke/Guardian communityI went out on to the street and saw everyone with their little contraptions – such a cool unifying event.Luke, 30, lawyer, Islington, London‘It was so exciting’View image in fullscreenSarah took her photo from her doorstep.Photograph: Sarah/Guardian communityI watched the eclipse through my camera from my front door – we were lucky enough to have a direct view from our doorstep. It was the first solar eclipse I can remember seeing, and it was so exciting. I kept calling my wife to come and look.Sarah, 31,admin worker, Alcester, Warwickshire‘We saw crescent circles of light shifting on the cardboard’View image in fullscreen‘It was a great chance to take a moment to be in nature,’ says Annayah.Photograph: Annayah/Guardian communityWe sat out by the green outside our house with a bunch of our neighbours, colanders and pizza boxes in hand! It was a great chance to take a moment to be in nature, surrounded by our community and folks of all ages, all pausing to observe the eclipse. We felt the heat shift and our shadows lengthen in the reflection of the sun, reflected through our colander on to a pizza box! We saw crescent circles of light shifting on the cardboard as the moon moved across the sun – it looked like scales. My partner and I were really young in 1999, so this is the first eclipse we’ve seen IRL. I’m so glad we could share the colander silliness with each other and our community.Annayah, 31, lecturer, Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire‘It was lovely to listen to children playing whilst taking in the atmosphere’View image in fullscreenA time lapse of the eclipse.Photograph: Laura Ngo/Guardian communityI’m a 41-year-old physics graduate who loves amateur astrophotography. I use my telescope in my back yard, but last night I took it to Brightlingsea, along with my dog. It’s one of the few west-facing beaches in the south-east. Lots of people made their way there. It was lovely to listen to children playing whilst taking in the atmosphere. All the kids were absolutely enjoying it. There was a very community feel on the beach. There was one child who didn’t have any glasses so I passed them mine and they said: “It just looks like the moon.”Laura Ngo, 41, Essex‘My sister called to say she had 10 pairs of glasses’View image in fullscreenPauline’s family watching the eclipse in northern Belgium.Photograph: Pauline Vandewiele/Guardian communityWe went with my siblings, parents and my husband to watch the eclipse. It was my sister who got the glasses because I thought we weren’t going to get to see it, and then she messaged everyone like, “Let’s gather, let’s go.” And I was telling her, “But we don’t have glasses.” but she had 10 pairs of glasses. We even gave some to the people there who didn’t have any so it was really very cosy. I loved capturing our little social gathering.Pauline Vandewiele, 30, interior architect, northern BelgiumExplore more on these topicsSolar eclipsesSpaceAstronomyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human history | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: It is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage too, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: It is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage too, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: A theatre in Mariupol, Ukraine, destroyed by Russian bombing, 25 April 2022.Photograph: Alexander Ermochenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenA theatre in Mariupol, Ukraine, destroyed by Russian bombing, 25 April 2022.Photograph: Alexander Ermochenko/ReutersOpinionHeritageUkrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human historySimon JenkinsIt is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage tooThu 13 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.13 EDTShareWars may not take summer holidays, but they do sometimes see exhaustion. As drones race back and forth acrossUkraineand the strait of Hormuz, a grim stalemate seems to have invaded the earth beneath. Aerial bombardment knows limited resistance and even less victory or defeat. Ukraine, Russia, Israel, Iran and their allies seem able to defy diplomacy and drop bombs on each other for ever.At which point the outside world can merely count some of the costs. Vladimir Putin’s known desire to eliminate Ukraine’s historical identity has led to its cultural devastation. Two weeks agoUnesco reportedthe destruction or dereliction of 545 of its historic buildings, including 156 religious sites and 43 museums. The attempted eradication of what Putin himself claims to be an intrinsic part of Russia’s own history is sickening.Russia’s bombing of Kyiv’s Pechersk Lavra complex andthe Dormition cathedral, coupled with shattering the magnificent St Sophia cathedral, are comparable to Ukraine bombing the Kremlin. So, too, is the attack on a cathedral and a museum in Odesa, andthe destructionof a theatre in Mariupol. These are defining monuments of Ukraine’s past. Yet their dereliction has received little publicity in the west.Meanwhile in Iran the beautiful city of Isfahan might surely have been spared Donald Trump’s egotistic bomb-fest. Not so.A Reuters surveyin June found the historic Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Jameh mosque and the governor’s palace partially destroyed. In Tehran, the Persian royal palace of Golestan has beenbadly damaged. Unesco reports of an attack on an 1,800-year-old fortress that embraced a prehistoric settlement reputedly 63,000 years old.The most savage consequence of the collapse of order in the Middle East is the reported damage or destruction of over 80% of the buildings in Gaza. The ancient city of Gaza itself is now largely rubble. Bombed by Israel are the medievalGreat Omari mosqueand the church of St Porphyrius, dating from the fifth century and one of Christianity’s most ancient sites.Gaza’s archives have been destroyed. The Omari mosque’s library and the adjacent cultural centre, whose thousands of ancient documents had survived the Crusades, havereportedly been lost. The Al Qarara museum wasbombed from the airand then bulldozed to the ground. A people’s entire past has been deliberately eradicated.As for Israel’s war on Lebanon, it culminated in June in what appeared to be the gratuitousbombing of the ancient port of Tyre. This included an attack on the site of the Roman hippodrome. The 1,000-year-old fortress of Beaufort was also damaged. The past is clearly without privilege.Aerial wars are unlike ground ones. Soldiers with guns have targets. So, we are constantly told, do modern missiles, but that does not explain the USbombing of an Iranian girls’ schoolin February. The reality is that bombers are casual because they are near invulnerable, while their victims appear small and anonymous. Bombers do not conquer territory or secure surrender. They are manifestations of leadership machismo.In the allied invasion of Italy in 1943-45, individual British and American officers were known to take steps to protect its monuments from destruction. As a result Italy’s ancient cities survived to a degree that Germany’s did not. In the aftermath, sincere efforts were made to evolve rules of war, including respect for cultural and historic monuments. War was still seen as a contest of professionals, not of cultures.The result was The Hague Conventionof 1954and the Convention for the Protection of Cultural Propertyin 1972. But recent years, in which we’ve seen a collapse of global governance, have left The Hague convention a paper tiger, like that other supposed discipline, the UN’s International Court of Justice. Victory today appears to lie in destroying an enemy’s identity and morale as much as in killing its people. When the Islamic State ruined much of the Iraqi city of Mosulin 2014, it set about eliminating all traces of its past. Trump’s threat to Iran, that “a whole civilisation will die tonight”, showed an equally primitive approach to conflict. It hardly warned his bombers to spare the mosques of Isfahan.Of international bodies,Unescois active in keeping a record of the fate of cultural heritage worldwide, but a record is just a record. Its listing of Russia’s and Israel’s devastation of their hated foes is like watching a historic tragedy unfold in real time. We might almost prefer it to happen behind our backs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne thing the outside world can do is help those seeking to help themselves. Thus theWorld Monuments Fund’s Crisis Response Programis invaluable. It sends aid, advice and materials to war zones, almost before the bombs have stopped falling. It was present in Mosul and its Ukraine Response Fund has many projects (26 of which are completed) helping to protect and stabilise bombed buildings, one day perhaps to restore them.As the west continues to meddle in foreign wars, perhaps this is the least that some of us can do. One of humanity’s deepest obligations is to its past. That past knows no national boundaries.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Borges, ballet and BDSM: 10 must-see movies at Edinburgh international film festival | Movies | The Guardian
description: The great Argentinian’s Highlands holiday, a mischievous doc about Jack the Ripper, the hypnotic latest from Nicolas Winding Refn and a kinky noir romp are among the best of this year’s lineup
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The great Argentinian’s Highlands holiday, a mischievous doc about Jack the Ripper, the hypnotic latest from Nicolas Winding Refn and a kinky noir romp are among the best of this year’s lineup
Content: A transformative riff on Shakespeare … These Violent Delights.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenA transformative riff on Shakespeare … These Violent Delights.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicMoviesBorges, ballet and BDSM: 10 must-see movies at Edinburgh international film festivalThe great Argentinian’s Highlands holiday, a mischievous doc about Jack the Ripper, the hypnotic latest from Nicolas Winding Refn and a kinky noir romp are among the best of this year’s lineupEdinburgh international film festival showcases a Scottish industry in rude healthPeter BradshawThu 13 Aug 2026 13.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMissionGeorge MacKay gives a viscerally intense performance in a new film fromFor Those in Peril’s Paul Wright. He plays a troubled restaurant worker called Dylan, who snaps during his asinine corporate “performance assessment” and heads off on an anguished and violent journey of despair into his own past.Borges and MeIt is a semi-legendary moment in Scottish literary history … when the great Argentinian poet and author Jorge Luis Borges was taken on a chaotic tour of the Highlands in 1971 by a hapless young PhD student, the blind author insisting on having everything described to him. This sweet and charming comedy, adapted fromJay Parini’s book, brings it to life, with Chilean comic actor Luis Gnecco playing Borges.SnapshotThis wayward and mischievous black-comic horror in flickering monochrome suggests that a mysterious Victorian inventor created cinema long before we all thought, and even found a way of recording lip-sync sound on a wax cylinder. And this cameraperson is shooting a fly-on-the-wall true-crime documentary about … attempts to unmask Jack the Ripper.View image in fullscreenFly on the wall? … Snapshot.Photograph: courtesy EIFF 2026These Violent DelightsScottish Ballet gives us an engrossing, transformative dance riff on the action of Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet. The ballet is fierce, athletic, knotty and sensual; it is not a filmed event under a proscenium arch but a film that inhabits its own theatrical space. A radically impressionistic compression, performed with commitment and style.Pretty BabiesThe time-honoured subject of Hollywood’s dark underbelly of shame, and the link between sex work and show business, is the subject of this stark drama from debut feature director Tyler-Marie Evans. Two young women escape their oppressive home town, believing that LA’s streets are paved with celebrity gold, and find themselves face to face with the sex industry.The Education of Jane Cumming review – sexuality, race and a real school scandalRead moreThe Education of Jane CummingGerman film-maker Sophie Heldman gives us an exhilaratingly candid and intelligent movie about the real-life libel case from 19th-century Scotland that inspired The Children’s Hour, about two female teachers accused of being lesbians in a homophobic age. Fiona Shaw has a delectable cameo as a haughty Scots aristocrat.View image in fullscreenA delectable cameo … Fiona Shaw in The Education of Jane Cumming.Photograph: © HeimatfilmHer Private HellThe dark master himself, Nicolas Winding Refn, is back with a bizarre new fantasia moonscape of dread, a twist on the British 60s pulp shocker of the same title by Norman J Warren. The film is set in a nightmarish hotel, occupying the inner space between hallucination and memory, a place where a film production is being discussed. The film executes a slow dervish swirl of hypnotic, toxic strangeness.Queen at SeaTom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall give unbearably powerful and award-winning performances in this drama about dementia, the endgame of care and the decisions that need to be taken when the spouse-carer is as vulnerable as the patient. To theatre historians, the Courtenay/Calder-Marshall pairing might poignantly recall their Hamlet and Ophelia on stage in 1968.‘I turned down Gandhi because I’m terrified of snakes’: the amazing movie memories of Bruce DernRead moreNorthbound/In Conversation: Bruce DernSeeing a Hollywood legend in the flesh as well as on screen is something not to be missed.Bruce Dern, the iconic star of Silent Running, Coming Home and Nebraska is appearing live on stage to talk about his life and times. His new film is also screening: in Northbound, he is an elder scallywag who recruits his prissy grandson to help him break out of his care home and head for freedom in Canada.View image in fullscreenA Hollywood legend in the flesh … Bruce Dern in NorthboundI Want Your SexGregg Araki, standard-bearer of new queer cinema and director of Mysterious Skin and Kaboom, now brings us a transgressive BDSM kink-positive neo-noir romp. Olivia Wilde is imperious dominatrix Erika, a black-clad contemporary artist and erotic conceptualist who has a complex relationship with her bedazzled assistant, muse and sub Elliot, played by Cooper Hoffman.Edinburgh international film festival runs from 13-19 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmEdinburgh film festivalFestivalsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump has amassed staggering wealth in ‘most openly corrupt’ presidency | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Ethics experts and Democrats express alarm as Trump uses office to grow his personal fortune to ‘unprecedented’ level
Author: Peter Stone
Headline: Ethics experts and Democrats express alarm as Trump uses office to grow his personal fortune to ‘unprecedented’ level
Content: Donald Trump waves as he boards Air Force One for departure on 7 August at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland.Photograph: Eric Lee/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump waves as he boards Air Force One for departure on 7 August at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland.Photograph: Eric Lee/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpAnalysisTrump has amassed staggering wealth in ‘most openly corrupt’ presidencyPeter Stonein WashingtonEthics experts and Democrats express alarm as Trump uses office to grow his personal fortune to ‘unprecedented’ levelThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 16.34 EDTShareDonald Trump’s use of his second presidency to grow his personal fortune has alarmed legal and ethics experts and congressional Democratsas he has reapedan “unprecedented” $2.2bn in 2025 revenues by amassing big cryptocurrency holdings, benefiting from wealthy foreign interests, expanding his Truth Social business and more, while federal oversight of his actions has waned.Trump last year raked in at least $1.4bn from his crypto ventures according to financial disclosure forms he filed in June. Simultaneously, about one million investors in a Trump crypto scheme suffered almost $3.8bnin lossesas their volatile crypto holdings tanked in value.Monetizing his presidency further this summer, Trump’s Truth Social media businessis pushing a new scheme that offers wealthy buyers special early access to his posts for a fee of $100,000 a month, which top Democrats and public interest groups say pose serious conflict of interest and corruption issues.Mark Warner, the Democratic senator of Virginia, in Julywrote to six majorWall Street financial trade groups urging them to reject a new Truth Social product, dubbed Truth API, that would enrich Trump by giving big investors early looks at Trump’s postings. Warner’s letter urged that they “not legitimize an arrangement that sells privileged access to market-moving presidential communications, especially for the president’s personal financial benefit”.On another monetization front, critics raised red flags about how Trump tapped his justice department to forge a potentially lucrative and sketchy deal to settle a $10bn lawsuit by Trump against the IRS about a leak of his tax returns that gives him and his family immunity from IRS audits of prior tax returns and could save him $100m.Likewise some analysts are troubled by how Trump has circumvented the constitution’s prohibition on foreign emoluments by accepting a $400m plane as a gift from Qatar, and how other wealthy foreigners have backed some Trump family hotel and golf deals abroad.Beyond his personal enrichment, Trump’s monetizing his office and transactional governing style has proved lucrative to his sons, some top advisers, billionaire buddies, big donors and other allies, say critics.ACNN poll in late July buttressed criticism of Trump’s monetizing his second term: the poll revealedthat 66% of 1,225 respondents said Trump doesn’t put the good of the country over his personal gain and only 34% said he does.Former federal officials, historians and other experts have raised “corruption” concerns and other red flags as Trump has monetized his presidency for personal gain in ways that far exceed any other president’s tenure.“Trump has figured out a way to monetize the presidency, political power and public policy in ways no other president has achieved,” Princeton historian Julian Zelizer told the Guardian. “In the first term, he created the thinnest of firewalls between his business and policy. In the second term, he didn’t put up any firewall and smashed all guardrails that existed.“The precedent is dangerous in general, as we are moving to a virtually unregulated era where there will be unending opportunities for corruption.”Former election officials concur that Trump is cashing in on his presidency to an unprecedented level.“Trump has openly rejected restraints on presidential conflicts of interests and is using the powers of the presidency, both real and imagined, to financially benefit his and his family’s business interests on an unprecedented level,” said Larry Noble, a former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission who now teaches law at American University. “In just the first year of this term, he reported his business holdings earned over $2bn.”Noble added: “While Trump’s second term is less than half over, it already looks like the most openly corrupt administration in our history.“Whether you’re a foreign country, a company or an individual who wants the government to approve a business deal, stop an investigation or just be a friend when you need a favor, the message is that this is a pay to play administration.”Other legal experts offer equally strong critiques.“I think the biggest concern is not simply that the president is making money from his office, but the potential for corruption,” said Barbara McQuade, a former federal prosecutorfor eastern Michigan who now teaches at the University of Michigan law school.“Trump’s settlement of his lawsuit against the IRS typifies his self-dealing. The judge assigned to the case later found that because Trump controlled both sides of the case, there was no adversity of parties to provide the court with jurisdiction. Instead, Trump used the court to legitimize what was essentially a gift to him at taxpayer expense.”Since his second term began, Trump has dismissed concerns about conflicts of interests, boasting to the New York Times in January that he has a “very honest family” and that he had never taken his presidential salary.Unlike prior presidents, though, Trump has declined to put his assets in a completely blind trust or divest from his businesses, although ethics experts have urged him to do so.Despite Trump’s protestations, Trump’s crypto earnings in 2025 are eye-popping – especially in contrast to the dismal returns for many investors and given Trump’s warnings in 2021 that crypto was a “scam”, and a “disaster waiting to happen”. Trump’s strong embrace of crypto came after the industry poured millions of dollars into his 2024 campaign, and hepledged to make the US“the crypto capital of the world” with less regulation.For instance, the crypto venture World Liberty Financial, which Trump and his sons launched in the fall of 2024 with the family of Steve Witkoff, who now is Trump’s special Middle East envoy, brought in $799m in 2025 for Trump,according to public filings.Last year too,Trump earnedanother $636m from his novelty memecoin $Trump which Trump began marketing just days before his inauguration in 2025.The Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Adam Schiff of California this year wrote a tough letter to the Trump-allied memecoin marketing firm Fight Fight Fight as Trump was poised to host an April event for buyers of $Trump at Mar-a-Lago similar to one Trump hosted at his Virginia golf club last year.“We have previously raised concerns with President Trump’s willingness to use the presidency for personal profit,” the lawmakers noted in their letter to the marketing firm for $Trump.The letter stressed that “not all $TRUMP holders have benefited from their investment”, and cited a February industry report that $TRUMP – and the first lady’s memecoin, $MELANIA – “erased an estimated $4.3 billion in retail wealth in recent months, with 2 million holders currently underwater”. In stark contrast, the samereportfound that 45 other crypto wallets that were early holders of $Trump coins had profited by about $1.2bn.After Trump’smemecoin bashin 2025 prompted conflict of interest questions and charges of corruption , the press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said Trump was “abiding by all conflict-of-interest laws that are applicable to the president”.But legal critics and experts say Trump’s monetization of his presidency has given short shrift to conflict of interest concerns, as his regulators have eased oversight and Trump has used his office to reward an array of wealthy allies in crypto and other fields.The Cornell economist Eswar Prasad faults the Trump administration’s regulatory laxness for some of the scandals and legal headaches that have plagued the crypto industry.“The Trump administration has clearly shifted the priorities and focus of the government’s regulatory apparatus to look past any and all sins of the crypto industry, thereby directly benefiting the Trump family’s financial interests,” Prasad said.A case in point, say critics, has been the weak oversight of Binance, the world’s biggest crypto exchange that has benefited Trump’s World Liberty Financial.WLF was tapped to play a central role in a $2bn investment by the Abu Dhabi financial fund MGX that is backed by theUnited Arab Emiratesin Binance. As part of the deal, the Abu Dhabi fund bought $2bn of a WLF stablecoin, dubbed USD1, to invest inBinance. Stablecoins are a popular type of cryptocurrency that are often pegged to the dollar.Trump’s $2bn bonanza heralds the rise of political grifters across the westRead moreThe WLF deal came after Binance in 2023 pleaded guilty to violating US money-laundering laws and other violations and the justice department fined it a whopping $4.3bn.Furthermore, Binance’s ex-CEO and founder, Changpeng Zhao, pleaded guilty in the US to violating the Bank Secrecy Act and failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program.Zhao, who still owns 90% of Binance, served a four-month jail term in 2024 and last yearreceived a pardonfrom Trump. Despite Binance pledges to crack down on crime, internal investigatorslast year foundthat about $1.7bn in crypto reportedly moved through Binance to Iranian entities linked to terrorism.Similarly, watchdog groups are sharply critical of Truth Social’s offer to sell Wall Street advance looks at Trump’s Truth Social posts for $100,000 per month.“Using the presidency to channel non-public information to his media company’s major institutional customers for profit is not simply Trump’s newest act in self-dealing,” said Virginia Canter, the chief counsel for ethics and anti-corruption with Democracy Defenders Action.“It is a significant escalation in exploiting and monetizing the presidency for his personal private gain. Providing Trump Media high-speed access to official non-public information is a step towards normalizing insider trading and public corruption, disregarding the damage it may cause to regular investors who will not have the same access as his wealthy institutional customers.”Canter added that “Trump is increasingly dependent on the presidency to generate business profits since his media company has been losing money over the past several quarters.”Trump Media & Technology, the company behind the Truth Social platform, on 10 Augustannounced it losta whopping $238m in the three months through June as it branched out into new businesses including crypto.Top Democrats echo these critiques.In a Julyletterto the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Senators Schiff and Warren called the new Truth Social deal “an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders”.Looking forward, McQuade urged “new rules and new consequences to protect the public from a president willing to put his own financial benefit ahead of the public interest”.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: What end-of-life experts know about living well: love your wrinkles, celebrate birthdays and don’t obsess over work | Death and dying | The Guardian
description: How can our understanding of mortality shape the way we live? Palliative care doctors and death doulas share the lessons they have learned
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: How can our understanding of mortality shape the way we live? Palliative care doctors and death doulas share the lessons they have learned
Content: Composite: Guardian Design; MoMo Productions;Tara Moore;Jonnie Miles/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design; MoMo Productions;Tara Moore;Jonnie Miles/Getty ImagesThe expertsDeath and dyingWhat end-of-life experts know about living well: love your wrinkles, celebrate birthdays and don’t obsess over workHow can our understanding of mortality shape the way we live? Palliative care doctors and death doulas share the lessons they have learnedSarah PhillipsThu 13 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe will all face death one day, but our attitude towards this is individual. How can our understanding of mortality shape our approach to life? Here, palliative care doctors and death doulas share what they know about the end – and how it informs the way they live.Prioritise people, not thingsDr Rachel Clarke is a palliative care doctor who works at an NHS hospital in Oxfordshire and is the author of several books, includingThe Story of a Heart. “I have learned what matters to my patients as they approach the end of their life,” says Clarke. “All the irrelevant stuff is stripped away. No one cares about how much power they had, how big their house is, how fancy their car is, how much status they had at work. What they care about is the people they love.” In short: “The way to live a life that is rich and deeply fulfilling is to build human connections. That matters more than anything else.”At the end of life, repairing relationships can be crucial, says Dr David Holland, a palliative care consultant who works in Norfolk. “People tend to have things they want to say, like ‘I’m sorry’, ‘I forgive you’, ‘Forgive me’, ‘I love you’ or ‘Thank you’. Not addressing those unsaid feelings can lead to people having regrets.”Keep work in proportion“If something is important to you, do as much of that as you can,” says Holland. “In my life, I really value what I do for work. It builds me up as a person, knowing that I can have those relationships with people and make a difference to people’s lives. It is a real privilege.”View image in fullscreen‘If something is important to you, do as much of that as you can.’Photograph: Piksel/Getty Images; posed by a modelBut it is important not to get too caught up in your career, saysRuby Love, an end-of-life doula in Bristol. “I’ve never met someone at the end of life who regretted not working more or not earning more money. If we can find a balance between what we need to live on and what we need to be happy, I think that is key.”Know that pleasure isn’t everything“Pleasure is a very superficial experience,” says Clarke. “It can be a distraction: you can eat or drink yourself into a stupor and have a fabulous time doing it, but it isn’t going to give you a sense of fulfilment.” Deeper experiences matter more, she says. “They are the moments of joy, awe and wonder at the world around us.”Be at one with natureWorking with people who are dying can be emotionally stressful. Holland finds relief through cultivating a plot of land. “I have always found great interest in wildlife and biodiversity,” he says. “I really enjoybeing out in natureand helping things to grow.”Clarke says:“The richness of life comes from our relations with other living creatures, human and also non-human. It could be animals or birds or plants, but it is living connections with the wider world that give life meaning. The more you can pour yourself into those connections, the more likely you are to have a deep sense of contentment and happiness.”Live with intention“Most of my life was spent focusing on living without regrets,” says Tan Ming Li, an end-of-life doula in Singapore and the founder ofthe Life Review, a charity that helps to normalise talking about death and dying. But one day someone said to her: “If you don’t have any regrets, you are not living life enough, you’re not daring to try things, you’re just feeling safe.” This caused Tan to have a rethink. “Now, my philosophy is more about living with intention. If I get invitations, do I really want to do this? If tomorrow is my last day, how do I want to spend it?”Focus on the small thingsView image in fullscreen‘Value those small moments.’Photograph: Galina Zhigalova/Getty Images; posed by a modelTan says the secret to a life well lived is “not just about joy but what lights a fire in your belly”. For example: “I have a dog and I love grooming him,” says Tan. “It’s not easy and it takes a few hours. Could I have spent that time doing other things, which could be more productive in society’s eyes? Of course.” But she values this time with her dog and would never send him to a groomer.“Value those small moments, like when the leaves first come back on the trees in the spring, or when you have a really good cup of tea,” says Love. “The big things are wonderful, but most of our life is the small things. So try to appreciate them.”Be a completistPeople often think about legacy at the end of their lives, says Holland. “I’ve had people who have wanted to hand over something important. This could be a business, memories or the building of a house.” So finish that novel, sort your family albums out, get your affairs in order.This year, Love arranged an exhibition for a client who used to be a photographer: “It was very small and low-key, but that was something that she really wanted to do.”Connect with othersView image in fullscreen‘Knowing you can make a difference is a real privilege.’Photograph: Luis Alvarez/Getty Images; posed by modelsClarke advises asking yourself: have you been a part of something that connects you to other people around you? “That could be through charitable work, working as a teacher or by being a loving figure at the centre of your family. It could be through artistic or creative endeavour. It could be a craft that you love doing and giving to your friends.”Holland says that he values “running a kids’ football team, having an input in village lifeand building relationships with neighbours”.Don’t worry about signs of ageing“The wrinkles, grey hairs and menopausal body that I now possess are all things that society wants us to feel distressed about because they want to make money selling products to try to fix our distress,” says Clarke. “All of those stigmas associated with ageing are a blessing and a privilege to have. Anybody who is old enough to feel anxious about those things should be saying: ‘I am so lucky. I have lived long enough to creak when I get out of bed in the morning.’ These are things that so many people are not lucky enough to experience.”Try to stay healthy – but don’t let it limit your life“The doctor in me makes me want to look after myself,” says Holland. “But, at the same time, I see a lot of patients where medical issues happen for no reason that we can identify. Therefore, it is important not to get too hung up on things and remember that life is for living. Time is precious.”View image in fullscreen‘Living connections with the wider world give our life meaning.’Photograph: Halfpoint Images/Getty Images; pPosed by a modelClarke says: “It is incredibly important to try to live healthy lives so that we can function as well as we can for as long as we can. But equally, ascetic lives are pretty hard and constrained. That is the opposite of life. Life is something to savour.“So, try to be healthy, but don’t beat yourself up for things that are often construed as minor sins of living, like eating delicious food and drinking beautiful wine. We are sensual creatures and celebrating that is part of living life richly.“I see health in the broadest sense and that embraces enjoying life, not just living it for as long as possible.”Celebrate birthdaysIf someone has a terminal diagnosis, Tan recommends having aliving funeral, where people gather to celebrate someone’s life with them before they die. “It doesn’t have to have the word funeral in it; just have a party. I want balloons and wine and people I love to be with me,” says Tan.If this doesn’t sit comfortably with you, or you are in good health, Tan advises to make sure you celebrate birthdays, especially big ones, as you are getting older.Love has had clients who have wanted a living funeral, but for others this can be overwhelming, especially when they are very unwell: “If you can’t face a big event, hanging out with people in smaller groups or one on one is a form of that.”Have a bucket list – and make it happen“I have about 100,000 things I want to do and experience before I die,” says Clarke. Seeing otters in the wild is a longstanding ambition. “I was recently on holiday with my family in Northumberland, dutifully going to nature reserves and deserted coastlines, trying to spot otters, which still eluded me. But I did manage to see and walk among thousands of nesting puffins. That was almost as wonderful as I think seeing my first otter in the wild will be.”Holland says: “The time when people are really poorly is important, because the knowledge of life being limited allows memories to be made and legacies to be left.” What is on his bucket list? “My son and I always talk about going to Costa Rica and seeing lots of wildlife.”View image in fullscreen‘A good death occurs when someone is at peace with the life they have lived.’Photograph: Tom Werner/Getty Images; posed by modelsAnd Love? “I would like to have a baby. I would love to have more time in nature. I want to get really good atmaking focaccia.” She recommends focusing on achievable and regular goals: “That way, if you suddenly get hit with an accident or a terminal diagnosis, hopefully you won’t have a long list of things that you’ve never done”.Talk about the kind of death you would like“A good death occurs when someone is at peace with the life they have lived,” says Clarke. “And they feel a sense of peace with the person they’ve been, the actions they’ve committed and, above everything, the relationships they have had with other people.”What sort of end of life does Clarke hope for? “My fantasy is to be a 90-year-old woman who is still engaged in and fiercely commenting on how she thinks the world should be, but also enjoying a glass of champagne with her grandchildren and doggedly going out at 5am trying to spot an otter.”Love says: “We are avoidant of thinking about any of these things, particularly younger people and those who are in good health. But actually, if we plan now for all the potential scenarios, we can then put those plans away and focus on living. And then, if or when a scenario arises where those plans are needed, they are already there and we’re not having to make decisions when everyone’s in a stressed state or when communication becomes less possible.”Does she have an end-of-life plan in place? “I’m in my early 30s and I am starting to do my own planning. My work has taught me that you have to make the most of what you have, every day. So go to see your friend, do something fun – because life isn’t infinite.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Britain’s scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would help | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: This summer’s extreme weather and wars in Iran and Ukraine have made our need for food stockpiles more pressing than ever, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: This summer’s extreme weather and wars in Iran and Ukraine have made our need for food stockpiles more pressing than ever, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: A car driving between dried-out farm fields, Lullingstone, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA car driving between dried-out farm fields, Lullingstone, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionFood securityBritain’s scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would helpGeorge MonbiotThis summer’s extreme weather and wars in Iran and Ukraine have made our need for food stockpiles more pressing than everThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTShareWhen a business makes long-term plans, they call it prudence. When a government makes long-term plans, they call it communism. Any sustained state intervention attracts the prefix “Soviet-style”, and triggers vicious attacks across the billionaire media. So governments have developed a bias against long-term thinking. This may explain why we no longer maintain strategic food reserves.In Britain, wheresoils have parched, market analysts warn that we’re facing themost severe food security crisisin decades. In normal years, crop failures at home don’t threaten our security, thanks to global trade. This is one of the reasons why hunger and famines arerarer and less deadlythan they used to be. But this is not a normal year, because the problem is now global.Similar impacts are hittingfarmers across Europeand in the US, whose wheat production this year isforecast to be lowerthan at any point since 1971. Until a few weeks ago, harvest forecasts in Canada were excellent, now itsspring wheat is also shrivellingin hot and dry conditions.Ukraine has had a good growing season, but exportforecasts have been cutas a result of Russia’s attacks on its ports. At the same time, crucial global pinch-points for food and farming supplies are tightening: Donald Trump’s aimless war with Iran has caused majorreductions in shippingthrough the strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Suez canal. These have become essential trade routes for fertiliser and, more recently, food, thanks to the Middle East’s emergence as amajor re-export hub.One impact of these disruptions has been todivert more shippingthrough the Panama canal. But the canal is now afflicted by drought, which has led torestrictions on ships’ draught(depth under water). The global circulation on which our food security depends no longer looks reliable.Country diary: This is how bad the heatwave has got for us arable farmers – I’m going on holiday | Colin ChappellRead moreIt’s not just that these impacts can immediately restrict the availability of food, even in wealthy importers such as the UK (poorer nations in the global south are, of course, hit much harder). It’s that they also land on a global food structure that has becomesystemically fragile. It is now highlyexposed to the riskof cascading collapse that nearly brought down the financial system in 2008. In fact, it suffers fromvery similar dysfunctions. The government knows this, because a report by its own security adviserswarns that our food supplyis “at strategic risk of catastrophic failure” by 2030. It responded bysuppressing the report.As with all potential system failures, it’s impossible to say where the tipping point may be. But what we can say is that if such an event occurs, the impacts would be beyond contemplation. It could be the most deadly global crisis in modern history.A world in which governments hold strategic stockpiles has a better chance of weathering either a temporary shortfall or a systemic failure. If food reserves were big enough, they would buy us enough time to rebuild the system. In their absence, if the food system collapses, so does society.The UK once held strategic food reserves, albeit very limited. But in the late 1970s and early 1980s, our governments decided they were no longer necessary, as private retailers would maintain sufficient stocks. As the National Preparedness Commissionpoints out, this policy coincided with decisions by the big retailers to stop holding stocks and switch to a just-in-time system: goodbye warehouses, hello logistics. No subsequent government appears to have noticed that its food-security assumptions are based on conditions that no longer exist. Perhaps they looked away out of the fear of being labelled interventionist. Perhaps they fear criticism more than crisis.Today, as far as I can tell, the government’s sole food storage intervention is a single unpublicised paragraph on itsPrepare website. It instructs us to “Put together an emergency kit of items at home. This could include: Non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking … how much you need will vary based on your own circumstances.” Invaluable advice, I’m sure. That scarcely anyone has seen it, that many people have no space for an emergency food store and no money to buy it with is just bad luck. Perhaps we don’t deserve to survive.6:05Why the UK has a food security problem – videoI write as though I’m confident that the UK does not maintain stockpiles. For several years, I have been asking the environment department this simple question: does it or does it not hold them? The Conservatives were honest enough to say “no”. But since Labour took office, it has repeatedly failed to answer. When I asked again last week, it sent me a long disquisition on related subjects, but signally failed to answer the question. I then asked why it hadn’t answered, and received no reply to that either. I find this response more eloquent than a candid “no”. It tells me two things: “the answer’s still no” and “we know the policy is wrong”. Otherwise, it would be happy to tell me about it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government also told me: “The UK has a highly resilient food system, drawing on both strong domestic production and international trade and we do not expect the recent dry weather to have any impact on national food security.” This claim, which defies warnings from the security services, market analysts and the food trade itself goesbeyond complacency. It’s denial.As far as I can tell, since he became prime minister, Andy Burnham and his office have not said one word in public about the climate crisis.On Wednesday he chaired anemergency Cobra meetingto discuss the extreme heat, the drought and the wildfires. But, at the time of writing, there has yet to be a public statement about what has caused this crisis, and how we might cause less of it.Yet No 10 did find time last week to intervene on Westminster council’s plan tolimit vertical drinkingin Soho. Good to know it is laser-focused on the crucial matters of state.The government’s disregard and denial sustains our proud tradition of heroic failure, from the charge of the Light Brigade to Brexit. Food reserves are for losers. Prudence is for suckers. Somehow the words “British” and “invulnerable” have become muddled up.In good times, government stockpiles look like a waste of money and effort. But the role of governments is not to prepare for the good times. Governments exist to defend us from harm. And this isn’t possible without long-term plans.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsFood securityOpinionExtreme heatcommentShareReuse this content

title: UK records hottest day of year as fifth summer heatwave reaches peak | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Kew Gardens in London hits 38.1C and 40C-plus recorded in parts of Europe with continent trapped under heat dome
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Kew Gardens in London hits 38.1C and 40C-plus recorded in parts of Europe with continent trapped under heat dome
Content: Waterloo Bridge with the City of London beyond.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenWaterloo Bridge with the City of London beyond.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersUK weatherUK records hottest day of year as fifth summer heatwave reaches peakKew Gardens in London hits 38.1C and 40C-plus recorded in parts of Europe with continent trapped under heat domeEurope heatwave – latest updatesSandra LavilleandAjit NiranjanThu 13 Aug 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK has recorded its hottest day of the year so far with a provisional temperature of 38.1C in southern England asEuropesweltered under a major heat dome.As temperatures on the continent surpassed 40C at the peak of the summer’s fifth heatwave, the thermometer at Kew Gardens in west London on Thursday surpassed the previous high of 38C on 28 June, the Met Office said.In France, which has recorded 17 days of extreme heat – one of the longest periods ever – Bordeaux reached 39C and Nantes 37C, Paris was on 37C and Montpellier 35C. In Spain, a maximum of 42.4C was recorded at Miranda de Ebro, prompting fresh fears of wildfires in the two countries.View image in fullscreenA plane drops retardant over a wildfire in Aznalcollar, Spain.Photograph: Marcelo del Pozo/ReutersIn the UK, Charlwood in Surrey recorded 37.1C, the second highest August maximum temperature since 2003. Teddington in London reached 36.1C, Pershore College in Worcestershire 36C, and temperatures in Wales reached 35C, according to provisional Met Office figures.An amber extreme weather warning was issued on Thursday across east and south-east England, including London, the Midlands, north-west England, south-west England and parts of Yorkshire and Humber.An extreme heat alert warning of significant impacts on health and social care services across the whole of England is in place until 9pm on Friday.mapThe Met Office has said this summer is on course to be the UK’shottest since records began, with 2026 likely to be the first year in which the country has recorded four separate days with temperatures of 36C or above.Spain has broken its burned area record for this time of year, data published by the European forest fire information system on Thursday shows, while in France, the area burned had already by the third week of July surpassed that of any full year on record. Fire weather in the EU since the start of the year has been more severe than ever before.The fires in many regions have been exacerbated by unusually dry conditions as heatwaves sap moisture from plants.Firefighters in the UK continued totackle a blaze in the New Forest in Hampshire. In the West Midlands, at least six homes were damaged and four people were taken to hospital for treatment because of anextensive grassfire near Stourbridge golf course. About 60 firefighters were sent to the scene, while the area’s town hall was set up to receive those fleeing their homes.“The apocalyptic scenes in Norton and across Stourbridge are sadly just a taste of what is to come if we don’t act,” said local councillor Andrew Tromans.Across parts of eastern and southern Scotland, there were warnings about a very high risk of wildfires. With record dry conditions in July and a dry start to August, nearlythree-quarters of Englandand the whole of Wales are in drought, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment.In mainland Europe, record-low water flows on the Danube have deprived thermal power plants of cooling water and forced some to reduce output as electricity demand for cooling grows. Romania on Thursday stopped the second of two reactors in its only nuclear power plant, which supplies about a fifth of the country’s electricity. The plant’s director told Agence France-Presse he did not foresee a restart within the next 10 days.In neighbouring Hungary, one of a number of central European countries to break national heat records last week, engineers have resorted to laying stones to boost the water level of the Danube by the Paks nuclear power plant, which avoided a full shutdown in July but is producing only 25% of its usual output, up from 10% earlier this month. The prime minister, Péter Magyar, said work was proceeding at a rapid pace on Thursday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Paks nuclear power plant on the banks of the Danube in Hungary.Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/ReutersThe human-driven climate crisis is primarily the result of burning fossil fuels, which releases greenhouse gases that trap heat, raising temperatures. The extra heat alters the planet’s water cycle and energy balance, making extreme events such as heatwaves, heavy downpours and severe drought significantly more frequent and intense.Britain’s scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would help | George MonbiotRead morePeople in the UK and Europe have felt the effects of extreme heat throughout the summer. Julia King, the peer who chairs the adaptation work of the Climate Change Committee, an independent advisory body to the UK government, has said extreme weather “gets worse from here” until net zero is reached.Doctors consider heat a “silent killer” because it greatly increases mortality rates while only occasionally being listed as the direct cause of death. In Germany, where meteorologists have issued heat warnings for a swathe of the west of the country for Friday, public health officials estimate that 12,500 people have died as a result of the heat so far this summer. More than 9,000 of these deaths occurred in an severely hot week in late June, when a national temperature record of 41.7C was set in eastern Brandenburg.NHS staff working in A&E departments across England have experienced their busiest summer ever, health leaders said. The Royal College of Nursing said its members were working ininhumane conditions, “dripping with sweat from head to toe” during the record-breaking heat.The RCN became the latest union to speak of unsafe working conditions for many members in hospital wards and care homes as the number of days of 30C-plus heat in the UK reached a record 35.Extreme heat has driven a surge in attendance at A&E departments over the summer, with more than 2.4 million patients attending each month in May, June and July – the three highest monthly totals ever recorded.The water industry regulator, Ofwat, said it would allow water companies in England and Wales to increase billsto spend £3.4bnmore than planned to meet supply demands, including for the building of new homes and datacentres.The Guardian has reported howLabour’s target of building 1.5m homesby the end of this parliament has come up against the reality of water scarcity in many of the areas where most development is planned.Explore more on these topicsUK weatherEurope weatherExtreme heatExtreme weatherClimate crisisEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UK universities face ‘financial crisis’ amid collapse in international students | University funding | The Guardian
description: Higher education figures call on Labour to reverse tax on fees and warn institutions at risk of ‘going under’
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Higher education figures call on Labour to reverse tax on fees and warn institutions at risk of ‘going under’
Content: Young graduates at the University of York, England. Education figures said universities may see further erosion of staff numbers and courses.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYoung graduates at the University of York, England. Education figures said universities may see further erosion of staff numbers and courses.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesUniversity fundingUK universities face ‘financial crisis’ amid collapse in international studentsHigher education figures call on Labour to reverse tax on fees and warn institutions at risk of ‘going under’Richard AdamsandRowena MasonThu 13 Aug 2026 13.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUniversity leaders are warning of financial turmoil in British higher education after new figures suggested a collapse in international student numbers would deprive the sector of vital income and undermine its future.The sector’s leaders called on the government to rethink the levy on international student fees imposed under Keir Starmer, as a former universities minister warned there was a risk of a university “going under” because of the financial crisis.Students face ‘ticking timebomb’ of debt and higher taxesRead moreWhile UK sixth-formersenjoyed improved A-level results, and a record 194,800 English 18-year-olds were accepted by their first choice of university, vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said it would not be enough to stave off further erosion in staff numbers and courses.Figures published by the Home Office showstudent visa applicationsto the end of July fell 11% compared with the previous year. With summer visa applications coming before the start of the academic year in autumn, the gloomy figures mean many UK universities will see significant losses if the trend continues, with some fearing international enrolments dropping by 30%.View image in fullscreenStudents at Harris academy in Wimbledon collect their A-level results on Thursday.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersProf Shitij Kapur, the vice-chancellor of King’s College London, said the fall in international student numbers was “in line with the pessimistic expectations” and may also reflect a drop in postgraduate applications earlier this year.Kapur said: “The critical thing is what this cycle will entail, which does not become clear till about October. The simple rubric is that every five international students impact one university job. And these falling numbers will invariably impact the financial health and staff complement of universities.“The silver lining in this gloomy picture is that the strength and desire to go to universities amongst our school leavers remains as strong as ever despite concerns about the loan schemes and graduate jobs, as you can see today.”Successive governments froze domestic undergraduate fees at £9,250 between 2017 and 2025, allowing inflation to erode their value by a third. Subsequent increases will be largely wiped out by universities paying a £925 levy on each international student.View image in fullscreenStudents celebrate their results at Barking and Dagenham college in Romford on Thursday.Photograph: Yui Mok/PADavid Willetts, the Conservative former universities minister and an architect of higher tuition fees, said universities were undoubtedly “under increasing financial pressure and that’s mainly because of the freeze in fees for eight years”.Willetts added: “There is indeed a risk of a university going under [through] financial crisis but what worries me more is just all the cutting back on the quality of the education experience of the students and I think we have an obligation to students to ensure their courses are properly funded, including by putting up fees so that the resource goes in.”Members of the Russell Group of research-intensive universities are being affected byincreased financial stress, with the University of Exeter announcing on Thursday that it was immediately scrapping geography courses at its Penryn campus in Cornwall, including for school leavers who had applied this year.A spokesperson for Exeter said: “We recognise that this is disappointing for affected applicants and difficult for colleagues associated with these programmes.”Libby Hackett, the chief executive of the Russell Group, said the group’s universities still attracted talented international students in an increasingly competitive global market, bringing cultural and economic benefits to their universities and to the UK more widely.But Hackett warned: “A series of policy decisions by successive governments, including the unpopular international student levy, risks undermining this success story. This isn’t just worrying for universities – it’s not good news for the UK as a whole. Recent analysis shows that the decline in international students means the UK has lost out on a net economic benefit of nearly £3bn.“The Burnham government recognises the critical role universities play in our national and local economies and our position on the world stage. We look forward to more consistent decision-making across government in support of economic growth, including measures that enable us to continue welcoming global talent.”Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of theUniversitiesUK group of vice-chancellors, said the student visa figures “should be a wake-up call” for policymakers.Humanities among degrees being ‘extinguished’ by hard-up universitiesRead more“There are plenty of people in government who understand the pressure on the sector, they understand how important universities are for local economies and for domestic students, and they are watching this with concern,” Stern said. “I hope those people are knocking on the door of the [Department for Education] and the Home Office, and saying that they can do one thing tomorrow that will help universities, and that is to quietly drop the idea of taxing international student fees.“I understand the political pressure around immigration, and the UK university sector has to be a good, responsive partner with government in making sure the system works the way it should. But if the government was seeking to reduce overseas student numbers, I think they have overcorrected. What we need is stability and a bit of help to recover our competitive position internationally.”Jacqui Smith, the skills minister whose portfolio includes higher education, told the BBC on Thursday that the government was concerned that university courses should be good value for money, and suggested future increases in tuition fees would be linked to teaching quality.“For most people, going to university is a very good and important investment in their future earning potential and in their life,” Smith said.Explore more on these topicsUniversity fundingInternational studentsAdmissionsStudentsA-levelsHigher educationUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage set for decisive but arguably empty victory in Clacton | Politics | The Guardian
description: Leader of Reform UK on course to defeat Count Binface and an assortment of fringe candidates as polls close in Essex
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Leader of Reform UK on course to defeat Count Binface and an assortment of fringe candidates as polls close in Essex
Content: Count Binface graffiti seen on Clacton pier on 13 August.Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCount Binface graffiti seen on Clacton pier on 13 August.Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesPoliticsNigel Farage set for decisive but arguably empty victory in ClactonLeader of Reform UK on course to defeat Count Binface and an assortment of fringe candidates as polls close in EssexPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentThu 13 Aug 2026 17.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVoting has closed in one of the UK’s more unusual and least tense byelections, withNigel Farageset for a decisive if arguably empty victory against dozens of independent, fringe, extreme or otherwise oddball opponents.The Reform UK leadersought re-electionto his Clacton seat in early July in an attempt to regain the political initiative following weeks of scrutiny over gifts he received and other aspects of his financial affairs.He framed the byelection as a chance for local voters to show their disdain for mainstream politics in a “people versus the establishment” contest, but was caught out after all the other main parties declined to stand candidates.Farage, 62, was instead left competing against a vast if decidedly niche field of 33 other hopefuls, including 20 independents, several representatives from tiny parties and no fewer than three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony party.The result, due to be announced from around 6am on Friday, will inevitably be a clear Farage win, with the only question being his margin of victoryover Count Binface, the self-styled campaigning alien who is the most prominent of his opponents.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage poses with a pint in a Clacton pub beer garden.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockWhile Reform will necessarily style the result as a clear endorsement of Farage’s record in the Essex seat, and of his tactic in calling the byelection, opponents will seize on any signs of a lower-than-expected majority or a slim turnout.Farageis being investigatedby the parliamentary standards watchdog over allegations he failed to declare gifts and donations, including a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne,first revealedby the Guardian.The process was paused when he resigned as an MP, but will resume once he is re-elected. If he is found to have breached declaration rules and suspended from the House of Commons, this could trigger a second byelection, which the other main parties would contest.While Farage insists he has relished a summer of knocking on doors in his constituency, he has been less visible on the national political stage – in part because of rules connected to how broadcasters must ensure balance during elections.Farage has insisted he did not need to declare the £5m from Harborne as it was given in advance of his return as Reform leader before the 2024 election. He has, however, given a series of explanations for the gift, including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit.The parliamentary inquiry is also looking into allegations that Farage wasfinancially supported by the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell, a close friend, afterthe Sunday Timesreported that Cottrell’s support included security and social media staff who worked on Farage’s online content in the year before he was elected.The 34-candidate field in the Clacton byelection is a UK record, beating the July 2008 contest in Haltemprice and Howden, East Yorkshire, regained by the Conservative MP David Davis after he resigned his seat and stood again as a protest over civil liberties.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsNigel FarageCount BinfacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Four taken to hospital and homes damaged in West Midlands fires | West Midlands | The Guardian
description: Grassfire covering about 16 hectares near golf course in Stourbridge was one of several large blazes in region
Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: Grassfire covering about 16 hectares near golf course in Stourbridge was one of several large blazes in region
Content: Smoke from the grassfire engulfs homes and woodland near Stourbridge.Photograph: West Midlands fire service/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenSmoke from the grassfire engulfs homes and woodland near Stourbridge.Photograph: West Midlands fire service/AFP/GettyWest MidlandsFour taken to hospital and homes damaged in West Midlands firesGrassfire covering about 16 hectares near golf course in Stourbridge was one of several large blazes in regionAngus ThomsonThu 13 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour people have been taken to hospital and several homes damaged as fires tore through residential neighbourhoods in theWest Midlands.A 16-hectare (40-acre) grassfire near a golf course in Stourbridge was one of several significant fires in the region on Thursday –the UK’s hottest day of the year.Twelve fire engines carrying about 60 crew were sent to the scene after West Midlands fire service was alerted to the fast-moving blaze just before 1.30pm on Thursday.Three firefighters and a child were taken to hospital for treatment, a fire service spokesperson said. A further six people were treated for smoke inhalation.Some local rail services were disrupted, while roads in the area were closed due to smoke, fire and fallen trees.View image in fullscreenA West Midlands fire service van arrives at the site of the wildfire in Stourbridge.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA firefighter working at the site of the fire in Stourbridge.Photograph: Matthew Cooper/PAImages released by the fire service showed the fire spreading to nearby woodland and homes. Six homes were damaged in the blaze, and other people in the area reported power problems.The fire service spokesperson said: “This is a wildfire with several points of origin, now involving multiple houses on fire.”Stourbridge town hall was opened to receive those forced to leave their homes, with the fire service helping to transport people who could not travel independently.View image in fullscreenA heat map shows flames threatening to engulf homes in the Stourbridge area.Photograph: West Midlands fire service/PACare home residents had also been evacuated, a local councillor, Andrew Southall, said.UK records hottest day of year as fifth summer heatwave reaches peakRead moreFire crews across the UK were battling multiple blazes on Thursday evening.Homes were destroyed by a fire in Sandyford, Stoke-on-Trent, and a woman was seriously injured when fire tore through homes in Castle Vale near Birmingham, the BBC reported.Northbound traffic on the M6 near Birmingham was temporarily closed due to smoke from a fire near the motorway, causing severe congestion and delays of more than two hours.Several homes were damaged, with 30 properties evacuated and a further 200 left without power due to a separate fire in Pershore, Worcestershire. One person was treated for smoke inhalation.In Warwickshire, the county’s fire and rescue service declared a major incident as crews fought a “large fire” in Salford Priors, Stratford-upon-Avon. That blaze was considered under control by Thursday evening.Dr Thomas Smith, an associate professor of environmental geography at the London School of Economics, said it was “highly unusual” for a wildfire to destroy homes in the UK.“To see wildfires once again destroying people’s homes is a deeply concerning sign that we are experiencing more extreme fire behaviour than we have historically,” he said. “The combination of exceptional heat and prolonged dry conditions is creating fires that spread faster, burn more intensely and increasingly threaten communities.”The Met Office gave a provisional reading of 38.1C (100.6F) on Thursday at Kew Gardens in west London.Forty locations across central and southernEnglandrecorded temperatures of 36C or above.Explore more on these topicsWest MidlandsFirefightersExtreme heatEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two seriously injured after passenger train derails near Lewes in East Sussex | Train crashes | The Guardian
description: Additional nine passengers sustain less serious injuries and major disruption to services reported
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Additional nine passengers sustain less serious injuries and major disruption to services reported
Content: The train derailed between Haywards Heath and Lewes.Photograph: Marcin Nowak/LNPView image in fullscreenThe train derailed between Haywards Heath and Lewes.Photograph: Marcin Nowak/LNPTrain crashesTwo seriously injured after passenger train derails near Lewes in East SussexAdditional nine passengers sustain less serious injuries and major disruption to services reportedMatthew WeaverandGwyn TophamThu 13 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people have been seriously injured after a passenger train derailed between Haywards Heath and Lewes inEast Sussexon Thursday.The South East Coast ambulance service said two people were taken to major trauma centres with severe injuries.Images of the aftermath appeared to show passengers standing on top of the toppled carriages while others could be seen in an area of heathland alongside emergency workers.BritishTransportPolice said: “At this time we believe that two people have sustained serious injuries and a further nine patients have sustained less serious injuries. Patients have been assessed and treated at the scene, with some transported to local hospitals.”View image in fullscreenEmergency services at the site of the derailed train between Haywards Heath and Lewes.Photograph: PAAssistant chief constable Ian Drummond-Smith said: “We’ve declared a major incident and a significant emergency service response is ongoing at the scene, but all passengers on the train have now been safely evacuated from the service.“Our thoughts are of course with everyone affected, and I’d like to reassure the public that we’re supporting the Rail Accident Investigation Branch [RAIB] to establish exactly what’s happened. We’ll provide further information as soon as we are able.”The RAIB has launched an inquiry into what went wrong.An aerial photograph of the scene showed three of the train’s eight carriages on their side.Rob Bradley and his six-year-old daughter Mabel were in the last of the carriages to stay upright.Speaking to the BBC he said: “We are doing OK. We were very lucky we were on the fourth carriage. The fifth went on its side.“We felt the train speeding up and started to rock. Then our carriage jumped vertically upwards and we could tell it was a derailment. The emergency brakes went on the train and everything got thrown forward.“The train skidded for quite a while before it stopped. We turned around and we saw the whole back of the train was open and smoke and dust were pouring into the carriage and we saw the fifth carriage had gone on its side.”Several rail routes were closed after theSouthernservice came off the tracks just before 4pm.Emergency services advised people to avoid the area, and said anyone travelling by rail in the area should allow up to 60 minutes extra for their journey.A spokesperson for Network Rail and Southern Rail said on Thursday evening: “We can confirm that the 14.24 Southern passenger service from Victoria to Eastbourne has derailed in the Lewes area of East Sussex.View image in fullscreenImages of the aftermath appear to show passengers standing on top of the toppled carriages.Photograph: @Defianc_e/Jeremy Veitch“Emergency services are on site and we will update with more information when we can. Trains through the area are suspended and passengers are advised to check online at southernrailway.com for the latest service information.”The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, tweeted: “Deeply concerned of reports of a derailment involving a Southern train in Lewes, Sussex.“Grateful to emergency services who are on the scene supporting those impacted. We are working quickly with the rail industry and local partners to assist passengers.”Southern said in an update on X at 5.47pm: “If you are travelling to Gatwick airport, please allow at least an extra 150 minutes for your journey to ensure you make your flight connections and use an alternative route.“We have requested rail replacement buses to the following stations: Haywards Heath, Lewes. We will update you here on X once confirmed, but for now, please continue to travel using your own alternative route.”In an earlierupdateit said the derailment had occurred between Haywards Heath and Lewes, meaning there were no trains running between Brighton and Lewes, Haywards Heath and Lewes and Seaford/Eastbourne and Lewes.The company told passengers: “You should delay your journey in this area until later on today, or use an alternative route to travel.”James MacCleary, the MP for Lewes, said: “I am aware of very concerning reports of a train crash in the Lewes area this afternoon. I am in touch with the relevant authorities now and will provide further updates as soon as I have more information.“This is clearly a very serious and developing incident, and my thoughts are with everyone affected. In the meantime, if you are concerned about someone or need urgent assistance, please contact the emergency services.”Explore more on these topicsTrain crashesRail transportEast SussexTransportEnglandSouthernnewsShareReuse this content

title: US conducted ‘mass spying campaign’ against leftwing groups and anti-ICE protesters, records reveal | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: DHS sent undercover agents to meetings and infiltrated chats of groups opposing Trump’s immigration crackdown
Author: Sam Levin
Headline: DHS sent undercover agents to meetings and infiltrated chats of groups opposing Trump’s immigration crackdown
