Content: Protesters march during a ‘Nationwide Shutdown’ demonstration against ICE enforcement on 30 January in Minneapolis, Minnesota.Photograph: Stephen Maturen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters march during a ‘Nationwide Shutdown’ demonstration against ICE enforcement on 30 January in Minneapolis, Minnesota.Photograph: Stephen Maturen/Getty ImagesTrump administrationUS conducted ‘mass spying campaign’ against leftwing groups and anti-ICE protesters, records revealDHS sent undercover agents to meetings and infiltrated chats of groups opposing Trump’s immigration crackdownSam Levinin Los Angeles andRachel Leingangin MinneapolisThu 13 Aug 2026 19.06 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 18.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNewly disclosed records reveal the US government extensively spied on prominent leftwing organizations and on protesters as part of a vast operation into groups opposing the immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year.Internal investigative reports show the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) sent undercover agents to community meetings in the Twin Cities andNew YorkCity, infiltrated Signal chats and obtained financial records of mainstream unions and left-leaning non-profit groups.Nearly 30 internal law enforcement reports were released on Thursday as part of a criminal case the Department of Justice (DoJ)has filed against 15 Minneapolis protesters.The defendants are accused of a “conspiracy” to “impede” US immigration officers during the Trump administration’s surge in the region.The DHS investigative reports were disclosed by the government and submitted to the court by an attorney for one of the defendants. The records show that in January, DHS launched an inquiry called “Operation Puppet Master” to identify a “network of conspirators” organizing against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The operation came as community organizing against ICE was swelling in the region in response to the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.A DHS report from February said the agency was looking into people who were “providing material support to violent opportunists and agitators”. The records suggest agents launched elaborate spying efforts targeting activists, protesters and mainstream progressive organizations opposing the Trump administration’s immigration policies.“I was shocked at the scope and the apparent lack of investigative discipline involved, but not totally surprised,” said Kevin Riach, an attorney for one of the indicted protesters, who filed the tranche of records in federal court.DHS spokespeople did not respond to inquiries and the DoJ declined to comment.The records indicate that the investigations followed the directive of Trump’s executive order last year that designated “antifa” a “domestic terrorist organization” responsible for “riots” against ICE. The investigations led to the criminal case filed in June against 15 protesters, which focused on Direct Action Minnesota, a loose coalition of organizers that the government says was part of a “conspiracy” opposing ICE’s surge in the region.The documents show that the government alleged major groups were connected to the criminal conspiracy, including the national labor unions AFL-CIO and Service Employees International Union; the local unionsMinneapolisFederation of Educators and the Minnesota Association of Professional Employees; and several large left-leaning groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and Showing Up for Racial Justice (SURJ).None of those organizations have been charged with any crimes.The records have added fuel to theconcerns of civil rights groups, who have argued that the federal government was criminalizing lawful protest activity under the guise of targeting leftwing “terrorism”.The documents show that DHS investigators obtained financial records of unions and non-profits, as part of an inquiry into “domestic terrorist financing”. One investigative record showed DHS used administrative subpoenas to obtain “wire transfers from various financial institutions to and from” SEIU, one of the largest unions in the US. Investigators also requested that the Federal Reserve Bank of New York provide financial data from the Communications Workers of America, an international union, the records showed.DHS further obtained financial records related to the Sunrise Movement, a national non-profit focused on the climate crisis.The records also provided detailed documentation of spying operations conducted by undercover agents who posed as activists and surveilled community activities.One DHS report documented “undercover agent activity” on 31 January at a Sunrise Movement “resistance skills training” at the Minneapolis public library. An agent described activists discussing recruitment and “de-escalation” at protests, with speakers suggesting having a “police liaison” and “safety marshal” at events. The report said: “It was clear that the Sunrise Movement organization focused on ‘peaceful’ protests.”The undercover agent actively engaged participants, according to the report. At one point, the agent told someone in attendance that he “works in construction and could build items that might assist other groups with more ‘direct-action’ protests”. That agent told the individual that “going to jail did not bother him” and gave out his phone number.The records documented the operations of another undercover agent who joined Signal groups of activists involved in protests.The records also showed undercover agents surveilling a virtual meeting at Hunter College in New York focused on “ICE brutality” and “responding to state violence”; a meeting at a labor center in Minneapolis during which activists discussed a wide range of political issues; a meeting in a Minneapolis public park about protest tactics; and a Direct Action Minnesota meeting at a church.The documents indicate that agents made audio recordings of the events.One undercover agent attended a “training” event at a gymnasium in a church and participated in “boxing/sparring practice”, according to a DHS report. The report noted that the agent was surreptitiously recording audio of the event, but that at one point the recorder “erroneously fell to the floor” and the agent had to return to the gym to retrieve the device.At one anti-ICE event at a church, agents documented the license plate information of attendees, the records showed. When two agents were approached by a man who “asked if they were ICE”, the agent responded, falsely, that they were not.Riach, the defense attorney, filed the records as part of a motion urging the court to compel the government to release additional records. In his filing, Riach accused the government of presenting “wild conspiracy allegations … born from the fantasies of political retribution that animate the Trump Administration”.He also alleged that DHS’s investigations were part of a “mass spying campaign” and said undercover agents “participated in organizing and directing the groups they were surveilling, at times working to entice people into discussing or committing crimes”.The records relate to activities that extend far beyond the allegations of the 15 defendants facing prosecution. That case alleges a vast conspiracy to organize against ICE, but across a 94-page indictment, there are no allegations of injuries to specific ICE officers caused by any defendants and no charges of serious violence.Emilia Gonzalez Avalos is the executive director of Unidos MN, a Minneapolis social justice non-profit group, whose activities were mentioned in the files.“I believe that this is a clear attempt to intimidate us, to punish and politically repress disagreement and difference,” she said. “And that is not the America that we have built through hundreds of years. And it’s definitely not the America that we are organizing for.”During trainings, organizers asked people not to record the sessions, Gonzalez Avalos said. But organizers would also say if there were any immigration agents or officers in the room, they were welcome to stay because the group had nothing to hide, because their work was “entirely grounded in the United States constitution”.Mike German, a former FBI agent andcivil liberties advocate, said it was striking that DHS was leading the investigations when typically the FBI would spearhead operations targeting potential “terrorist” activity. He said it was also notable that DHS was using administrative subpoenas, which don’t require judicial authorization, to obtain records.The government, German said, also appeared to be relying on theories of “guilt by association” to justify surveillance instead of narrower investigations focused on specific alleged criminal activity. German, who previously served as an undercover agent, further scoffed at the notion of undercover agents spying on what appeared to be accessible, community events.“You’re talking about meetings that are open to the public, where they are recruiting among the public, saying: ‘Please come to this protest,’” he said. “It’s hardly a challenge to ‘infiltrate’ this kind of meeting, and that should be a clue this isn’t a criminal group. It’s very rare for criminals to [publicize] discussion of their criminal activities.”The investigations, he added, fit patterns in US history of the government targeting leftwing activist and labor organizing. After 9/11, he said, those powers to spy on communities were greatly expanded.“Nobody should be surprised that the government would use these authorities to target political opposition rather than target criminals, particularly so under this administration,” he said.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS immigrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US politicsMinneapolisNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Unemployed young people to join AI boot camps to get job-ready | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Pilot scheme will provide three weeks of training as part of UK government’s latest attempt to address Neets crisis
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Pilot scheme will provide three weeks of training as part of UK government’s latest attempt to address Neets crisis
Content: The government wants the majority of attenders at the boot camp to gain an apprenticeship.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe government wants the majority of attenders at the boot camp to gain an apprenticeship.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianYouth unemploymentUnemployed young people to join AI boot camps to get job-readyPilot scheme will provide three weeks of training as part of UK government’s latest attempt to address Neets crisisDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 13 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYoung peopleout of work or at risk of unemployment in the UKare to join “AI boot camps” where they harness the technology to get a foothold in the workplace.The government’s latest attempt to address the crisis in Neets – young people not in work or education – involves turning to a technology that many view as a potential threat to employment.A pilot in north-westEnglandwill provide up to 70 people aged 16 to 21 with three weeks of AI training, including learning to build AI tools, understanding how businesses use AI and learning to use the technology responsibly. There will also be workplace skills training such as in using office IT systems and timekeeping.The government wants the majority of attenders at the boot camp to gain an apprenticeship at local businesses that have signed up, including the defence firm BAE Systems and the food company Heinz.Lisa Nandy, the digital, culture, media and sport secretary, said the scheme would “support young people at a crucial juncture in their lives”. The pilot will be used to refine an England-wide AI skills scheme due to roll out next summer.The boot camp will use AI tools from US tech firms including Microsoft, the ChatGPT developer OpenAI and Anthropic, the startup behind the Claude chatbot.Bouke Klein Teeselink, an academic at King’s College London and an expert on the impact of AI on work, said the boot camp was a “good idea in principle”.“What we need to do is make juniors more attractive to companies and one way to do that is make them more productive by teaching them how to do AI well,” he said.However, Teeselink said he was sceptical that a three-week programme would be enough to make teens “AI-ready”, because AI readiness required continuous learning and updating of skills.Fears of AI’s impact on jobs have focused heavily on school leavers and graduates because AI tools are viewed as capable of performing the “grunt work” that is typically set aside for workforce newcomers, with white-collar industries such as law, finance and marketing among the most vulnerable.This weekStanford University in the USflagged a decline in the employment of young workers in AI-exposed occupations such as software engineering and customer service.The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said the programme would give young people “the skills they need to thrive in the AI workplace”, amid signs of growing pressure on youth employment.The latest data, published in May, showed the number of young people aged 16 to 24 neither working nor learning surpassed 1 million for the first time since 2013, reaching 1.01 million in the three months from January to March.Aninterim report by the former Labour minister Alan Milburn, also published in May, warned that the figure could rise to one in six by 2031 and that Britain risked leaving behind a “lost generation” of young people ill-prepared for work.Last month Andy Burnham committed to cutting the number of Neets but declined to set a target deadline.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentUnemploymentYoung peopleAI (artificial intelligence)Work & careersEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Edinburgh international film festival showcases a Scottish industry in rude health | Movies | The Guardian
description: This year’s festival is superpowered by a strong year for Scottish cinema, showing it can thrive under the ‘four dimensional perpetual catch-22’ of global ambitions
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: This year’s festival is superpowered by a strong year for Scottish cinema, showing it can thrive under the ‘four dimensional perpetual catch-22’ of global ambitions
Content: Part of a strong clutch… Domnhall Gleeson in The IncomerPhotograph: Courtesy of EIFFView image in fullscreenPart of a strong clutch… Domnhall Gleeson in The IncomerPhotograph: Courtesy of EIFFMoviesEdinburgh international film festival showcases a Scottish industry in rude healthThis year’s festival is superpowered by a strong year for Scottish cinema, showing it can thrive under the ‘four dimensional perpetual catch-22’ of global ambitionsBorges, ballet and BDSM: Peter Bradshaw’s 10 must-see movies at Edinburgh international film festivalAndrew PulverThu 13 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNow that itsdisastrous collapse and speedy rebirthis a trauma slowly receding in the rear-view mirror, the Edinburgh international film festival can set its sights on bigger things. Apart from its traditional role providing a showcase for the best of current world cinema, the festival has an ace up its sleeve for 2026: the undeniable confidence and conspicuous achievement of its home film industry in Scotland. Just as Cannes likes to give a decent amount of houseroom to favoured French directors, and Sundance sees at least part of its job to talk up US independent cinema, Edinburgh acts as a vector for Scottish film-makers to gain valuable exposure and get their work in front of significant festival audiences. Inevitably, some years are harder than others, but Edinburgh’s 2026 edition feels stronger than it has been for years.The festival’s opening gala slot, traditionally a local film, has been given to The Incomer, a surreal comedy starring Domhnall Gleeson and set Scotland’s far north, and which picked up a major award at the Sundance festival earlier this year. Among a clutch of strong films are Borges and Me, based on Jay Parini’s memoir of escorting author Jorge Luis Borges on a trip around the Highlands; andThe Education of Jane Cumming, the extraordinary true life story of the 19th-century Edinburgh schoolkeeper who inspired The Children’s Hour. Scottish artist Douglas Gordon is the focus of a new documentary, Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon, while Scottish Ballet perform in These Violent Delights, a film rendering their dance version of Romeo and Juliet. Past glories are due to live again with a 30th anniversary screening of junkie classic Trainspotting (with the added bonus of a live club night featuring a DJ set from Irvine Welsh).View image in fullscreenThe Education of Jane CummingPhotograph: © HeimatfilmPaul Ridd, the festival director, is aware of the potential minefield of sticking up for Scottish cinema. “It’s great to have all those movies in the mix, these films deserve to be at the big table. But we never want to think we’ve got to promote this stuff. What we want to avoid is the sense that there’s any film in our lineup that is in there for any other reason than it’s just top quality. We’re not quota driven. It’s always about the quality. And I’m just very happy that there’s such a wealth of great Scottish work to showcase.”Ridd points to the influence of Screen Scotland, the state-and-lottery funded agency founded in 2018 that was designed to act as a specialist funding unit for Scottish film. “All these great films are testament to what the whole organisation has been doing to put those film-makers and those films on the map.” The recent appointment of Screen Scotland’s executive director Isabel Davis ashead of the British Film Institute’s £20m film-making fund– itself seen as a vote of confidence in the way the Scottish film industry has evolved.Davis, who takes up her new post in October, is clear that increased and targeted project development has been vital. “We were put together with the notion that really good creative development support was going to be the key to all of that film-making success, and it has paid off. It takes years, project by project. It means giving tough love to people on scripts, saying that things could be better, pushing people to be more ambitious – and then backing that up with more development support and then production support.”Festival success is a major marker, and the fact that seven Scottish films were selected for Sundance earlier this year was a major cause for celebration; as well as The Incomer, the picks included andThe Story of Documentary Film (The 1980s), the newest in a stream of film-history essays from critic-turned-film-maker Mark Cousins – who is described by Davis as “the gift that keeps on giving” as far as the Scottish film industry is concerned. Conversely the recent Scottish film that appears to elicit the most fervent admiration from across the Scottish industry is the most hyperlocal of all: Everybody to Kenmure Street, documentaryabout the mobilisation of local activists to prevent the arrest of two men by immigration enforcement officials. Davis says “it’s just connected to people so far beyond Scotland, it’s unbelievable.”Producer Ken Petrie, whose new film Sunny Dancer is releasing UK cinemas this week, is one of the new generation of Scottish film-makers who have benefited from Screen Scotland’s involvement, but says the going is still tough. “You know, it’s always been a hard business. It’s never been so hard or expensive to make something that has so little financial reward. The whole value chain of the film industry at the moment is a challenge, especially for independent producers.”View image in fullscreenHighlands tale … Borges and Me.Photograph: Courtesy EIFF 2026Petrie, who started out as a special effects technician on projects such as The Wolfman, Robin Hood and World War Z, says that, for him at least, the challenge is to avoid staying too close to home. “Scotland is in a good place, but I think we need to have a bit more courage to try to really blossom on to the global stage. The question for me is: how do you make that stuff that’s going to travel internationally, entertain Scotland and the UK, but also the rest of the world?”He adds: “The ugly fact is the UK film business is centred in London. I don’t know if it’s possible that people can live and work in Scotland in isolation and be able to build global companies. I’m trying to make stuff for global audiences, so surely you have to go and find out what the global marketplace is saying.”On the other hand, Petrie is concerned that Scotland’s record as an international production base – which has seen projects of the calibre of Spiderman: Brand New Day, The Odyssey, Frankenstein and The Buccaneers shoot in the country – may be hampered by Westminster over the level of subsidy it can offer to attract these productions. “Should we be trying to grow more in Scotland? It’s like a kind of four-dimensional perpetual catch-22.“I mean, Scotland’s an exciting place. Everybody loves the Scots. Certainly when I’m out in the marketplace that’s what comes across. There’s a lot of goodwill out there towards Scotland. I try to always be an optimistic realist and I think that’s what we need to be in Scotland at the moment.”Edinburgh international film festival starts on 13 August and runs until 19 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmEdinburgh film festivalScotlandFilm industryFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Behind England’s bumper A-level results lie record levels of regional disparities | A-levels | The Guardian
description: Need for Burnham to tackle regional inequality could not be clearer as London becomes ‘educational outlier’
Author: Sally Weale
Headline: Need for Burnham to tackle regional inequality could not be clearer as London becomes ‘educational outlier’
Content: In London, nearly a third of A-level candidates gained A*s and As. In the East Midlands and north-east, the figure was less than a quarter.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyView image in fullscreenIn London, nearly a third of A-level candidates gained A*s and As. In the East Midlands and north-east, the figure was less than a quarter.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyA-levelsAnalysisBehind England’s bumper A-level results lie record levels of regional disparitiesSally WealeEducation correspondentNeed for Burnham to tackle regional inequality could not be clearer as London becomes ‘educational outlier’Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAndy Burnham has put regional inequality at the top of his agenda as prime minister, and nowhere is the need for doing so clearer than in education.As England’s A-level results were published on Thursday morning, students across the country were pictured celebrating a bumper crop of results, withrecord rates of As and A*s.Drill down into the detail, however, and the regional disparities are shocking, with the gap between London and the lowest performing areas of the country also at record levels.Nearly a third of A-level candidates in the capital (32.7%) gained A*s and As, up six percentage points on last year.In the East Midlands, however, less than a quarter (23.1%) secured top grades, down from 23.8% in 2025, putting it level with the north-east, which increased its share of top grades marginally from 22.9% last year.The results reveal the gap in A and A* grades between London and the north-east has grown to an alarming 9.6 percentage points, the largest since the pandemic and significantly higher than the 2019 pre-pandemic disparity of 3.9 points.Chart showing percentages of A* and A grades in English regionsThe gap in A* grades is up from two percentage points in 2019 to 5.1 points in 2026. Experts are hoping the prime minister’s devolution plans to give regional areas the independence to adapt their approach to local conditions will help learners outside London.Lee Elliot Major, a professor of social mobility at Exeter University, said: “Our capital has become an educational outlier while too many young people in the north-east, East Midlands and other parts of the country are growing up in very different worlds of opportunity.“England is no longer defined by a simple north-south divide. It is increasingly a story of London pulling away from much of the country. Talent is spread evenly across the country; opportunity is not.”The reasons for London’s runaway success are many. Tony Blair’s London Challenge started the process of transformation in the capital’s schools in 2003. Since then higher pay and cultural attractiveness have incentivised more teachers to join the capital’s schools, while ambitious migrant families have helped raise standards.The Department for Education says its Rise teams (regional improvement for standards and excellence) are putting “a laser focus” on areas and schools where performance is weakest.A proposal in the schools white paper to use household income to vary funding rates according to the level of disadvantage so that children with more entrenched disadvantage attract more funding has also been welcomed.But the scale and persistence of the disparities laid bare in Thursday’s results clearly require significant intervention.Chris Zarraga, the director ofSchoolsNorth East, which represents 1,150 schools in the region, said schools in different parts of England were not operating on a level playing field.“In the north-east, schools are working within communities facing entrenched disadvantage, intense pressure on public services, growing Send [special educational needs and disabilities] needs and very different access to opportunities and infrastructure.“Increasingly, schools are being asked to compensate for all of those things. That does not mean accepting lower outcomes. These divides are not inevitable. But we will not close them simply by demanding more from schools while leaving the conditions around them unchanged. Government needs to treat this as a system challenge.”He called for a long-term approach encompassing education, early years, health, Send, transport, skills and economic development, alongside high-quality academic and vocational pathways.Elliot Major said an “ambitious, region-first approach” was needed. “Too many rural, coastal and post-industrial communities have been left with fewer educational and economic opportunities.“The warning lights are flashing: persistent attainment gaps by background and place, historically high levels of school absence, and growing divides outside the school gates.Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union, said more funding was needed. “Schools do everything they can to respond to poverty but the pressures and strains on schools in areas of disadvantage must be addressed by Andy Burnham’s government, including all our schools and colleges to be properly funded.”Zarraga said: “Results day should reflect young people’s potential and hard work, not the structural advantages or disadvantages of where they happen to grow up.”Explore more on these topicsA-levelsYoung peopleEnglandExamsSchoolsSecondary schoolsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Imelda Staunton: ‘Umbridge’s giggle needed to be short and sharp. So I just did a boom, boom’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor answers your questions on working with her dog, becoming a dame, Harry Potter, and making televisual history in The Singing Detective
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The actor answers your questions on working with her dog, becoming a dame, Harry Potter, and making televisual history in The Singing Detective
Content: Imelda Staunton … ‘Having my dog in the show was fantastic because she liked everything I did.’Photograph: Nick ThompsonView image in fullscreenImelda Staunton … ‘Having my dog in the show was fantastic because she liked everything I did.’Photograph: Nick ThompsonFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterviewImelda Staunton: ‘Umbridge’s giggle needed to be short and sharp. So I just did a boom, boom’As told toRich PelleyThe actor answers your questions on working with her dog, becoming a dame, Harry Potter, and making televisual history in The Singing DetectiveThu 13 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou andBill Nighywere comrades inPride, but play estranged spouses in & Sons. Was it more fun marching alongside him or giving him a piece of your mind?MrSOBaldrickIt’s fun doing anything with Bill Nighy!View image in fullscreenStaunton and Bill Nighy in & Sons.Photograph: Icon Film DistributionI once saw you atRHS Garden Wisley. Are you a keen gardener? What’s your favourite plant?HeyJudithBYes, I am a gardener. We love doing the garden. My favourite plant – this week – is the rose Munstead Wood, which has an incredible scent, and a deep, dark raspberry colour. It’s a rose we might be in danger of losing because of climate change. Roses need water, so I think we’re going to have to change our planting.View image in fullscreenWith her husband, Jim Carter, at the RHS Hampton Court flower show in 2022.Photograph: Karl Black/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.How’s your garden coping in the heatwave?irenehandalIt looks like Africa. We’re obeying the hosepipe ban, getting our steps in, and our weight work with watering cans, hour upon hour. Considering we live on a tiny island, you’d think they could just desalinate seawater for farmers, or for us to use on plants or gardens or whatever. However! Next question …You were in the year above me atLa Sainte Union Catholic School in Highgate,north London. I remember a girl with an amazing voice singingWouldn’t It Be Loverly as Eliza Doolittle in My Fair Lady, and I’ve always wondered: was it you?Anne210No, I don’t think it was me. But I did sing Blue Suede Shoes with my mate Angela Robinson – who I still know – with a guitar and a recorder. You can only imagine what that was like. However, we felt like pop stars, and we won the music festival, although there was no prize – apart from the kudos.View image in fullscreenStaunton as Mrs Kitty Warren with her daughter Bessie Carter as Vivie Warren in Mrs Warren’s Profession.Photograph: Johan PerssonWho was easiest to work with: your husband,Jim Carter, in Guys and Dolls; your daughter,Bessie, in Mrs Warren’s Profession; or yourdog, Molly, who played Chowsie in Gypsy at Chichester Festival theatrein2014?TopTrampThe dog, obviously. Because she was the easiest to carry. I carried the dog on stage. Try doing that with Jim Carter – not going to happen. And my daughter, who’s 5ft 9in, that’s not going to happen either. Having my dog in the show was fantastic because she liked everything I did, so that was quite useful. Did Molly have to audition? No, she knew someone in the show.My daughters know you first as the voice of their favourite books:Zog,The Smeds and the Smoosetc. Did all that stage and film discipline mean ittook only one or two takes in the booth?GH_ParisI think it was more to do with having done quite a lot of radio. I did a lot of Radio 4 plays in the early 80s, where all you’ve got is your voice. The microphone becomes the other character. That really laid the groundwork for all of the animation voices I’ve done in films and children’s books, including Julia Donaldson’s books. I love doing that because you can’t escape. You’ve only got the voice. It’s got to be so contained and the discipline comes from that, I think.Did gettingmade a dame in 2024feel like a bit of a demotion after playing the Queen?Dr_J_A_ZoidbergI’m still trying to cope with it.View image in fullscreenAs Dolores Umbridge in Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyHow did you come up with that chilling giggle forDolores Umbridge? Was your menacing performance based on any of your real teachers?Shannon_78676andDrMTobogganThankfully, it wasn’t based on any real-life teachers. I didn’t want it to be a silly giggle. I wanted it to be quite hard, but with a very high tone. I remember thinking I didn’t want it to take too long, so the laugh needed to be short and sharp. So I just did a boom, boom – two notes that didn’t take up too much time.What was it like working with the late, greatPete Postlethwaite, as he gradually turned into a rat in the2000 comedy Rat?maryfinnView image in fullscreenPete Postlewaite … ‘It was so good of him to come out of the fridge stark naked.’Photograph: Karen Robinson/The ObserverWell, the thing is – we never saw him turn into a rat. We saw him turn back into a human. Pete only did about three days on that film. It was so good of him to come over to Dublin and come out of the fridge stark naked. I don’t know why he came out of the fridge, but it was a pretty extraordinary effect. But that was him. Of course, I’d worked with Pete back in 1986 – we did a swashbuckling romp at the Royal Shakespeare Company, The Fair Maid of the West, with Sean Bean and Simon Russell Beale. Pete Postlethwaite was a genius. End of. Timing, heart and soul. I mean, he was just a genius, so it was a real joy that he came over and did three days on this mad little film.Which is harder on stage: delivering a page-long speech, or sitting silently with too much time to think about your next line?nivlek47Look, it’s always heaven when it’s someone else doing the work. It’s funny – when you start out in your career, you want all the big speeches. As it goes on, you start to think: “Oh, I’ve done that. Can someone else have a go?” So, at the moment, it’s quite nice. I loved doing George Bernard Shaw’s Mrs Warren’s Profession with my daughter last year, which has a lot of words. I was so relieved when it was her turn. I thought: “Off you go, you do it now.”When you were making The Singing Detective, did you feel you were making something extraordinary that would be remembered as part of televisual history?CaptainLibAbsolutely. You knew it was something completely off the wall, so unlike anything we’d ever seen on television before. I still remember the read-through: sitting in that room with Dennis Potter and the rest of the cast, not really knowing how we were going to put what was on the page on screen. That was Jon Amiel’s job as director, and Michael Gambon was sublime. Dennis Potter’s writing made me feel so inadequate. I thought: “How could I possibly be in this? How can I help bring this to life?” It was extraordinary. I’m sure Jon would agree it was one of his greatest pieces of work.View image in fullscreenAs Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown.Photograph: Alex Bailey/APYour parents came from County Mayo. Were you screaming at the TV whenMayo beat Kerryto win their firstGAA All-Ireland Senior FootballChampionshipin 75 years this July?ExileCuChulainnStrangely, in May this year, I was in Kerry for four weeks doing a film. I’d never been to that part of Kerry. It’s absolutely stunning. The people, the place, the scenery – everything was stunning. So my heart was completely in Kerry. Then a couple of months later, the football happened, so I’m afraid I was conflicted.You move between the West End and film/TV constantly. What does one give you that the other doesn’t?ethd58One is more knackering.I once saw you at RHS Chelsea opening a bottle of champagne with a sabre! Is this how you open it at home?dalyFoleyAlways.& Sons is in UK cinemas from 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewImelda StauntonBill NighyHarry PotterTelevisionScience fiction and fantasy filmsFilm adaptationsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Schoolgirl Terrorist? review – by the end of this documentary you feel like you have sat through a nightmare | Television | The Guardian
description: A vulnerable girl took her life at 16 having faced terror charges and online grooming by neo-fascists. The catalogue of failures by British authorities is utterly enraging
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: A vulnerable girl took her life at 16 having faced terror charges and online grooming by neo-fascists. The catalogue of failures by British authorities is utterly enraging
Content: Manipulated … Rhianan Rudd.Photograph: Emily CarterView image in fullscreenManipulated … Rhianan Rudd.Photograph: Emily CarterTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Schoolgirl Terrorist? review – by the end of this documentary you feel like you have sat through a nightmareA vulnerable girl took her life at 16 having faced terror charges and online grooming by neo-fascists. The catalogue of failures by British authorities is utterly enragingLucy ManganThu 13 Aug 2026 18.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Schoolgirl Terrorist? contains its answer within its very question. Titles are designed to catch your attention. Normally they contain the baldest, most extreme possible summary suggestion of what you are about to see that the makers think they can get away with. A question mark introduces the idea of interrogation, of nuance, of doubt from the off – all things commissioners believe will put people off.The exception is when the subject is so clearly an abominable, Kafkaesque tale of mismanagement and incompetence visited upon ordinary people. To pretend otherwise even for a titular moment would be to undermine your programme’s integrity from the start.So, then to The Schoolgirl Terrorist? and the story of Rhianan Rudd, who in 2020 became the youngest girl ever charged with terror offences in the UK. She was 15. She was 16 when she died by suicide at a Nottinghamshire children’s home.Rhianan’s mother Emily and her older brother Brandon recall a child who always had “a very big whiplash in personalities” and whose mental health seems to have caused her mother concerns from the earliest days. At three she would often insist she was not Rhianan and later invent alternative characters – often “solemn, critical” - in a way that seems to have gone beyond the normal practice of imaginative children. “I was always called a neurotic mother … How can you say that when you don’t live with her?” Emily says she had undiagnosed autism. Brandon says he does not remember a time in the family’s life when social services were not involved and that, by the time his sister was 11, she seemed “depressed a lot of the time, if I’m honest”.View image in fullscreenRhianan’s brother Brandon … cannot remember a time when social services not involved with family.Photograph: CandourTo this mix was soon added Emily’s new boyfriend, an American called Dax Mallaburn, an ex-member of a right-wing gang who said he was trying to be a better man and who was approved by social services to live with them in their post-refuge home. Then came the pandemic and lockdown, and a computer in Rhianan’s own room for the first time. Online, unbeknown to Emily, she met a neo-fascist called Chris Cook. Not understanding why her daughter suddenly began spouting hateful rhetoric of various kinds to family and friends, and after Rhianan told her she had downloaded a bomb-making manual, Emily referred her to the deradicalisation programme Prevent. Soon after that, Rhianan was arrested. Her Prevent case was closed while she was investigated by MI5, as is protocol at such a time. This is perhaps the most striking of the many assaults on common sense already accrued – and that will continue to line the path to tragedy.She should, after the investigation began, have been referred by either the police or social services to the Home Office unit that deals with modern slavery and trafficking, and exploitative practices like online grooming and radicalisation. Instead, this was only done at the insistence of her defence team long after she had been charged with six counts of terrorism. By then she had also been remanded to custody in a children’s home which seemed ill-equipped to deal with the problems she had, and where Rhianan was able to self-harm despite her mother warning the staff of her history of doing so.The charges against the 15-year-old were dropped in 2021 when the Home Office made a formal finding that Rhianan had been a victim of exploitation. The inquest into her death would also note the influence of Mallaburn (who Emily had split from by this point), of which her mother was unaware. Therapy via Prevent began. When it started to focus on the “darker” aspects of Cook’s manipulation of her, which involved sexual content, Rhianan took her own life.View image in fullscreenAn animation from the programme.Photograph: CandourBy the end of the hour you feel like you have sat through a nightmare, watching Emily and others who loved Rhianan shout into voids that were supposedly filled with people trained and ready to help those in exactly their situation. Instead, it is a catalogue of missed opportunities, failures and – almost the most frustrating, maddening, galling thing – the simple sense that there was no one, or certainly no one high enough up the food chain to make a difference – who had the wit or courage to look at the situation in the round early on and say: this child is not what we mean by terrorist. We have gone badly wrong and we must fix this.The programme ends, as these programmes always do, with the rights of reply from the other parties involved. MI5 and Prevent point to findings by the coroner’s court that absolve them of blame. The children’s home stands by its care plan and treatment of Rhianan.“How does anyone know that anything has moved on … I want to know what you’ve done to change what you did with Rhianan,” says Emily. Prevent says her daughter’s death “has informed multiple strategies in our approach to young people and mental health.” I’d say we need more question marks.The Schoolgirl Terrorist? is on Channel 4In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewYoung peopleOnline abuseFactual TVUK security and counter-terrorismreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Billion-streamers, Beyoncé and heart-bruising beauty: Frank Ocean’s 20 best songs – ranked!  | Frank Ocean | The Guardian
description: It’s a decade since the Los Angeles musician released the seminal album Blonde. To lessen the pain of his hiatus, we count down the best of an artist who redefined R&B
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: It’s a decade since the Los Angeles musician released the seminal album Blonde. To lessen the pain of his hiatus, we count down the best of an artist who redefined R&B
Content: Eclectic and inventive … Frank Ocean.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenEclectic and inventive … Frank Ocean.Photograph: Publicity imageRankedFrank OceanBillion-streamers, Beyoncé and heart-bruising beauty: Frank Ocean’s 20 best songs – ranked!It’s a decade since the Los Angeles musician released the seminal album Blonde. To lessen the pain of his hiatus, we count down the best of an artist who redefined R&BAlexis PetridisThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Acura Integurl (2011)Frank Ocean’s pre-fame demos are hard to find – there’s a fan-made, 64-track compilation called The Lonny Breaux Collection floating around – but worth checking out, as evinced by this brief but potent piano ballad. Sweet but heartsore, it packs an emotional punch; it would have been a highlight of the mixtapeNostalgia, Ultra, had it made the cut.19. Higgs (2016)The stark penultimate track onOcean’s “visual album” Endless– just vocals and gently fingerpicked acoustic guitar – takes its name from the invisible energy of the Higgs field, which the lyrics seem to equate with love. It presents the emotion as mysterious and fleeting; Ocean’s voice is racked, the melody haunting.18. Dear April (2020)One of a string of singles Ocean put out between 2017 and 2020 – his last releases to date, although he obliquely mentioned a new album duringhis chaotic Coachella appearance in 2023. Dear April was billed as acoustic, but it’s built around jazzy electric guitar and synth washes – understated, but truly beautiful.17. American Wedding (2011)Several tracks on Nostalgia, Ultra featured Ocean singing over other people’s music, but American Wedding – based on the Eagles’ Hotel California – prompted legal action. It’s understandably a fan favourite: he may nick the tune, but Ocean replaces the original’s coked-out ennui with anguish that snags against the slickly familiar backing.View image in fullscreenPlaying Coachella in Indio, California, 2012.Photograph: C Flanigan/FilmMagic16. Slide on Me (2016)The visual aspect of Endless – in which Ocean assembled a flight of stairs – may have been wilfully boring, but the music that accompanied it boasted tension between its hazy, dreamlike quality and its raw, mixtape-like roughness. This is audible to spectacular effect on Slide on Me’s blend of bumping R&B, lo-fi ambience and vocals that sit somewhere between nonchalant and pained.15. Cayendo (2020)Another of Ocean’s one-off single releases, the bilingual Cayendo fitted its moment perfectly. Released at the height of the Covid pandemic, it sounded as if it had been recorded by someone locked in their bedroom. Its muffled, grumbling guitar and vocal – shifting from deep and effect-smothered into anguished and emotive – captured a mood of troubled introspection.14. Nikes (2016)The first taste of Ocean’s second album, Blonde, threw listeners a curveball – a spare, crestfallen song that referencesthe murder of Trayvon Martin, over half of which is sung by Ocean with his voice sped up to the point where it sounds nasal and cartoonish. Inexplicably, it works, musically and as a statement of leftfield intent.Listen to Biking.13. Biking (2017)Take your pick from either version of Biking. The A-side pulls Jay-Z andTyler, the Creatorinto Ocean’s strange sound-world – Jay-Z sounds as if he is rapping after being locked in a cupboard. The “solo” version lops off the lo-fi intro and features Ocean’s urgent vocal over an unhurried beat and languidly strummed acoustic guitar.12. Rushes (2016)Rushes seems to reflect on a relationship gone wrong: “First I was rushing for a wait / This time I’m waiting for a rush.” It makes fantastic use of Ocean’s chief vocal foil on Endless, Jazmine Sullivan, burying her powerful voice in the mix so it functions like another instrument, adding suitably heady uplift to the chorus.11. Bad Religion (2012)Bad Religion is effectively the sound of Ocean coming out, tormented by his love for another man and his closeted status. It would have been a bold move whatever it sounded like, but it’s also a fantastic song, deploying the dramatic sound of a church organ and delaying the arrival of the beat until its immense climax.10. White Ferrari (2016)White Ferrari is far from the usual driving anthem; rather, it evokes someone lost in thoughts and memories as they motor along. It’s daring – there is no chorus, the arrangement keeps changing – and beautifully done, from the fleeting interpolation of the Beatles’ Here There and Everywhere toJustin Vernon’s heart-stopping guest vocal.View image in fullscreenAt Bonnaroo festival in Manchester, Tennessee, 2014.Photograph: Josh Brasted/WireImage9. Pink Matter (2012)Should you require evidence of how different Ocean was, consider Pink Matter, a complex, thoughtful rumination on the female anatomy – presented as a dialogue with a sensei – that’s about as far from your standard male R&B star’s approach to the subject as you could get. Plus: a fantastic guest verse fromAndré 3000.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion8. Nights (2016)One offourbillion-streaming tracks from Blonde, Nights’ exploration of a mind working overtime in the small hours – picking through childhood memories, the pressures of fame, failing relationships – sounds amazing. It warps and changes with each passing thought: clanging alt-rock guitar; eerie synth ambience; heavy-metal arpeggios; warm, beat-forward R&B.Queer sounds: our writers on their favourite LGBTQ+ songsRead more7. Lost (2012)The topic of drug use hangs over Channel Orange (see also: Crack Rock). On Lost, Ocean deploys one of his sweetest, poppiest melodies to depict the relationship between two co-dependent dealers. Despite the narrator’s promise of a better life, it isn’t clear who is dragging whom further into coked-out oblivion.6. Ivy (2016)Partly inspired by the Strokes – you can hear their influence in the muted guitar chug that underpins the track – Ivy splits the difference between indie rock and R&B ballad so skilfully that it’s impossible to categorise as either. The lyrics deal with memories and regrets; the closing scream isn’t so much cathartic as chilling.5. Self Control (2016)More relationship drama – has a relationshipevergone smoothly in an Ocean song? – originally intended to be sung as a duet; the female voice was eventually replaced by Ocean’s own, sped up. A wonderfully subtle string arrangement and a chorus of multitracked backing vocals amp up the infectious mood of sadness mixed with resignation.View image in fullscreenOn stage at Parklife festival in Manchester, England, 2017.Photograph: Visionhaus/Corbis/Getty Images4. Chanel (2017)The best of Ocean’s string of one-off singles, Chanel delves straight into the topic of sexual fluidity and notions of masculinity: “My guy pretty like a girl / And he got fight stories to tell.” The production is stripped back – there are moments when the music is barely there – focusing attention on Ocean’s gripping vocal.3. Pink + White (2016)An all-star cast – production by Pharrell, a Jon Brion string arrangement, Beyoncé on backing vocals – but it’s all about the song nevertheless. The haunting earworm of the piano figure, the 60s soul mood, the ache in Ocean’s voice as he sings “you showed me love”: Pink + White makes misery sound worth wallowing in.Frank Ocean at Coachella review – a rollercoaster ending in disappointmentRead more2. Novacane (2011)Amid the delightfully scrappy eclecticism of Nostalgia, Ultra is Ocean’s first classic. The brilliantly original storytelling – a dental student who dabbles in pornography and gets high on local anaesthetic – blends darkness and disquiet with flashes of wit, a fabulous, pulsing, slowly building production and a bright, pop-facing melody. It’s got the lot.1. Pyramids (2012)As statements of intent go, the first single from Channel Orange takes some beating. It’s nearly 10 shapeshifting minutes long, initially driven by a house rhythm and a riff that recalls Capella’s 90s Eurodance anthem U Got 2 Know. It changes completely midway through, first to an ambient interlude, then to spaced-out R&B, before concluding with a burst of rock guitar. (It also boasts an incomprehensible narrative about ancient Egypt and strippers.) Compelling and compulsive, it underlined that, rather than being an upstart kid fromthe Odd Future stable, Ocean was an artist whose musical ambition would have impressed his idol, Prince.Listen to the playlist. Note: five of the tracks in this article are not available to stream onSpotifyExplore more on these topicsFrank OceanRankedR&Bbest ofShareReuse this content

title: What is the MMR vaccine and how does Trump’s executive order affect parents and children? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: President’s order calls for several changes to childhood vaccinations – and experts say it’ll lead to confusion
Author: Sarah Sloat
Headline: President’s order calls for several changes to childhood vaccinations – and experts say it’ll lead to confusion
Content: A nurse prepares to administer a vaccines in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on 28 April 2017.Photograph: Courtney Perry for the Washington Post via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA nurse prepares to administer a vaccines in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on 28 April 2017.Photograph: Courtney Perry for the Washington Post via Getty ImagesWell actuallyWhat is the MMR vaccine and how does Trump’s executive order affect parents and children?President’s order calls for several changes to childhood vaccinations – and experts say it’ll lead to confusionSarah SloatThu 13 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Monday,Donald Trumpsigned anexecutive orderpushing for revisions to how children in the US are vaccinated.The executive order calls for several changes. These includefewer vaccinationsoverall and a recommendation that the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine be replaced with separate shots for each diseaseadministeredduring separate medical visits. The latter direction is currently impossible to implement because no stand-alone shots for these diseases are licensed in the US.“I think the biggest impact of this executive order is that it’s going to cause more confusion,” says Dr David Diemert, a professor of medicine and director of the George Washington University Vaccine Research Unit. “And confusion for things like vaccination schedules for kids is never a good thing.”Here’s what you need to know about the executive order’s potential impact and the science behind the debate.What does Trump’s executive order mean for the vaccine schedule?Critically, the executive order does not actually “change anything about current recommendations”, says Dr James Campbell, chair of the committee on infectious diseases for the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). While the executive order puts pressure on states to change their vaccine policies, it is the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) rather than the president that sets federal recommendations.How Trump’s order on vaccines is sowing confusion, doubt and fearRead moreFor now, the proposed changesdo not limitaccess to vaccines or limit insurance coverage.“Parents should absolutely proceed with getting their child’s vaccines as currently recommended, and explore any questions with their pediatrician,” says Dr Sallie Permar, chair of pediatrics at Weill Cornell Medicine.Because of the Trump administration’s attempts to change vaccine policy, many states have opted not to follow CDC childhood vaccine recommendations. As of January 2026, at least 28 states, as well as the District of Columbia,announcedthat they would follow vaccine recommendations from other entities; most of these states indicated they would follow AAP guidance.Regardless of the executive order, “[the AAP] guidelines will be what we continue to follow. We know these are backed by decades of studies, studying millions of patients, showing the vaccine schedule is safe and effective,” says Dr Katherine Piwnica-Worms, system chief of pediatrics at NYCHealth+ Hospitals.This is the latest attempt to change the US childhood vaccine schedule. In March, a courtblockedsimilarchangesadvocated for by the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr.What is the MMR vaccine?The MMR vaccine protects against three viral infections: measles, mumps and rubella. All threespread easily.Measlescan be serious for all age groups, but can beespecially dangerousfor babies and young children. In early stages, it’s characterized by a high fever, small spots inside the mouth and a rash. Severecomplications, like pneumonia or brain swelling, can lead to hospitalization and death.While measles was declared eliminated from the US in 2000, cases are now increasing: in August, approximately2,465 caseswere confirmed, a riselinkedto slumping immunization rates.Mumps is another contagious viral infection;symptomsinclude painful jaw swelling, fever and appetite loss. People who are vaccinated may still get the disease, but can expect milder symptoms and fewer complications.Though it’s sometimes called “German measles”,rubellais not caused by the same virus as measles. It’s spread through coughs and sneezes, and is especially dangerous during pregnancy for developing babies. One dose of the MMR vaccine is about 97% effective at preventing rubella.Is the combined MMR vaccine safe?The CDC currentlyrecommendschildren get two doses of the combined MMR vaccine.When signing the executive order, Trumpclaimed: “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal, and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective.”But the suggestion that the combination vaccine could be “quite lethal” is unsupported by any evidence, says Permar.“At this point, decades upon decades of data and real-world expertise show otherwise,” she says. TheMMRvaccine has been “among the most life-saving of all vaccines”.There is no evidence that spreading out shots would be safe,accordingto the AAP. Instead, longer times between vaccinations can leave a child vulnerable to preventable diseases, and multiple shots do not “overwhelm” a child’s immune system.Do individual vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella exist in the US?Single shots for measles, mumps and rubella arenot availablein the US. For them to exist, manufacturers would need to make new lots of the separated vaccines and then test them.“It would be very costly and take a long time,” says Campbell. “There’s no reason to believe that separating them would have any benefit.”Why is the MMR a combined vaccine?The combined vaccine wasdevelopedin 1971. Children typically receive their first dose between 12 and 15 months, and their second dose between the ages of four and six years old. The second doseincreasesthe protective immune response to measles and decreases outbreaks of all three diseases overall.Combination vaccines protect children with fewer shots, and in turn, require fewer appointments. Worldwide, there is an effort to combine more vaccines, says Diemert. “We know that the more injections you include in a schedule, the less likely a child is going to get fully vaccinated,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExtensiveresearchshows that the MMR vaccine is safe. Careful review of vaccine combinations is also how researchers found that a different combination vaccine called the MMRV vaccine – which also protects againstvaricella, or chickenpox – is associated with a small increased risk of febrile seizures, says Permar. These brief convulsions are frightening, butdon’t causepermanent harm.In the UK, the MMRV vaccinereplacedthe MMR vaccine in the National Health Service vaccine schedule. In 2009, the CDC advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP) updated its guidance torecommendusing MMR and a separate varicella vaccine for the first dose, due to the risk of febrile seizures. The AAPrecommendseither two doses of the MMR or MMRV vaccine.Does the combined MMR vaccine have any links to autism?Two dozen studies have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism,accordingto the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. A 2020Cochrane Reviewof the MMR vaccine – considered by the scientific community to be the “gold standard” for high-quality medical information – also found the vaccine to be effective, safe and unrelated to autism.The original report that suggested the potential link has since beendiscreditedfor faulty methodologies.“There’s never been any data to support that vaccines cause or contribute to autism, but there have been many studies showing no association with autism,” says Campbell.Further, “there’s better evidence that vaccines can prevent the type of brain damage that may link to autism”, says Permar. For example, contracting rubella during pregnancy can lead to fetal brain damage and anincreased riskof autism.What other vaccines are included in the executive order?The executive order recommends immunizations for 11 diseases. According to a White Housestatement, this is a reduction from the 18 diseases recommended by the CDC in 2024.It also recommends limiting vaccinations for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, influenza, meningitis, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and rotavirus to children with a heightened risk of suffering complications from certain illnesses, or tocasesin which a healthcare provider and guardian decide vaccination is appropriate, rather than recommending them routinely.What effect will Donald Trump’s childhood vaccine recommendations have in the US and beyond?Read moreHowever, scientific evidence suggests all children, not just those in “high risk” categories, benefit from these vaccinations, says Piwnica-Worms.The proposed limitations to the RSV vaccine especially stood out to Permar, who describes the vaccine as a “success story of American ingenuity”. Researchshowsthat the vaccine made an immediate positive impact after it wasapprovedin 2023,decreasingthe number of babies hospitalized from the virus.Critically, the executive order does not mean there have been any changes tothe current vaccine schedulerecommendations issued by the CDC. These shots are still recommended to all children.The AAP’s 2026childhood immunization schedulealso still recommends routine vaccinations against 18 different diseases. The AAP schedule isendorsedby 12 health professional societies.“The executive order doesn’t change what we need to do in terms of continuing to review vaccine data to help pediatricians and families make good decisions,” says Campbell.What do experts think of Trump’s executive order on vaccinations?Declining a vaccination is linked to an increased risk of developing the illness the vaccine is designed to prevent.But Campbell observes another risk linked to the new executive order: it can cause confusion, leading to lower immunization rates overall. Researchsuggeststhatconflicting information, along with misinformation, contributes to declining vaccination rates.The recommendation to split the MMR vaccine when that is not technically possible could be especially damaging. “I think that may lead some people to think, ‘If I don’t have a choice, then I’m not going to vaccinate,’” says Campbell. “And unfortunately, this is happening in the same year when we’ve had more measles cases since 1991.”Recent changes and questions to the US vaccine schedule have led to confusion and anxiety in parents, explains Piwnica-Worms. When Kennedy attempted to change the childhood immunization schedule in January, “there was a large rise in questions and hesitancy from families”, she says.A possible silver lining is that the executive order inspires productive conversations about vaccines, says Diemert, before adding: “I’m struggling to think of a positive.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyMMRVaccines and immunisationTrump administrationRobert F Kennedy JrDonald TrumpChildren's healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘At any moment I might fade out’: archives reveal fearless era of land speed record breakers | Motor sport | The Guardian
description: Unseen material gives an insight into how the death-defying land speed record attempts by drivers going down the generations made a profound impact on the public imagination
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Unseen material gives an insight into how the death-defying land speed record attempts by drivers going down the generations made a profound impact on the public imagination
Content: Malcolm Campbell’s Blue Bird car tears across the Bonneville salt flats in 1935. Photograph: FIA/Bill ShiplerUnseen material gives insight into how death-defying attempts by drivers made impact on public imaginationByGiles RichardsThu 13 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith the Bonneville salt flats in Utah echoing to the sound of a new land speed record achieved by a British team, the timing could not be more apposite. The historical legacy of the challenge of pushing the envelope of pace is being dusted down and made public in the form of an extraordinary archive from more than a century of record-breaking machines and their singularly driven pilots.On Tuesday, JCB’s Hydromax car took the hydrogen-powered International Automobile Federation (FIA) land speed record,reaching 406.320mph at Bonneville.Appropriately the car was driven by Andy Green, the former RAF wing commander who holds the current outright land speed record of 763.035mph, set in 1997 in the ThrustSSC car in which he also became the only person to have broken the sound barrier on land.His efforts in the ThrustSSC and now the JCB Hydromax join a rich history of land speed records, the archive of which is being re-examined, much of it seeing the light of day for the first time.The FIA is in the process of digitising for public viewing more than two million documents and pictures from its archive. Its collection relating to the land speed record, held in the FIA storage facility in Valleiry, France, is one of the first projects to be undertaken and will be made public shortly.“This is the first time they’ve been available outside of the boxes that were stored in Valleiry,” said Roger Banowetz, the president of the FIA land speed records commission. “I was pushing to get the land speed record archive digitised, it’s really important to have that material available for everybody.”Alongside the documents and pictures are hand-written notes, letters and official records, annotated by those witnessing or taking part in the record attempts, a distinct, human element reaching back through the years.View image in fullscreenCamille Jenatzy of Belgium in the La Jamais Contente car in 1899.Photograph: Courtesy of RenaultThe battle to be the fastest had begun shortly after the invention of the motorcar at the end of the 19th century,but initially under electric combustion power. The Frenchman Count Gaston de Chasseloup-Laubat set the first mark in 1898 at 39.24mph in a Jeantaud car but the baton was swiftly taken up.Belgium’s Camille Jenatzy joined the fray and the pair swapped records for two years until Jenatzy broke the 100kmh mark in his car La Jamais Contente (“The Never Contented”), a striking, torpedo-shaped beast in which Jenatzy sat bolt upright from the knees upward.What followed became a furious competition as men and women in machines from around the world vied to take the top spot and swiftly caught the public’s imagination. In what might be considered the competition’s golden age, the British were front and centre. Kenelm Lee Guinness took the record in a Sunbeam 350HP after the first world war, followed by four more successes from Malcolm Campbell, the latter becoming a household name and a key player in a frenetic contest in the 1930s as he and his fellow Britons George Eyston and John Cobb went at it. When the decade began the record stood at 231mph. By its close it was 367mph.The archive reflects a period when the exploits were front page news. Pictures of Cobb’s Railton Special being assembled speak evocatively of the time while the technical report of his records included understated remarks noting that the course was “unusually rough”.View image in fullscreenMalcolm Campbell (left) on the Bonneville salt flats in 1935 with assorted equipment.Photograph: Bill ShiplerPhotos of Campbell’s efforts in 1935 at Bonneville include a picture of the time scorer and calculator, with a handwritten note on the back reading “early morning – clothes not yet removed”, and of his Blue Bird car hurtling across the salt. That year in Utah, Campbell broke the 300mph mark but it had been far from an easy ride, as he later recalled.“Suddenly a film of oil started to cover the windscreen and deadly fumes from the engine commenced to enter the cockpit and I realised that at any moment I might fade out,” he said. “However, we were fast approaching the end of the mile when there was a terrific explosion. The near-side front tyre had burst. By now the screen was opaque. I had a feeling as though dozens of nails were being driven through the top of my head, this being caused through inhaling the exhaust fumes, and in consequence regaining full control of the car was not very easy.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA letter from Colonel Péron, who was the general secretary of the Association Internationale des Automobile Clubs Reconnus, to Malcolm Campbell, regarding locations for his land speed record attempt.Photograph: _FIA/FIAIn a sport where the speeds made the threat of death a constant possibility, it was a stark reminder of how dangerous it was and the bravery of those participating.“You just don’t get in the thing and put it on cruise control and go down the course,” observed Banowetz in Utah.“We’re out here on the salt right now. Some of the other records have been done on mud, dry land surfaces. All have very reduced traction compared to a tarmac surface. So it really increases the challenge exponentially.”Included too is the correspondence between Campbell and Colonel CG Péron, who was the general secretary of the Association Internationale des Automobile Clubs Reconnus, which set the rules and ratified new records and would ultimately evolve into the FIA. As Campbell tried to find a suitable venue for his efforts between 1928 and 1931 Péron did his best to assist, including enlisting the help of the French military in Algeria. “Mon General …” begins the letter of introduction he supplied to Campbell.The competition continued in the postwar period, not just for outright speed but for timed endurance runs too. In 1959, the archive charts a record in the international class G by what might have been considered the most unlikely contender, an aerodynamic-bodied Austin-Healey Sprite. The record was set over 12 hours across 1,665 miles at an average speed of 138.75mph, the details of which were meticulously filled in by hand, including a laconic note recording when one of the drivers, Gus Ehrman, endured a huge spin when the engine cover came off at 135mph: “Car spun outside measured line in 5th lap – run continued.”View image in fullscreenArt Arfons in the Green Monster, breaking the world land speed record in 1965 on Bonneville flats.Photograph: _FIA/Courtesy of FIAIn the 60s the contest changed drastically as the cars ceased to be wheel-driven but rather propelled by jet and rocket engine power. Campbell’s son Duncan was the last to hold the wheel-driven record at 403.10 mph in 1964 before the FIA allowed the use of thrust power and ushered in a new era.It was led by Craig Breedlove from California who had shown the future when he put a fighter jet engine on to a three-wheel chassis called Spirit of America and reached 407mph at Bonneville in 1963, a record that was not recognised at the time as it was not within regulations.When they were changed he and another young charger, Art Arfons, enjoyed an enthralling to and fro. Between 1963 and 1965 they exchanged the fastest time repeatedly, with Arfons’ wonderfully named Green Monster taking on Spirit of America as the record went from just over 400mph to Breedlove making it to 600.601mph in November 1965.The FIA documents include a telegram Breedlove sent confirming the new record and noting that, this time, his car did have four wheels.This week the competition continued with Green and JCB on the flats to set another record. The motto of the team, “never content”, has stood the test of time, as the archive aptly demonstrates. “The people that do this sport are admired because it’s unique in so much as if you can dream it, you can build it and you can race it,” said Banowetz.Explore more on these topicsMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content
