title: I got married in the Vegas of Europe. It was the most romantic 20 minutes of my life | Jules Darmanin | The Guardian
description: Post-Brexit visa rules and faceless pen-pushers were keeping me and my partner apart. But love finds a way, writes French journalist Jules Darmanin
Author: Jules Darmanin
Headline: Post-Brexit visa rules and faceless pen-pushers were keeping me and my partner apart. But love finds a way, writes French journalist Jules Darmanin
Content: A newly married couple in the Nyhavn old town area of CopenhagenPhotograph: Jeppe Gustafsson/AlamyView image in fullscreenA newly married couple in the Nyhavn old town area of CopenhagenPhotograph: Jeppe Gustafsson/AlamyOpinionWeddingsI got married in the Vegas of Europe. It was the most romantic 20 minutes of my lifeJules DarmaninPost-Brexit visa rules and faceless pen-pushers were keeping me and my partner apart. But love finds a wayThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.33 EDTShareConsider your ideal wedding. You may picture religious pageantry, majestic domes and the auspicious light of the Divine beaming on a white dress. Maybe you see friends dancing on a pub’s veranda, cheering for you in front of a town hall, or anywhere really – the people you love are there, and it’s all that matters.What you are probablynotpicturing is a meet-up with Chris and Mitch, two complete strangers waiting for you and your future spouse by a nondescript fountain in the middle of Copenhagen. Judging by my soon-to-be-wife’s bewildered laugh throughout the entire 20 minutes of our wedding, this is not what she was picturing either. Should I add that neither of us is Danish, or lives inDenmark?My wife, who is attached to her privacy and thus will remain “my wife” for the purpose of this piece, is British-Polish, and made her life in the UK. I am French.Brexitmeans Brexit. To live happily ever after under the same London roof, we had to prove our commitment to the relevant authorities.Our immigration adviser – an odd but knowledgable fellow – was unsubtle about it. On a Zoom call about a year ago, he mimed a rifle being reloaded. To end ourlong-distance relationshipand build a life together, it was time for a shotgun wedding.But while love doesn’t wait, administrations around Europe like to take their sweet time. Marrying in Britain required a “fiance visa”, which would have allowed me to stay in the UK while waiting to get married, but not to work, making it financially unviable. Doing it in my home country would have required dealing with French bureaucracy – you can appreciate why we ruled that out. If only there was a simple way to marry abroad, we thought.A single Google search was enough to find an agency called Marry Abroad Simply.Despite the hundreds of five-star reviews praising “excellent communication”, “genuine kindness” and a “completely stress-free experience”, I couldn’t shake the feeling that getting wed with Marry Abroad Simply was a bit like going for a haircut to a salon named Best Haircuts. One would hope for a bit more mystique.But so be it – I dialled the WhatsApp number on the website and mumbled something to the effect of: “Hello, I’d like to marry my partner as soon as possible, please.” Instead of saying, “Sounds a bit dodgy, love”, a charming woman called Leanne laid out her fast-and-furious pitch.Plan A, she said, was Gibraltar, the easiest option when it comes to paperwork. However, the marriage certificate can take a few weeks to arrive in the post. Plan B was Denmark, but city halls were crowded, so we would need to pay extra for a quicker ceremony in the park. Finally, she added, “I can get you married in Georgia in a couple of weeks.”We opted for a compromise between speed and familiarity, and picked the “Copenhagen Express” package.Denmark, we found out in the process, is theVegas of Europe. Thanks to its lenient, multilingual administration, couples from around the world flock to the Scandinavian kingdom to elope. The trend startedmore than a decade ago, with Germans crossing the border to marry their partner from outside the Schengen area. It’s not a bad business: international couples bring about120m kroner (about £13.7m)to the economy every year.Leanne, who spoke to me after our blitz wedding, reckons her company helps 150 couples in Denmark every month. She often deals with cases more complex than ours, such as same-sex unions where one spouse comes from a country still denying them their rights. A former government document specialist, in 2013 she joined this industry specialising in quick, fuss-free wedding planning.Our own wedding attained summits of fusslessness you wouldn’t believe. The day before, our suitcases barely unpacked, we got to Copenhagen city hall, where the civil registrar desk also serves as a gift shop. We queued with other couples to prove our identity to the Danish government. Fake bouquets were displayed on a table next to a sign saying “Flowers (for rent) on your wedding day”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenFlowers for rent in Copenhagen city hall.Photograph: handoutWe passed on the offer and the next morning rushed to the flower shop at Copenhagen train station. The white and purple bouquet my partner chose would look splendid under the grey Danish sky. With our prêt-à-porter suit and dress, she was gorgeous and I was dapper enough. We were ready to walk down the aisle.After a 15-minute stroll through Copenhagen’s Latin Quarter, under the gaze of curious tourists and blase locals, we arrived at our venue: thegardens of the Royal Library. It’s a nice but unassuming park in the heart of the city. We had no guests, as you can imagine, and Marry Abroad Simply procured us Chris and Mitch.Chris and Mitch – bless them – were our professional and only witnesses. They introduced us to our officiant, a mild-mannered gentleman named Jesper. We then stood awkwardly in front of the building that housed centuries of Danish literature. Jesper gave a brief speech about how we, too, were writing the first page of our common book. Listening to the sniffs on the video Chris took of that moment, I believe he shed a tear. But Leanne since told me they could do several of these a day, so he may just have had a cold.We were so engrossed in the absurdity of the situation that we didn’t pay that much attention to Jesper’s speech. We said our vows, exchanged our rings, and kissed under the golf clap of onlookers. After some pictures, including a selfie with the gang, we crouched down on a bench to sign the papers. My wife and I were married.You might find this unromantic, but I couldn’t disagree more. Throughout our Danish escapade, we kept bumping into other couples roaming in and around city hall. We could often guess from their looks and their accents that they were there for reasons similar to us. They were lovers seeking to tear down the borders erected between them, to prove their most intimate devotion to faceless pen-pushers.That day was for us against the world. It was a day of boldness and belief in a bright future. To my readers longing for marriage, I say: forget bridesmaids, distant cousins and nervy photographers. What I wish for you is to marry abroad simply.Jules Darmanin is a French journalistExplore more on these topicsWeddingsOpinionEuropeMarriageDenmarkBrexitcommentShareReuse this content

title: Lost jobs, inequality, rogue agents: why are we accepting oligarchs’ AI agenda? | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: The dangers of AI become clearer every day. Why are we still acting as if we have no choice about our future?
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: The dangers of AI become clearer every day. Why are we still acting as if we have no choice about our future?
Content: ‘Lost jobs. Lost wages. Widening inequality. Datacenters using up water and electricity and polluting the climate.’Photograph: Brandon Dill/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Lost jobs. Lost wages. Widening inequality. Datacenters using up water and electricity and polluting the climate.’Photograph: Brandon Dill/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Lost jobs, inequality, rogue agents: why are we accepting oligarchs’ AI agenda?Robert ReichThe dangers of AI become clearer every day. Why are we still acting as if we have no choice about our future?Supported byAbout this contentThu 13 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTShareRather than producing jobs, the US economy actually lost 23,000 jobs in July, according toBureau of Labor Statisticsdata released on Friday. In addition, May and June’s job numbers were revised downward, showing a combined 103,000 fewer jobs than previously reported.As if this weren’t bad enough, wage growth has also slowed. Average hourly earnings rose by just 0.1% from June.This isn’t just a single month’s slow wage growth, either. Average hourly earnings increased just 3.2% over the pastyear– the lowest annual growth rate in five years.What’s going on? It’s too early to tell. But evidence is mounting that artificial intelligence is playing a role.New research by economists at Morgan Stanleyshowsthat the rate of unemployment is half a percentage point higher than it would otherwise be in occupations significantly exposed toAI, which they put at about30%of all employment. The effect is even more dramatic among younger people.Workers in these exposed occupations are also finding it more difficult to transition from unemployment back into employment than workers in less exposed occupations, leading to longer spells of joblessness.And according toresearchby the economists Sania Edlich and Apollo Global Management’s Torsten Slok, wage growth in jobs exposed to AI has contracted by 6.7% since 2023. This slowdown in wage growth has already resulted in at least $28bn inlossesfor 5.8 million affected workers.Billionaires are trying to lull us into AI complacency. Don’t let them | Steven GreenhouseRead moreThese findings still don’t explain the startling loss of jobs in July or the downward revisions for May and June. There are probably many factors at play. But they suggest that employers may be anticipating they’ll need fewer workers in the future – and won’t need to pay them all that much in order to attract them.It doesn’t matter that AI may create more jobs over the long term. As John Maynard Keynes once noted, over the long term we’re all dead.More thanhalfof Americans surveyed by Reuters/Ipsos in June said they were worried AI will put someone in the household out of work.Edlich and Slok write: “The critical policy question is not whether AI will reshape the labor market more broadly, but how quickly, and whether workers will have the support they need when it does.”As a former secretary of labor who’s kept his eyes focused on the Trump regime, I can assure you workerswon’thave the support they need any time soon.Even if AI begins to generate the productivity bonanza its advocates predict – but that it hasn’t yet – there’s no reason to assume US workers will see any of the benefits in their paychecks. If you hadn’t noticed, wages have been stuck even as the stock market has roared.To the contrary, all signs point to vast riches for a few major AI investors and executives, while most Americans are left behind.Wealth inequality is already at record levels, and wealth at the top is quickly morphing into political power.AI is already breeding a vast wave of campaign money. The pro-AI Super Pac Leading the Future, backed by executives at OpenAI and Palantir,had amassed more than $140mas of April, while Public First Action,backed by Anthropic,isn’t far behind.As the great jurist Louis Brandeis is reputed to have said: “America has a choice. We can have great wealth in the hands of a few. Or we can have a democracy. But we can’t have both.”AI is pushing us further toward the first option.Meanwhile, there’s the planet to consider.Amazon is now investing in a natural-gas power plant linked to a Pecos county, Texas, datacenter. The site could become the country’slargest single source of climate pollution, the New York Times reported. According to regulatory records reviewed by the Times, the plant will be allowed to release 33m tonnes of carbon dioxide a year.So much forAmazon’s promiseto reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040 as part of its Climate Pledge. You can bet other giants in the AI race will be turning to natural gas, too.Oh, and I haven’t even mentioned the Frankenstein in the room. A few weeks ago, OpenAIadmittedthat two of its artificial intelligence models had gone rogue and hacked into another company.How soon before AI models escape all their cages?Just last week, scientists published a study documenting how they used AI tocreate new kinds of viruses, raising the frightening possibility that the technology could be used to invent dangerous pathogens.Lost jobs. Lost wages. Widening inequality. Datacenters using up water and electricity and polluting the climate. Vastly more money polluting our politics. Models escaping their cages and hacking into everything, possibly threatening human life on this planet.Can we pause for a moment and talk about what’s really happening here?As the sociologist Tressie McMillan Cottom says, AI has merged regressive politics with unchecked economic power under the guise of technological innovation. Far too much money is giving a small group of unelected people extraordinary power to determine our future in ways that are likely to remake – and could possibly destroy – our lives.We’re watching all of this roll out as if we have no choice, as if it’s inevitable, as if AI is just something we’re going to have to adapt to.But why shouldwehave to adapt toit, whenitis the product of people like Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Mark Zuckerberg and Dario Amodei?If the markets reject OpenAI and Anthropic, the US should nationalize them | Bruce Schneier and Nathan E SandersRead moreWhy shouldwebe confined to being spectators at their enormously dangerous game? Why shouldwehave to accept all these hugely negative, potentially life-threatening consequences?The fact is, we don’t.Communities across the US are organizing against datacenters near them. Maga supporters and progressives are joining together to say “no” to the noise, higher electricity bills and water shortages.Well, then, why can’t we stop the whole thing? Why can’t we decide that, to the vast majority of us, the incalculable costs and risks of AI aren’t worth the potential benefits?Critics argue that stopping or even pausing AI in the United States would risk American industry falling behind competitors overseas.But if the costs and risks exceed known benefits, why not let China or any other competitor try AI out first? Why shouldwebe the canary in this extraordinarily dangerous coalmine?Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSuper PacsOpenAIAnthropicAmazonTexasUS unemployment and employment statisticscommentShareReuse this content

title: AOC’s public egg-freezing shouldn’t feel radical. But in today’s US, it does | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The congresswoman’s decision is an assertion of women’s freedom and dignity at a time when our status is rapidly eroding
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The congresswoman’s decision is an assertion of women’s freedom and dignity at a time when our status is rapidly eroding
Content: ‘The principle that women can and should pursue ambitions other than marriage and motherhood turns out to be much more endangered than I thought it was.’Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The principle that women can and should pursue ambitions other than marriage and motherhood turns out to be much more endangered than I thought it was.’Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesOpinionAlexandria Ocasio-CortezAOC’s public egg-freezing shouldn’t feel radical. But in today’s US, it doesMoira DoneganThe congresswoman’s decision is an assertion of women’s freedom and dignity at a time when our status is rapidly erodingThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTShare“Don’t be weird about this,” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive star and rumored 2028 presidential contender, said on herlive video broadcastas she raised her shirt to angle the syringe into her abdomen. Then, with resignation, “even though I know all of you will be.”The New York Democrat is 36 years old, and this week she revealed that she is beginning the process of freezing her eggs during Congress’s August recess. In the video, Ocasio-Cortez said that she was seeking to destigmatize the realities of women’s lives as they navigate the conflicting demands of professional aspiration and family building; she explained to viewers the process of the hormonal injections she was administering to herself, showing them the drugs and injector she was using arrayed on a paper towel, beside a disinfecting towelette. The procedure, Ocasio-Cortez explained, was not covered by her insurance, and she would be paying “100% out of pocket”. She had been saving to afford it for some time. “This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life,” she said, going on to assert her hope that transparency about such questions will destigmatize women’s reproductive lives and promote their dignity.It’s a bold move from a likely presidential contender. The decision to go public with her egg-freezing distinguishes Ocasio-Cortez as the rare Democrat willing to articulate an alternative vision of gender politics in an era when the Trump administration and its allies have rapidly eroded women’s civil rights protections, reproductive rights and workforce access, but whenmany mainstream Democratshave eschewed a robust defense of women’s 20th-century gains in favor ofcoveting white male votesand making overtures to the manosphere. Still, more than a political statement of values, the move may also serve as an early confrontation with what may be among the future-candidate AOC’s thorniest electoral vulnerabilities: her sex.‘Bold and ethical’: doctors on AOC’s egg-freezing journey - and Maga’s criticisms of itRead moreBy now, it is hardly controversial to say that the status of women has rapidly eroded over the past decade. The culture has turned against women’s freedom and dignity. In 2016, Donald Trump was elected just weeks after the nation heard him proudly declare that hegrabbed women“by the pussy”, defeating the first electorally viable female presidential candidate in a huge symbolic defeat for women’s advancement that has still not been reckoned with. In 2022, the national right to an abortion was killed off by the supreme court in the Dobbs case, decimating women’s dignity still further and materially harming their health and economic prosperity. The rise of the manosphere has initiated adolescent boys and grown men alike into a vulgar, domineering style of public misogynist contempt; a rash of so-called “wellness” influencers have encouraged women to abandon their reliable hormonal birth control in deference to scientifically dubious superstitions; tradwives have told girls and women to abandon workforce participation, education, ambition, financial independence and basic self-respect in favor of a gauzy, aproned life of baking a lot and thinking very little. Meanwhile, the rise of AI and deepfake technology means that now any woman or girl whose face appears in public must subject herself to the possibility, and frequently the reality, of being humiliated and degraded withdigital pornography of her likeness, as a punishment for being female.Policy, too, has turned against women’s historic gains. The Trump administration’s dismantling of theDepartment of Educationmeans that there is now very little in the way of enforcement of Title IX, the law that was supposed to secure women’s equal right to education. The administration hasweaponized the Equal Employment Opportunity Commissionin an effort to combat fictitious discrimination against white men, turning the organization away from its mission of fighting the kind of discrimination that keeps women out of the workforce. Officials have threatened to cut educational funding for students inwomen-dominated fields, and they havedecimated Title X, turning the program meant to help low-income women meet their reproductive health and family planning needs into one that encourages childbearing instead. Programs meant tocombat teen pregnancy– a wildly successful investment in young girls’ gifts and potential – have been cut. Birth control hasbeen burned. There has been dispiritingly little pushback: shockingly few prominent political figures seem willing to mount a meaningful defense of the rights and dignity of women and girls.In this context, AOC’s earnest willingness to draw attention to the status of women, and to argue for herself – and, implicitly, for others – as valuable for their intellects and gifts, and not merely for their reproductive capacities, is notable in itself. In her video, Ocasio-Cortez noted that she would be undergoing the treatment while continuing to work, including before an appearance on ABC’s This Week this past Sunday. “I want you all to see that,”she said. “And because women can do anything, and I think it’s badass that I’m going to be giving myself shots in the green room [as I] get my glam on.”On the show, she was blunt about the political moment motivating her disclosure. “In this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country and normalize them,” Ocasio-Cortez said.Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez should run for president | Bhaskar SunkaraRead moreRadical feminism this is not. Ocasio-Cortez’s assertions of women’s worthiness and capacity for public life, and her celebration of her own reproductive choices and pledge to help make such freedom possible for others, would have been considered tepid, even banal, a decade ago, during the “girlboss” era, when women’s reproductive freedom and workplace access were more culturally accepted and less directly threatened by policy. Back then, I would have rolled my eyes at such a display; now, I could weep with gratitude. The principle that women can and should pursue ambitions other than marriage and motherhood turns out to be much more endangered than I thought it was then; the example of a prominent woman doing so turns out to be more precious.But AOC’s egg-freezing saga, coming as 2028 speculation mounts, raises another question: how voters will respond to a female candidate of childbearing age. Historically, female politicians of AOC’s national profile and political ambition have largely been post-menopausal, and already mothers. Ocasio-Cortez’s youth and beauty have at times been a political asset – it’s hard to imagine any female politician achieving her level of national prominence while looking like, say, JD Vance – but it has also presented her with unique obstacles and humiliations, and prompted contempt for her on the part of her opponents that at times is so virulent and obsessive that it seems downright Freudian. As the first in her cohort of millennial progressives, and an early innovator in vertical video engagement with her constituents, AOC has long been willing to buck conventional wisdom about what a successful candidate should do or say in public. As she mulls a presidential run, she now has to contend with something else that no other candidate has ever done successfully before: running as a woman.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAlexandria Ocasio-CortezOpinionWomenPregnancyGenderFeminismTrump administrationReproductive rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on solar eclipses: moments of wonder that bring us together | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Wednesday’s eerie spectacle united crowds beneath the sky, continuing a human fascination that stretches from ancient myth to modern physics
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Wednesday’s eerie spectacle united crowds beneath the sky, continuing a human fascination that stretches from ancient myth to modern physics
Content: A total solar eclipse is seen from Castronuevo de los Arcos, Spain, on 12 August 2026.Photograph: Manuel Balles/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA total solar eclipse is seen from Castronuevo de los Arcos, Spain, on 12 August 2026.Photograph: Manuel Balles/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionSolar eclipsesThe Guardian view on solar eclipses: moments of wonder that bring us togetherEditorialWednesday’s eerie spectacle united crowds beneath the sky, continuing a human fascination that stretches from ancient myth to modern physicsThu 13 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 20.09 EDTShare“I’d describe it as a magical eeriness.” Lisa Redfern’sdescriptionto the Guardian conveys the combination of beauty and wrongness that accompanied Wednesday’s partial solar eclipse in Britain. Crowds across the country assembled as the sun’s power seemed to wane, twilight changed tone abruptly, the temperature fell and the familiar landscape took on an unnatural appearance. In a divided world, there is comfort in coming together in awe. Ms Redfern, speaking from Cornwall, was right that Britons “may not see another one. We have to make the most of these moments.” The country has to wait 55 years for another comparably deep partial eclipse.To experience the true marvel of the eclipse, one had to be in thepath of totality– which this week crossed over Greenland, Iceland and Spain. There the sun was completely obscured. Britain saw a partial version, with the moon covering part of the sun, with only a thin yellow crescent showing. Totality is another world of wonder: for a few minutes a black disc appears where the sun should be, surrounded by a fiery corona in a purplish firmament. It is64 yearsbefore a total eclipse of the sun will be seen over Britain.View image in fullscreenAlbert Einstein.Photograph: Bettmann ArchiveToday we understand that eclipses occur when the moon passes directly between the sun and the Earth, a rare three-way alignment known as asyzygy. The moon blocks the sun and casts a shadow across the Earth. As the moon orbits and the Earth rotates beneath it, that shadow races across our planet, tracing a thin ribbon where, for a few extraordinary minutes, day turns suddenly to darkness.For ancient peoples without such knowledge, something appeared to be eating the sun. In China, the cosmic order appeared threatened by dragons. In India, thedisruptionwas attributed to a demon’s disembodied head. It was a Greek philosopher,Anaxagoras, who arguably first proposed the correct theory of eclipses after experiencing one in 478BC. Astronomical knowledge became political power most memorably in 1504, when Columbusexploitedhis knowledge of an approachinglunar eclipse– “blood moon” – to frighten Jamaica’s Indigenous people into giving him food after they had refused.Britain and its empire made adistinctivecontribution to understanding the heavens, turning eclipse expeditions into laboratories for the emerging science of astrophysics. It was the1868 solar eclipseover colonial India that led to the element helium being discovered jointly by the astronomersPierre Janssenof France andNorman Lockyerof Britain. By the late 19th century, the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society had a “joint permanent eclipse committee”, government funding and privileged access to the navy and colonial administrations.The committee organised the 1919 eclipse expeditions to Príncipe island, off west Africa, and Brazil that changed science for ever. Theirobservationsfound that the sun’s gravity deflected light from distant stars, just as Einstein’s theory of general relativity had predicted four years earlier. Though the 1919 resultsremaindebated, the irony was that British imperial scientific power ended up making aGerman-born physicistthe most famous scientist in the world, just months after Britain and Germany had finished fighting a catastrophic war. Then science transcended divisions; today the eclipse itself does as we gather beneath it in shared amazement. It is also a reminder that some experiences still belong not to nations or individuals, but to humanity as a whole.Explore more on these topicsSolar eclipsesOpinionAstronomySpaceThe moonThe sunAlbert EinsteineditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on A-level and T-level results: a boost to the nation’s confidence | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Young people should be proud of their achievements. Ministers should focus on what comes next
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Young people should be proud of their achievements. Ministers should focus on what comes next
Content: Students at Neath Port Talbot College react as they receive their results.Photograph: Gareth Everett/Huw Evans/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStudents at Neath Port Talbot College react as they receive their results.Photograph: Gareth Everett/Huw Evans/ShutterstockOpinionA-levelsThe Guardian view on A-level and T-level results: a boost to the nation’s confidenceEditorialYoung people should be proud of their achievements. Ministers should focus on what comes nextThu 13 Aug 2026 13.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTShareAstrong set ofA-level resultsshould raise confidence in Britain’s future. These aredifficult exams, and schools and colleges across England, Wales and Northern Ireland are rightly proud of their achievements. Top grades are up, especially in maths, which remains the most popular subject. A total of 262,820 18-year-olds have gained a place at university or college – 3% more than last year.But the headline success masks some troubling trends. The humanities made up only a quarter of entries, while subject choices are becoming more specialised. Huge gender gaps are also striking: girls made up 79% of English A-level entries but just 19% in computing. In T-levels there has been an improvement, although their newness makes this year’s results harder to assess or compare. But the dropout rate remains higher than in the qualifications that T-levels are supposed to replace, while take-up remains low. Five years in, suchongoing issuescannot be dismissed as teething troubles.More worrying still are the geographical disparities dividing economically disadvantaged parts of the north and Midlands from the wealthy south - and especially London. Young people in the capital are almost twice as likely to apply to university as those in north-east England – the widest gap on record. Educational opportunities are diverging in parallel with economic ones.Nor are these inequalities only spatial. There may be relief in government that private schools did not take more of the top grades; the 46.8% of their pupils receiving an A* or A was only slightly up on last year. But the fact that just13% of college learnersachieved these marks should concern everyone who wants to see all young people reach their full potential. This is arguably made more concerning by the severe financial difficulties facing some universities. The stakes in admissions have always been high, and widening inequalities between institutions could lift them higher. A 2% rise in international students accepted on to undergraduate courses should ease the sense of crisis slightly.So far, Andy Burnham’s statements on education have pointed to devolution as his preferred method of rebalancing the system, along with a renewed focus on vocational options including new GCSEs (or equivalents). But while more firmly embedding colleges within local economies is a good idea, givingmayors responsibility for sixth forms, along with the full range of post-16 options, would be a huge shift. It must not be rushed. Rather than reorganising existing budgets, ministers should work towards a boost to spending on disadvantaged 16-19s with a scheme modelled on the pupil premium.Looking across the qualifications landscape,A-levelsare a bright spot. For too many teenagers, GCSEs are an overly restrictive or demoralising ordeal. The ability to make choices at 16 about what to study is broadly welcomed. Sixth-form and college courses can be rewarding for teachers as well as pupils – as could be seen in the videos of staff on results day. These courses and exams are not perfect; greater breadth should be a medium-term aim. But if politicians want to do right by young people, there are two things they should do right away. One is to revise the unfair terms of student loans. The other is to address the financial crisis facing the universities where many of them will be enrolling in a few weeks’ time.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Parkrun is a joy for many. Get involved | Running | The Guardian
description: Letters: Bill Hunter says the weekly 5k race at locations across the UK and beyond is for everyone, and should be celebrated, while Helen Beioley says it is the perfect excuse to meet friends and consume a croissant after
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Bill Hunter says the weekly 5k race at locations across the UK and beyond is for everyone, and should be celebrated, while Helen Beioley says it is the perfect excuse to meet friends and consume a croissant after
Content: ‘Many would tell of the camaraderie and their improved physical and mental health. Strangers become friends and even partners.’Photograph: Neil Hall/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Many would tell of the camaraderie and their improved physical and mental health. Strangers become friends and even partners.’Photograph: Neil Hall/ReutersRunningLettersParkrun is a joy for many. Get involvedBill Huntersays the weekly 5k race at locations across the UK and beyond is for everyone, and should be celebrated, whileHelen Beioleysays it is the perfect excuse to meet friends and consume a croissant afterThu 13 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTShareI am sorry that the parkrun spoils Janet Knowlson’s experience of her local park (Letters, 7 August). I wonder if she has ever spoken to a parkrunner or a volunteer? Many would tell of the camaraderie and their improved physical and mental health. Strangers become friends and even partners. We do not take over the park, as she alleges, rather we recognise that we share the space with other park users and are respectful of their rights and needs. Parkrun is for everyone and anyone, from children upwards, and not only runners. It is only competitive if you want it to be, and is equally welcoming to walkers. Parkrun is a huge success story, both in the UK and many other countries, and should be celebrated. It receives no public funding and each event relies on an army of volunteers, without whom it wouldn’t happen. Long may it continue.Bill HunterHonley, West YorkshireIn response to Janet Knowlson’s letter complaining about the disruption to her daily peaceful walk through her park by parkrun, please can I suggest that she avoid just this one specific hour a week? Parkrun is an inclusive joy for hundreds of thousands of runners and walkers of all shapes, sizes, ages and levels of fitness. For me, it’s the perfect excuse to meet up with mates and wallop down a huge almond croissant as a post-run(walk) reward.Helen BeioleyFrance Lynch, StroudHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A timely warning on the rise of the ‘tech bros’ from the author of The Nerd Reich | Silicon Valley | The Guardian
description: Letter: Gil Durán is right, writes Catherine Austin Fitts – we must reject the limited vision of Silicon Valley with a revolution in consciousness
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Gil Durán is right, writes Catherine Austin Fitts – we must reject the limited vision of Silicon Valley with a revolution in consciousness
Content: Silicon Valley: ‘Gil Durán underestimates the darkness being contemplated.’Photograph: Steve Proehl/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSilicon Valley: ‘Gil Durán underestimates the darkness being contemplated.’Photograph: Steve Proehl/Getty ImagesSilicon ValleyLettersA timely warning on the rise of the ‘tech bros’ from the author of The Nerd ReichGil Durán is right, writesCatherine Austin Fitts– we must reject the limited vision of Silicon Valley with a revolution in consciousnessThu 13 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTShareThank you for your interview with Gil Durán, the author of The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy (‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley, 5 August).Durán is right – the antipathy towards the “tech bros” is growing. However, Durán underestimates the darkness being contemplated. The plan is for complete spatial and financial transaction control. This is not the end of democracy – it is a slavery system. Many of the people involved believe technology can dramatically extend their lifespan and they can replace most of the population with robots and automation. Now is the time to reject their limited vision with a revolution in consciousness. Thanks to Durán for the inspiration.Catherine Austin FittsHickory Valley, Tennessee, USHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Food Standards Agency should do more in the fight against ultra-processed foods | Ultra-processed foods | The Guardian
description: Letter: Mike Pender responds to an article by Felicity Lawrence in which she reflects on why food firms are panicking and suing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Mike Pender responds to an article by Felicity Lawrence in which she reflects on why food firms are panicking and suing
Content: ‘Regulation is surely the most effective way to control profit-oriented companies, many of which pay little regard to the possible negative impact of their products.’Photograph: Alamy/PAView image in fullscreen‘Regulation is surely the most effective way to control profit-oriented companies, many of which pay little regard to the possible negative impact of their products.’Photograph: Alamy/PAUltra-processed foodsLettersFood Standards Agency should do more in the fight against ultra-processed foodsMike Penderresponds to an article by Felicity Lawrence in which she reflects on why food firms are panicking and suingThu 13 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTShareFelicity Lawrence’s alarming piece on ultra-processed foods (Why are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running out, 7 August) made no mention of the UK’s Food Standards Agency, whose primary statutory objective is to protect public health from risks arising from the consumption of food.The FSA is an independent, non-ministerial government department. Its advice to ministers, and guidance to consumers, is informed by the most up-to-date scientific evidence, free of political or commercial considerations.As Lawrence pointed out, food manufacturers see government action as a threat. And regulation is surely the most effective way to control profit-oriented companies, many of which pay little regard to the possible negative impact of their products until compelled to do so.The FSA lastpublished guidanceto consumers on ultra-processed foods in February 2025. Given that “the science on harm caused by foods high in fat, salt and sugar is now settled”, it is perhaps time for it to consider updating this guidance and also whether to recommend government intervention.Mike PenderCardiffHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Andy Burnham’s great British rip-off list just got even longer | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the prime minister’s promise to end unexpected payments and hidden catches for consumers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the prime minister’s promise to end unexpected payments and hidden catches for consumers
Content: ‘For millions of households, the problem is not finding the “unsubscribe” button. It is finding that £50 buys remarkably little at the supermarket.’Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreen‘For millions of households, the problem is not finding the “unsubscribe” button. It is finding that £50 buys remarkably little at the supermarket.’Photograph: Yui Mok/PAConsumer affairsLettersAndy Burnham’s great British rip-off list just got even longerReaders respond to the prime minister’s promise to end unexpected payments and hidden catches for consumersThu 13 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTShareMisleading discounts and obstructive cancellation procedures certainly deserve regulation. But presenting this as a significant response to the cost of living crisis feels like rearranging the cushions while the sofa is on fire (Subscriptions you can’t easily cancel, sales that aren’t sales – I’ll end the rip-offs that British people hate, 9 August).For millions of households, the problem is not finding the “unsubscribe” button. It is finding that £50 buys remarkably little at the supermarket, while housing and essential bills consume ever more of their income.Perhaps this is merely the appetiser and something considerably more substantial is coming for the main course. I sincerely hope so. Otherwise, perhaps ministers could extend their new consumer-friendly approach to democracy: one-click cancellation for political subscriptions that no longer offer value for money.Fernando Quintana MarreroLondonThe issue thatAndy Burnhamintends to address stems from what Cory Doctorow has described as “enshittification” – that is, the intentional process of making tech services worse to increase profits once customers are hooked in.The PM needs to be careful not to end up sweating the small stuff and finding that all efforts are futile as his government’s apparent fixation with the likes ofPalantirand desire to build more and more datacentres creates a dependency on foreign corporations that undermines our economic, environmental and national security, and the only jobs that arise are for serfs in the warehouses and delivery vans of the techno-feudal overlords.Dave HunterBristol“Every ‘sale’ seems to come with an asterisk,” writes Andy Burnham. Was your inclusion of a large asterisk next to his name at the bottom of the article in the print edition a cheeky nod to a sales pitch by the PM?Thomas RyderNottinghamMaybe Andy Burnham should look at the practice, used by energy companies, of “standing charges”?Dougie FirthLondonHow about ending the scandal of the rip-off student loan scheme?Richard HollisSt AlbansHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Quicksilver Amy Hunt flies to glorious golden double with 200m triumph | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Britain’s Amy Hunt struck gold in the 200m to complete the sprint double, while Mark English became Ireland’s first European Championship men’s gold medallist by winning the 800m
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Britain’s Amy Hunt struck gold in the 200m to complete the sprint double, while Mark English became Ireland’s first European Championship men’s gold medallist by winning the 800m
Content: Amy Hunt hopes to add to her medal collection in the relays.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAmy Hunt hopes to add to her medal collection in the relays.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsQuicksilver Amy Hunt flies to glorious golden double with 200m triumphHunt had won 100m already; Asher-Smith wins bronzeMark English wins 800m for Ireland’s first men’s goldSean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamThu 13 Aug 2026 17.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid the adrenalised delirium of her second European title in three days, Amy Hunt walked to the nearest TV camera, held up her hands and, in homage to Russell Crowe’s character in Gladiator screamed: “Are you not entertained?”It quickly transpired that the 24-year-old Cambridge graduate had been quite the warrior off the track too. Because, as she revealed after collecting a 200m gold medal to go alongsideMonday’s 100m title, she has been nearly fainting this year when running over the longer distance.European Athletics Championship 2026: Hunt beats Adeleke and Asher-Smith to win women’s 200m gold – as it happenedRead more“I have had a lot of health things going on this year – some really, really low pressure,” Hunt explained. “The 200s have been really scary. I have been nearly fainting after a lot of my 200s this year. I had just to go into that one and get on the bend and be really brave.”Hunt had entered the 200m final as the overwhelming favourite, but she had to work to chase down the two-time champion, Dina Asher-Smith, one lane outside her, around the bend.Having done that, the raucous 20,000 crowd at the Alexander Stadium expected to see a coronation. Instead it turned into a struggle, and Hunt only just had enough in the tank to cross the line in 22.19sec, ahead of Ireland’s fast-finishing Rhasidat Adeleke, who ran a national record of 22.28. Britain’s Asher-Smith took bronze a further 0.01 further back.It means that Hunt’s dream of winning an historic quadruple of gold medals at these European Championships is alive – as she made clear afterwards by holding two fingers up in her right hand, before flipping the hand to show four fingers.“Two out of four,” she said. “Honestly, I think the 100 is the hardest mentally. And the 200 is the hardest physically.“I was thinking about my coach,” he said before I went in: ‘Just imagine me in lane 10 with a stopwatch and a whistle. Just keep those thighs up, girl.’“But there’s no celebrating, no champagne until Sunday night because I have a debt to the ladies,” Hunt explained, as she set her sights on the 4x100m and mixed relays over the weekend. “We have to make sure we come here and make sure we show them who is the best sprint nation in Europe.After 92 years, Ireland finally has a male European championship gold medallist. And his name is English – Mark English. The 33-year-old doctor from Donegal, produced a surgical performance to take gold, tracking and then overtaking Croatian Marino Bloudek in the home straight to win in 1:45.26.“Just relief,” said English. “I have been trying for a lifetime to get a title. I had planned to go to Sierra Nevada at 6am tomorrow, so I’m going to have to try to rebook that flight. These moments don’t come around often. I have a life that’s never come around for me before, so I’ll have to try to celebrate it somehow.”Bloudek clung on to take silver with Spain’s Mohamed Attaoui winning bronze. As the huge Irish contingent celebrated, the heart also went out to Britain’s Max Burgin, who was forced to pull out minutes before the race after suffering an injury in the warmup.View image in fullscreenMark English crosses the line to become the first Irishman to win European gold.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAIt caps a summer of woe for Burgin, who also picked up a virus at the Commonwealth Games and didn’t make it out of the semi-finals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was also no medal for another British contender, Elise Thorner, in the 3,000m steeplechase. The 25-year-old had entered the race as the fastest European over the distance in 2026 but she could only finish fifth behind Germany’s Gesa Felicitas Krause.The race was also notable for a faceplant by another German, Lea Meyer, into the water jump while running in the medal positions. While Meyer got up, she could only finish fourth.“It was gutting to see Lea actually fall, because I know her quite well,” said Thorner. “She is an amazing athlete. Shocking to see and trying to get over was a bit mad. But I was pretty spent with 200m so I was hanging on anyway.”View image in fullscreenElise Thorner (right) could finish only fifth in the women’s 3000m steeplechase final.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAFurther success Germany as Leo Neugebauer hung on to win the men’s decathlon from his compatriot Niklas Kaul after collapsing over the line. His score of 8,611 points proved enough by 38 points, even though the 6ft 7in Neugebauer looked to be wading through treacle over the last 50 metres before collapsing over the line.But the event was marred by extraordinary scenes earlier on day two in the pole vault, after officials forgot to raise the bar from 4.70m to 4.80m. As a result athletes were under the impression that they were attempting 4.80m, while the bar was in fact still at 4.70m.A EuropeanAthleticsstatement said that the “results of this additional 4.70m round were cancelled, and the competition was resumed at 4.80m, with all athletes given the opportunity to attempt the height.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 9: Everton | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: Modest but sensible-looking recruitment befits the club’s new air of stability but a continuation of their spring slump could test David Moyes’s appetite for the fight
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Modest but sensible-looking recruitment befits the club’s new air of stability but a continuation of their spring slump could test David Moyes’s appetite for the fight
Content: Thierno Barry has shown promising signs during Everton’s pre-season matches. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersModest but sensible-looking recruitment befits the club’s new air of stability but a continuation of their spring slump could test David Moyes’s appetite for the fightByAndy HunterThu 13 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:10th (NB: this is not necessarily Andy Hunter’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:13thProspectsA season stripped of the fear of relegation, featuring more proactive, front-footed football and the return of some hope: hadEvertonbeen offered that package before their relocation to Hill Dickinson Stadium last summer it would have been accepted gratefully given the turmoil of the previous four years. For four fifths of last season it was accepted gratefully, but then came a collapse that transformed perceptions of David Moyes’s first full season back in charge. Talk of progress requires more supporting evidence this time around.Everton were three points off the fifth and final Champions League qualification spot on 21 Marchhaving dismantled Chelseain their finest performance at the club’s new stadium. They did not win another game all season and slumped to 13th on the final day – the same position as the previous campaign under Sean Dyche and Moyes, with only one point more but an inferior goal difference. European football may well have been an ambitious target for a club adjusting to a new home and the loss of 10 players following the expiry of their contracts, loans included. But the opportunity presented itself to Moyes’s team and they blew it.Without the upheaval of last summer, with midfield resources improved and young players having had the benefit of a year’s experience of thePremier League, European qualification could be a more realistic proposition this season. Provided a few glaring holes in Moyes’s squad are finally filled. An upgrade on the limited centre-forward options of Beto and Thierno Barry is essential, although the latter has shown more promising signs in pre-season. Likewise a successor to Séamus Coleman – one of several big Evertonian losses behind the scenes recently. Everton’s quest for a new right-back is their very own Odyssey, while central defence was another area of concern last season. Genuine progress, the measure of which is not open to debate, rests on the final moves of the window.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureThe consequences of Farhad Moshiri’s calamitous ownership are still being felt with Evertonordered to pay almost £40m in compensationto Burnley over the latter’s relegation in 2021-22. Everton are appealing against the can-of-worms verdict by a Premier League independent disciplinary commission, along with the biggest financial penalty ever imposed on a Premier League club, but claim their latest punishment has not affected this summer’s transfer plans. Many season ticket holders have been hit by above-inflation price increases – in some instances of almost 10% – and the club have extended a sponsorship deal with Stake, despite the UK governmentpledging to crack downon unlicensed gambling operators sponsoring British sports teams.Owner-fan relationshipThe Friedkin Group (TFG) has brought the financial stability that Everton desperately needed but it would be a stretch to suggest fans have connected with a low-key ownership group that rarely attend games. The man they appointed to run the club, chief executive, Angus Kinnear, annoyed supporters at the end of last season by claiming the hierarchy was “happily dissatisfied” with the first campaign at Hill Dickinson Stadium. The comment was portrayed as fresh evidence of Everton accepting mediocrity but in fairness to Kinnear, who was writing about TFG’s determination to banish the threats of financial instability, relegation and regulatory sanction, he did add: “The progress is clear but we have not achieved anything yet.”The managerDavid Moyes turns 64 in April and, while the Premier League’s oldest manager clearly retains the hunger and ambition to rebuild Everton on a stronger footing, it will be interesting to see whether he retains the appetite for a fight with his critics in the event of a poor start. Particularly as the Scotland job remains available and he would appear the ideal candidate to succeed Steve Clarke. Moyes was exceeding his brief until the dismal end to last season cost Everton a shot at Europe and placed his team selections under an unforgiving spotlight. Talk of a contract extension has since gone quiet.Star signingView image in fullscreenBrennan Johnson struggled at Crystal Palace but could have just the attacking qualities Everton need.Photograph: Everton FCIt has been a sensible window rather than a sexy one from Everton so far – see replacing Idrissa Gana Gueye with the £7m Christian Nørgaard – but they might have delivered in swapping Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. No one would dispute that the Wales’ international’s move from Tottenham to Crystal Palace in January fell flat, least of all Palace who were willing to take a significant hit on their £35m, one-time record investment only seven months later. But if the 25-year-old recaptures the form he showed at Nottingham Forest, or when scoring 18 goals for Spurs in 2024-25, he could prove a steal who addresses several problems in the Everton frontline.Stat attackDavid Moyes loves to keep a settled side. Everton averaged the fewest changes to their starting XI of any team in the 2025-26 Premier League. With the squad looking largely the same as last season, this trend should continue. But what if injuries bite?StatSet for a breakthroughTyler Dibling would have been a strong candidate for this category last summer following his arrival from Southampton for an initial £35m. It reflects a nonevent of a debut season on Merseyside that he can be nominated 12 months on. Everton invested a lot of time and money into their pursuit of the England Under-21 international, who remains the most expensive signing of Moyes’s second spell in charge, but the return was a huge disappointment. The attacking midfielder started only four league games and was not given a single minute after the 2-0 win over Burnley on 3 March. The manager did not hide his frustration with what he was seeing on the training ground.World Cup impactThe longest World Cup in history should not have too onerous an impact on Moyes’s squad. Only three of his players were involved and, of those, only Jordan Pickford was in action after 1 July. Pickford came in for familiar criticism following his performances against Ghana and Argentina despite reinforcing his status as England’s undisputed No 1 goalkeeper across the tournament. Iliman Ndiaye started once for Senegal and was subbed in the 73rd minute with his country leading Belgium 2-0 in the last-32 tie. They ultimately lost 3-2. Nathan Patterson, whose Everton future is uncertain, featured in all three of Scotland’s forgettable group campaign.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27EvertonPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Championship spending hits record levels and likely to go higher as playoffs expand | Championship | The Guardian
description: With a top-eight finish offering at least a playoff place, the temptation to spend big in pursuit of the Premier League will grow – but so will the risks
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: With a top-eight finish offering at least a playoff place, the temptation to spend big in pursuit of the Premier League will grow – but so will the risks
Content: Ollie McBurnie celebrates Hull’s lucrative playoff final winner with Matt Crooks. The Tigers spent 142% of their revenue on wages in 2024-25.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenOllie McBurnie celebrates Hull’s lucrative playoff final winner with Matt Crooks. The Tigers spent 142% of their revenue on wages in 2024-25.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersChampionshipChampionship spending hits record levels and likely to go higher as playoffs expandWith a top-eight finish offering at least a playoff place, the temptation to spend big in pursuit of the Premier League will grow – but so will the risksAndrew BeasleyThu 13 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Championship’s collective wage bill grew to a record £903m in 2024-25, according to Deloitte’s latest Annual Review of Football Finance. Clubs are paying players enormous sums in their pursuit of Premier League football. With the playoffsexpanding this season, the number of owners willing to risk even more money in the hope of securing promotion is only likely to increase.In isolation, the figure of £903m does not signify much. Compared to the Premier League’s £4.4bn salary outlay, it almost looks small. But England’s top division can afford that gargantuan commitment to wages whereas the second tier cannot. The 24 clubs in theChampionshipearned £942m, meaning salaries consumed 96% of revenue. If there was any surprise in their collective net debt being £1.4bn at the end of 2024-25, it was only that it had reduced from the £1.5bn it was a year earlier.While qualifying for European competitions is not on the immediate agenda for clubs at that level, Uefa’s financial sustainability regulations restrict spending on wages, transfers and agent fees to 70% of club revenues. Luton and Sheffield United spent about 59% of their income on salaries in 2024-25, with the parachute payments they received for being relegated from the Premier League the previous season helping them keep a grip on their finances.Chart showing percentage of income spent on wages by clubs in the 2024-25 ChampionshipBut only four other clubs were below 80%, with 13 – more than half the division – spending more on wages than they earned. Cardiff spent £39m on salaries against £26m income, giving them the worst wages to revenue percentage in the division (150%). The reward for their ambition was to finish bottom of the table.The reason for such risk-taking is obvious. Deloitte estimates that the newly promoted Coventry and Hull will see their revenue rise by at least £210m over the next three seasons, with the windfall potentially reaching £365m if they can retain their Premier League status into 2027-28. Ipswich’s figures are lower thanks to receiving parachute payments last season, but they are still thought to be around £170m and £325m respectively.These sums are helping to form a strata of clubs that regularly flit between the top two tiers of English football. Burnley have either enjoyed promotion from the Championship or suffered Premier League relegation for five consecutive seasons. The Clarets are fourth favourites with bookmakers to go up once again next May, with their fellow relegated sides West Ham and Wolves leading the Championship promotion market.Their advantage is obvious. Capology estimates West Ham have the 15th highest wage bill in the world outside the Premier League and Saudi Pro League. Wolves are only two spots behind them in these amended standings, with Burnley a further six places back.The majority of top division teams in France, Germany, Italy and Spain can’t keep pace with the salary spend of these clubs so how can most Championship teams expect to compete? Jarrod Bowen alone is thought to earn £7.8m per year at West Ham, more than the entire squads of Lincoln (£5.8m) or Bolton (£6.3m).Chart showing the top 10 club wage bills in the 2026-27 ChampionshipThe new playoff system in the Championship at least offers more clubs the chance of a Premier League golden ticket. The teams that finish between third and eighth will qualify, with third and fourth going straight through to the traditional two-legged semi-finals. Their opponents in those ties will be decided by one-legged quarter-finals that feature the teams in fifth and sixth at home to those in eighth and seventh respectively.This will leave the tantalising possibility of a playoff berth open to plenty of clubs until very late in the season. Few will be entirely out of the running in January, when the transfer window offers an opportunity for squad investment. The fate of Leicester highlights the possible risks though. When the winter window closed earlier this year, they were six points from eighth, nine above the bottom three. Clubs in a similar position next January may gamble on going for a playoff spot but could end up being relegatedas Leicester were.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChart showing National League playoff wins by position in the final table since 2017-18The National League also highlights how unlikely it is that teams that take the additional playoff spots go up. The highest tier of non-league football has employed a six-team playoff format since 2017-18, with only the division winner earning automatic promotion. The club finishing seventh have yet to win the playoffs, with the side in sixth succeeding only once. Even then, the team in question (Grimsby in 2022) were in their only season outside League Two in the past 10. They were below their regular level, not climbing up to reach sixth.The Championship has a similar theme for playoff success. No team finishing sixth have gone up since 2010, with Aston Villa the most recent fifth-placed side to earn promotion,in 2019. None of the previous seven teams that finished eighth in the second flight averaged more than 1.5 points-per-game or won more than 43.4% of their matches. If they can’t win every other game at that level, how can they hope to compete in the Premier League in the unlikely event they go up?No one cares about that when there’s a reward in the region of £200m simply for getting there. Supporters might care if the owner drives their club’s finances further into the red chasing an unlikely playoff dream though.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Leigh dent Leeds’ title ambitions as Super League set to reject NRL’s opening £7m offer | Super League | The Guardian
description: Title-chasing Leeds Rhinos fell to a 16-20 defeat by Leigh Leopards on a day when Super League clubs indicated they would hold out for a better NRL offer
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Title-chasing Leeds Rhinos fell to a 16-20 defeat by Leigh Leopards on a day when Super League clubs indicated they would hold out for a better NRL offer
Content: Umyla Hanley runs in for the match-winning try as Leigh inflict a first home defeat of the season on Leeds.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenUmyla Hanley runs in for the match-winning try as Leigh inflict a first home defeat of the season on Leeds.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueLeigh dent Leeds’ title ambitions as Super League set to reject NRL’s opening £7m offerLeeds 16-20 LeighClubs optimistic of securing better offer soonAaron Bowerat AMT HeadingleyThu 13 Aug 2026 17.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 20.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn what may prove to be the most significant day in Super League’s modern history away from the field,Leigh Leopardsblew wide open the race for top spot in this year’s competition on it with a stunning victory against the league leaders, Leeds Rhinos.Super League clubs were finally informed on Thursday morning of a long-awaited opening offer from the NRL to invest in the competition. A figure of around £7m per season, for the next five years, has been tabled but is set to be turned down by clubs – who believe the competition’s value is much higher. In return, the NRL would get a 10% stake inSuper Leaguein each year it invests, but this is probably the first of several negotiationsbetween the two competitions, with some leading figures who were in that meeting telling the Guardian a crucial get-together of the clubs next Thursday will probably lead to Super League rejecting that opening bid.St Helens’ decline reaches breaking point with stench of failure lingeringRead moreHowever, Thursday is still a watershed moment, with expectation high that by the timeNRLofficials arrive at the end of this month, the two parties will be closer together and able to strike a deal that could revitalise Super League’s prospects, long-term financial picture and potentially its broadcast future.The NRL is understood to have introduced the broadcaster DAZN into negotiations on Thursday as part of its offer, with Sky Sports – Super League’s longstanding partner since its inception in 1996 – showing three games a week from the start of next year and DAZN potentially the rest. It promises to be a deal that will change how Super League is viewed for ever.But before then, the competition is heading for a thrilling finale which took another twist here. Leeds had not lost at Headingley all season but came unstuck against one of their main playoff rivals in an exciting contest, with Wigan able to go joint-top if they beat Bradford on Saturday. “We have to learn from that,” Leeds’ coach, Brad Arthur said.The lead changed hands on no fewer than four occasions on the night, but it was ultimately Umyla Hanley’s fantastic try with 25 minutes remaining which proved decisive and gave Leigh a huge victory. That was the only try of an engrossing and high-quality second half.The Rhinos led after three minutes when Ryan Hall capitalised on a sublime Jake Connor pass but three minutes later Leigh levelled through Josh Charnley. Innes Senior finished a magnificent team move from the visitors to put them in front for the first time before Brodie Croft strode through a gap in the Leigh defence to make it 14-10. By half-time it was level though, as Senior claimed his second try to leave it finely poised going into the interval. Connor’s second penalty of the night shortly after the restart put Leeds back in front, but then Hanley responded after a long-range move that caught the league leaders off guard.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDespite a barrage of attacks from Leeds, they couldn’t breach the Leopards’ line again – a world-class tackle from Hanley to deny Hall in the final minute epitomising how brilliant Leigh were when it mattered. “Courage is the word I’d use,” their coach, Adrian Lam, said. That courage will stand them in good stead for what lies ahead.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueLeeds RhinosLeigh LeopardsNRLRugby leaguematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Rangers crash out of Europa League as Derek McInnes’s winless start goes on | Europa League | The Guardian
description: Rangers drew 1-1 with Jagiellonia Bialystok but lost 3-2 on aggregate, while Hearts held Benfica but also went out of the competition, having lost the first leg 6-1
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rangers drew 1-1 with Jagiellonia Bialystok but lost 3-2 on aggregate, while Hearts held Benfica but also went out of the competition, having lost the first leg 6-1
Content: Ross McCrorie (centre) and his Rangers teammates trudge off the field after the match.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoss McCrorie (centre) and his Rangers teammates trudge off the field after the match.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersEuropa LeagueRangers crash out of Europa League as Derek McInnes’s winless start goes onRangers 1-1 Jagiellonia Bialystok (2-3 agg)Spirited Hearts hold Benfica but also out of competitionPA MediaThu 13 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDerek McInnes’s fledgling tenure as Rangers manager is in disarray after his side exited theEuropa Leaguequalifiers with a 3-2 aggregate defeat to Jagiellonia Bialystok after drawing 1-1 at Ibrox.Fog and on time (nearly): Lech Poznan reach Faroe Islands for fixture after two-day tripRead moreRangers had lost 2-1 in the first leg in Poland last week but there was optimism when the captain, Lawrence Shankland, levelled the tie on aggregate with a penalty on 19 minutes.However, in the 65th minute, the visitors deservedly equalised through the attacker Nik Prelec and the disjointed home side could not get a foothold in the game again despite changes in formation and personnel, with the boos ringing out around the ground at full time from fans frustrated atthe dismal start to the season.McInnes has failed to register a win in four competitive matchessince moving from Hearts in the summerand the dispiriting performance means Rangers will take on Jablonec, from Czechia, in the Conference League playoff round.Hearts, meanwhile, restored some pride in a 1-1 draw withBenficaas they too dropped out of the Europa League.Tómas Magnússon had the home fans dreaming of a famous win over their illustrious opponents after firing in the opener in the 77th minute. But the Portuguese giants, cruising from a 6-1 first leg win a week earlier, levelled less than a minute later through Dodi Lukébakio to wrap up a 7-2 aggregate triumph.View image in fullscreenTómas Magnússon (left) is congratulated by his teammates after scoring for Hearts against Benfica.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAIt was nevertheless an encouraging display from Wouter Vrancken’s side against a team who made seven changes from the first leg.The consolation for Hearts is a place in theConference Leagueplayoffs, where they will face Rapid Vienna of Austria.David Gray revealed hisHibernianplayers had their heads in ice buckets as he lauded them for “an incredible achievement” after closing out a 2-1 aggregate victory over Shkendija to set up a Conference League playoff round showdown with the Belgian side Gent. The two teams played out a tightly contested 0-0 draw in the second leg in the searing heat of the Todor Proeski National Arena.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHibernian fans in the stands at the Todor Proeski National Arena.Photograph: Nikola Krstic/Shutterstock“I’m delighted for the players,” the Hibs manager told BBC Sport. “It’s a brilliant time to get your first clean sheet of the season.“I just said to the players, don’t underestimate how big an achievement that is against a really good side who made it to the knockout stages of the competition last season.“Added to that, the conditions, the heat, we had to deal with all these things. I don’t think it was a brilliant game, but we put our bodies on the line and the attitude was there.”Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueRangersHeartsBenficaConference LeagueHiberniannewsShareReuse this content

title: Jack Draper ‘in difficult place’ after defeat by Martín Landaluce at Cincinnati Open | Jack Draper | The Guardian
description: Former world No 4 Jack Draper slumped to a 6-3, 7-5 defeat against Martín Landaluce in the first round of the Cincinnati Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Former world No 4 Jack Draper slumped to a 6-3, 7-5 defeat against Martín Landaluce in the first round of the Cincinnati Open
Content: Jack Draper never recovered from a poor start against Martín Landaluce.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJack Draper never recovered from a poor start against Martín Landaluce.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesJack DraperJack Draper ‘in difficult place’ after defeat by Martín Landaluce at Cincinnati OpenFormer world No 4 slumps to 6-3, 7-5 first-round lossDraper still recovering from long-term arm injuryTumaini Carayolin CincinnatiThu 13 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe minuscule amount of confidence and self-beliefJack Drapercurrently has to call upon in the most difficult period of his career was underscored in the first game of his opening match in Cincinnati. Draper began his service game by shanking a forehand into the back fence, which he followed up with two double faults. He immediately fell down a break and never recovered.A few fleeting positive moments followed, but this miserable start set the tone for another excruciating day for the former world No 4 as he could not escape the mental fatigue borne out of battling serious injury for 15 months and counting. Draper fell 6-3, 7-5 to Martín Landaluce, the world No 64.Jack Draper: ‘When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again’Read more“It’s the same as last week, the way I’m usually able to fight for every ball and conduct myself, it’s just missing,” Draper said. “After last week, I put in a lot of hard work to play a bit better this week. Obviously, the conditions and all the things that I’m changing is very hard to manage, but I think from just an internal point of view, it’s a difficult place to be right now.”Draper spent the final stretch of his first-round loss at the Canadian Openlast week in tears. On Wednesday, as he tried to put on a brave face and remain positive, the 24-year-old described his emotions as a reaction to the mental toll of both his injury – bone bruising in his left arm – and the disruptive changes he has made in order to lessen the strain on it. There were no tears this time, but between a poor first set and the way he squandered six set points in set two after leading with a double break at 5-2, Draper was a shadow of himself.He said: “From the start of the match, you’re battling it a lot and you’re trying to keep going with it and moving forwards throughout the match and trying to … pump stuff up and give you energy, but it just suppresses you down. It’s got to a point with me where it’s taken probably one of my biggest qualities, my fighting spirit.”Since Wimbledon, Draper has changed his strings, his racket and he continues to adjust to his service motion. Thesechanges have all been madein service of reducing the strain on his arm and at the expense of optimising his performance. Although Draper said his injury did not directly contribute to the loss, the great uncertainty surrounding the condition of his arm remains the defining problem.View image in fullscreenJack Draper is likely to need to progress through qualifying to compete at the US Open.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesUnlike most injuries, this is not a case of resting for some time and coming back. “I think that’s the toughest part,” he said. “It’s like there are no right answers. You have to figure it out. A lot of it’s probably, I found out in the end, biomechanics and changing rackets. It’s a tough injury because you have to start again with what you do.“There’s a level of chronic pain that’s always with you. That starts to go away, but obviously the arm is linked to the elbow. It’s linked to bicep tendinitis, it’s linked to so many nerves around that area. So when you have an injury to that area, the whole arm is kind of lit up. It’s like someone taking blood pressure. And your arm’s just [struggling].“When you’ve got that on your playing arm – this is my life, this is my career, you know? It’s tough enough as it is to play such an intense sport and the amount we have to give to it. And when you’ve got an injury that is tough to come past and tough to understand, there’s many challenges, there’s many obstacles. For a normal person, they’d go and probably have six months off and it might recover and heal. Truth is, I’m playing tennis and so it’s not as simple as taking time off and it’s going to go because it doesn’t [work]. I’ve tried it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is more uncertainty on the horizon. Since he is ranked No 143 and does not have a protected ranking, Draper has been reliant on wildcards to enter ATP events.He does not expect to receive a wildcard for the US Open, meaning he will have to play in the qualifying draw in order to compete in New York. “I think it’s the fatigue in my mind and my body from a long period of setback and struggle and isolation and just trying to get back all the time. The level of my fall almost from where I was last year and the amount of things that I’m having to change in my tennis. Yeah, the mountain seems very, very big.”Cameron Norrie, the British No 2, set up an intriguing second-round match against the top seed, Alexander Zverev, after he recovered from a set down to defeat Dino Prizmic 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. Norrie, who missed out on being seeded by one ranking spot, has begun to find his form during the hard court swing after a rib injury hurt his momentum during the clay and grass court seasons. His meeting on Saturday with the French Open champion will provide him with a clear measure of his level.Explore more on these topicsJack DraperTennisnewsShareReuse this content
