title: Carrick rules out £100m signing for Manchester United as Rashford rejoins squad | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick has stated that Manchester United will not make a £100m signing due to finances as Marcus Rashford joined up with the squad again
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Michael Carrick has stated that Manchester United will not make a £100m signing due to finances as Marcus Rashford joined up with the squad again
Content: Marcus Rashford did not play for Manchester United in their friendly against Leeds.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarcus Rashford did not play for Manchester United in their friendly against Leeds.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedCarrick rules out £100m signing for Manchester United as Rashford rejoins squadUnited unable to financially compete with rivalsRashford back after Barcelona loan but could leaveJamie Jacksonin County KildareThu 13 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick has stated thatManchester Unitedwill not make a £100m signing this summer due to their finances, with the manager also insisting that Marcus Rashford “is our player” despite the forward and club preferring him to depart.In the current window United have invested a total of £85mon Youri Tielemansand Andrey Santos but have never spent £100m on a single transfer.Chelsea set Friday deadline for Fernández suitors as City reject new £51m Barça bid for RodriRead moreThis is in contrast to Manchester City, Tottenham, Liverpool, Arsenal, and Chelsea, the rest of the traditional big six, who have all spent £100m-plus on a player in recent years.Carrick was asked how United can compete. “Money’s money. I get that,” said the manager. “It’s still about football and that’s where the competition lies. What we feel naturally as a group is to try and win games. So there’s a lot that goes into that, but certainly the situation is what it is as well, whether that’s finances or whatever.”Carrick guided United to third last season and was asked why the money from Champions League qualification cannot be invested in expensive elite players.“To be honest, I haven’t got the answers for that. We’re working with pushing everything that we can to make the best of it,” he said. “For now, we’ve got to make the most of it, push everything in every boundary that we can to be able to win again, basically.”Quick GuideTielemans apologises for offending Villa fans with United boastShowYouri Tielemans has apologised to Aston Villa after saying he joined Manchester United because they are a bigger club than his former team.Tielemans made a £35m move to Old Trafford in July, when United triggered a release clause in his Villa contract. The Belgium midfielder helped Villa end their 30-year trophy drought by winning the Europa League last season, but Tielemans had no qualms about joining United, who finished one spot above fourth-placed Villa in the Premier League last season."There are clubs above Villa, and Manchester United is one of them," he said on Wednesday – before taking to social media on Thursday to make peace with his former club."Never meant for my words in the press yesterday to offend anyone or the institution of Aston Villa Football Club, which I massively respect and I’m grateful for the past three years," the 29-year-old wrote on Instagram."I must however admit my mistake and apologise for my choice of words, will be more careful in the future. Wishing the club the best in the future."AFPWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The 45-year-old was asked whether United can win the title without any players worth £100m or more in the squad.Carrick said: “A little bit depends on what position that is and what you’ve got and the dynamics you need at certain points. Sometimes you do need that if it’s the right player. Again, it’s not purely on money. Obviously over time we need to be pushing to look to enhance the squad. So, yeah, 100% we need to do that.“We’ve done really good business. So we’re delighted with that [but] we want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that, so that never stops.”View image in fullscreenYouri Tielemans, who arrived from Aston Villa, was one of United’s big summer signings.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesRashford joined the squad at their County Kildare training camp base on Sunday following a post-World Cup break. The 28-year-old has been on loan the past season and a half at Barcelona and Aston Villa respectively, due to a breakdown in his relationship with the club’s executive and the former United head coach Ruben Amorim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRelations have eased andRashford is focused on workingunder Carrick, though the player’s preference is to depart. The club want the same as they seek to reduce the wage bill. The forward’s final two years of his deal are worth £35m.Disney+ secures rights to Gary Neville’s Overlap content in riposte to Lineker’s Netflix dealRead moreCarrick was asked if Rashford will stay beyond the 1 September deadline. “He’s our player and has trained really well,” said Carrick. “It’s been good to have him around the group again.”The manager was asked if he wants Rashford to remain. “He’s a very good player, Marcus, and if you’re going to have a career over 10 or 15 years, there’s going to be times when things go in a direction and maybe a different direction. All right, that happens,” he said. “There’s ups and downs, and that doesn’t judge you as a one-off kind of [state]. It’s what happens over time, and now we’re in a positive place as a group, and Marcus can offer us so much. He has done, and he can do again, so it’s quite exciting.”Asked if Carrick views Rashford as not for sale, he said: “No, he’s our player and he gives something a little bit different in the group.”Harry Maguire, Noussair Mazraoui and Tielemans have all indicated United can win the title. “We’ve definitely got the potential to achieve something really special,” said Carrick. “I’m not hiding from the fact, and we should aim to do that, but I can’t give you a definite answer on that – it’s certainly what we’re pushing to do because that’s the club we are.”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMarcus RashfordMichael CarricknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Absolutely unacceptable’: Japan condemns visit by Vladimir Putin to disputed Kuril Islands | Japan | The Guardian
description: Japanese PM says islands seized by Soviets late in second world war are part of her country under international law
Author: Gavin Blair
Headline: Japanese PM says islands seized by Soviets late in second world war are part of her country under international law
Content: Vladimir Putin at a fish processing plant on the disputed Kuril Islands.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/ReutersView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin at a fish processing plant on the disputed Kuril Islands.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/ReutersJapan‘Absolutely unacceptable’: Japan condemns visit by Vladimir Putin to disputed Kuril IslandsJapanese PM says islands seized by Soviets late in second world war are part of her country under international lawGavin Blairin TokyoThu 13 Aug 2026 08.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Japanese government has reacted angrily to Vladimir Putin’s first visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, which are claimed by both Tokyo and Moscow.Japan’s foreign minister, Toshimitsu Motegi, summoned the Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev, while the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, called Putin’s actions “absolutely unacceptable”.Known inJapanas the Northern Territories and by Russia as the Southern Kurils, the islands were seized by the then Soviet Union in the closing stages of the second world war and have been a source of contention ever since.The Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945 as Tokyo was about to surrender, and the dispute has prevented the two nations from signing a formal peace treaty.View image in fullscreenPutin visits a hospital.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL/EPATakaichi told reporters in Tokyo that the islands, which are just off Hokkaido, were “both historically and under international law” a part of Japan and called the visit by the Russian leader “incompatible with Japan’s consistent position” on the territory.Japanese television showed footage of Putin on the island of Etorofu, or Iturup in Russian, visiting a hospital, meeting residents and trying caviar at a processing plant, as well as comments condemning the visit by former Japanese residents who were deported when Russia took control of the islands.About 17,000 Japanese formerly lived on the islands, which today are occupied by about 20,000 Russian citizens.As well as its strategic significance, the island chain – consisting of Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group – provides access to rich fishing grounds and valuable mineral deposits.On Wednesday, Putin travelled to the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where he inspected navy drills and declared that the four disputed islands were recognised as Russian in international documents.Shinzo Abe, the late Japanese prime minister, had reached an entente with Putin over the territory, with visits by Japanese citizens to family graves resuming and talk of a future peace treaty. However, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine prompted Japan to impose sanctions on personnel and entities linked to Moscow, souring bilateral relations.The Russian president acknowledged Abe’s actions in his remarks on Wednesday and went to call the recent sanctions “unprovoked”. He said: “Japan has identified Russia as a major source of threats. I would like to point out that we are not threatening Japan. On the contrary, it has territorial claims against our country.”Though it is Putin’s first visit to the islands, Dmitry Medvedev went to Kunashiri in 2010 when he was president. Medvedev was widely seen as loyal to Putin, who was prime minister at the time.Explore more on these topicsJapanRussiaVladimir PutinAsia PacificEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: BAE Systems to pay $36m penalty after 104 violations of US arms export rules | BAE Systems | The Guardian
description: State department says it has reached administrative settlement with company’s US arm to resolve breaches
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: State department says it has reached administrative settlement with company’s US arm to resolve breaches
Content: BAE Systems unveils its unmanned fighter aircraft Brontanax in July. BAE voluntarily disclosed all but one of the alleged violations by its US arm.Photograph: Sarah Young/ReutersView image in fullscreenBAE Systems unveils its unmanned fighter aircraft Brontanax in July. BAE voluntarily disclosed all but one of the alleged violations by its US arm.Photograph: Sarah Young/ReutersBAE SystemsBAE Systems to pay $36m penalty after 104 violations of US arms export rulesState departmentsays it has reached administrative settlement with company’s US arm to resolve breachesGraeme WeardenThu 13 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK defence company BAE Systems is to pay a $36m (£26.7m) civil penalty after breachingUS arms exports regulationsmore than 100 times.The US Department of State announcedon Thursday that it had reached an administrative settlement with the US arm of BAE to resolve 104 violations of the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations.The breaches included the unauthorised exports of technical data to multiple countries, including China, and violations of directorate of defense trade controls authorisations involving various countries.BAE voluntarily disclosed all but one of the alleged violations, which helped it avoid a higher penalty. It also persuaded the state department to suspend half of the penalty, on the condition that the $18m was used to strengthen BAE’s compliance programme.BAE Systems said it remained committed to ensuring full compliance with all applicable export control laws, and had “thoroughly cooperated” with the state department’s review.“We have been working diligently to implement improvements to our BAE Systems Inc compliance programme over the last several years, and we will continue to do so. We take seriously our responsibility to protect critical information and support all our customers’ security,” the company added.The state department said the settlement highlighted “the importance of exporting defence articles pursuant only to appropriate authorisation from the department”.BAE was accused of sending technical data related to printed wiring boards for use in global positioning system (GPS) to a manufacturer in China in December 2023. According to the state department, the company “recognised its supply chain team did not fully understand the export control and compliance regulations” and that its secure file transfer networks did not highlight export control warnings before the data was sent.The company also sent data related to printed wiring boards for use with military GPS to Canada in September 2021, after a licence agreement had expired, and the technical specification of an “explosive mixture” to the UK. In another breach, technical data related to a US navy guided-missile destroyer were sent to Germany.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA BAE subcontractor also “furnished defence services without authorisation” on more than 17 separate occasions in Italy and France, and also in Indonesia, according to the state department.The company also accidentally exported without authorization a control system for a military gas-turbine engine to Switzerland.Explore more on these topicsBAE SystemsArms tradeInternational tradeManufacturing sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Fake sex worker and accomplice jailed for fatally spiking men’s drinks | UK news | The Guardian
description: Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru from Essex jailed for 17 years for drugging four men to steal from them, two of whom died
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru from Essex jailed for 17 years for drugging four men to steal from them, two of whom died
Content: Madalin Dumitru, left, and Adina Mihai pleaded guilty to manslaughter after targeting men who had been seeking sexual services.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenMadalin Dumitru, left, and Adina Mihai pleaded guilty to manslaughter after targeting men who had been seeking sexual services.Photograph: PAUK newsFake sex worker and accomplice jailed for fatally spiking men’s drinksAdina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru from Essex jailed for 17 years for drugging  four men to steal from them, two of whom diedSteven MorrisThu 13 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman who posed as a sex worker and administered a deadly amount of sedative to two men has been jailed for 17 years, along with her accomplice.Adina Mihai, 31, and her partner Madalin Dumitru, 30, who arranged for her to meet men at their homes, drugged their victims to steal from them.She spiked the glasses of wine of four men with the sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL). Two,Malcolm King, 80, of Gloucestershire, and Gary Mouat, 36, of Oxfordshire, died.Jailing Mihai and Dumitru, from Ilford, Essex, atOxfordcrown court, Mrs Justice Brunner said: “Your intention was to incapacitate each victim making them deeply unconscious.“The administration of the drug was haphazard and depended on the strength of each batch, the amount put into drinks, and the amount they drunk.“If you had stopped for a moment to consider the risks, as you should have done, you would have realised that it carried a high risk of serious injury or death at the very moment you administered that drug. If you had done the most cursory research, you would know that GBL can be extremely toxic.”The pair pleaded guilty to two charges of manslaughter and to administering poison to the two survivors, who cannot be identified.Julian Evans KC, prosecuting, said: “While Dumitru waited nearby, Mihai would enter the victim’s home. There, she would persuade the victim to drink alcohol laced with GBL.“Once the victim was unconscious, Mihai would look for property to steal. Then she would rejoin Dumitru, leaving the victim alone and unconscious.”No sexual services were provided but the pair worked on the premise that victims would not report what had happened to the police out of embarrassment.The court heard Mihai advertised online and the couple would take cash deposits before meeting the men. When their victims fell unconscious, she would steal watches, jewellery, aftershave and cash.In a victim personal statement, Mouat’s son, aged eight, said the defendants had ruined his life.He asked the couple: “Why did you have to kill my dad, you could have just taken the money, he was really kind, he would have given it to you.“He was my dad and now he’s gone. I miss him every day and will never get to see him again. I will never be able to get another dad and that makes me feel so sad. You have ruined my life and all the plans we had to do things together. My family is destroyed now.”King’s daughter, Caroline, said: “When my father was killed, the defendants did not only end his future. They stole mine as well.”His younger sister, Jacky Seagroatt, said: “What haunts me every day is the way he died. I might have been able to come to terms with losing my brother if he had died naturally or as the result of a tragic accident. I cannot stop imagining what he went through or how frightened he may have been.”Charles White, the senior crown prosecutor with the CPS, described the case as “unique”.No other deaths, poisonings or thefts have been linked to the pair but police are keeping an open mind about the possibility of other victims.Explore more on these topicsUK newsCrimeEssexDrugsOxfordShareReuse this content

title: Israeli troops force families from homes amid settler terror campaign in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Former PM of Israel calls events ‘concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing’ against Palestinians
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Former PM of Israel calls events ‘concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing’ against Palestinians
Content: The Israeli army entered Qusra after days of a settler siege on Palestinian homes in the area.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Israeli army entered Qusra after days of a settler siege on Palestinian homes in the area.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAWest BankIsraeli troops force families from homes amid settler terror campaign in West BankFormer PM of Israel calls events ‘concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing’ against PalestiniansEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemThu 13 Aug 2026 14.54 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli troops have forced two Palestinian families to leave their besiegedWest Bankhomes, the day after a top Israeli commander personally promised he would end a violent settler campaign to drive them out.Israeli soldiers also took over eight other homes in Qusra early on Thursday, telling the village’s mayor, Abdul Azim Wadi, that the buildings were needed for a days-long operation to remove the settlers. They later relinquished six. Settlers still roam the village.The Palestinians’ ordeal began on Sunday when Israeli settlers and soldiers set up a tent blocking the entrance to three homes on the edge of the village. They severed water and electricity supplies and prevented an ambulance from reaching a sick toddler.Amid mounting international pressure over the siege, Maj Gen Avi Bluth, who commands all Israeli troops in the occupied West Bank, visited Qusra on Wednesday to meet the trapped Palestinians andcommittedto “evacuate” the settlers from the village.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers stand guard next to settlers in front of Palestinian houses in the village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/GettyBluth’s troops later removed the tent but left the militants, their bedding and other equipment. Soldiers retreated after a failed attempt to drive out the Israeli settler group with riot control techniques. The siege continued into a fifth day on Thursday, with the impact on the village only expanding after Bluth’s visit.“The army arrived at around 10am and asked us to evacuate the houses because of a military operation in the area that would last for three days. We refused to leave,” said Qusai Ridi, one of the besieged Palestinians. “The army then moved us all into one house.”He was allowed to return home in the afternoon, where he found Israeli soldiers had damaged a security camera system and stolen some equipment. They are still occupying the home of his neighbour Yousef Hassan, who is staying with Ridi.Settlers are still patrolling outside in the area where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh waskilledby a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault.“I am afraid and do not trust that the army will actually evacuate the settlers. But I sincerely hope they do,” Ridi said.View image in fullscreenCritics in Israel say a lack of will on the part of soldiers in Qusra has led to the siege continuing.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyHis brother is an American citizen, and the US ambassador to Israel,Mike Huckabee, who is generally supportive of Israel’s settlement project, described the siege as a “horrific act of terror” carried out by Israeli terrorists.On Thursday afternoon, Israeli soldiers left six homes they had taken over in the morning. The returning Palestinian families reported damage including a Qur’an with pages torn out and destroyed decorations.Israel’s former prime ministerEhud Olmertsaid the siege was a “concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing”, which left him disgusted and ashamed.“These are crimes against humanity which are actively supported by the Israeli government and are assisted by the indifference and total lack of action by the IDF and the Israeli police. It’s unforgettable and unforgivable.”The same terrortacticswere used to force another Palestinian family out of their home in the neighbouring village of Jalud in July. Soldiers and settlers were filmed playing with a football together on the terrace of that house on Thursday.An Israeli military spokesperson said soldiers had been ordered not to displace Palestinian residents of Qusra and would not operate inside the besieged homes.“The soldiers were instructed that the Qusra residents will remain in their homes,” the military said in a statement. The spokesperson declined to comment on why those orders were being violated.The chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), Eyal Zamir, has ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank. Domestic critics said the army’s failures in Qusra were more the result of a lack of will than shortage of forces.Abandoned by the US: Palestinian Americans trapped in a surge of Israeli settler violenceRead more“Yesterday’s events in Qusra illustrate the impotence of the IDF, the police, the GSS [Shin Bet] and other security organizations in the face of a group of bullies,” the commentator Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Israeli newspaper Ma’ariv.“Instead of bringing a police van [and] arresting the criminals … [security forces] have been trying to negotiate with them. They are thugs. They believe themselves to be the lords of the land.”Israeli militants target Palestinians with neartotal impunityin the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only oneindictmentover those deaths.Violence isdeployedas part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, the rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes.Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineMike HuckabeeEhud OlmertnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fossils show huge carbon emissions harm forests, not ‘green the planet’ | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Study of 56m-year-old leaves counters claims from Trump administration members of ‘benefits’ of fossil fuel pollution
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Study of 56m-year-old leaves counters claims from Trump administration members of ‘benefits’ of fossil fuel pollution
Content: Dead trees near Mammoth Lakes, California, in 2022.Photograph: David McNew/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDead trees near Mammoth Lakes, California, in 2022.Photograph: David McNew/Getty ImagesClimate crisisFossils show huge carbon emissions harm forests, not ‘green the planet’Study of 56m-year-old leaves counters claims from Trump administration members of ‘benefits’ of fossil fuel pollutionOliver MilmanThu 13 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdding huge quantities of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere is set to cause the Earth’s forests to wither and die rather than flourish, according to a new study that counters erroneous claims that fossil fuel pollution will green the planet.An analysis of fossilized leaf cells from a period known as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (or PETM), which occurred about 56m years ago, has helped reconstruct how the world’s forests responded when planet-heating gases were previously being released at a rapid rate.The current galloping pace of carbon emissions from the burning of fossil fuels is unmatched in historic and prehistoric records but the PETM, when huge amounts of carbon were released over a 130,000-year period and the worldheated upby as much as 8C (14F), is the closest comparison.The authors of the new paper found this prehistoric change caused a retreat in the forests that blanketed the Paleocene-Eocene world, causing them to die off as the Earth browned rather than greened, a finding they state has “chilling implications” for today’s world.View image in fullscreenFragments of fossilized leaves like these helped the authors re-create the forest canopies of 56m years ago.Photograph: Dr Regan Dunn“What we see is that as the carbon dioxide ramped up, the forests became very dense but then subsequently collapsed, opening up dramatically,” said Regan Dunn, a researcher at La Brea Tar Pits and the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, who led the study.“Around 60% of the biomass of the standing vegetation was gone; it was a huge loss. This should be a concern because the rate of carbon release has never been higher than now.”Dun added: “Forests are some of our best friends and allies but we are already seeing them die back, be cut down and consumed by wildfires. It’s happening quickly; every summer the change seems faster and faster.”Trees may store less planet-heating carbon than hoped, study suggestsRead morePlants like trees require carbon to build their structures and, along with water and sunlight, provide food. Once the world started to burn coal, oil and gas in huge volumes from the industrial revolution onwards, the amount of emitted carbon dioxide surged at an unprecedented rate, with atmospheric concentrations of CO2risingby more than 50% in little over a century.This increase in carbon did initially helpboostsome plant life, a change that has been seized upon by those who question the facts of climate science. Prominent figures in Donald Trump’s administration have argued that burning fossil fuels is good for the environment.“CO2was never a pollutant,” Doug Burgum, the interior secretary,toldFox Business earlier this year as the federal governmentmoved to eraseits own power to address the climate crisis. “When we breathe, we emit CO2. Plants need CO2to survive and grow. They thrive with more CO2.”On the same TV network last year, Chris Wright, Trump’s energy secretary,saidthat there were “pluses” to global heating as well as negatives. “A warmer planet with more CO2is better for growing plants,” Wright claimed.View image in fullscreenThe authors compared the cuticle structure of modern leaves (pictured above under epifluorescence microscopy) with fossil leaf cuticles to create a model for canopy cover. Scale bar is 50 microns (0.05 mm).Photograph: Dr Regan DunnExperts have previouslyrejectedsuch claims as false, with the new research paper, published in Science, showing that the Earth’s past experience demonstrates that trees require much more than CO2to thrive.Extra carbon dioxide traps more heat, causing trees to struggle amid extreme temperatures and a lack of key nutrients. Hotter conditions can also trigger outbreaks of pests and disease, weakening trees further, and dry out vegetation that then explodes into huge wildfires, such as those that haveengulfedmuch of Canada and western Europe this summer.The switch from greening forests to browning forests occurred around 2000, the new paper states, when the impacts of drought and heat stress overtook the benefits of extra CO2. Since then, evidence haspiledupof escalating global tree mortality, including trees in the tropicsdyingof dehydration.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Once the climate becomes too warm, plants aren’t able to handle it; it affects their physiology and their relationship with water,” said Dunn. “Once they can’t survive because the CO2and temperatures are too high, that’s when you see forests die back.”There was “quite a lot of tree mortality” now occurring in Europe, North America and the Amazon, Dunn said, requiring swift cuts to carbon emissions to ensure that the world doesn’t barrel down the same path as it did 56m years ago.“There is still time to prevent the worst outcomes and best thing we can do is keep fossil fuels in the ground,” she said. “It’s important for people to understand that once we pass thresholds it takes a long time to recover from them. The 130,000 years of the PETM change on human timescales is basically forever.”Dunn and her colleagues ascertained the extent of ancient forests by analyzing fossilized cells of leaves called leaf cuticle fragments. This enabled them to determine the density of the forest canopy during the PETM, allowing them to calculate the advance and retreat of forests over time.View image in fullscreenThe field crew excavating a trench through PETM strata in the Hanna Basin, Wyoming.Photograph: Marieke Dechesne, USGSIn that past era, forests covered a much larger extent of the world than now, with no ice at the poles and much higher seas than today. But while the PETM changes occurred over many thousands of years via carbon released by the natural forces of volcanic activity, current climate change is much faster and caused by our deliberate combustion of fossil fuels.The paper is a “genuine advance” and provides a record over tens of thousands of years that shows the knock-on impacts of thinning forests, according to Trevor Keenan, a scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the new research.“The headline is that warming won,” Keenan said. “Carbon dioxide rose sharply, and any benefit that gave the forests was not enough to stop canopies from opening up and staying open for tens of thousands of years.”This is worrying because the pace of change today, he added. “The ancient carbon release happened over thousands of years; ours is happening over decades,” he said. “Faster forcing gives ecosystems less room to adjust.“Second, those forests faced climate change alone. Today’s forests are dealing with the same warming while also being fragmented, logged, converted to agriculture and exposed to altered fire regimes. If forests thinned under the slower and cleaner version of this experiment, that is not a reassuring precedent.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisTrees and forestsGreenhouse gas emissionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wing and a prayer: how probiotics might save bat species from a killer fungus | Global development | The Guardian
description: Bat experts were shocked at how fast white-nose syndrome had spread to Canada’s northernmost colonies from the US. Now, the race is on to find a cure before species disappear
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bat experts were shocked at how fast white-nose syndrome had spread to Canada’s northernmost colonies from the US. Now, the race is on to find a cure before species disappear
Content: Jesika Reimer holds a bat in Katmai, Alaska. For 20 years, white-nose syndrome has swept across North America, killing at least 6.7m bats. Now, scientists hope a ‘probiotic cocktail’ developed from the microbiome on bats’ wings may give vulnerable species a ‘fighting chance’ against the disease.Photograph: Michael CodeView image in fullscreenJesika Reimer holds a bat in Katmai, Alaska. For 20 years, white-nose syndrome has swept across North America, killing at least 6.7m bats. Now, scientists hope a ‘probiotic cocktail’ developed from the microbiome on bats’ wings may give vulnerable species a ‘fighting chance’ against the disease.Photograph: Michael CodeThe age of extinctionGlobal developmentWing and a prayer: how probiotics might save bat species from a killer fungusBat experts were shocked at how fast white-nose syndrome had spread to Canada’s northernmost colonies from the US. Now, the race is on to find a cure before species disappearThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentTrina MoylesThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCrawling through a narrow passage in a cave beneath a boreal forest near Fort Smith in Canada’s Northwest Territories in May, two biologists spotted a lifeless bat on a limestone ledge, its body covered in a spindly white fungus.When they shone their headlamps to get a closer look, they saw another bat with the fungus on its forearms. “It hissed at us and crawled back into a crack,” Jesika Reimer says.For Reimer, an ecologist specialising in bat populations in northern Canada and Alaska, there was little doubt. For 20 years, white-nose syndrome, a lethal disease caused by the fungusPseudogymnoascus destructans(known as Pd), has swept west across North America, spreading from bat to bat and cave to cave,killing more than 6.7 million bats.The fungus attacks their face, wings and arms while they are hibernating. They stir from rest and groom themselves, burning through the fat and energy reserves they need to survive the winter, and eventually die from dehydration or starvation. Smaller bats with lesser fat reserves are particularly at risk.View image in fullscreenJesika Reimer frees a bat from a net in Alaska’s Katmai national park.Photograph: Michael CodeNow it had reached Fort Smith, a town about 450 miles (725km) south of the Arctic Circle. “For 20 years, we’ve been tracking the spread of white-nose syndrome across the continent,” says Reimer’s colleague, Joanna Wilson, a biologist for the Northwest Territories government. “We always knew it would eventually get here.”Even so, the biologists were shocked by what they saw. They had hoped to do a baseline survey of healthy, stable populations before the fungus arrived. In 2025,white-nose syndromehad been discovered in a cave in Fort McKay, Alberta, nearly 200 miles south. “We thought we’d have a year or two,” Reimer says.View image in fullscreenA brown bat with white-nose syndrome in New York. The disease has moved north with a speed that has alarmed scientists in Canada.Photograph: Ryan von Linden/APNow the fungus has reached the northernmost-known hibernaculum, where bats shelter during the North American winter, it has raised urgent questions about its potential impact on bat populations in Canada andAlaska, Reimer says.The caves near Fort Smith were first discovered in 2010, when a wildlife technician flying over the area noticed a distinctive karst feature below. A karst landscape is formed when bedrock such as limestone or dolomite dissolves, forming underground caves and sinkholes that provide an ideal habitat for wintering bats. The technician later hiked back on foot and confirmed it was, indeed, a hibernaculum. Two additional caves were found in the region.View image in fullscreenThe bat caves near Fort Smith, in Canada’s Northwest Territories.Photograph: Jesika ReimerUntil then, biologists had not known where the Northwest Territories’ hibernating bat species – including little brown bats (Myotis lucifugus), big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) and northern long-eared bats (Myotis septentrionalis) – were spending the winter.They had located summer colonies, or roosts, which tipped them off that bats were sticking around through the winter months, but they did not know where or in what numbers. The 11-chambered cave shelters an estimated 3,000 bats, making it the largest hibernaculum in western Canada. It has been key to understanding the behaviour of northern bats.In 2011, Reimer focused her postgraduate research on the cave to discover how bats survived at such an extreme northern latitude, where the summer months are cooler, shorter and the sun hardly sets. She found that northern bats had to adapt to survive, such as taking more risks than their southern counterparts, flying at dusk instead of in true darkness to forage for mosquitoes and moths, and eating more orb-weaver spiders –higher in energy content – to keep fuel levels up.But no matter their adaptive abilities, smaller species of bats, such aslittle brownandnorthern long-eared myotisbats, are particularly susceptible to white-nose syndrome. Both are listed as species of special concern in the Northwest Territories. Since the fungus arrived in New York state in 2007 – thought to have been brought over from Europe on the shoes of a caver – ithas killed 90% of little brownand99% of northern long-eared myotisbats in the caves where it has spread.Some little brown populations are slowly rebounding, Reimer points out. They are genetically adapting their metabolic rates to burn less fat and withstand infection.View image in fullscreenBats illuminated by scientists’ headlamps in a hibernaculum in Canada’s Northwest Territories.Photograph: Julie Thomas/Jesika ReimerHowever, there is a less hopeful prognosis for the northern long-eared myotis, a species that weighs just 6-9g, and lacks the fat and energy reserves to outlast white-nose syndrome through the winter. “If it hits them as hard as it has elsewhere in their range, we can expect them to completely disappear from the ecosystem,” Reimer says.In May, Reimer and Wilson led research efforts to capture bats outside the cave entrance using lightweight mist nets, documenting little browns and northern long-eared myotis with white fungus “riddling the wing membranes”, Reimer says, adding that there were clear signs of necrosis, when living tissue dies. They also used a UV light to scan for orange fluorescence on their wings, which indicates Pd.They witnessed other unusual behaviours, too, including bats flying outside the cave in daylight. “That can be a sign of bats that are sick, or trying to recover,” Wilson says.One of their colleagues discovered an infected bat, badly dehydrated, at a nearby lake. “It couldn’t fly,” Reimer says. When they examined its wings they found they were as “brittle as tissue paper”, she says. They gave the bat food and water, though they think it probably died later.View image in fullscreenSigns of necrosis in a bat’s wing caused by white-nose fungus.Photograph: Jesika ReimerWhile laboratory tests recently came back positive for white-nose syndrome, Reimer and Wilson were relieved that they did not see the same mass die-offs as documented in large caves in the south, including most recently in Alberta’s Rocky Mountains. They are not sure if it is because the fungus has only just arrived and has not yet become established, or if the cave’s sub-arctic latitude gives bats an adaptive edge.One factor could be the temperature of caves. While the fungus thrives at 10C (50F), Reimer says, the northern caves are much cooler. “Some of the chambers drop below freezing throughout the winter,” she says.And while Pd can still grow, it might not grow as quickly as it would in a warmer cave. That, says Wilson, gives researchers some “cautious hope”.“We might see different outcomes,” she says.And there is an additional reason for hope. Researchers are applying anexperimental “probiotic cocktail”, developed by scientists at Ontario’s McMaster University from samples taken from the microbiomes on bats’ wings, to the surface of summer roosts. The substance gets on to their body and spreads from bat to bat in much the same way that Pd spreads.It is thought that the probiotic – beneficial microbes that have anti-fungal properties – could improve the bats’ resilience to Pd infection by slowing its growth. Early field trials in British Columbia and Washington are yielding promising results: among Pd-infected bats, those with the highest amount of probiotic microbes had the least Pd.“We see it as a treatment option that has a very good chance of helping and very little chance of harm,” Wilson says.But further complicating the advance of white-nose syndrome is another big factor: wildfires. In 2023, large wildfires torched the trees surrounding the caves near Fort Smith. “It’s matchsticks. There is not a single piece of foliage to be found,” Reimer says.The loss of habitat forces bats to fly longer distances to find food, summer roosts in old decayed trees, and mates during the autumn breeding season.View image in fullscreenJesika Reimer releases a bat after taking samples for her research. Scientists hope a probiotic could improve bats’ resilience to Pd infection.Photograph: Michael CodeReimer also wonders if wildfires could have played a role in the rate at which the fungus spread, forcing bats from the Northwest Territories to move south and mix with Pd-infected bats – then bringing it back to the northernmost caves.For now, there are more questions than answers, including what mitigation measures biologists will take – and if they will choose to mitigate at all, says Reimer. While the little brown bats may be able to bounce back on their own, interventions could give the northern long-eared myotis a “fighting chance” to survive and adapt, she adds.Nothing more will be known until next spring, when Reimer and Wilson return to the caves to see how the bats have fared – and to search for more answers.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentThe age of extinctionWildlifeConservationCanadaAmericasAnimalsBiologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How our food became so dependent on oil | Cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: The oil and gas industry is far more integrated in food production than many of us realise. Josh Toussaint-Strauss looks at the processes for meat, processed staples and fruit and vegetables
Author: Alex Healey
Headline: The oil and gas industry is far more integrated in food production than many of us realise. Josh Toussaint-Strauss looks at the processes for meat, processed staples and fruit and vegetables
Content: 6:20It's complicatedCost of living crisisHow our food became so dependent on oilGlobal food prices have hit their highest level in over three years. We are told this is due to rising oil and energy costs, but how exactly do they affect prices? The most reported reason is that transport and fertiliser are to blame, but the reality is that the oil and gas industry is far more integrated in our food production than many of us realise. To get a better understanding, Josh Toussaint-Strauss takes a closer look at the production processes of three categories of food: meat, processed staples and fruit and vegetables. What he discovers is a level of involvement that is shockingJosh Toussaint-Strauss,Alex Healey,Sarah Verrall,Ali AssafandRyan BaxterThu 13 Aug 2026 06.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 09.39 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsCost of living crisisIt's complicatedAgricultureFarmingFood & drink industryOil and gas companiesEnergy industryFood

title: India fuels worldwide jump in planned coal production  | Coal | The Guardian
description: Rise in new mine proposals, mainly in states of Odisha and Jharkhand, comes despite plateau in global demand
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Rise in new mine proposals, mainly in states of Odisha and Jharkhand, comes despite plateau in global demand
Content: Coal is loaded into a truck at an open-cast mine near Dhanbad, India. The country plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes.Photograph: Altaf Qadri/APView image in fullscreenCoal is loaded into a truck at an open-cast mine near Dhanbad, India. The country plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes.Photograph: Altaf Qadri/APCoalIndia fuels worldwide jump in planned coal productionRise in new mine proposals, mainly in states of Odisha and Jharkhand, comes despite plateau in global demandJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.The Guardian view on India’s green growth gamble: it will need more than private finance | EditorialRead moreIndia plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth andcontend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour ofrenewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the GlobalEnergyMonitor’s latest report.It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWind and solar power surpassed coal generation in the global electricity mix for the first time last year, according to aseparate report from energy thinktank Ember, in a “milestone moment” for climate action.China and India were largely responsible for the rise in renewables, according to the Ember report, while the US and Europe continued to rely more heavily on fossil fuels.Tiffany Means, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor and co-author of the report said: “The economic rationale for expanding coalmining becomes progressively weaker as low-cost clean energy continues to displace coal.“Rather than locking in decades of additional coal production, governments have an opportunity to cancel projects that remain in the development pipeline before they advance to construction.”Explore more on these topicsCoalEnergyIndiaFossil fuelsEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everyone is scared’: flood-hit Porto Alegre braces for another El Niño | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: Two years after southern Brazil’s worst climate disaster ravaged the city, and with poor areas still recovering, many fear official neglect has left them exposed once again
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two years after southern Brazil’s worst climate disaster ravaged the city, and with poor areas still recovering, many fear official neglect has left them exposed once again
Content: Devastation in Sarandi, Porto Alegre. In May 2024, flooding killed 183 people in the state of Rio Grande do Sul and displaced more than 600,000. All photographs by Alass DerivasView image in fullscreenDevastation in Sarandi, Porto Alegre. In May 2024, flooding killed 183 people in the state of Rio Grande do Sul and displaced more than 600,000. All photographs by Alass DerivasSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanEl Niño southern oscillation‘Everyone is scared’: flood-hit Porto Alegre braces for another El NiñoTwo years after southern Brazil’s worst climate disaster ravaged the city, and with poor areas still recovering, many fear official neglect has left them exposed once againSupported byAbout this contentAlass Derivas and Sara Van Horn in Porto Alegre, BrazilThu 13 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the backstreets of Porto Alegre, a state capital in southernBrazil, you can still see signs of the devastating flood that swept through the city two years ago: scattered debris, waterlogged homes and destroyed businesses.In May 2024,flooding killed 183 peoplein the state of Rio Grande do Sul and displacedmore than 600,000. The neighbourhood of Sarandi was one of thehardest-hit parts of Porto Alegre, with water levels reaching up to 5 metres above normal, completely submerging many of its streets.“Most people are still suffering the mental health consequences of the flood,” says Luís Rogério “Jamaika” Machado, a community leader in Sarandi.“They lost absolutely everything. Unable to rebuild their houses, most have become deeply depressed.”View image in fullscreenJamaika at the cultural centre in Quilombo dos Machado. His community provided food, clothing and medical assistance to thousands of families during the 2024 floodsLast month, meteorologists announced theimminent return of El Niño, the naturally occurring phenomenon caused by rising sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific but the effects of which aregreatly aggravated by the climate crisis. El Niño, which disrupts weather patterns across the globe, is likely to cause extreme rainfall and flooding in southern Brazil.Jamaika lives in an urbanquilombo, a Brazilian settlement founded by escaped enslaved people or their descendants. Quilombo dos Machado is one of 11 such territories in Porto Alegre and served as a centre of solidarity for the entire Sarandi area during the flood, distributing food, clothing and medical assistance to thousands of families.Now Porto Alegre’s flood-hit communities, though still recovering from one of Brazil’s deadliest climate disasters, face renewed threats from this year’s developing El Niño as incomplete flood defences and government relocation schemes fuel fears of displacement and deepen a climate justice crisis.View image in fullscreenA man walks through the rubble of destroyed homes in Sarandi, Porto Alegre, one of the worst affected nighbourhoods in the 2024 floodingSarandi, along with other poorer areas of the city, is one such example. Despite being among those who are the least responsible for the emissions that cause climate breakdown, people there experienced the worst effects of the 2024 flood.This imbalance has led the Porto Alegre research group at the Metropolis Observatory, part of Brazil’s National Institutes of Science and Technology (INCT), to call the flooda climate justice crisis.Now, these same people are bracing for yet another climate-induced disaster.The first storms caused by the latest El Niño arrived in Rio Grande do Sul last month, with rain and strong winds disrupting the region. Rising river levels affected at least 200municipalities, leaving 1,800 people homelessand many more outraged by the government’s inaction over the past two years.Map showing location of Rio Grande do Sul within Brazil and South America“El Niño peaks in December, January and February,” says Wilfran Moufouma-Okia, chief of climate prediction at World Meteorological Organization. “So we are just at the beginning.”For people in Porto Alegre, the headlines bring renewed fears.“Our house was completely submerged. We lost everything,” says Suelen Telles, a pre-school teacher who lives in Sarandi. “We’ve since returned to our house, and we’re terrified of losing everything again. Everyone on our street is scared.”View image in fullscreenSolange Rodrigues Correa, who lost her home in 2024 and has moved in with her grandsonAfter losing her house in 2024, Solange Rodrigues Correa moved in with her grandson in Ilha Grande dos Marinheiros, an archipelago on the margins of the city. News reports have caused her to worry about the flood waters returning, and Correa, who suffered a stroke due to the stress of the 2024 floods, has not slept for several nights in a row.“Once again, what will become of us?” she says.Rudimar Dal Asta, a priest in Ilha Grande dos Marinheiros and one of the community leaders who helped in rescue missions during the previous flood, says the government has given assurances that there is an evacuation plan, but they have not seen it yet. “Our escape route is to run to the bridge, just like we did in 2024,” he says.Over the past few months, Porto Alegre has repaired floodgates, replaced sewer covers, and rebuilt a section of the Sarandi dyke. Mayor Sebastião Melo announced that improvements to pumping stations – which were shut off in 2024 due to the risk of electric shock – would be completed by November.“We’ve finished many projects,” says Melo. “Others are now under construction, and others have yet to be started. Porto Alegre is now a much more protected city.”In the south of the city, however, the preparations remain makeshift: sandbags, movable barriers and floating pumps. Certain neighbourhoods, such as Ilha Grande dos Marinheiros, do not have adequate protective infrastructure and people are apprehensive.View image in fullscreenThe Sarandi dyke was damaged in 2024 and was partly rebuilt by the Porto Alegre authorities“The flood protection systems are still incomplete,” says Leonardo Bauer Maggi of the Movement of People Affected by Dams (MAB), a large grassroots social movement that supports the affected population.“They installed emergency sirens, but we don’t know where to run if they sound,” he says. “No shelters have been prepared.”The Porto Alegre administration isnow being suedfor the failures of the flood protection system in 2024. Last year, the state court of auditors revealed that a lack of investment and a series of otherfailures combined to weaken flood-protection measures in Porto Alegre.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAuditors held Melo, as well as the former mayor Nelson Marchezan Júnior, responsible for a “serious disregard for the duty of care”. The public prosecutors’ office has since sued the city of Porto Alegre for 50m reais (£7.3m) to reimburse 19 neighbourhoods affected by the flood.“We want to prepare for El Niño, but we still don’t know how,” says Jamaika. “When the water rises, the only alternative presented by the government is to leave the area in an emergency.”View image in fullscreenHundreds of people wait for help on a street above the flood waters in Porto Alegre in 2024Last month, the state government launchedPrepara RS, an emergency initiativeto assist policymakers, organise volunteers and provide public guidance about imminent storms to the people of Rio Grande do Sul. The initiative has transferred 32.3m reais to 138 municipalities across the state.In a statement praising the quality of its monitoring systems and its flood defences, the state government said: “In recent years, the government has been making progress in a series of structural, operational and strategic improvements to prepare the state to face extreme events, including possible negative effects of El Niño.”Yet the state government acknowledged that it had failed to predict the recent rise of river levels, which have now flooded cities across the region.A recent studyby the Celso Furtado International Centre for Development Policy and the Climate and Society Institute revealed that the state government had spentless than 0.5% of its climate budgeton mitigating future disasters.Maggi says the people most affected by the floods are working class, who had to borrow money to rebuild their homes. “The water receded, but the flood didn’t pass,” he says.View image in fullscreenWhile homes in Quilombo Kédi, a black area of Porto Alegre, were destroyed, new towers and a golf course are built around themAbouttwo-thirds of people affected in Rio Grande do Sulhad a family income at or below 5,000 reais (£730) a month, according to theBrazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics.Jamaika says nearly 7,000 families in his quilombo were affected by the flood – and 4,500 of them have not yet recovered, which he blames on a lack of government assistance.In 2024, the federal government distributed 5,100 reais of “reconstruction aid” to about 430,000 affected families, totalling 2.2bn reais,based on government data. But Jamaika says this aid was woefully inadequate for those in his community. “Rebuilding their lives becomes almost impossible. What house can you rebuild with 5,000 reais?”Many in Porto Alegre accuse the city and state governments of using floods to displace them. Betânia Alfonsin, a law professor and member of the Metropolis Observatory, says houses in flood-risk areas are demolished when people relocate and are often refurbished for wealthier owners who can afford risk mitigation.The classification of “risk area” is often used selectively, says Alfonsin. “It’s a stamp of expulsion for the poor.”View image in fullscreenCritics say houses are being built on cleared sites by wealthier owners when poor families are forced to relocateMost people in these areas are relocated through government programmes such asMy Home, My Life, which offers financing for new homes. However, people say the mortgage is burdensome. “They push My Home, My Life as a solution, which we call ‘My Debt’,” jokes Solange Correa. “You had a house – now you get a debt for life.”‘I’ve seen things no one should go through’: the overwhelming scale of loss in Brazil’s floodsRead moreAnother federal government housing programme, Assisted Purchase, gives 200,000 reais towards a new property. In Porto Alegre, 9,477 people applied, with 5,800 of those approved. After receiving funds, the old homes are demolished, leaving people remaining in rubble in neighbourhoods such as Ilha Grande dos Marinheiros and Sarandi, which resemble war zones.“This programme is problematic because it negotiates family by family rather than community,” says Alfonsin, who argues that it promotes the dispersal and destruction of communities.More than 50% of Assisted Purchase recipients bought homes in other cities. For Jamaika, the programme “is yet another expression of gentrification”.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanFloodingBrazilExtreme weatherAmericasClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Man, 102, dies after alleged assault in south Wales pub | Wales | The Guardian
description: Phillip Ormerod was taken to hospital after the incident in the Crow’s Nest in Cwmbran and later died of his injuries
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Phillip Ormerod was taken to hospital after the incident in the Crow’s Nest in Cwmbran and later died of his injuries
Content: The Crow’s Nest pub in Cwmbran, where the incident took place.Photograph: Google StreetviewView image in fullscreenThe Crow’s Nest pub in Cwmbran, where the incident took place.Photograph: Google StreetviewWalesMan, 102, dies after alleged assault in south Wales pubPhillip Ormerod was taken to hospital after the incident in the Crow’s Nest in Cwmbran and later died of his injuriesBethan McKernanThu 13 Aug 2026 09.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 102-year-old man has died of his injuries after allegedly being assaulted at a pub in south Wales.Phillip Ormerod, of Cwmbran in the Welsh valleys, was taken to hospital after the incident at the Crow’s Nest pub on 1 August. Gwent police said on Thursday that he had since died.A 56-year-old man from Llanelli was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm in connection with the case. He has been released but remains under investigation.The senior investigating officer, DCI Shelley Comley, said: “We understand the public interest in this incident but want to remind people that not only is this an active criminal investigation but there is a family at the heart of it processing the loss of a loved one.“Please consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments – particularly online commentary – could have on them and the ongoing investigation as a whole.”Emergency services were called to the Crow’s Nest at about 10.25pm on the night of the incident after Ormerod had fallen from a stage.According to reports, he had walked up three steps on to the stage where the Llanelli-based band SuperHans were playing to ask for the volume to be turned down when he was knocked over.Ormerod reportedly suffered critical injuries after falling backwards and hitting the floor.His son, Robert Ormerod, told the Press Association his father had lived in the Llanyrafon neighbourhood for decades and was a popular regular at the Crow’s Nest, where younger people would buy drinks for him.The great-grandfather was a draughtsman before he retired. He lived alone after the death of his wife 40 years ago and was recently diagnosed with dementia.Ormerod said: “I feel sad – even though he could be difficult because of his age and dementia, still, you get used to him being around. Even though I suppose he wouldn’t go on forever, he would’ve carried on I think for a bit.”Gwent police have appealed for anyone who was in the pub between 10pm and 11pm on the night of the incident to get in touch directly or via Crimestoppers.Explore more on these topicsWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Birmingham Four’ lawyers hope spycops inquiry will help reopen case | Criminal Cases Review Commission | The Guardian
description: Undercover officers working for West Midlands ‘special projects team’ planted evidence to convict men, lawyers claim
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Undercover officers working for West Midlands ‘special projects team’ planted evidence to convict men, lawyers claim
Content: From left: Tahir Aziz, Naweed Ali, Mohibur Rahman and Khobaib Hussain, who were arrested in 2017 and convicted of planning a terrorist attack.Photograph: West Midlands police/PAView image in fullscreenFrom left: Tahir Aziz, Naweed Ali, Mohibur Rahman and Khobaib Hussain, who were arrested in 2017 and convicted of planning a terrorist attack.Photograph: West Midlands police/PASpycops scandalCriminal Cases Review Commission‘Birmingham Four’ lawyers hope spycops inquiry will help reopen caseUndercover officers working for West Midlands ‘special projects team’ planted evidence to convict men, lawyers claimNeha GohilMidlands correspondentThu 13 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawyers representing four men convicted of terror offences are increasingly hopeful that revelations from the undercover policing inquiry could boost the chances of their case being reopened.Ten years ago, Khobaib Hussain, Naweed Ali, Mohibur Rahman and Tahir Aziz were arrested and later convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the UK after an elaborate covert police operation.As part of the undercover operation, police set up a fake delivery firm, Hero Couriers, to snare Hussain and Ali, who, like one of the other “Birmingham Four”, had a previous terror-related conviction.The investigation involved an undercover police officer working for theWest Midlands“special projects team” under the alias Vincent. On Ali’s first day working for Hero Couriers, MI5 officers discovered a bag under the seat containing a “partially constructed” pipe bomb, a suspected handgun and a meat cleaver with “kafir” scratched on to it.View image in fullscreenAn imitation handgun with an empty magazine strapped to it that was found in Naweed Ali’s car.Photograph: West Midlands police/PALawyers representing the Birmingham Four have long expressed their belief that Vincent planted the evidence in the vehicle – a claim ridiculed by the undercover police officer during the trial and rejected by the jury.The lawyers submitted an initial application to the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) to investigate the men’s convictionsin 2024and are still waiting for a response.Gareth Peirce, a lawyer known for successfully fighting miscarriage of justice cases, told the Guardian she had submitted further information to the CCRC earlier this year which included, but was not limited to, evidence heard at the undercover policing inquiry.The inquiry is examining the conduct of undercover police officers who spied on more than 1,000 political groupsbetween 1968 and at least 2010.View image in fullscreenA meat cleaver with ‘kafir’ scratched on to it that was also found under the seat of Naweed Ali’s vehicle.Photograph: West Midlands police/PAPeirce said the submission, although broad, cited evidence heard at the inquiry in November last year, where the managers of an undercover police officerbelieved he had concocted a gun plotto frame an animal rights activist. She said this incident had parallels with the Birmingham Four.She said: “The coincidences and parallels with the Birmingham Four prosecution evidence are exact – an undercover officer, with access to firearms, claims to stumble upon a plot by an individual he is spying on. Both cases rest on the improbable ‘discovery’ of firearms and other weaponry in cars recently driven by the activists.”Peirce said evidence heard during the undercover policing inquiry demonstrated the “easy ability of an undercover officer to fabricate evidence” as well as “how easy [it is] to rely on an organisational cover-up”.Hussain’s sister, Mariam, has been fighting for the group’s case to be reopened with the Muslim advocacy group Cage. She said: “We’re in a position now, unfortunately, where you’re having to spoon-feed and redirect the CCRC to ‘go look here, go do this’ because we’re not getting regular updates so we don’t really know what’s going on and how they’re investigating.”On Wednesday, Cage issued a joint statement signed by several organisations, including the miscarriage of justice charity Appeal and Muslim advocacy groups, calling for the CCRC to immediately review and reopen the case.Stephen Kamlish, who represented Ali during the 2017 trial, said the evidence presented during the trial showed his client was innocent, including the fact Ali had willingly given his car keys to Vincent.“I have no doubt at all that the defendants are innocent – all of them,” Kamlish said.Mariam said: “There was no evidence to point that this bag belonged to any of the four men that were convicted.”As the 10-year anniversary of their arrests approaches, Mariam said her brother continued to have many unanswered questions.She said: “It hasn’t ended for us. That pain, it’s every day. We’re living a nightmare every day. You feel so helpless. There’s not a moment where [you] can switch off and just get on with our lives as normal. It’s truly horrific.”A CCRC spokesperson said: “A review into these applications is ongoing. It would be inappropriate for us to discuss the case or make any further comment while the applications are being reviewed.”A West Midlands police spokesperson said: “In 2017, all four men were unanimously found guilty by a jury. In 2018, Judge Hon Mr Justice Openshaw rejected their leave to appeal, saying: ‘In my judgment there was abundant evidence of [Naweed Ali’s] extreme jihadist beliefs, to the effect that it was his duty to attack those whom he considered to be ‘unbelievers’ in this country.“‘The exchange of messages in the heavily encrypted‘three musketeers’ Telegram groupaccount and elsewhere were only explicable upon the basis that he was plotting an imminent attack. A partially made pipe bomb was found in his van. He answered no questions in interview and did not give evidence to give any explanation for the many incriminating pieces of evidence against him. In my judgment, the evidence against him was overwhelming; the conviction is safe and his application for leave to appeal against conviction is accordingly refused.’”The police spokesperson continued: “In 2018, a full court of appeal examined the safety of these convictions in great detail and upheld the findings of the jury, with Lord Justice Holroyde stating: ‘We have considered whether anything put before us casts doubt on the safety of the convictions. We are satisfied that there is nothing that does so. The jury by their verdicts plainly rejected that the evidence had been planted. Having done so there was ample circumstantial evidence against each of the accused to support the convictions.’”Explore more on these topicsCriminal Cases Review CommissionSpycops scandalUK criminal justicePoliceBirminghamWest MidlandsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nearly 100 children detained as adults under UK-France migration deal | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Figures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilities
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Figures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilities
Content: People thought to be migrants attempt to board a small boat off the coast of Neufchâtel-Hardelot, France, in July.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenPeople thought to be migrants attempt to board a small boat off the coast of Neufchâtel-Hardelot, France, in July.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAImmigration and asylumNearly 100 children detained as adults under UK-France migration dealFigures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilitiesRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 13 Aug 2026 14.13 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly 100 children have been wrongly identified and detained as adults under Shabana Mahmood’s “one in, one out” deal withFrance, the Guardian can disclose.Home Office staff said that of 304 age-disputed cases arising from the scheme over nine months, 94 (31%) – were ultimately found to be minors. Children are supposed to be excluded from the scheme, while government policy limits immigration detention of unaccompanied children to 24 hours.The figures have emerged in a letter sent to the Home Office minister Anna Turley from Jane Leech, the interim chair of independent monitoring boards (IMBs), which scrutinise prisons and immigration detention facilities.In the highly critical letter, Leech also said some people detained under the scheme:Had been awaiting deportation for more than six months, despite being supposed be held for up to 28 days only “in exceptional cases”.Were being readied for removal to France despite having TB or requiring hospital treatment.Faced removal after being separated from family members with whom they had travelled, which she said had a “particularly damaging impact”.French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since springRead moreThe “one in, one out” initiative, launched last August, allows the UK to send somepeople who arrive by small boat back to France while agreeing to take the same number of people from France if they are judged to have a legitimate claim.Leech said the deal was “placing highly vulnerable, newly arrived individuals, including children and survivors of abuse, in detention”.In the letter to Turley, she wrote: “Your officials have informed the IMB that 304 age disputes have taken place between 15 August 2025 and 1 May 2026, of which 94 (31%) were assessed to be children.“The IMB is therefore concerned that child safeguarding mechanisms are ineffective, and believes more should be done to ensure that those whose age is under dispute are not detained in the first place.”Leech criticised the length of time it took for officials to complete age assessments. “In two cases observed by the Heathrow Board, it took 40 days or more from arrival at the IRC [immigration removal centre]to age assessment,” she wrote.Referring to the deal as Operation Hillmore, its official name within the Home Office, Leech said she had “significant concerns” about the vulnerabilities of those detained under the scheme.She wrote: “Many of those who have recently arrived present as psychologically distressed, and Boards have observed records and heard testimonies showing that many are survivors of torture and abuse.”There was evidence of poor health screening at Manston among the Hillmore detainees, Leech wrote. “Gatwick IRC recently received one individual from Manston with tuberculosis, while a second was refused admission to Brook House because of the critical state of their health, and referred directly to hospital.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe said people were being held for lengthy periods despite the scheme being intended to operate at pace, with one man detained for 27 weeks.Government figures covering 4 August 2025 to 30 June 2026 show that1,087 people were returned to Franceunder the deal. During the same period, 27,920 people arrived in the UK on small boats.Imran Hussain, the executive director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, described the figures as “disturbing” and said they were the latest example of children being wrongly treated as adults by the Home Office.“Too often refugee children are being treated as adults and put into unsafe situations, at risk of abuse and neglect, and exposed to significant safeguarding risks,” he said.“We call on the government to prioritise professional assessments led by trained social workers, which has been found to be the most accurate way to determine age and therefore avoid these risks.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “Robust age assessments are essential to maintaining the integrity of our border and ensuring migrants receive appropriate safeguarding and access to services.“We will continue to strengthen and modernise this process, including through the rollout of cutting-edge AI technology from next year to support age assessment.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeFranceEuropeMigrationForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Italian businessman admits organising bomb attack ‘to boost friend’s security’ | Italy | The Guardian
description: Valter Lavitola has confessed to masterminding bombing at home of investigative reporter Sigfrido Ranucci
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Valter Lavitola has confessed to masterminding bombing at home of investigative reporter Sigfrido Ranucci
Content: The blast outside Sigfrido Ranucci’s home near Rome in October last year almost destroyed his car and another owned by his daughter.Photograph: Cecilia Fabiano/APView image in fullscreenThe blast outside Sigfrido Ranucci’s home near Rome in October last year almost destroyed his car and another owned by his daughter.Photograph: Cecilia Fabiano/APItalyItalian businessman admits organising bomb attack ‘to boost friend’s security’Valter Lavitola has confessed to masterminding bombing at home of investigative reporter Sigfrido RanucciAngela Giuffridain RomeThu 13 Aug 2026 09.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Italian businessman has admitted to masterminding a bomb attack at the home of Sigfrido Ranucci, a prominent investigative journalist, claiming it was intended to boost his security protection.Valter Lavitola, who was friends with Ranucci, the host of Report, an investigative programme aired by the state broadcaster, Rai, made the confession to investigators after his arrest earlier this week in connection with the case,the businessman’s lawyer, Sergio Cola, told the Italian media.It was originally thought that the mafia had been behind the attack in October last yearwhen a rudimentary but powerful bombwas detonated outside Ranucci’s home in a town near Rome, almost destroying his car and another owned by his daughter.Four other peopleallegedly commissioned by Lavitolawere arrested in late June on suspicion of carrying out the attack.Cola said Lavitola had orchestrated the attack in order to boost Ranucci’s security detail amid threats to his life from the mafia.“He did it for Ranucci’s good, because he was a target of attacks,” he said.View image in fullscreenSigfrido Ranucci.Photograph: Cecilia Fabiano/LaPresse/ShutterstockLativola denied allegations that the motive had been to enhance Ranucci’s popularity with the aim of him entering politics, something Lativola allegedly hoped to benefit from too.The allegations were outlined in an investigative report, seen by the Guardian, which included telephone conservations including one allegedly from Lavitola telling Ranucci “you will be prime minister in two years”.There has been no suggestion from investigators that Ranucci, who previously expressed shock over Lavitola’s alleged involvement, was aware of the plot.Ranucci, whose investigations for Report focus on alleged crime and corruption, often involving government ministers, is suing unnamed commentators and politicians who accused him of staging the attack for his own
