benefit for defamation.His lawyer, Roberto De Vita,said that if the allegations of Lavitola’s motivewere correct then Ranucci was “a victim three times over”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“He is a victim of a serious, dangerous attack, of betrayal, of being exploited by a friend in a delirious show of madness and, last but not least – and perhaps most seriously – of a massive and persistent campaign of media and political lynching that, through conjecture and insinuations, has sought to portray the victim as the more-or-less-willing beneficiary of the attack.”The case has unfolded amid a broader debate about press freedom inItalyand journalists’ safety.Ranucci has been outspoken about thealleged interference in Raiby Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government. The broadcaster opened an internal audit into his journalistic methods after it emerged in early July that Lavitola was being interrogated in connection with the bomb attack. The deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, has called for him to be suspended.There have been questions over Ranucci’s relationship with Lavitola, a former journalist who owns a restaurant in Rome. They became friends in 2019 after Ranucci conducted an investigation into Lavitola, who has been embroiled in several legal proceedings in the past, including one resulting in a conviction for extorting the late former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi.Ranucci told Corriere della Sella in early July that he had “never hidden” the friendship, describing it as perhaps a case of “Stockholm syndrome”.Explore more on these topicsItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever
Content: People in protective clothing lower the coffin of an Ebola victim into a grave in Bunia, Ituri province, on Tuesday.Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/APView image in fullscreenPeople in protective clothing lower the coffin of an Ebola victim into a grave in Bunia, Ituri province, on Tuesday.Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/APEbolaDRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth provinceMan dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest everRachel Savageand agenciesThu 13 Aug 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ebola outbreak in theDemocratic Republic of the Congohas spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago.The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in westAfrica, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data.Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said.There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak.The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace.Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded.The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming thatEbolais not real.Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials sayRead moreHealth workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months.The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February.Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate.Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”.Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months.Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time.This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in apaper published this weekin the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola.Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the viruscould be mutatingand that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate.Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.Explore more on these topicsEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaWorld Health OrganizationGlobal healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: French ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of women  | Central African Republic | The Guardian
description: Disciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residence
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Disciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residence
Content: Foucher, pictured in 2018 during his posting to Lebanon, has served as France’s ambassador to Central African Republic since 2023.Photograph: Wael Hamzeh/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFoucher, pictured in 2018 during his posting to Lebanon, has served as France’s ambassador to Central African Republic since 2023.Photograph: Wael Hamzeh/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockCentral African RepublicFrench ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of womenDisciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residenceAgence France-PresseThu 13 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance has opened disciplinary proceedings against its ambassador toCentral African Republicover allegations of misconduct, after claims he brought dozens of women into his official residence, raising potential security concerns.The investigation comes as Paris seeks to rebuild relations with CAR after their sharp deterioration in recent years amid Russia’s expanding influence in the former French colony.The French weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported that the ambassador, Bruno Foucher, 65, brought about 30 women between the ages of 20 and 30 into his residence during the period of January 2024 to March 2026, with some of them staying overnight. The visits prompted officials to report a security breach.The ambassador acknowledged having had sexual relations with two young women, the weekly said.The French foreign ministry said: “At the initiative of the ministry, an administrative investigation was carried out in Bangui in 2026. Upon receipt of the findings of this mission, and at the request of the minister, the ministry initiated disciplinary proceedings against the ambassador. These proceedings are ongoing.”The ministry conducted an on-site inspection in April, which led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings.Foucher is a career diplomat who has served as ambassador to CAR since 2023. He was ambassador to Lebanon from 2017 to 2020, to Iran from 2011 to 2016, and to Chad between 2006 and 2011.According to Le Canard enchaîné, which said it obtained the inspection report, the ambassador received about 15 visits a month.He also allegedly instructed staff to allow one of the young women to stay at the residence during his absence.Russia maintains a strong foothold in CAR, primarily through the Wagner paramilitary group, which plays a key role in providing security for the country’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra.French officials have accused Russians of fostering anti-French sentiment in a number of African countries.The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, praised the “complete restoration of relations” betweenFranceand CAR when he visited Bangui in March.Explore more on these topicsCentral African RepublicFranceAfricaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror
Content: Refqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAView image in fullscreenRefqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAWest BankIsraeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homesSettlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terrorEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemThu 13 Aug 2026 02.45 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in theWest Bankvillage of Qusra through a campaign of terror.A group of settlers and soldiers set up a tent outside the home of Yousef Hassan’s family on Sunday afternoon, trapping him inside with his wife and two young daughters.The Israeli men gathered just metres away from the spot where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh waskilledby a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault.“Every night, the settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night. We are living in a state of terror,” Hassan said. His mother, brother and sister, and three neighbours have also been blockaded inside, and their power and water have been cut off.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers stand guard next to settlers in front of Palestinian homes that they have blockaded in the village of Qusra.Photograph: Nidal Eshtayeh/APSettlers used thesame tacticsto steal another Palestinian home in neighbouring Jalud village, driving the al Tubasi family out in July after a months-long siege.They cut off water and electricity to the homes, although a solar panel allows Hassan to keep some devices charged in Qusra. They have also blocked medical care.When his younger daughter, aged two, fell ill with vomiting and a high fever on Monday, settlers blocked an ambulance from reaching the house. The girls and their mother were eventually evacuated on Tuesday.Hassan said those in the house were short on food and were drinking water and juice delivered by the ambulance that came to collect his daughter. “The situation is extremely dire.”On Wednesday morning, the commander of Israeli forces in the region, Gen Avi Bluth, visited the families and promised to lift the siege, an Israeli military spokesperson said. Hassan confirmed the visit.“Today, the area commander came and spoke with us and assured us that he would evacuate the settlers. For the first time, I feel that there is some seriousness on the part of the army in dealing with the settlers,” Hassan said, but added that it had not yet produced tangible results.Soldiers removed the tent but not the bedding and other possessions and, after brief clashes with the settlers, withdrew. “The settlers are still there in front of the house, and we are still unable to leave.”View image in fullscreenYousef Hassan said Israeli settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAAn Israeli military spokesperson said commanders were “gravely concerned” about the settlers’ actions and that soldiers who supported them would face disciplinary action, but declined to give a timeline for lifting the siege.On Wednesday evening, the chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Eyal Zamir, met other senior commanders to discuss the situation in Qusra. He ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank.“The battalion, which is currently undergoing a period of refreshment and training, will be deployed to the sector in order to strengthen operational control. Furthermore, additional soldiers will remain on standby for deployment as necessary,” a military spokesperson said.The military was working with the police to bring “those responsible for the disturbances to justice”, the spokesperson added.The incident has become an international issue for Israel. On Thursday, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, whosupportsthe wider settler movement,calledthe group who surrounded the homes “Israeli terrorists”.Israeli militants target Palestinians with neartotal impunityin the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only oneindictmentover those deaths.Violence isdeployedas part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, the rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes.View image in fullscreenAn Israeli settler tends to his animals as settlers besiege a Palestinian home.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA“What is happening in Qusra is not an isolated incident,” said B’Tselem’s executive director, Yuli Novak.“Settler militias, backed by the Israeli military, are expanding their attacks into Palestinian villages and towns – seizing land, attacking homes and forcing families out. Israel’s ethnic cleansing of the West Bank is accelerating and expanding in plain sight.”Dozens of Israelis from the country’s security, political and cultural elite havethreatenedlegal action against their government over its failure to tackle “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank.As the occupying power in the West Bank, Israel is responsible under international law for ensuring the safety of Palestinian civilians and meeting their basic needs.The Israeli military has declared the area a closed military zone and blocked journalists from approaching the Palestinian homes. Israeli settlers are subject to the same orders but have not been removed.Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Sports Direct owner Mike Ashley buys Harvey Nichols  | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Frasers Group acquires majority of upmarket retailer’s sites from the administrators
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Frasers Group acquires majority of upmarket retailer’s sites from the administrators
Content: The Harvey Nichols in Knightsbridge. The chain has 13 stores and 1,200 staff.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Harvey Nichols in Knightsbridge. The chain has 13 stores and 1,200 staff.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersRetail industrySports Direct owner Mike Ashley buys Harvey NicholsFrasers Group acquires majority of upmarket retailer’s sites from the administratorsBusiness live – latest updatesSarah ButlerThu 13 Aug 2026 12.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 08.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe owner of Sports Direct has bought Harvey Nichols out of administration after the upmarket department store chain warned it could run out of money if it did not find new funding.Mike Ashley’sFrasers Groupsaid on Thursday it had bought the chain, which is headquartered at its store in Knightsbridge, for an undisclosed sum on the day it was put into administration. Sources said he had paid about £40m for Harvey Nichols, which has 1,200 employees and 13 stores.These consist of five large stores – in London, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester – and a smaller one in Bristol plus outlets in Dublin, Riyadh, Dubai, Doha, Kuwait and two in Hong Kong.Consumer confidence at near two-year high as World Cup and UK holidaying lift summer spendingRead moreFrasers said it was acquiring the London, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Leeds, Bristol and Manchester stores. Discussions over the future of the Dublin shop were “ongoing” but Frasers said it had already bought certain stock and fixtures and “continues to support” trading there. The franchise agreements for the overseas stores will continue under the deal.Harvey Nichols’s restaurant in the Oxo Tower in London is not included in the deal, and is being sold off separately. The administrator, FTI Consulting, said a sale was being finalised that would preserve 100 jobs and the ongoing operation of the business.Frasers said in a statement: “Significant restructuring and integration of Harvey Nichols into the Frasers Group ecosystem will be required to create a sustainable business for the future, including a review and rationalisation of the store portfolio, organisational structure, operating model and cost base.”Frasers bought the House of Fraser department store chain out of administration in 2018 and has since closed about 40 of its 60 stores. The group has been building its interests in luxury fashion with the Flannels chain and large stakes in the German brand Hugo Boss and the British handbag maker Mulberry.Ashley has bought aseries of struggling premium brandsin recent years after starting out with a single sports shop. He has said he would keep Harvey Nichols’s Knightsbridge and Edinburgh stores, but rebrand the four other UK stores – in Birmingham, Leeds, Manchester and Bristol – as House of Fraser or Flannels.The veteran retail analyst Richard Hyman said: “We can be certain that Harvey Nichols won’t be the same, because being the way it was has racked up huge losses and that won’t be tolerated byMike Ashley.”It is not clear if Ashley plans to keep the entire Knightsbridge flagship store as a retail and restaurants operation under the Harvey Nichols brand long-term, or if he might redevelop it bringing in some of his other brands such as Sports Direct, Flannels or gyms and other partners, such as a hotel, to fill the space more profitably.Hyman teased: “Sports Direct might go well on that corner”, pointing to Lillywhites, the former department store on London’s Piccadilly, which Ashley has owned for decades and is now in effect a Sports Direct outlet.View image in fullscreenMike Ashley’s bid was said to have been more attractive than a potential offer from Next.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAHarvey Nichols, which was founded in 1831 as a linen shop, became the flag-bearer for 1990s chic highlighted in popular culture by regular mentions in TV sitcom Absolutely Fabulous. It was put up for sale by its long-term owner Dickson Poon after failing to make a profitsince the coronavirus pandemiclocked out big-spending foreign tourists.The Frasers Groupchief executive, Michael Murray – who is Ashley’s son-in-law – said: “Harvey Nichols is an iconic British institution with significant potential, but it is clear meaningful change is needed.“The turnaround will require tough choices, and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term, to create a stronger and more sustainable Harvey Nichols for the long term.”Julia Goddard, chief executive of Harvey Nichols, said: “I look forward to working closely with Frasers Group to build on the momentum already under way.”Lindsay Hallam, senior managing director at FTI Consulting which acted as administrator to Harvey Nichols, said the deal secured more than 1,000 jobs and “provides a strong platform for its next chapter”.The Knightsbridge store opened in 1889. In the last century it was owned by the Burton Group, the former owner of Debenhams, before Poon bought it in 1991 for £53m and listed it on the London Stock Exchange in 1996.In recent years the business has suffered from increased competition from Harrods and Selfridges as well as a host of online players, while its aspirational shoppers’ budgets have come under pressure from the cost of living crisis.It reported aloss after tax of £105mafter writing off inter-company loans for the year to 29 March 2025, according to accounts published over the weekend. The directors said the company was not a going concern, because it would run out of money within the next year and that it had no agreements for new funding.The FTSE 100 retailer Next had been interested in taking over the business but sources said it wanted only one or two of Harvey Nichols’s stores, so Ashley’s bid was seen as more attractive.Ashley, the controlling shareholder in Frasers, told the Financial Times last Friday that Harvey Nichols was in a “death spiral” and that it would be a “huge challenge” to turn it around.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryFrasers GroupMergers and acquisitionsMike AshleynewsShareReuse this content

title: Tesla paid Elon Musk 2.5m times more as CEO than its average worker in 2025 | Business | The Guardian
description: Tech billionaire’s $158.3bn deal an outlier in report showing widening gap of CEO to worker pay at top companies
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Tech billionaire’s $158.3bn deal an outlier in report showing widening gap of CEO to worker pay at top companies
Content: Elon Musk attends a session during the Cannes Lions international festival of creativity on 19 June 2024 in Cannes, France.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElon Musk attends a session during the Cannes Lions international festival of creativity on 19 June 2024 in Cannes, France.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty ImagesBusinessTesla paid Elon Musk 2.5m times more as CEO than its average worker in 2025Tech billionaire’s $158.3bn deal an outlier in report showing widening gap of CEO to worker pay at top companiesMichael SainatoThu 13 Aug 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Muskreceived over 2.5m times as much compensation atTeslaas the company’s average worker, according to anew reporton the growing gap between top corporate executives and their workers.Musk’s $158.3bn pay deal was an outlier but came as the gap between CEO and worker paycontinued to grow. Excluding Musk, last year the average ratio of CEO to worker pay for the top S&P 500 companies was 312 to 1, up from a285:1 ratioin 2024. With Musk, the average pay ratio was 5,387:1, according to the executive pay watch report released this week by the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US.“In 2025,Elon Muskreceived the median Tesla worker’s pay every 4.23 seconds – less time than it takes to read this sentence,” states the report. “A majority of S&P 500 CEOs made more in one day than the median US worker made in one year.”Average CEO pay, excluding Musk, was $22.8m in 2025, up from $18.9m in 2024. With Tesla accounted for, the average increases to $340.1m.The report notes workers’ share of US national income has fallen to the lowest level since the second world war.Tesla stock suffers double-digit drop on carmaker’s worst day in yearsRead moreThe report also looks atDonald Trump’sincomein 2025. At$2.2bn, largely from his crypto holdings, Trump’s income rose nearly 254% from 2024. The median US worker would require 43,154 years to earn what Trump received in 2025.“This is political grift unlike what we have ever seen in our lifetimes, perhaps ever, but it only tells part of the story of how CEOs and the Trump administration has rigged our economy to enrich themselves at the expense of working people,” said Fred Redmond, AFL-CIO’s secretary-treasurer.“Trump’s radical budget bill that Republicans rammed through Congress last year, it made drastic cuts to healthcare, food assistance for children and families in order to give massive tax cuts for corporations and the wealthy.”The report cited data demonstrating theeconomic strugglesofmost Americans; 33% of US adults have no retirement savings, 37% of adults do not have enough money to cover a $400 emergency expense, 26% of US adults have skipped medical care due to costs, and 23% of renters in the US have fallen behind on rent over the past year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.“As President Trump said, he has a lot of assets because he was a massively successful businessman prior to becoming President, which was why he was elected to office in the first place,” said a White House spokesperson in an email. “All of the President’s assets are in held in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party financial institutions. There are no conflicts of interest.”Explore more on these topicsBusinessUS income inequalityElon MusknewsShareReuse this content

title: UK economic growth slows down as Iran war pushes up energy prices | Economic growth (GDP) | The Guardian
description: GDP expanded by 0.4% in three months to June, but analysts warn growth is ‘likely to fade’
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: GDP expanded by 0.4% in three months to June, but analysts warn growth is ‘likely to fade’
Content: The latest GDP data suggests continued high energy prices are starting to weigh on growth.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenThe latest GDP data suggests continued high energy prices are starting to weigh on growth.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAEconomic growth (GDP)UK economic growth slows down as Iran war pushes up energy pricesGDP expanded by 0.4% in three months to June, but analysts warn growth is ‘likely to fade’UK economy shows surprising resilienceBusiness live – latest updatesHeather StewartThu 13 Aug 2026 02.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEconomic growth slowed in the second quarter of the year, as the disruption unleashed by the Iran war began to take its toll, official figures show.The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said GDP expanded by 0.4% in the three months to June,down from 0.6% in the first quarter, in line with City economists’ expectations.While it marked a slowdown, analysts said the data suggested the UK economy had been more resilient in the face of the ongoing Middle East conflict than feared.UK economy grows by 0.4% in second quarter as some businesses helped by World Cup and hot weather – business liveRead moreYael Selfin, the chief economist at KPMG, said: “Consumers have faced a series of shocks since the start of the year but have weathered them remarkably well.”However, she warned the second half of the year was likely to be weaker. “The UK economy closed out the first half of the year on strong footing, but momentum is likely to fade over the coming months,” she said.The news comes as the new chancellor, John Healey, prepares to present his first budget on 28 October.The ONS said services output expanded by 0.5% across the second quarter, and construction by 0.3%, while industrial production – which includes manufacturing and energy – was flat.UK economic growth chartWithin the important services sector, the strongest growth was in information and communication businesses, which was up 2.7%, led by an upturn in computer programming.GDP growth in the single month of June was a better-than-expected 0.3% – City economists had forecast no growth.Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said warm weather and World Cup-related spending may have helped to buoy demand.“In short, households spent more than anticipated,” he said. “Hotter weather saw consumers ramp up spending. The World Cup may have also had an effect in keeping June GDP on an upward trajectory with retail, hospitality, and advertising revenues all up on the month.”However, economists still expect rising energy costs to dampen growth through the remainder of 2026.Oil and gas prices shot up in the wake of Donald Trump’s attacks on Iran at the end of February – though consumer utility bills were protected until July by the energy price cap, which thenjumped by 13%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith prices remaining high, Healey could come under pressure to offer additional support to households and businesses this winter.Andy Burnham announced a VAT cut for electricity bills last month, but told the BBC on Wednesday that he would like to go further. “I can accept criticism that this isn’t enough, because I wouldn’t say it’s enough,” he said.The British Chambers of Commerce responded to the GDP data by sounding the alarm about continued high business costs.Stuart Morrison, its research manager, said: “Faced with global headwinds from the Iran conflict, the UK economy showed welcome resilience in Q2. But the headline figures shouldn’t disguise the cocktail of cost pressures choking long-term business growth.”Inflation figures for July will be published next week and are expected to show a higher reading than June’s 2.6%, reflecting rising utility bills. Sustained high inflation will increase pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates.Healey said: “I know people are worried about the impact of the conflict in the Middle East on their cost of living, which has been too high for too long and it has added pressure on British businesses.“This is an active, hands-on government, putting British interests first – giving breathing space to those feeling the strain, making our country more resilient and bringing hope back.”Explore more on these topicsEconomic growth (GDP)EconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs
Content: It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001.Photograph: LegoCamera/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIt is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001.Photograph: LegoCamera/ShutterstockAir transportSouth Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran warIncheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubsRaphael Rashidin SeoulThu 13 Aug 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for international passengers, in part owing to disruption in the Middle East caused by the Iran war.The airport, South Korea’s main gateway, about 30 miles (48km) west of Seoul, handled 38.39 million international passengers in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Airports Council International (ACI), the global trade body for airports.Heathrow in the UK was second, with 37.79 million, followed by Changi airport in Singapore with 34.53 million.It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. The airport was 10th in the world in 2002, rising to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024 and 2025.Part of the increase was attributed to disruption caused by theUS-Iran conflict, which weakened the role of Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and diverted some transfer traffic to alternative routes through east Asia, Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC) wasquoted as sayingby the Yonhap news agency.Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airportRead moreIncheon’s international passenger traffic was up 6.3% year on year overall, with rising numbers of foreign visitors also contributing to the increase.Foreigners accounted for 39.3% of Incheon’s passengers in the first half of the year, up from 35.2% for the whole of 2025. The proportion reached a record 44.4% in the second quarter, with IIAC attributing the increase largely to growing numbers of visitors from China and Japan, according to local media.Heathrow, in west London,recorded 40 million passengersin total in the first half of the year, including both domestic and international travellers, its busiest first half on record. Passenger traffic to Asia-Pacific rose 7.9%, while capacity to the Middle Eastreportedly fell16.5% owing to the regional conflict.Earlier this weekIstanbul overtook Heathrowas Europe’s busiest airport by total passenger numbers. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.Incheon has also expanded its role as an international hub. It serves 101 airlines flying to 183 cities, including 158 international passenger destinations.A four-phase expansion completed in late 2024 increased the airport’s annual capacity to 106 million passengers.Kim Beom-ho, the acting president of IIAC, said the ranking reflected “the support of the government, the public’s encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport”.South Korea also lays claim to theworld’s busiest air route. The domestic corridor between Gimpo airport and Jeju island had 14.4 million seats scheduled in 2025, according to the aviation data provider OAG, more than any other route in the world.Explore more on these topicsAir transportSouth KoreaMiddle East and north AfricaUS-Israel war on IranAirline industryAsia PacificHeathrow airportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Come Back Home review – loss and love in Palestinian artist’s intriguing fringe hour | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Fadi Murad’s unconventional drama is a collage structured with the free-form imagination of a poet
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Fadi Murad’s unconventional drama is a collage structured with the free-form imagination of a poet
Content: Water and war … Fadi Murad’s Come Back HomeView image in fullscreenWater and war … Fadi Murad’s Come Back HomeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewCome Back Home review – loss and love in Palestinian artist’s intriguing fringe hourSummerhall, EdinburghFadi Murad’s unconventional drama is a collage structured with the free-form imagination of a poetMark FisherThu 13 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast year, a group of Scottish producers staged a four-day mini festival calledWelcome to the Fringe, Palestine. One of the excerpts was a scratch performance by Fadi Murad, which now returns as a full-length show. It is not a conventional drama. Rather, Come Back Home is structured with the free-ranging imagination of a poet, an impressionistic collage that resists straightforward interpretation.Murad’s theme is one of loss and the pull of home, focusing in particular on the death of his mother in a car accident when he was nine. He speaks touchingly from a child’s perspective of what it meant to lose the nurturer in his life, the one he turned to in just such a moment of distress. And he shares video footage of his younger self singing Mad World byTears for Fearsat her memorial. It is as cute as it is sad.That death was formative; elsewhere in the performance, he leaves the violence and killings of a troubled Jerusalem for us to intuit, although he does talk of those who are willing to kill for God. This is not a war play in any strident sense: its reflections are more personal and elliptical, even if, in such circumstances, the personal is political.Mrs Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library review – interrogating Hannah ArendtRead moreFrom his passages of heavily alliterative poetry, atmospheric video and low-key clowning, a theme of water emerges: his mother was a hydrologist, there is a baptism in holy water, a link between water and war, and a striking opening image of Murad wetting himself – a forlorn figure, man or boy, under horrific pressure.Impressionism can only go so far and we could do with a clearer key to unlock what Murad has to say, but he has a gentle, endearing energy that keeps the show always intriguing.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatrePalestinereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was fun to get pushed around’: Andrew Rannells on ‘razzle dazzle’, kissing co-stars and being a better friend to Lena Dunham | Movies | The Guardian
description: The star of Girls and The Book of Mormon talks about coming out, turning a showmance into a romance, and going toe to toe with the West Wing’s Allison Janney in new film Miss You Love You
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: The star of Girls and The Book of Mormon talks about coming out, turning a showmance into a romance, and going toe to toe with the West Wing’s Allison Janney in new film Miss You Love You
Content: ‘I’d rather do porn than Pokémon’ … Andrew Rannells.Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for SCADView image in fullscreen‘I’d rather do porn than Pokémon’ … Andrew Rannells.Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for SCADMoviesInterview‘It was fun to get pushed around’: Andrew Rannells on ‘razzle dazzle’, kissing co-stars and being a better friend to Lena DunhamRyan GilbeyThe star of Girls and The Book of Mormon talks about coming out, turning a showmance into a romance, and going toe to toe with the West Wing’s Allison Janney in new film Miss You Love YouThu 13 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImagine a cute, young, gay Jim Carrey with a withering line in put-downs: that is Andrew Rannells. Or rather, it was, back when he starred inLena Dunham’s HBO series Girlsas Elijah, the formerly closeted ex of her character, Hannah. Dunham had seen Rannells playing Elder Price, the zealous missionary spreading the good word in the original 2011 Broadway production of the bad-taste musicalThe Book of Mormon, for which he received a Tony nomination. Girls, in turn, spread the good word about him. To this day, fans still shout “Your dad is gay!” at him in the street, a call-back to the moment when Elijah tartly advises Hannah that she might want to fine-tune her gaydar.It is an older, gentler, salt-and-pepper-bearded Rannells who stars in the comedy-dramaMiss You, Love You. He plays Jamie, a personal assistant arriving in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to shepherd the spiky and recently widowed Diane (Allison Janney)through the initial weeks after her husband’s death from Parkinson’s. As it dawns on them that Diane’s son – Jamie’s employer – may not make it to his stepfather’s funeral, these strangers navigate their way through the grey area of their flung-together friendship.Initially, Jamie struggles to retain composure in the face of Diane’s gale-force disdain, as she picks and pecks at his every word. “I was just trying to keep up with what Allison was doing,” says Rannells, who is wearing a silvery-grey shirt and running a hand through his chestnut quiff. He knew Janney from starring together in thecomic thriller Another Simple Favor, but nothing prepared him for being harangued by her during the new film’s extended takes. “She is relentless. She goes and goes and goes. All her years on The West Wing really prepped her.”Watch the trailer for Miss You, Love You.Rannells is hardly low-energy himself. Whether in his impish US television appearances, collected in YouTube compilations with titles such as “andrew rannells being a little TOO ICONIC on talk shows”, or in his shopping-mall song-and-dance number as an incorrigible Juilliard graduate inRyan Murphy’s The Prom, he is all razzle-dazzle. “Yeah, I’m usually in that position,” he concedes. “It was fun this time to be on the other side of it and to feel what it’s like to get pushed around and bullied.”It is a few weeks before his 48th birthday and Rannells is speaking on a video call from the home in Los Angeles he shares with the actorTuc Watkinsand the latter’s twin teenage children. The room behind him is blurred, so it is impossible to identify the three paintings on the wall, but since Rannells put his stylish Manhattan apartment on the market last year for nearly $2.5m (£1.8m), Dogs Playing Poker is unlikely to be among them.He and Watkins met on the 2018 Broadway revival of the pre-Stonewall chamber-pieceThe Boys in the Band. Their first kiss was in character. “We would end each show making out on stage. Ten minutes of us rolling around while Jim Parsons was crying.” They hooked up but didn’t start dating until a year later, when the cast reconvened forMurphy’s Netflix version. “We turned a showmance into a relationship,” he says with a little twitch of the eyebrow.View image in fullscreenWithering put-downs … Rannells and Lena Dunham in Girls, 2017.Photograph: Apatow Productions/Kobal/ShutterstockGiven his success, it is natural to assume that Rannells’ performance as Jamie in Miss You, Love You was based on his own experience of having PAs. On the contrary, he says – he has never hired one. This may make him something of an outlier in Hollywood. “One of my closest friends has an assistant. At times, I’m closer to the assistant than I am to him.” Why has Rannells resisted? “Maybe it comes from years of working in theatre. I got in the habit of doing things for myself. To relinquish that control now would be, I think, hard for me.”Knowing when and how to ask for help is one of the lessons that Jamie must learn in the film. Rannells can sympathise. “You are raised in the midwest to take care of your own problems: don’t make waves, fix it, move on. Sometimes I do myself a disservice by not asking for what I need. I’m getting better at it. But I’ve certainly seen it abused. A lot of actors take advantage of people and I don’t want to be that person.”He grew up next door to a children’s theatre in Omaha, Nebraska, and took drama classes from a young age. Performing soon began to pay: from 13 to 31, he was a prolific voice actor in cartoons including Pokémon and Yu-Gi-Oh!. That spilled over into his burgeoning stage career: at 21, he toured the US in Pokémon Live!. “In retrospect, [I] would rather have done a snuff film or porn,” he said later.His big, gay New York life was under way by then. He came out to his parents shortly before leaving home to study drama at 19. “My family was mostly – what’s the best way to say this? – not shocked,” he wrote in Too Much Is Not Enough: A Memoir of Fumbling Toward Adulthood. That 2019 book also revealed, in a chapter entitled It’s Never the Priest YouWantto Kiss, that he had been sexually assaulted as a teenager by a Catholic priest.View image in fullscreenThe boys in the band …(from left)Zachary Quinto, Andrew Rannells, Matt Bomer and Jim Parsons at the 2018 Tony awards in New York.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Tony Awards Productions“My mum accepted my sexuality,” he says. “My dad said: ‘I don’t think you have to be this way, but I love you.’ I was like: ‘Eh, that’s not exactly what I wanted to hear, but whatever.’” A few months later, his father reached a different conclusion. “He said: ‘I realise you’ve always been this way and I’m sorry I said that.’” Hadn’t his dad introduced him to 1940s musicals from a young age? “Exactly! It was his fault.”Coming out was relatively plain sailing, but there was a crisis ahead. When Rannells was 22, he brought a date back to his apartment. In the bathroom later, he checked the phone messages he had been ignoring for the previous few hours and found that his family had been frantically trying to reach him. His father was in a coma; a few days later, he died.That night, with its intermingling of sex, intimacy and mortality, left an impression on Rannells. In 2017, he wrote about the awkwardness of being consoled in this devastating moment by a naked man he hardly knew: “After I hung up, he tried to hug me: ‘What happened?’ I wanted to shout: ‘Clearly nothing good! Put on some pants!’”That essay inspired him to write and direct How Do You Remember Me?, his half-hour contribution tothe Amazon series Modern Love. In the screen version, he highlights the disparity that exists between separate recollections of identical events. “I’m sure that guy has gone off and told that story, especially as I’ve become successful,” he says. “And I’m sure it’s mostly the same as mine – but also pretty different.”View image in fullscreenGale-force disdain … Rannells and Allison Janney in Miss You, Love You.Photograph: HBORannells had his own experience of seeing the familiar from a revealing new angle when he readDunham’s recent memoir, Famesick. Its tales of behind-the-scenes horrors on Girls include theallegedly hostile behaviour of Adam Driver, who Dunham claims berated her for forgetting her lines before hurling a chair at the wall next to her. “That book is a great example of seeing things differently,” Rannells says. “Girls was my first TV job and when I showed up on set I saw the fun, exciting part. At times, Lena would open up to me and I’d read things in the press that were untrue or unfair. But the book was hard to read as someone who is close to her now. I felt terrible that I wasn’t a better friend.”What could he have done? “Been more available. I let a lot of shit slide because so much was happening. I had a break-up, then a new relationship. I was doing The Book of Mormon eight times a week and working on Girls.” He left to shoot 22 episodes of Murphy’s 2012 gay-dads sitcom,The New Normal, before returning to Girls when The New Normal was cancelled. “Of course, there was another part of reading her book,” he says. “I was, like: ‘Why didn’t she talk about me more?’” Joking he might be, but there is a Reddit thread on that very topic. “I would like to say I started that thread, but I did not,” he says. The eyebrow twitches again. Did he or didn’t he? As ever with Rannells, you are left with a tantalising question mark.Miss You, Love You is on HBO Max in the UK and Ireland, the US and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsComedy filmsRyan MurphyComedyGirlsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I ran away to Paris to be a writer and ended up begging’: Bill Nighy on dashed dreams, golf emojis and playing a cranky novelist | Movies | The Guardian
description: As his new film & Sons hits the screen, the actor turned podcast agony uncle relives his ‘cliched’ ambitions, deplores working lunches – and yearns to do the splits like Prince
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: As his new film & Sons hits the screen, the actor turned podcast agony uncle relives his ‘cliched’ ambitions, deplores working lunches – and yearns to do the splits like Prince
Content: ‘I don’t do smiley emojis’ … Bill Nighy.Photograph: Charlie GrayView image in fullscreen‘I don’t do smiley emojis’ … Bill Nighy.Photograph: Charlie GrayMoviesInterview‘I ran away to Paris to be a writer and ended up begging’: Bill Nighy on dashed dreams, golf emojis and playing a cranky novelistRyan GilbeyAs his new film & Sons hits the screen, the actor turned podcast agony uncle relives his ‘cliched’ ambitions, deplores working lunches – and yearns to do the splits like PrinceThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 04.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdying patriarch summons his brood for a dramatic announcement. It may not be the most original starting point for a movie, but & Sons adds an eccentric twist – one that it would be unfair to reveal here but which nudges the material into the realm of science fiction. The father in question is a revered novelist who is as reclusive as JD Salinger and as whiskery and dishevelled as Catweazle. Dormant for decades, the fictional AN Dyer is first glimpsed in a horizontal position on the sofa, refusing to come to the telephone: “I don’t do phonecalls,” he grumbles.That is patently not true of the actor who plays him. “I spend a lot of time on the phone,”Bill Nighysays breezily. He is speaking to me from north-west London, where he has been nosing around bookshops. “I’m also an enthusiastic texter. I was always very quick on the old Nokia. Quite proud of myself, I was.” Where does he stand on emojis? “I used to be philosophically opposed. Most of them are a bit naff.” He then proceeds to list the exceptions. “I like the flamingo and the purple dahlia. I like the leaping shark. Sometimes I combine it with the leaping dolphin. Very occasionally, I like the golfer in mid-swing if I’m congratulating someone. I don’t do smiley faces.”double quotation markWhat one thing would make me turn down an acting job? TogasCommunicating over Zoom is a no-go, hence our phone conversation today. “It got to the point where every time I had a Zoom call, it made me unhappy. I’m old enough to be able to say, ‘Can I retire from Zoom?’” At 76, he has ruled out other undesirable experiences. “Food where you talk about work. That’s one. Particularly lunch. You have to sit there for so long and it just confuses the issue. Working lunches are absolutely out of the question now.” He has never been much of a partygoer either, and used to get what he calls “a thrill, or a kind of anti-thrill” from putting invitations, especially highly prized ones, straight in the bin. When I ask if there is any one thing that is likely to make him turn down an acting job, his answer is instant and unequivocal: “Togas.”View image in fullscreen‘No fireworks, no reaching for prizes’ … Imelda Staunton and Bill Nighy in & Sons.Photograph: Icon Film DistributionNo such garments in & Sons, which pits Nighy as Dyer against his vexed older offspring (played by Johnny Flynn and George MacKay) and the ex-wife (Imelda Staunton) who has never forgiven him for siring a son (Hamnet’s Noah Jupe) by another woman. The old man has been an abrasive and emotionally absent parent, but appears to believe his literary talent excuses that. Nighy has no time for such guff. “It’s like when footballers behave badly on the pitch and people say, ‘Temperament is part of his genius.’ Give me a break. That’s anathema to me. I don’t believe it in the least.”Dyer claims his goal as a father was to “do no harm”. Nighy himself has a daughter – the actor-director Mary Nighy – by his ex-partner, the actor Diana Quick, whom he was with for 27 years until 2008. Did he start out with a parenting philosophy? “Blimey, Ryan. It’s a long time ago.” Indeed: he has two grandchildren now. “But no. Not really. You make it up as you go along. You make mistakes, then correct them, and hopefully you arrive at something that works. My parents were not oppressive or unkind, and I didn’t want to be either.”Unkindness is fully part of Dyer’s repertoire in & Sons, along with rage and misanthropy – none of them qualities that Nighy is typically asked to play. “I’m not thought of in those terms,” he agrees. “Though of course, half my work is not in living memory. You get to the stage where everyone who watched it is dead.”View image in fullscreen‘I’ll never be Steve McQueen’ … Nighy as Davy Jones in Pirates Of The Caribbean: At World’s End.Photograph: Disney/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockStrangers still commend him on his performance as the unvarnished ex-rocker Billy Mack, who blithely admits that his new Christmas single is a “festering turd”, in Richard Curtis’s 2003 romcom Love Actually. Nighy has made his share of blockbusters, including two voyages with the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise, where he was hidden behind a beard of writhing, computer-generated tentacles. But it is the gentler figures, endearingly flawed, for which he is truly cherished, whether bracingly frank like Billy or sweetly diffident: the terminally ill, buttoned-up bureaucrat in Living, which earned the actor his only Oscar nomination to date; the husband who chickens out of cheating on his wife in Lawless Heart; or the Scrabble enthusiast searching for his missing son in Sometimes Always Never.Don’t count him out as a sex symbol either. One early success was The Men’s Room, the raunchy 1991 BBC series in which his explicit scenes as a libidinous academic earned the censure of the Broadcasting Standards Council. After playing Nighy’s wife in Notes on a Scandal, Cate Blanchett asked a journalist: “What thinking western woman do you know who wouldn’t want to embrace him?”If he is typecast today, it doesn’t faze him. “Maybe there are people out there who like it when I do the things I always do. Just like I always want Steve McQueen to do what he does.” What has Nighy learned from the minimalist star of The Great Escape? “That I’ll never be Steve McQueen,” he sighs. “You need a lot of confidence to do what he did. No fireworks, no reaching for prizes. It’s a kind of reckless restraint.” Prince is another hero. “Everything Prince did was attractive. Anyone who can do the splits and come back up on the backbeat … well, I’ll follow them anywhere.”It was writers who were the object of his youthful idolatry: Hemingway, Fitzgerald. There is a special poignancy, then, in seeing Nighy as a novelist in & Sons, since that is what he wanted to be for many years. Blame Mr Weir, the English teacher at his Catholic grammar school. “He told me, ‘You might want to try your hand at the novel.’ I must have been 14. I’m not claiming this as an early sign of my neglected genius. But it was like a bomb going off in my head.”View image in fullscreenOscar-nominated buttoned-up bureaucrat … Nighy in Living, 2022.Photograph: Album/AlamyAt 15, he got a job on The Field, the hunting and fishing magazine. What were his responsibilities? “I changed the roller towel in the ladies’ room. All the girls from the typing pool used to come in. Not because of my animal magnetism, I hasten to add, but because they knew they could make me blush. Those roller towels are quite tricky. I’d bugger it up and they’d start laughing.”Then there was the day he landed in trouble with the boss. “I’m from a small town – Caterham in Surrey – and I used to become very excited if I saw a Roller or a Bentley in the street. I got pulled up in front of the CEO because he’d driven past me and I’d started jumping up and down and waving. He said, ‘That’s not what I expect from an employee.’”Nighy’s next stop was Paris. “I am a walking, talking cliche,” he says. “I ran away to be a writer. Like a million others, I went straight to [the bookshop] Shakespeare & Company and hung about thinking I’d write killer sentences and find a girlfriend. Neither of which happened. I ended up begging on the Trocadéro.” He didn’t relinquish his literary dreams so much as let them wilt. “Someone suggested I go to drama school, and that became what I did. I thought I’d get around to writing eventually. I’m still thinking it. I’m just very good at procrastination.”He may not have a novel in the works but a kind of verbal memoir is unspooling, 25 minutes at a time, in the form of his podcast,Ill-Advised, in which he serves as a soothing agony uncle, meanderingly answering listeners’ queries about everything from fashion to avoiding social faux pas. Off-the-cuff being his preferred mode, he never sees the questions before recording. “I ramble on the spot but I find that I’ve thought about whatever the subject might be. I’ve already thought about trousers, for instance, because I’m a bit of a fetishist about lounge suits and shirt collars.”Ill-Advised, which is about to launch its third series, has more than 300,000 monthly listeners and was named 2026 Podcast of the Year by the Broadcasting Press Guild. That doesn’t stop Nighy being comically apologetic about it. “I triednotto have a podcast,” he assures me, giving the impression, as he usually does, that he has secured his tremendous career and the esteem of audiences, critics and contemporaries simply by the happy accident of stepping off the lift at the wrong floor. Perhaps he won’t ever be mistaken for Steve McQueen. His compliments about that actor, though, could plainly be applied to him, too. No fireworks, no reaching for prizes. A master of reckless restraint.& Sons is in cinemas from 21 August. The third series of Ill-Advised begins on 3 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmBill NighyPodcastsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: My Brilliant Career review – a joyous heroine lights up this rare and beautiful period drama | Television | The Guardian
description: Phillipa Northeast is brilliant as a young woman rebelling against society’s expectations in 1890s Australia. It is witty, intelligent and absolutely glorious to watch
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Phillipa Northeast is brilliant as a young woman rebelling against society’s expectations in 1890s Australia. It is witty, intelligent and absolutely glorious to watch
Content: Irrepressibly charming … Philippa Northeast, right, and Genevieve O’Reilly in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Ian Routledge/NetflixView image in fullscreenIrrepressibly charming … Philippa Northeast, right, and Genevieve O’Reilly in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Ian Routledge/NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewMy Brilliant Career review – a joyous heroine lights up this rare and beautiful period dramaPhillipa Northeast is brilliant as a young woman rebelling against society’s expectations in 1890s Australia. It is witty, intelligent and absolutely glorious to watchLucy ManganThu 13 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m hot headed, with a snub nose, and that’s why I prefer a direct gaze.”So speaks Sybylla, the charmingly irrepressible and irrepressibly charming heroine of My Brilliant Career, played utterly convincingly and with vim, vigour and joy by Philippa Northeast in the new adaptation of Miles Franklin’s 1901 Australian classic of the same name. Creator Liz Doran must have wept with happiness when they found an actor capable of bringing so much to an already glorious script – and who embodies the joie de vivre upon which so much of the plot, as everyone she meets becomes part of her orbit, depends.Sybylla is one of too many children for her hardworking mother and debt-ridden, irresponsible father to support. So she is sent from their impoverished farm in Possum Gully to stay with her maternal grandmother (Anna Chancellor), the aptly named Mrs Bossier. She is a successful horse breeder who lives in widowed splendour, with her other daughter Helen (Genevieve O’Reilly) miles away in a grand mansion. She has plenty of time on her hands to shape Sybylla into a proper model of womanhood and get her married off to a rich man who can take care of her and the rest of her family.Sybylla does not take kindly to the revelation of Granny’s plans. “I’m being gussied up! … Slowly turned on a spit of propriety!” she writes in horror to her sister Gertie back home. Sybylla had thought she was going to be at Caddagat House, see the wider world and fuel her ambition to become a writer. Knowing that husbands do not help this mission, she practises a cheerful kind of resistance against Mrs B while throwing herself into the rest of her new life. She makes friends with Nell (Sherry-Lee Watson), the talented horse trainer from an Indigenous family who dreams of becoming Caddagat’s foreman despite the handicap, in 1890s rural Australia, of both her background and her sex.Sybylla makes frenemies (but! He’s extremely attractive) with an English guest at the house, Frank (Jake Dunn), and becomes a mentee of sorts to their high society neighbour, the glamorously eccentric Augusta (Kate Mulvany, having a wild time). Augusta’s nephew Harry (Christopher Chung) is, like Frank, like all of us, drawn to this new, iconoclastic free spirit who has appeared in their midst – but the limits to Augusta’s bohemianism and other factors mean he is not as free in his turn as he might be to choose a wife.The Sybylla-Frank-Harry love triangle evolves slowly and convincingly as the three young people make their mistakes, are overheard saying things to each other that they shouldn’t and generally explore the different kinds of attraction that different people offer each other. But, refreshingly, it doesn’t become the dominant tale. Sybylla’s writing ambitions remain important, with Augusta urging her to try to get stories published in magazines as an alternative way of supporting herself and her family that would also allow her to retain her independence. The ramifications of her father’s incompetence increase. Bailiffs gradually strip the home of its few valuables and eventually another daughter must be sacrificed – this time to become a governess/maid of all work to a local family – to help manage his debts. The pressure on Sybylla to marry, and marry well, mounts as her friendships with Harry and Frank deepen in different ways. It is a rare and beautiful thing to watch people not flirt but connect by degrees.Mixed in with these parts most faithful to the novel are more modern elements. A male homosexual relationship, and the terrible fear and misery it brings in a time and place that finds it completely unacceptable, is movingly shown. Nell and her family – especially her sister’s secret relationship with the (white) neighbourhood policeman – demonstrate the forces of racism and colonialism at work. And sexism, if not outright misogyny, is in the air everyone breathes. From the need to get married for security (nicely thrown into relief by the freedom enjoyed by the various widows among the local folk), to Aunt Helen running the household and business for years only to be passed over without a word when it is deemed time for her brother to inherit everything, to Nell’s talents always being assumed to be simply the result of what her father taught her, no woman can escape its effects.Doran’s creation retains all the book’s sense of defiance but adds a welcome soupcon of more optimism too. It crackles with intelligence and wit, gives all of its characters room to breathe (although it may ultimately be Sybylla’s show, everyone has something meaningful to do and contribute, and the cast is all-round magnificent) and, without ever becoming superficial, never loses its lightness of touch. A joy. A brilliant, brilliant joy.My Brilliant Career is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon review – an engrossing story, if you can stomach it | Television | The Guardian
description: This documentary follows the shocking case of Neil Hopper, a top surgeon who had his own legs removed due to a fetish.
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: This documentary follows the shocking case of Neil Hopper, a top surgeon who had his own legs removed due to a fetish.
Content: Neil Hopper, the vascular surgeon, who faked sepsis and had both legs amputated.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenNeil Hopper, the vascular surgeon, who faked sepsis and had both legs amputated.Photograph: BBCTV reviewTelevisionReviewAn Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon review – an engrossing story, if you can stomach itThis documentary follows the shocking case of Neil Hopper, a top surgeon who had his own legs removed due to a fetish.Jack SealeThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo fetish or obsession is unique, and the internet can always connect you with others whose minds work the same way. It’s one of the great blessings and curses of the digital age, and central to An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon, a two-part documentary on which the “contains material some viewers may find disturbing” disclaimer is no exaggeration.We begin at the Royal Cornwall hospital, known locally as Treliske, in Truro, Cornwall. It used to have a man on its staff who was a minor medical superstar: Neil Hopper, a vascular surgeon, was well known for his clinical expertise and comforting bedside manner, particularly when advising on and performing amputations. He acquired full hero status in 2019, when he was diagnosed with sepsis and had both legs amputated below the knee but miraculously returned to work within six months, astonishing physiotherapists and other medical professionals with how well he adapted to disability.Documentary crews shadowed Hopper at work; he was welcomed on to the BBC Breakfast sofa to tell presenter Naga Munchetty his inspiring tale. Patients facing amputation were desperate for a consultation. Life without legs almost seemed like an improvement for Hopper, not least because a £466,653 insurance payout got him a new car, high-grade prosthetic limbs and an accessible extension on his home.‘I felt sick that he was near my mum’: a top amputation surgeon had his own legs removed due to a fetish. Were his patients safe?Read moreHaving set all that up, the programme switches to London for the lurchingly horrific saga of Marius Gustavson. Before beingimprisoned for life in 2024on multiple counts of grievous bodily harm with intent, Gustavson made a very good living from running an illicit website called the Eunuch Maker, which sold its users videos of … well, of what the name of the site implies. Men volunteered – although some seemed to have been carefully groomed by Gustavson, and none could legally consent to what happened next in any case – to attend Gustavson’s basement flat, where they were filmed undergoing amateur medical procedures in a non-sterile environment. Many were taken away by ambulance, having sustained irreversible injury. The more gruesome the content, the more the torture-porn addicts in the Eunuch Maker community – which had more than 20,000 members – enjoyed it. A good few of the butchered men were fulfilling a long-held desire to lose a part of their own body. Some performed the procedure themselves.Hopper was one of the Eunuch Maker viewers, which is partly why he is also in prison, having committed the offence of possessing extreme pornography. We see some of the incriminating messages Hopper exchanged with Gustavson, where his polite articulacy and medical idioms – “penectomy” is the term he used for what was done in videos he watched “thousands of times” – clang against the horror of what he is discussing.That Hopper had a Eunuch Maker login doesn’t count as a revelation since it’s the obvious explanation for being in the same documentary as Gustavson. The other crime Hopper was found guilty of last year constitutes the twist in the narrative, which arrives at the halfway point and is fairly guessable in a “No … nooooo, surely not. NO!” sort of way, although the first episode rather mischievously misleads viewers in order to conceal it.From there we have an exploration of body integrity identity disorder, a rare condition in which the patient rejects a body part in much the same way someone with gender dysphoria has an insistent feeling that their assigned gender is incorrect. That warrants sympathy rather than revulsion, but then we face the awful possibility of Hopper’s professional decisions having been compromised. The latter suspicion has, it is a great relief to hear, been allayed by reviews of his work that found no evidence of malpractice.It is quite the story – equally repellent and engrossing – but how should it be told? Any documentary like this has to earn the right to demand an hour and a half of your time when it would take 10 minutes to read an article about the case. Here, it’s not clear that television wins. The two main characters are unavailable because they are in prison, although Hopper’s TV appearances and social media content, filmed before his arrest, sharpen the picture of the gentle, self-effacing man colleagues and patients thought they knew. One of Gustavson’s victims speaks compellingly, but “Michael” inevitably has his face and voice disguised. An awful lot of the details are ably filled in by veteran local news reporter Olivier Vergnault, who is in it so much he ought to invoice the producers for a presenter’s fee instead of a contributor’s.This perfectly well-made programme sets it all out, but if it feels like too much time to invest in such strong ick, you could always search for Hopper and Gustavson online instead. You can find anything there, as this show proves so grimly.An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon is on Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryFactual TVCrimePornographyNHSreviewsShareReuse this content

title: James: Getting Away With It review – hippies, hardnuts and dreamers unite | Movies | The Guardian
description: Auto-hagiography it may be – most of the interviewees were in the band at some point – but this portrait of the seminal Manchester indie group is charming stuff
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Auto-hagiography it may be – most of the interviewees were in the band at some point – but this portrait of the seminal Manchester indie group is charming stuff
Content: Say Something or Sit Down … James in their heyday.View image in fullscreenSay Something or Sit Down … James in their heyday.MoviesReviewJames: Getting Away With It review – hippies, hardnuts and dreamers uniteAuto-hagiography it may be – most of the interviewees were in the band at some point – but this portrait of the seminal Manchester indie group is charming stuffLaurence PhelanThu 13 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time of their first flush of success – concomitant with the turn-of-the-90s Mancunian baggy scene, when indie discos thronged with people in big daisy petal T-shirts, and the anthemic Sit Down was only kept off the No 1 spot in the charts by Chesney Hawkes – James had already had as many ups, downs and near misses as most bands have in a lifetime.Subtitled Sects, Trance and Rock’n’Roll, this good-natured, funny and occasionally rousing documentary portrait details them all. It begins when their middle-class, boarding school-educated soon-to-be-singer Tim Booth meets cute with a bunch of working-class borderline hooligans in a band, after they sneak into the University of Manchester’s student union bar and swipe his drinks. Described by their manager as “a band that took all the wrong turns and made every mistake possible”, they turned down Factory Records’ offer to release a first album because they didn’t want to have a product number. They then turned down a support slot on the Smiths’ US tour because half the group had by then joined an esoteric meditation cult and the scheduling would have clashed with the bassist’s enlightenment.Later, the non-enlightened ones earned a reputation for being the party-hardiest reprobates on the 1997 Lollapalooza tour – the same year Korn, Snoop Dogg and the Prodigy were on the bill, no less. Mind you we only have their own word for it; Getting Away With It is a very insider account, to a fault, and other than sometime producer Brian Eno and lifelong superfan Chris Martin, virtually every interviewee in this documentary is or has been in James. The film is far more concerned with the internal dynamics of the band than their times or even their songs.James review – special band still filling arenas with anthems of warmth and humanityRead moreBut fair enough; the interpersonal dynamics are fascinating. They’re a mixture of hippies and hardnuts, dreamers and pragmatists, united by music. “We’re not alike but we share an ethos,” says one of them. And, quite deliberately it starts to seem, they have maintained a position on the brink of implosion, always dancing on the edge of chaos, generating drama to keep the sparks and the embers of their creativity glowing.James: Getting Away With It is in UK cinemas on 17 August for one night only.Explore more on these topicsFilmMusic documentaryDocumentary filmsIndiePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bruckner Symphony No 3 album review – Anima Eterna’s period instruments bring visceral drama | Classical music | The Guardian
description: There’s bone-crushing intensity in this striking recording of the original version of the Bruckner’s third. Pablo Heras-Casado teases out vital, almost operatic detail
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: There’s bone-crushing intensity in this striking recording of the original version of the Bruckner’s third. Pablo Heras-Casado teases out vital, almost operatic detail
Content: Measured but vital… conductor Pablo Heras-Casado.Photograph: Javier SalasView image in fullscreenMeasured but vital… conductor Pablo Heras-Casado.Photograph: Javier SalasClassical musicReviewBruckner Symphony No 3 album review – Anima Eterna’s period instruments bring visceral dramaAnima Eterna Brugge/Heras-Casado(Harmonia Mundi)There’s bone-crushing intensity in this striking recording of the original version of the Bruckner’s third. Pablo Heras-Casado teases out vital, almost operatic detailClive PagetThu 13 Aug 2026 11.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAccording to legend, in the summer of 1873 Anton Bruckner travelled to Bayreuth intending to dedicate one of a pair of scores to his hero, Wagner. Apparently, the two composers got legless and by the time Bruckner arrived back home, he could no longer remember which symphony the master preferred. In a flap, he put pen to paper: “Symphony in D Minor, where the trumpet begins the theme?” he fished. “Yes! Best wishes! Richard Wagner,” was the reply.View image in fullscreenAnton Bruckner: Symphony No 3 in D MinorPhotograph: Harmonia MundiWith its mighty peaks and faint reminiscences of the operas, the Wagnerian aesthetic looms large over the Third Symphony in D minor, especially in its more radical original version, presented here by period instrument specialistsAnima Eterna. Gut strings and original woodwind and brass are more pungent than their modern counterparts, but they sometimes struggle to summon the weight necessary for Bruckner. Not here. Pablo Heras-Casado conducts one of the most explosive and visceral accounts on record with his Belgian orchestra laying into the score with bone-crushing intensity.Compared with Roger Norrington, who opted for period instrument lite, and François-Xavier Roth’s foot-on-the-gas approach, Heras-Casado is more measured but no less vital. The results are almost operatic: his long-breathed Adagio comes across as an achingly lyrical aria; the furious Scherzo a frenetic micro-drama. The finale swings from rugged turmoil to broad good humour at the flick of a switch. Harmonia Mundi’s recording is strikingly immediate, revealing plenty of instrumental detail without stinting the music’s sonic amplitude.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
