title: ‘I feel like I’m at war’: are we losing the battle against machine-made music? | Music | The Guardian
description: Despite outcry from musicians, AI slop is creeping into the charts as record labels scramble to adapt to a new normal where hits can be made at the click of a button
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Despite outcry from musicians, AI slop is creeping into the charts as record labels scramble to adapt to a new normal where hits can be made at the click of a button
Content: Illustration: Brendan Conroy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Brendan Conroy/The GuardianMusic‘I feel like I’m at war’: are we losing the battle against machine-made music?Despite outcry from musicians, AI slop is creeping into the charts as record labels scramble to adapt to a new normal where hits can be made at the click of a buttonJason LamphierThu 13 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.04 EDTShareThis year, the battle for song of the summer has been eclipsed by a much more complicated – some would even say disturbing – debate. That’s because we find ourselves asking not “What’s the song of the summer?” but rather “Is the song of the summer evenreal?”Among the top contenders for the title is Fenix Flexin’sRubberz, a single released in June that has ascended to No 58 on the BillboardHot 100 and racked up more than 35m Spotify streams. It’s not the sort of fare Fenix usually cooks up. The artist is known for his trap music as part of the rap duo Shoreline Mafia, but Rubberz is a mildly noirish, 80s-inspired synth-pop track featuring a voice nothing like his. The song has drawn comparisons to Morrissey, but it more closely resembles Men at Work’s Down Under, or a Weird Al Yankovic parody of Men at Work. It’s pretty awful. But more importantly, it has an uncanny quality to it. It soundsoff.Almost immediately after it came out, skeptics accused Fenix of employingartificial intelligenceto create the track, if not entirely at least partly. He and the song’s credited producer, Purps on the Beat, initially denied it, with Fenix insisting that he’d justused Auto-Tuneand a phoney British accent. The kerfuffle culminated this month when indie DJ-producer Medasin posted avideothat he said proved that Rubberz had been made using the free generative music tool Treblo.Medasin then captured himself giving Treblo prompts to pump out his own track. Its sound and lyrics were eerily close to those of Rubberz. Fenix rejected Medasin’s claims, posting what he said were clips of the song’s stems, or its fundamental components, but then Medasin posted a rebuttal of him demonstrating how AI songs, too, can be broken down into stems. A few days later, Fenix finallyadmittedto using AI to make Rubberz, writing: “never said I didn’t use AI, i said it had nun to do w recording process.”This is in line with the findings of the platform’s own open-source classifier,Was This Made With Treblo?, which finds Rubberz to be “very likely Treblo” according toWired. The tool hasn’t been independently reviewed, but the Treblo co-founder Ryan Tremblay confirmed to the Guardian that the classifier returns a very high probability score (“higher by far than any false positive”) for Rubberz, indicating that Treblo generated the song. “We built Treblo for everyone, from normal people experimenting at home to charting artists looking for new sounds,” Tremblay said. “Some artists appear to have used our model to find a sound that millions of people connected with, and that’s exciting.” When reached by the Guardian, Fenix’s representative declined to comment.The uproar over Rubberz coincided with another major development in music in recent weeks. On 29 July, several record companies, including “the big three” – Universal Music Group, Sony Music and Warner Music Group – issued a proposal calling for global music charts to disqualify AI-generated tracks from consideration if they did not meet certain criteria. According to their suggested guidelines, a song could enter the charts only if it was properly authorized, lawful and substantially human-made, and does not raise concerns of streaming or chart manipulation. The issue, as the record companies stated in apress release, is that a significant number of AI-generated tracks hitting streaming services like Spotify have used tools trained on artists’ music without their consent and are often linked to fraudulently boosted streaming numbers. Under the proposed rules, these songs would not be allowed to enter charts such as the BillboardHot 100.At the same time, all the major record labels have announced partnerships with the likes of Nvidia, Spotify and Stability AI to develop AI music tools, with BMGannouncinga partnership with the AI music-creation platform Suno this week. The rapper Tyga, a labelmate of Fenix, proudly toldVibemagazine recently that his new album $tarface was created with AI, saying: “There’s nothing wrong with using technology as a tool.” (The album received Pitchfork’s first 0.0reviewin nearly two decades.)He is not alone in his permissive attitude. While Rubberz is the first AI-generated single to crack theHot 100, it is not the first to land on the Billboardcharts. In November, the AI act Breaking Rust hit No 1 on the country digital song sales chart withWalk My Walk, a track credited to a person who goes by Aubierre Rivaldo Taylor. That same month, the AI-powered R&B singerXania Monet– whose name instantly conjures actual human R&B singersVictoria MonétandJanelle Monáe– became the first AI act to enter a Billboard radio airplay chart, later climbing to No 1 on the R&B digital song sales chart. An avatar that the Mississippi poet Telisha “Nikki” Jones invented with Suno, she reportedly landed a multimillion-dollar record deal last fall.Xania Monet, an AI artist created by Telisha ‘Nikki’ Jones.Illustration: Talisha JonesAfter XaniaMonet’s milestone, Billboardreportedthat a total of at least six AI-generated or AI-assisted artists had debuted on its various charts in 2025. The publication admitted, however, that the tally could be higher because it has become harder and harder to determine which songs have used AI, and just how much. This was validated a week later when a study by the French streaming platformDeezerand research firm Ipsos revealed that 97% of its participants couldn’t tell the difference between AI-generated music and human-made music.Spotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending themRead moreUnsurprisingly, the proliferation of AI artists has struck a nerve with the human ones. SZA toldi-D: “I feel like I’m at war because of AI.” Last month, sheslammedAI generators like Suno and alleged that they were being trained on her songs without her permission. “If you’re a musician and you support this degenerate shit? You’re disgusting and there’s nothing you could ever say to me to make this OK,” she said. Jack Antonoff recentlycalledAI-music makers “godless whores”. Billie Eilish, Bad Bunny, Kate Bush, Annie Lennox, Nick Cave, Sting, Stevie Wonder and Paul McCartney have allprotestedagainst the heavy use of generative AI in music.And why shouldn’t they? Yes, dictating what one wants to create to an app requires a sliver of inspiration and imagination, but it pales in comparison with the blood, sweat and tears artists pour into music of their own – music that hasn’t been trained, often without permission, on reams of pre-existing copyrighted work. If those artists’ labor is grueling, the results, performed live and perfected in a studio by bands and session players with real instruments, can be deeply moving and totally exhilarating. Directing prompts to AI music generators like Suno, Udio and Treblo to spit out fully formed songs for mass consumption is a faster, cheaper, easier way to make music. It also disrespects and debases the art form, reducing hard-earned craft to half-assed mimicry.If the outcry against AI sounds like a bunch of intransigent luddites shaking their fists at the inevitable arrival of a new era, know that naysaying artists and wary record companies are not alone. A recent report published by the music and entertainment insights company Luminate showed that listeners, especially members of gen Z and gen Alpha, are increasingly uneasy with AI-generated songs. The study found that 44% of US respondents felt less inclined to listen to a song if it involves generative AI. “Consumers are net negative,” a Luminate analyst toldNPRin May. “People are more likely to feel uncomfortable than to feel comfortable with AI use.”View image in fullscreenThe AI tool Suno lets users generate prompt-based songs at the click of a button.Photograph: Courtesy of SunoUniversal, Sony and Warner are not demanding an outright ban on AI music from charts and streaming services. Though all three sued the AI music generators Suno and Udio in 2024, alleging they had trained their platforms on the labels’ artists without their permission, Universalsettled with Udioand Warnersettled with both Suno and Udiolast year. (Sony has yet to settle with either.) The labels continue to work with Spotify and AI companies to develop generative music tools, in a move that effectively keeps their options open. Warner executive Robert Kynclsaidthe deals would foster “new creative and commercial possibilities”, adding: “Now, we are entering the next phase of innovation. The democratization of music creation.” Universal, Sony and Warner did not respond when approached by the Guardian for comment.Meanwhile, other artists have expressed support of AI as a means to enhance songwriting. “With new technology, I try to use it as a tool to grow, not a crutch,” Björk wrote in a 2025poston X. “If there is no soul in tomorrow’s music made by AI, it is because no one put it there … Anything that is mass-manufactured without the attention of creativity is that way, AI or not. So it is not about the tool – it is what you do with it.” Even McCartney enlisted AI to isolate John Lennon’s vocals for the final Beatles song, 2023’sNow and Then. What these labels and so many musicians want is a system of guardrails to ensure that AI use is limited, honest and transparent.There is hope. In January,Bandcampbanned all music fully or substantially created by AI from the platform. ThoughTidalallows fully AI-generated songs on its app if they are not linked to fraud or artist impersonation, they cannot collect streaming royalties or direct-to-fan sales revenue, and get tagged with an “AI” label. A coalition of music industry organizations, including the Grammys and the Recording Industry Association of America, recentlyannouncedthat it was taking steps to notify listeners of AI use in recordings. This month, Spotifysaidthat it would label AI artists with an “AI Persona” tag and exclude these artists from its personalized recommendations, while its optional “AI Credits” feature allows artists to note whether AI was used in a song’s creation.Per the record companies’ proposed criteria, such AI Personas would not be chart-eligible. If Deezer’s findings are any indication, plenty of listeners would support this. Its 2025 survey results showed that 80% of respondentsagreed that entirely AI-generated music should be clearly labeled to listeners, while 52% thought entirely AI-generated songs should not be included alongside human-made songs in the main charts.Author and journalist CJ Farley echoed this sentiment in a recent column forTime. He dismissed the terms “AI artists” and “AI musicians”, suggesting that we instead refer to AI releases as “AI products”. Then he took it a step further, arguing that these products should be confined to their own chart “away from human musicians with real lives and with real financial obligations”.If Rubberz is a joke, Fenix Flexin might have been trying to see exactly how much he could get away with. (That would at least explain why the song is such dreck.) But what about all the AI products with more nefarious purposes floating around out there undetected, the slop created by impostors and opportunists attempting to steal the work of others and pass it off as their own? There’s more at stake here than chart rankings. Artists’ livelihoods and legacies are on the line. If we don’t act now, tomorrow’s song of the summer may just be a sad, hollow shell of yesterday’s.

title: Universality by Natasha Brown audiobook review – a sparkling multi-voiced satire | Books | The Guardian
description: A magazine article about stolen gold sparks a culture war between a cast of politically polarised characters
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: A magazine article about stolen gold sparks a culture war between a cast of politically polarised characters
Content: Striking gold in Universality.Photograph: BA E Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenStriking gold in Universality.Photograph: BA E Inc./AlamyAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewUniversality by Natasha Brown audiobook review – a sparkling multi-voiced satireA magazine article about stolen gold sparks a culture war between a cast of politically polarised charactersFiona SturgesThu 13 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstinging dissection of wealth, class and the media, Natasha Brown’s satire begins with a man named Jake gazing at a gold bar he has found at a farm in West Yorkshire. Outside, an illegal rave is taking place which will end in three hospitalisations and property damage. Pondering what to do with the ingot that he has just used to bludgeon a stranger, Jake decides to do a runner.The story of the stolen gold is told by a journalist, Hannah, in a magazine article named A Fool’s Gold, replicated in full here, which she claims exposes “the fraying fabric of British society, worn thin by late capitalism’s relentless abrasion”. Her piece, which goes viral, features Richard Spencer, an arrogant, philandering banker and the owner of the farm, whose reputation is left in tatters; a contrarian rightwing newspaper columnist named Miriam Leonard, known as Lenny; and a group of radical anarchist squatters who call themselves The Universalists.Universality goes on to dissect the fallout from the article via the varying perspectives of its protagonists, all of which makes it ideal for the multi-voice audio treatment: Norma Butikofer narrates Hannah’s article while Hannah herself, a burnt-out literary journalist who stumbles on a scoop, is voiced by Anushka Chakravarti. Clare Corbett reads Lenny, antihero of the culture wars, and Daniel Weyman reads from the viewpoint of the self-pitying Richard, who calls Hannah’s actions “a cruel confidence trick”. Though we come to understand that each of the characters has an axe to grind; which of them, if any, can we trust?Further listeningThe Calamity ClubKathryn Stockett,Penguin Audio, 28hr 45minMeg, a young orphan deemed “unadoptable”, has her fortunes changed when she meets Birdie, the new bookkeeper at her orphanage. This Depression-era novel from the author of The Help is read by January LaVoy and Jenna Lamia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Chelsea Wolfe: The Dark review – existential reflection goes from whisper to gothic scream | Music | The Guardian
description: The genre-blending Californian artist casts off past toxic influences with a powerful set of tender, brooding and emotionally charged songs that wouldn’t feel out of place as festival anthems
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: The genre-blending Californian artist casts off past toxic influences with a powerful set of tender, brooding and emotionally charged songs that wouldn’t feel out of place as festival anthems
Content: ‘It’s not party music’ … Chelsea Wolfe.Photograph: Magdalena WosinskaView image in fullscreen‘It’s not party music’ … Chelsea Wolfe.Photograph: Magdalena WosinskaMusicReviewChelsea Wolfe: The Dark review – existential reflection goes from whisper to gothic scream(Loma Vista)The genre-blending Californian artist casts off past toxic influences with a powerful set of tender, brooding and emotionally charged songs that wouldn’t feel out of place as festival anthemsDave SimpsonThu 13 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Chelsea Wolfe wasinterviewed by the Guardian in 2015about her fourth album, Abyss, she revealed that her music had been informed by the bouts of sleep paralysis she’d suffered from since childhood. The condition – a transitional state between being awake and asleep – affects sufferers in different ways. Some wake up feeling paralysed, others see ghosts or demonic figures. For the California-born singer-songwriter, it meant “waking up, and you can move your body and your eyes are open, but there are figures and people from your dreams still present in your room”.View image in fullscreenChelsea Wolfe: The DarkNo surprise, then, that her music – a blend of drone, alt, folk, industrial and doom metal – had ended up so spookily unsettling. She appeared on album covers with pupil-less eyes, spoke in interviews about “following the path of witchcraft” and even covered Norwegian black metal act and convicted arsonist/murderer Burzum. She did have a sense of humour about it all, however, telling one interviewer, with a chuckle: “It’s not party music.” Since then, though, much has changed. Wolfe left Los Angeles for the mountains above the city – where she’s finally been able to enjoy a good night’s sleep. Sobriety since 2021 has also brought what she calls “a new clarity”. Both developments inform The Dark.The sublime opener Cold is again driven by lack of sleep, but for entirely different reasons as she taps into the insomnia that can result from a fracturing relationship. “Baby, when I’m next to you / Feels so cold / And it’s hard to sleep / And it’s hard to feel so alone,” she sings, dramatically ending up feeling as if she is “crying underwater / Screaming at the surface”. With its strummed folk beginning, brushed drums and layers of piano and acoustic guitars, the yearning gothic ballad is closer to, say, Annie Lennox than Ethel Cain and sets the scene for this much more accessible ninth album which channels her darker urges into something more universal.After 2024’s largely electronic, David Sitek-produced She Reaches Out to She Reaches Out to She, Wolfe felt as if she was continually returning to “a version of my old self”. So The Dark turns to Grammy-winning producer/co-writer Jennifer Decilveo, whose credits include Hozier and Miley Cyrus, and returns to a core of guitar, bass and drums (alongside longtime collaborator Ben Chisholm). Drone and doom metal has almost entirely made way for brooding bass lines, wailing guitars, dramatic dynamic shifts and subtle orchestrations. The dreamier, more gothic tracks recall Evanescence or, on Swallower, the Cure, while Wolfe’s haunting vocals literally span the spectrum from a whisper to a scream – or, on the driving, windswept Seethe, a blood-curdling howl. Her ethereal singing suggests, of all things, Cocteau Twins’ Elizabeth Fraser fronting the Sisters of Mercy.Chelsea Wolfe: The Dark (Live at Mono lake) – videoNow 42, the singer has talked about how The Dark has been driven by “letting go … being in my early 40s as a woman, growing older and wanting to be who I am now”. This process has involved letting go of old behaviours and toxic relationships as well as her old music, which has driven some emotionally powerful songs. In the beautifully sad I’m Not There, she tells someone: “It’s too late, we’re already strangers,” a sentiment which recalls Carole King’s It’s Too Late. In the slightly Lana Del Rey-ish Halo, she directly quotes Martha and the Vandellas – “Nowhere to run, nowhere to hide” – another unexpected reference point from an artist with Wolfe’s history.‘Techno in a monastery – are you ready?’ The Greek priest whose doom metal album is the year’s hippest recordRead moreWolfe subsequently disowned her more conventionally singer-songwriterly self-released 2006 debut Mistake In Parting as a “shitty breakup album”, but seems to be reacquainting with classic songcraft as well as allowing herself more warmth and introspection. The folky title track is a beautifully observed “love letter” to the comfort of the black (“Our love glows in darkness / In a world that feels so heartless”) which builds to a finale featuring Warpaint drummer Stella Mozgawa and former Nine Inch Nails bassist Justin Meldal-Johnsen.Death Is Not The End – not the Bob Dylan song – is a tender largely acoustic folk rumination on the afterlife. Wolfe gently whispers “I’ll see you again” as one might over a dearly departed’s coffin, before Nine Inch Nails guitarist Robin Finck lets fly with guttural, chilling noise. Dancer in the Sky is the closest Wolfe has come to an epic, anthemic love song, with an exquisite arrangement and a chorus made for people to sing along. In fact, a lot of these songs wouldn’t sound incongruous being performed before huge crowds holding phones or lighters in the air. Wolfe recently became the unlikely face of a perfume range (Ghosts, obviously) and is clearly edging towards to the mainstream, but after two decades at the culty coal face this powerful, mature collection should take her to a wider audience.This week Dave listened toShearwater and Laurie Anderson– You and Your DogThe Texans’ cascading clarinet, bass and cymbals make a beautiful backdrop for the art-pop legend’s moving reminisce about a beach walk and days long gone.The Dark is released on 21 August. Alexis Petridis is awayExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockMetalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Can Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh review – US family saga is a late-career triumph | Irvine Welsh | The Guardian
description: The Scottish author focuses on gun culture and generational conflict in this darkly satirical tale about a great power in decline
Author: Jake Arnott
Headline: The Scottish author focuses on gun culture and generational conflict in this darkly satirical tale about a great power in decline
Content: Irvine Welsh.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIrvine Welsh.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesBook of the dayIrvine WelshReviewCan Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh review – US family saga is a late-career triumphThe Scottish author focuses on gun culture and generational conflict in this darkly satirical tale about a great power in declineJake ArnottThu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Why expect unconditional love from somebody you’ve brought into a fucked, dying planet, who then has to sit around and watch you screw it up even more?” So muses twentysomething college dropout Luke Ayrton on his parental lineage as he works the Las Vegas Strip, “comping girls for clubs” in Sin City. His job is to trawl the “plankton” of bacherlorette parties in order to lure the “whales” – rich men willing to spend to try to impress young women.“In this game your sociology skills sharpened,” it’s observed, but beyond the seedy side hustle lie weightier concerns: the matter of his family legacy. Electronic dance music aficionado and aspiring writer Luke is estranged from his Maga-positive Mom and Dad, and now lives with grandparents George and Molly, affluent boomers with a countercultural past.Vietnam vet and retired lawyer George sees himself as a “hippy sellout”, his dream of pursuing human rights advocacy corrupted by real estate deals and entertainment law. Actor Molly’s early theatre and independent cinema success led only to small parts in low-budget film and TV. Grandson Luke is set to inherit their fortune, yet struggles for meaning against a background of disappointment and growing despair: an intergenerational nihilism that deepens like a coastal shelf.double quotation markThis is a bold and ambitious work, in which Welsh deftly shifts point of view with confidence and convictionIrvine Welsh’s 16th novel Can Nothing Save Us? comes as something of a surprise. An epic American family saga, it explores a collective emotional malaise at the heart of a great power in decline. This is a bold and ambitious work, in which Welsh deftly shifts point of view with confidence and conviction: his ability to jump generations and to capture the voices and feelings of his disparate cast of characters is at times quite astonishing.Our author’s way into this garish universe is clearly via his familiarity with the Las Vegas club scene. There’s an early namecheck of Scottish DJ Calvin Harris, friend and collaborator with a long-term residency on the Strip. Welsh’s ear for the demotic is as strong as ever as he conveys the slang and grammar of Luke’s world, as well as the sense of being a small player on the periphery of a bewildering, drug-addled circuit. The theme of generational trench warfare is neatly set up at a legal meeting where Luke’s parents, Gina and Don, are informed of their disinheritance by Molly and George. A standard trope of family drama takes a Rabelaisian turn. “Me grow up?” Gina retorts at maternal accusations of immaturity. “You drink your own urine and walk around naked.” The elderly couple’s “urotherapy” remains a rather desperate last vestige of an alternative lifestyle, perhaps a metaphor for the diminished returns of a dying idealism. Welsh’s knack for absurd social satire is regularly deployed to interrogate serious themes and visit dark places.In Vietnam, George was a witness to the My Lai massacre, when hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese civilians were murdered by US soldiers. He is also a survivor of a lone gunman’s attack on the Las Vegas Strip from the Mandalay Bay Hotel in 2017. The buried trauma of past atrocities seems to feed a societal yearning for the freedom to bear arms. “The mass-shooting at Mandalay Bay had no long-term impact,” Welsh comments. “White Americans, at least on a conceptual level, didn’t mind being shot at by other white Americans; some even considered it their birthright.”Facing his own mortality, George excavates the past with his PTSD-ridden fellow veterans, as elsewhere in the land of the free a resigned feeling of rearmament reigns. An anonymous and ultra-disaffected “weapons engineer” is tooling up to settle his score with society. An ayahuasca ceremony at a desert commune descends into gun-toting mayhem. And on a hunting trip planned as a family bonding exercise, Luke finds himself aiming a rifle at his father, Don.The plot develops a mercilessly ballistic energy of its own as multiple storylines converge on another mass shooting, this time at an outdoor festival called Our Rave’s Electric. A complex and explosive denouement almost succumbs to the chaos it depicts, though in the end the only control on the narrative seems the fateful trajectory of a familiar American tragedy. Its inevitability only makes it all the more pitiful.We are left with a poignant coda of post-trauma, and a disturbing sense that this is merely part of an unending, generational cycle. Can Nothing Save Us? has apparently had a long gestation period, at one time in development as a TV project. That Welsh has finally realised this story in such an expansive, compelling and heartfelt novel is something of a literary triumph, proof that this medium remains the best kind of long-form narrative. And it’s certainly a late-career tour de force for the author himself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. title: Agent 64: Spies Never Die review – licence to kill time like the 90s never ended | Games | The Guardian
description: This GoldenEye 007-styled retro shooter is an agreeable set of straightahead shooting missions that hark back to a simpler time, with simpler controls
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This GoldenEye 007-styled retro shooter is an agreeable set of straightahead shooting missions that hark back to a simpler time, with simpler controls
Content: Polygon fighter … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Illustration: Replicant D6View image in fullscreenPolygon fighter … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Illustration: Replicant D6GamesReviewAgent 64: Spies Never Die review – licence to kill time like the 90s never endedPC; Replicant D6This GoldenEye 007-styled retro shooter is an agreeable set of straightahead shooting missions that hark back to a simpler time, with simpler controlsAlex SpencerThu 13 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith007 First Light, 2026 has already given us the best James Bond game in more than three decades, since the release of Rare’s N64 classic GoldenEye 007. But what about those players whose loyalties lie not with the super-spy himself but the particulars of that 90s interpretation of his adventures?Enter Agent 64: Spies Never Die. Made almost entirely by a single developer (who goes by the very cloak-and-dagger alias Replicant D6), its production values couldn’t be much further from the blockbuster First Light. There’s no voice acting, with all dialogue instead delivered via subtitles, while each location on your globe-trotting adventure is depicted by a repeating texture wallpapered over scenery so blocky you can count the individual polygons.View image in fullscreenFired up … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Illustration: Replicant D6In lieu of any high-budget flash, Agent 64’s big special effect is nostalgia. From the title onwards, this retro shooter is one long homage to GoldenEye, and to its un-Bonded successor, 2000’s Perfect Dark.Enemies have pinched facial features – a result of taking photographs of real people’s faces and wrapping them around diamond-shaped heads – and roll acrobatically from behind cover to take their next potshot, just as they used to. And yes, there’s a Big Head mode that swells those diamonds into enormous target-practice balloons.View image in fullscreenBrand new retro … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Illustration: Replicant D6Less explicably, Agent 64 retains the slightly strange control scheme of its inspirations, even though it doesn’t have to work around the (iconic but unwieldy) N64 pad that made it a necessity. You can pull a trigger for a zoomed-in precision aim, but somehow this is even fiddlier to steer with a modern analogue stick or mouse than it was back then. The first level features a pair of locks you must manually shoot; they remain the game’s toughest bosses.Better by far to just run and gun, letting the generous auto-aim do its thing. OK, the target your gun seeks out might not always be the one you expected, or wanted, but playing this way unlocks a hectic pace of action that – nostalgic warmth aside – is Agent 64’s greatest asset.It’s essential to the joys of split-screen deathmatch multiplayer, which generates the same kind of giggly fun that filled so many late 90s living rooms, especially once the match rules have been tweaked to allow only proximity mines or melee judo chops. (Youcanplay online, but this is so counter to the elbows-on-the-sofa appeal of the thing that I never actually attempt it.)Meanwhile, the story mode (which can be played solo or co-op with a partner) is so in hock to games of old that it ignores the subsequent 30 years of level-design knowhow. The number of dead ends and looping identical corridors can be infuriating, especially since dying means starting over from the beginning, but this is offset by the briskness of the missions. Each can be finished in less than five minutes, at which point the game will challenge you with a “par time” that often comes in undertwominutes.As you revisit these levels, trying to shave off vital seconds, their layouts begin to make much more sense. These are obstacle courses, really, where enemies aren’t so much a threat as they are something to be hurdled – or better yet, avoided. On top of this, Agent 64 piles hidden collectibles and challenge variants that recycle the levels in yet more ways, and their size makes them incredibly moreish.The fantasy on offer here isn’t really beingJames Bond. It’s being young again, with one illicitly acquired copy of GoldenEye to last you the summer and all the time in the world to pick the cartridge clean. For all its rough edges, that’s a mission Agent 64 pulls off with aplomb.Agent 64: Spies Never Die is out now, £19.64Explore more on these topicsGamesPCJames BondShooting gamesAdventure gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ham review – vegan take on Hamlet delivers meaty rebuke to carnivores | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Vengeance for a slaughtered pig is the starting point for a riotous parody that suggests the meat industry poses an existential threat to human survival
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Vengeance for a slaughtered pig is the starting point for a riotous parody that suggests the meat industry poses an existential threat to human survival
Content: Comeuppance for the sausage queen … Mary Higgins, left, and Ell Potter in Ham.Photograph: Jonny RuffView image in fullscreenComeuppance for the sausage queen … Mary Higgins, left, and Ell Potter in Ham.Photograph: Jonny RuffEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHam review – vegan take on Hamlet delivers meaty rebuke to carnivoresSummerhall, EdinburghVengeance for a slaughtered pig is the starting point for a riotous parody that suggests the meat industry poses an existential threat to human survivalKate WyverThu 13 Aug 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThat’s my next hotdog ruined. Shakespeare’s “too solid flesh” is squeezed into a sausage-shaped form in Mary Higgins and Ell Potter’s inventively guilt-trippy new show. Leaping wildly fromHamlet, this outrageous, confrontational performance-activism layers hooting comedy with world-ending dread as Mary (a vegan) attempts to persuade Potter (nicknamed “the sausage queen” by their dad) to change their meat-eating ways.Transposing Hamlet’s existential questions to the future survival of humanity via the meat industry’s impact on the planet, Higgins takes on the role of our stubborn, sauntering prince, seeking vengeance for the ghost of a poor, slaughtered, strangely seductive pig. Suave and silly, Potter is both ghost and Gertrude, the latter reading madness into the truth only her son is brave enough to face.Easy laughs are won through winking Shakespearean parody, but the further off-piste the show goes, the more Ham swerves what we already know and ignore, and jolts us into looking anew. Through naked dancing, a pet funeral, and a dom/sub relationship with a meat-eating member of the audience, this anarchic duo directs our avoidant gaze to our own impact on the planet. Though Higgins is on higher moral ground, Potter’s role is essential, with their effusive love of food stopping this from being purely haranguing – both for them and us – and twirling it into a genuine personal dilemma.Spin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundryRead moreThis isn’t about the murders of animals, Higgins says, but the suicide of the human race. (It’s also a bit about the murders of animals; they’re not afraid to show brutal, scarring images.) Inescapably a little preachy, the show is also riotously funny – until the very end when footage of recent forest fires blazes behind the performers. The clips start across the ocean and get closer: to Europe; the UK; Arthur’s Seat. It’s no longer a question of what might, or might not be.At Summerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Culture)TheatreFoodEdinburgh festivalFestivalsImmersive theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: As Far As We Know review – strange solo goes full pelt down the mean streets | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With increasing speed, Sam Ward tells the story of a woman who finds holes in her garden – but is it just a shaggy dog story?
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: With increasing speed, Sam Ward tells the story of a woman who finds holes in her garden – but is it just a shaggy dog story?
Content: Speed reader … Sam Ward in As Far As We Know.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenSpeed reader … Sam Ward in As Far As We Know.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAs Far As We Know review – strange solo goes full pelt down the mean streetsSummerhall, EdinburghWith increasing speed, Sam Ward tells the story of a woman who finds holes in her garden – but is it just a shaggy dog story?Mark FisherThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnd there is a man sitting at a desk, welcoming us to the theatre and opening a folder. And the folder contains a sheaf of paper that the man proceeds to read. And the more the man reads, the faster he goes. And the man hits such a speed we realise why he did not learn this script: it would be too prodigious a feat of memory.And as if to emphasise the pace, the man is soon accompanied by a percussive score byCarmel Smickersgill, which has a jazz freedom as well as a sense of urgency and is rather good. And as the story rattles out, so Han Sayles’s lighting design closes in on the man, who is the writer Sam Ward in this solo show by his companyYESYESNONOand he seems to be going faster still.And the story he tells is of a woman who discovers holes appearing in her garden and they are emitting a sound she cannot quite recognise. And as she tries to figure out the reason they are proliferating, she finds herself in a bank where there are next to no employees and even less money.Ten Ways to Die Happy review – gameshow invites you to don a robe and treasure timeRead moreAnd she is taken under the wing of a private detective straight out ofRaymond Chandlerwho only adds to her sense of disorientation, as do all the other strange events: the cave and the rooftop forest and the enigmatic messages telling her to look for the horizon.And as it plays out, you wonder whether this is a dreamlike odyssey with some insight to share – about what: uncertainty, alienation, the futile search for meaning? – or just a shaggy dog story that, for all the cool polish of its staging, goes around the houses for its own uncertain ends.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalFestivalsSummerhallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jordan Brookes: The Part of You That’s Always Screaming review – former fringe champ’s chewy croissant tale | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: This is a spiky, interrogative and surprisingly conventional set from an act who usually pushes standup to its limits
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: This is a spiky, interrogative and surprisingly conventional set from an act who usually pushes standup to its limits
Content: How are we affected by another’s gaze – or our own? …Jordan Brookes in The Part of You That's Always Screaming.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHow are we affected by another’s gaze – or our own? …Jordan Brookes in The Part of You That's Always Screaming.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewJordan Brookes: The Part of You That’s Always Screaming review – former fringe champ’s chewy croissant talePleasance Dome, EdinburghThis is a spiky, interrogative and surprisingly conventional set from an act who usually pushes standup to its limitsBrian LoganThu 13 Aug 2026 04.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 04.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can fall victim to your own high standards – and few comics have set higher standards than Jordan Brookes. A new show fromthe 2019 comedy award champis an event, at which half the fun is seeing how he’s monstered the form into some unforeseen new shape. If this year’s offering, The Part of You That’s Always Screaming, were delivered by any other comic, I’d be hailing it as one of the twistiest and deepest-thinking hours on the fringe. But it lacks Brookes’ usual ambition: its delivery is fairly conventional; things aren’t pushed as far as we expect.It’s all relative, mind you: this is still a set in which, at one unexpected moment, our comedian turns down the lights, turns up some disturbing industrial soundscape, and jerks threateningly across the stage. But then we act differently when we’re being watched – which is Brookes’ point here, in a show that worries intensely at the relationship between selfhood and being seen. It’s structured, deliciously, around an innocuous experience on a train, when Brookes snacking on a croissant becomes a performative act, awkwardly positioned as he is between the window and a window-gazing fellow passenger.Harriet Dyer: Easily Distra … review – how to sell a single shoe on eBay and other storiesRead moreHow are we affected by another’s gaze – or our own? Do you ever get tired of your own POV? What’s the worst thing cyber-hackers might see through your webcam? It’s always entertaining to trace the knotted thread of Brookes’ thinking, even as it spools away from the main subject, towards amusing standalone riffs on pickup artistry and (very droll, this) the idea of the super-strong mother who can lift a car to save her child.Really, I should be satisfied with the high quality of the comedy alone. But with Brookes, we’ve been trained to expect more, and I kept wondering when the opening routine, about the early film Train Pulling Into a Station, was going to get its stunt payoff, or what dramatic ending was in store for the croissant tale. These expectations were thwarted – but dial your expectations down merely to spiky and interrogative comedy, and they will be amply rewarded.AtPleasance Dome, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalJordan BrookesComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)FestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: We’re going to party like it’s 1629… the masques, the music and the mayhem of Banqueting House | Classical music | The Guardian
description: What music soundtracked 17th-century England? Ahead of a DJ set in Banqueting House, Georgia Mann looks at the wild, the experimental, the melancholic – and why a theorbo caused a security alert
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What music soundtracked 17th-century England? Ahead of a DJ set in Banqueting House, Georgia Mann looks at the wild, the experimental, the melancholic – and why a theorbo caused a security alert
Content: A scene from The Tempest at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, Stratford Upon Avon in 2016. Shakespeare’s play had its first recorded performance at the old Banqueting House in 1611.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from The Tempest at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, Stratford Upon Avon in 2016. Shakespeare’s play had its first recorded performance at the old Banqueting House in 1611.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianClassical musicWe’re going to party like it’s 1629… the masques, the music and the mayhem of Banqueting HouseWhat music soundtracked 17th-century England? Ahead of a DJ set in Banqueting House, Georgia Mann looks at the wild, the experimental, the melancholic – and why a theorbo caused a security alertGeorgia MannThu 13 Aug 2026 05.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 05.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing Charles is on the throne, there’s anxiety around the power-brokers of Whitehall, and an age of deep political division and conspiracy obsession is under way.That’s right, I’m referring to the middle years of the 17th century, a period I’m immersed in as I’m putting together a Jacobean-Carolean Classical DJ set, where the beats are to be dropped beneath one of the UK’s most awesome works of art: theRubens painted ceilingat the Banqueting House in Whitehall.After a period of restoration and conservation, the ceiling is on view again – and this weekend you’ll be able to feast your eyes on cherubim, goddesses and James I ascending to the celestial realm while listening to music that matches the visuals.double quotation markMasques were the 17th-century equivalent of a VIP ticket to Glastonbury, Glyndebourne and a Killing Kittens sex partyThe DJ set will see us segueing between music first performed in theBanqueting Housefour centuries ago, with lute songs and choral anthems employed as testament to the pioneering and introspective spirit of the age. This was an era in which amateur musicians had access, for the first time, to printed manuscripts; it was an era of heightened melancholy perfected by the Morrissey of his day, John Dowland; when the lute ushered in musical improvisation that John Coltrane and Jimi Hendrix would have relished. It was also an era of masques.Masqueswere the 17th-century equivalent of a VIP ticket to Glastonbury, Glyndebourne and a Killing Kittens sex party. Banqueting House’s architect, Inigo Jones, was also the set and costume designer of these masques, which encompassed opera, theatre, ballet and balland were always allegorical affairs, with mythological gods and goddesses parading around in outrageous costumes. These extravagant performances reinforced the divine right of the Stuart monarchy, and the audiencecourtiers, aristocracy dignitaries and diplomats – was seated according to status and rank. Masques also involved plenty of bad behaviour, with reports of performers in outrageous costume sometimes so hammered on stage that they vomited, and a chaotic tradition of the audience smashing up the refreshments table at the end of the show.View image in fullscreenOne of the last things Charles I saw on this earth: the Apotheosis of James I painted ceiling by  Rubens inside Banqueting House Royal Palace, Whitehall, London.Photograph: John Bingham/AlamyMusic was intrinsic to the power play at the Banqueting House, and much of it was wildly experimental. Jacobean music specialist and lutenist Elizabeth Kenny showcases some of the best of it on her album,The Masque of Moments. Masques would generally have featured three groups of instruments, she says: “A brass group, which often represented the underworld; a big band of violins, which accompanied the dancing that went on for hours; and a group in the middle made up of voices, lutes and viols. That group experimented with coloratura singing – cascades of notes – that would have blown people’s minds at the time.”The aristos were fully in on the action. Charles I’s wife, Henrietta Maria, danced the lead role in the masque Tempe Restored, in which she was lowered from the ceiling on a jewelled chariot. Strong Beyoncé energy. She was also rumoured to have been romantically involved with a star lutenist of the day, Jacques Gaultier – who obtained rock-star status for the way he played the treble lute, a tiny instrument that became a major element of the masques. (The lute section ranged from the teeny treble all the way through to a new-fangled beast of an instrument from Italy: the theorbo, a bass lute with an enormously long neck.) Importing musical ideas from Italy was de rigeur in the early 17th-century. Inigo Jones is said to be the person who brought the first theorbo to England. Apparently he was detained at the Jacobean version of customs because officials thought he had smuggled in a “popish machine” with which to assassinate the King.It was a lutenist, Robert Johnson, who composed music for the first ever performance of Shakespeare’s The Tempest at the Banqueting House in November 1611. Johnson wrote the song settings for Where the Bee Sucks and Full Fathom Five, music we still use today. Ruby Hughes performsFull Fathom Fiveon her recent album, Amidst the Shades; her pared back purity of tone perfectly captures the sense of an otherworldly, mournful spirit.Dowland was another contemporary of Shakespeare’s. He was a lutenist, composer, singer and master of melancholy, opting for cheery titles to his songs such as In Darkness Let Me Dwell and Flow My Tears. His greatest modern-day interpreter is the countertenor Iestyn Davies.“We have to really tune in to these songs,” Davies says. “We misunderstand this music as delicate and quiet, [but] it’s incredibly expressive. That’s why people like Sting get so hooked on it.” (Sting released an album of Dowland’s musicin 2006.) Listen to Davies singFlow My Tearsto experience what sadness meant in this era. “You need melancholy to cure your melancholy,” explains Davies of the belief at the time. “Songs were a way to access a deep sadness, and then get through it.”A year before Dowland’s death, Charles I ascended to the throne, an altogether different kingly creature to his father, James. Charles’s absolutist tendencies led to the schism with parliament, the civil war and, eventually, his death on the scaffold erected just outside the Banqueting House, where he was beheaded on 30 January 1649. Rubens’ epic painted ceiling was one of the last things Charles saw on this earth.Charles’s favourite composer was William Lawes, who fought and died for the king as a royalist soldier. Lawes’ Royal Consort Sets are written for viol consort, accompanied by a bass line of two plucked string instruments. They have a shadowy depth to them, flitting between dance forms of the day and a soulful solemnity that make for a poignant underscore to Charles’s final words: “I go from a corruptible to an incorruptible crown, where no disturbance can be.”View image in fullscreenPortrait of the composer John Dowland (1563-1626).Photograph: Album/AlamyLawes also wrote some exquisite sacred vocal music. The French early music ensemble Près de votre oreille (Close to your ear) recorded an album of it calledLighten Mine Eieslast year; the opening funeral elegy,Music, the Master of thy Art is Dead, is surely some of the most ethereally lovely music ever written about death.A new era at the Banqueting House dawned: that of the Lord Protector himself, Oliver Cromwell. I was surprised to discover that the man who led the Puritan government, which banned Christmas carols and shut down theatres, made the lavish environs of the Banqueting House his primary hall of audience in 1654.The Lord Protector was, in fact, a music lover who had his favourite organ from Magdalen College, Oxford, installed at his lavish apartments at Hampton Court, and employed various musicians to perform there. AsCromwell biographer Paul Layputs it, there’s a “spectrum of puritanism” and, ironically enough, Cromwell was at the milder end of it.And yet, thanks to the zealots, the theatres were shut and many musicians of the era found themselves forced to make a living playing in taverns and alehouses – the inspiration behind the hugely enjoyable Alehouse Sessions album by Norwegian early music ensemble Barokksolistene. It’s thought that these musical meetings during the Commonwealth era were the earliest public concerts in Britain.England’s republic was not destined to last anywhere near as long as Rubens’ ceiling, and the Interregnum officially ended on 29 May 1660. That same day, on his 30th birthday, Charles II made a triumphant return, processing through London and arriving at the Banqueting House to have his hand kissed by the gathered parliamentarians. This king had a taste for the theatre, and for actresses, and under the Merry Monarch the playhouses returned with ever more spectacular restoration entertainment.The 17th century closed with the destruction of almost all of the old palace at Whitehall in a massive fire. Banqueting House was left standing – but there were no more masquesthere – under the Georgians it became a chapel and under Victoria a military museum.As we prepare to return this music to the gloriously opulent space where it would have been heard 400 years ago, I’m reminded of lines from The Tempest, a play all about the power of theatre and the thin walls between fantasy and reality. Those ascendant Rubens paintings of a divinely ordained monarch will once again resound, as Prospero and Caliban’s island did, a place: “full of noises, Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight, and hurt not”.Classical DJ is at the Banqueting House, London, on 15 and 16 August.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicMonarchyOperafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: RSC postpones Othello while leading actor Sharon D Clarke has cancer treatment | Sharon D Clarke | The Guardian
description: Radical reimagining of Shakespeare play was due to run at Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon from 13 February to 3 April 2027
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Radical reimagining of Shakespeare play was due to run at Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon from 13 February to 3 April 2027
Content: Clarke, a three-time Olivier winner, said she had been overwhelmed by the ‘tidal wave of love’.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClarke, a three-time Olivier winner, said she had been overwhelmed by the ‘tidal wave of love’.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianSharon D ClarkeRSC postpones Othello while leading actor Sharon D Clarke has cancer treatmentRadical reimagining of Shakespeare play was due to run at Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon from 13 February to 3 April 2027Nadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentThu 13 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheRoyal Shakespeare Companyhas announced that it will postpone its radical production of Othello starring Sharon D Clarke, while the Olivier-winning actor undergoes treatment for cancer.The production, directed by Monique Touko, was scheduled to run from 13 February to 3 April 2027 at the Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon. Clarke, 60, is best known for her role as Lola Griffin in the BBC medical drama Holby City, as well as for her theatrical performances in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom and Caroline, or Change.In a statement on Thursday, Clarke said: “I would like to thank all the beautiful people at the RSC for their understanding, love, support and healing energy. Othello will be my north star as I undergo treatment.”She added that she, her family and wife – the writer and director Susie McKenna – had been “overwhelmed, humbled and buoyed by the tidal wave of love that we have received and are so blessed to have an army of strength and support to hold us up. Love and thanks to my beautiful people.”The RSC said anyone with tickets to see Clarke in Othello would be automatically refunded and a replacement production period would be announced at a later date.Touko, whose recent work has included Marie & Rosetta at @sohoplace and Jaja’s African Hair Braiding at the Lyric Hammersmith, said: “On behalf of the entire creative team, we send Sharon all the love for her ongoing treatment and recovery.“As a director, I have been incredibly blessed to collaborate with Sharon on this major reframing of Shakespeare’s tragedy, which reimagines Shakespeare’s Othello through the lens of misogynoir. Sharon is the ultimate collaborator. Her generosity and passion for this project continues to astound me and I look forward to us coming back together when the time is right to share this production with the world.”The RSC described the show as “set in a climate-threatened future in which a Black lesbian holds a seat of power”.It said it “re-imagines Shakespeare’s 400-year-old story through the lens of misogynoir, as an unsanctioned marriage perilously crosses boundaries of race, sex and status, allowing jealousy, suspicion and malign intent to close in.”The RSC’s co-artistic directors, Daniel Evans and Tamara Harvey, said Clarke’s casting as Othello was integral to Touko’s adaptation, “which is why we have taken the difficult decision to postpone, to give Sharon the time and space she needs to undertake treatment”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey added: “Sharon is, in every sense of the word, a warrior, and we know she will meet this challenge with the unwavering strength and indomitable spirit that she brings to so many aspects of her life and work. We look forward to revisiting this thrilling collaboration in the future and, on behalf of everyone at the RSC, we send Sharon our love and strength for a full recovery.”A three-time Olivier winner, Clarke has worked consistently on stage and screen since her first TV role in 1986’s The Singing Detective. Most recently, she starred as Lady Bracknell opposite Ncuti Gatwa in the National Theatre’s production of The Importance of Being Earnest.Explore more on these topicsSharon D ClarkeRoyal Shakespeare CompanyTheatrenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I wanted to capture the range of British culture at the time’: the photographer who documented late nights on the 90s London tube | Photography | The Guardian
description: In the 1990s, Mark McEvoy took portraits of punks, partiers and late-night lovers on the underground. His images show city life before smartphones – when people still had to rush to make the final train
Author: Luke Turner
Headline: In the 1990s, Mark McEvoy took portraits of punks, partiers and late-night lovers on the underground. His images show city life before smartphones – when people still had to rush to make the final train
Content: Crush hour … A couple on the Victoria line, 1993.Photograph: Mark McEvoyView image in fullscreenCrush hour … A couple on the Victoria line, 1993.Photograph: Mark McEvoyPhotography‘I wanted to capture the range of British culture at the time’: the photographer who documented late nights on the 90s London tubeIn the 1990s, Mark McEvoy took portraits of punks, partiers and late-night lovers on the underground. His images show city life before smartphones – when people still had to rush to make the final trainLuke TurnerThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark McEvoy’s tube photographs, taken inLondon Undergroundcarriages at around 11pm on Friday and Saturday nights from 1992 to 1995, capture moments that may seem superficially frivolous, but might be the most significant of our lives. These are the golden hours of the end of the week, where friendships are found and sealed; gabbled conversation rolls along with the sway of the carriages; and new lovers meet up en route for an encounter that may turn out to be a fleeting one-off, or in fact the beginnings of a lifelong companionship.All are swept along in the scramble to hop onboard the last tube – a panic that ended when all-night services began on some lines 10 years ago this month. The night tube arrived when my time of going out all weekend was fading, and gave me a slight feeling of missing out. Looking at photos of other people’s social lives can make one feel like that too; at the same time, it’s not hard to see ourselves in these tired, happy and thoughtful faces.These images feel so natural in part because McEvoy was not a voyeur but a participant in London’s mid-90s nightlife. Living in a shared flat in Camden Town, northLondon, he was part of the capital’s music scene, describing himself as “slightly hippy-ish, trendy, kind of casual, into funk, jazz and reggae”; he “smoked a lot of weed”. One night, travelling home from Brixton, he was struck by being surrounded by a very London mixture of people of different ages, races, sexualities and pop-cultural scenes – the tube carriage became a beautiful stage. “We’ve all been there,” he says of the underground train. “We can straight away relate to that space.”Thus inspired, he spent the next two years going underground around traditional pub closing time on Friday and Saturday nights. Most of the pictures were taken after McEvoy had asked his subjects for permission, and he found that usually they’d pose for a shot, then just carry on doing what they were doing before.The images are rooted in their time by the old wooden-floored rolling stock and tube seat patterns, and by the fashions of London’s subcultures: casuals, rockabillies, goths, and punks doing the punk thing and responding to requests for a photo by baring their arses. McEvoy documented the last years of the fiercely tribal nature of British youth culture before it was flattened out by the internet, as streaming homogenised music tastes.The lack of smartphones in these photos is striking. Yet the energy in them feels curiously universal, expressive of a particularly British shedding of reserve and the joy of closing time and just before, when a good night brings up the feeling that there’s always the potential for something more.Even today, with gen Z drinking far less than their predecessors, you still see similar scenes on the underground, although at 4am the train rattles along more quietly, carrying more wreckage. The life in the faces that McEvoy snapped three decades ago endures in a new generation, and even in those of us who are old enough to know better but still sometimes find ourselves rushing for the night tube. How can it not? It’s the eternal energy of London, written on skin and flesh; rage and laughter, smiles and tears.‘We’ve all been there, we can all relate’: Mark McEvoy on five of his night tube photographs(Main picture, above) “This couple were nuzzling up to each other, and when I asked if I could take a picture, they said yes straight away and started kissing. It was kind of a performance, but then it wasn’t. They thought: oh, this guy’s asked to take a picture; come on, let’s give him this. Or maybe they were about to kiss anyway.”View image in fullscreenSunglasses at night … An American Londoner on the Northern line, 1992.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“This passenger told me he’d just moved from the States. The big reason was because he got shot in the shoulder in gang crossfire. We started talking about the difference between America and England, and he said it was getting as bad here. I guess he was feeling the London tension.”View image in fullscreenMind the gap … A passenger seeming to pray on the Piccadilly line, 1994.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“The other side of my photography is capturing these moments. This is one of my favourite pictures in a way, because I obviously didn’t ask him to sit there, and he may or may not be praying. There were a few candid ones like that; people just crashed out, maybe having a rough time.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSubway sect … Punks larking about on the Northern line, circa 1990.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“I was very aware of all these different lives just passing each other, different backgrounds, ages, groups, tribes. I wanted to try to capture the variety of that: the wide range of British culture in that space at that moment.”View image in fullscreenTrain in vain … Revellers look for the party on New Year’s Eve, Jubilee line, 1994.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“These guys were running through the compartments. New Year’s Eve had just struck, so they thought: well, we’re not going to be able to make it up to Trafalgar Square, so let’s go crazy here.”View image in fullscreenUninvited guest … A lairy fellow traveller on the Northern line, 1993.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“He was drunk. As I stood up to get off, he said he wanted to be my assistant and followed me everywhere I went. He started talking to this Irish couple. I didn’t even know what they said, but within five seconds they started punching each other; it was mayhem. Then the train stopped. I just backed off the train very slowly and watched the doors close and the whole commotion disappear.”Mark McEvoy’s zineLondon Underground 1992-1995is out now. A selection of the tube series photos is planned for display at the London Transport Museum in spring 2027.Explore more on these topicsPhotographyArtLondonLondon UndergroundTransportfeaturesShareReuse this content
