title: You be the judge: should my girlfriend stop annotating her books? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Julie makes notes in the margin as she’s reading, but Charlie says she’s ruining books he may want to read. Should they get on the same page? You decide
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Julie makes notes in the margin as she’s reading, but Charlie says she’s ruining books he may want to read. Should they get on the same page? You decide
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my girlfriend stop annotating her books?Julie makes notes in the margin as she’s reading, but Charlie says she’s ruining books he may want to read. Should they get on the same page? You decideFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution:Charliedouble quotation markIt breaks my immersion in the stories – like when someone says ‘This next bit is so good’Julie can’t read without a pen in her hand. She writes all over every book: underlining, writing over things, crossing things out. When she explains it to people, she makes it sound fun. She says it’s because she’s an author – her first book is due out this year. She makes it sound like she’s adding quality, writerly insights to the pages, but it’s actually just random connective comments like “lol” written in the margins.I’ve asked her to stop as it breaks my immersion in the stories. It’s like when someone says “This next bit is so good” when you’re watching a film. She doesn’t write spoilers and some of her comments are interesting, but they still distract you from the story. It also denies me the opportunity of a relationship with the writer of the book. Julie is a writer herself, so should value this. We read the same books, but I have to buy an extra copy because I can’t bear reading hers. In our small flat – and in a cost of living crisis – we have too many books and too little space. We can’t afford to keep buying books. She uses a pen for her annotations, which makes it even harder to ignore. She should ask herself: “Is this a book that Charlie wants to read?”double quotation markShe accuses me of skim-reading … It hurts when she dismisses my feelings about thisI am in a book club and I ask Julie for recommendations, but we can’t lend books to friends because of her annotations. Julie says I shouldn’t care about this as she buys her own books. She accuses me of skim-reading and said it shouldn’t affect me, but I’m a deep reader. It hurts when she dismisses my feelings about this.We’ve been together for two years and it’s always been an issue. She says she wants us to read more of the same books but her annotations put me off.Reading books covered in graffiti is not fun. It’s a bit like how kids shouldn’t put toys in their mouth if others want to play with them. However, I know I will have to continue reading Julie’s books with the annotations because she won’t change.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThe defence: Juliedouble quotation markHe says what I write doesn’t make sense, but it does to me – I’m a writer, it’s part of my workI get that it’s distracting if I underline or write a comment in a book, but I shouldn’t have to justify my actions if it’s a book I’ve bought.My own book is due out later this year and this is how I work. I don’t think Charlie and me have to share everything if it’s work-related. I don’t say to him: “Stop doing that thing for your job, so I can make more use of it.”Charlie says what I write in the books doesn’t make sense, but it does to me. Annotating books is part of my work. When I’m struggling to write, reading a book really helps me. I’ll often circle or underline words like “and”, “but”, “she” and “he”. When I write in the margins, it is sometimes as brief as “lol”; others it’s an insight, such as “but what about the impact on her daughter?”double quotation markI can count on one hand the amount of times our book choices might have overlappedI’m an avid reader, whereas Charlie isn’t. He is in a book club with his friends but only reads for that. He skim-reads and usually we read different books. He says I shouldn’t annotate my books in case he wants to read one, but I can count on one hand the amount of times our book choices might have overlapped.On holiday once, Charlie borrowed a book of mine and said: “This is quite a distracting thing you do.” But I don’t think annotating is unusual. I always see people writing in books on the train or on Instagram. Charlie says we need to buy two copies of each book but I disagree. He could just go and borrow one from the library.Recently, he asked to borrow a book. Before I lent it to him, I showed him the writing inside and he said it was fine and readable, so it’s clearly not a consistent issue.Charlie says we can’t lend annotated books to friends but I’ve never given away a book, so that’s not an issue. I like to go back and re-read them, and as we live near my parents, we have space to keep all my books there. I shouldn’t have to change the way I read. I could write in pencil to appease Charlie, but he said it wouldn’t make a difference to his reading experience.Names have been changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersJulie’s habit might help her, but it’s preventing Charlie from enjoying books. If she wants to annotate them, she could use sticky notes or page-marker tabs, which would also make it easy for her to find the sections she finds inspiring or interesting.Iris, 28I would never write in a book myself, but this is obviously important to Julie’s enjoyment of reading. Charlie wants to stop her annotating “in case” he decides to read the book after her. If they plan to share a book in future, he should read it first.Tricia, 64Books are sacrosanct. It is allowable to mark up one’s own textbooks, but never acceptable to write on someone else’s prose – and certainly not if it’s little more than graffiti.Andrew, 70I was pro-Charlie when he said they both read the same books, but Julie denied that. So she’s entitled to mess up her own books if she must. Personally, I’ve underlined etc when researching, but otherwise I respect authors too much to deface their work.Peter, 75I see how Julie’s notes could distract Charlie, but reading is a personal, private activity and everyone interacts with books differently, especially the likes of Julie, who is a writer herself. They’re lucky to have a library nearby – that sounds like a solution.Victoria, 59Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us who you will throw the book atThe poll closes on Wednesday 19 August at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked:should Declan put the brakes on his road rage93%of you said yes –Declan is guilty7%of you said no –Declan is not guiltyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgeRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve been on plenty of dates – but nothing happened’: are we looking at the death of the kiss? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Call it a crisis, call it a decline, call it a recession: the long, lusty snog is in trouble, harder to experience in real life or even watch on screen. But why? And what’s it like to think you may never lock lips with another?
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Call it a crisis, call it a decline, call it a recession: the long, lusty snog is in trouble, harder to experience in real life or even watch on screen. But why? And what’s it like to think you may never lock lips with another?
Content: The way we were … George Peppard and Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany’s, 1961.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe way we were … George Peppard and Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany’s, 1961.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyLife and style‘I’ve been on plenty of dates – but nothing happened’: are we looking at the death of the kiss?Call it a crisis, call it a decline, call it a recession: the long, lusty snog is in trouble, harder to experience in real life or even watch on screen. But why? And what’s it like to think you may never lock lips with another?Elle HuntThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpencer’s last kiss was two years ago, on a first date. It started off promisingly: after matching on Tinder, they met for a walk, then got drinks and ice-cream, before having dinner at her place. Finally, they kissed. “I didn’t like it,” says Spencer. He still struggles to identify why. “I found her attractive. There was chemistry, but something was lacking. There was nothing behind the kiss – it felt like a mechanical thing to do.”That wasn’t just Spencer’s most recent kiss – it was his first ever, at the age of 29. Now 31, he says a second kiss in some ways feels less possible than having sex: “The jump feels way bigger.”We are living through a crisis of intimacy: more people are reportedly single and having less sex. But behind those headlines there is a smaller but no less significant finding: we may also be in a kissing recession. In a recent YouGov survey, commissioned by oral care brand Waken, more than a third of British adults reported kissing romantically less often than they did five years ago. Nearly one in five hadn’t been kissed in more than a year, while 27% believed kissing is becoming less common.For gen Z in particular, self-consciousness may be a factor. The Waken survey found that those aged 18 to 24 fretted about the “right moment” for a kiss, and whether they might be bad at it. A third said they had avoided a kiss because they lacked confidence. This tallies with research consistently showing that young people today are more risk-averse than those in the past, abstaining not just from sex but also from alcohol and drugs.Blair, who is 24 and non-binary, has only had three kisses in total since their teens, despite a six-year long-distance relationship. “Even though we had been together for years, I felt quite self-conscious, insecure and daunted by having so little experience,” they say. Now, “the thought of kissing someone I don’t know to the same degree makes me want to shrink away like a turtle”. They say they’ve always lacked confidence, but it worsened through the Covid-19 pandemic. Today, like many in their generation, they prefer the homebody lifestyle. “I have never been to a bar or club, I have never tried dating … I barely go anywhere that isn’t work or the cinema – which is to say, I never find or put myself in situations where kissing someone is even a possibility,” they say. “Even if I did, I don’t think I could find the nerve.”Though more pronounced in gen Z, this risk aversion – linked to less time spent face-to-face with friends – goes broader. “People are not talking to strangers, or asking each other on dates,” says Sarah Stein Lubrano, a social theorist who is writing a book about this “social atrophy”. Kissing is a telling example, because it makes use of skills such as reading facial expressions, body language and subtle social cues that may be getting rusty with our dependence on tech. Its reported decline should concern us all, Lubrano says, “not because everyone needs to be in romantic relationships, but because overall it means less social connection, less commitment, less belonging”.Compared with the challenges of finding a partner or having sex, kisses may seem trivial, especially to older generations who exchanged them freely. But the reported kissing recession is part of a broader breakdown in connection, attributed to the rise in digital communication, the decline of shared spaces and nightlife, shifting gender relations and even fears of surveillance. When two people were filmed kissing in New York’s Central Park last month, the clip went viral, attracting 4 million views on TikTok and manymocking comments.Kissing has always been a mirror of its times, says Katie Barclay, a professor at Macquarie University, Sydney. In her new book The Kiss: A History of Passion and Power, she traces its evolution since medieval times and concludes that we really are kissing less today. Through the 19th century the kiss became the main symbol of romantic and physical intimacy, but as culture has become more visual and explicit, romantic kissing has receded in prominence and meaning. “It’s not as interesting – it doesn’t have the same erotic capacity as it used to, which is maybe why people are kissing less in general,” Barclay says.View image in fullscreen‘Romantic kissing has receded in prominence’ … Dev Patel and Freida Pinto in Slumdog Millionaire.Photograph: PictureLux/The Hollywood Archive/AlamyIn these pornified times, first base scarcely registers. A 2022 studyfound that kissingwas “significantly less prevalent” in male-female pornographic videos than in the typical experiences of American adults. Even romantic comedies might foreground sex over the “snog on the couch” leading up to it, Barclay points out. And while kissing may be glossed over publicly, privately the issue has become more fraught, with the #MeToo movement raising awareness of the importance of consent. Though a positive shift, this adds another layer of complexity and raises the stakes of misjudging the moment. “Now it can be, and is, seen as a harm,” Barclay says.That seriousness has complicated a youthful rite of passage. “I’m definitely very self-conscious about romantic intimacy – but it’s not for lack of trying,” says Carrie, 23. Her final two-and-a-half years of secondary school were conducted online due to the pandemic: “I do feel like I missed out.” Carrie has been on “plenty” of dates since, “but nothing has happened – it’s frustrating”. She feels scared and too inexperienced to make a move; her dates may have felt the same, she adds. “I’m not sure how to take charge in those situations. I don’t want to look like an idiot.”Carrie nonetheless remains hopeful. Older people who have missed out on the milestone fear their moment has passed. “I put myself out there, but no one is interested,” says Joseph, 36. He uses dating apps, has gone to singles events and feels confident approaching women, but says it has never led to an opportunity to kiss. “In the past, you had places to connect locally and strike up relationships, whether platonic or not. It allowed you to build up social skills. Nowadays, people are glued to their phones and stay at home.”View image in fullscreenToulouse-Lautrec’s In Bed, the Kiss, 1892.Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesEven if it didn’t lead to more, Joseph says a kiss would give him confidence and hope, “the sense of being wanted – the experience of it”. He worries that there is something wrong with him, and that he will for ever be unloved and alone. Therapy hasn’t helped. “I’ve learned not to hope any more because it just brings about a lot of pain.”Joseph emphasises that he doesn’t hold women responsible for his situation, but he fears his inexperience will become more of a disadvantage as he gets older. “Let’s face it: a guy that hasn’t had a kiss in his mid-30s is seen as a major red flag to some women, consciously or unconsciously.”Rodrigo, 31, conceals his lack of experience from friends, afraid of ridicule and being judged as a misogynistic “incel”. “Unfortunately, we all get grouped in that negative category,” he says. He has no time for men who blame their lack of sexual success on women, instead of looking inward. “Some of those guys have become really blind to what’s wrong with them.”Rodrigo believes his barrier is dating apps: in 12 years, he’s never landed a date. “I think people like myself, who are below-average attractiveness, feel we have no chance at all.” Social media, circulating dating horror stories, has stoked his fear of rejection. He tries to stay positive, take breaks from dating and busies himself with work, but periodically feels “depressed and sad and angry at myself”. He still desires a relationship, and the validation of a kiss, but even that increasingly feels impossible. “I think, deep down, I’ve given up hope.”Dolly, 35, has not had a kiss since early 2020. Before the pandemic, she says: “I was the kind of person who could just kiss someone on a night out, and it would be fun and silly – then something changed.” She puts this down to intimacy issues stemming from past traumas, which have felt more pronounced with age, and clarity about the connection she is looking for. As a lesbian, she feels grateful to be spared the increasingly fraught heterosexual dating scene, but says kissing has come to feel more weighty and consequential. “Now, if I’m going to kiss someone, they have to be someone I really, really trust,” she says.Dolly admits she misses how easy kissing used to feel, when she was younger “and things didn’t really matter”, but she doesn’t feel any urgency. “I have my friends, who I adore. I don’t feel like something is missing.” She has noticed her straight teenage sister is also unbothered by dating, focusing instead on her social life and studies. “Apparently her and her friends just don’t care. When I was at school it was all about who you fancied.” It reflects a broader reported trend of women giving less priority to romance and love, often citing a lack of desirable partners and stubbornly unequal dynamics, with kissing the casualty – or sacrifice.For Catriona, 55, the eight-year gap since her last kiss reflects her flourishing, not failing. She says she has “opted out” of dating because of the lack of emotionally intelligent men ready for a mature, equal relationship, and that many gen X women are doing the same: “I want to date a partner, not a project.” That precludes kissing, with Catriona preferring her own company to being intimate “for intimacy’s sake. Long, lingering kisses are wonderful, and something I miss from time to time, but I am no longer willing to just kiss anyone.” She “wouldn’t be concerned about kissing someone after all these years,” she adds, “but only after hours of conversation, and after I’d looked for green flags.”View image in fullscreen‘Long, lingering kisses are wonderful’ … the kiss scene in the film Moonlight.Photograph: A24Catriona is grateful for the experiences of her youth. “My God, I am glad I did all my kissing practice before the modern internet,” she says – mostly in nightclubs, “with random boys”. She has sympathy for younger generations, who don’t feel so “free to goof around and make mistakes”. Factoring in the UK’sdeclining nightlifesector, rising costs and dangers such as drink-spiking, “it’s far harder to meet someone to kiss than it was in the 1990s”, she says.If kissing really is in decline, that is a societal problem, down to the absence of social infrastructure for young adults in particular, Lubrano says. “We need places where people can hang out for extended periods and maybe eventually get to a position where they would want to kiss.” But that doesn’t mean, in the meantime, that individuals are powerless.Kissing’s challenges and complications might be being overstated relative to the rewards, Lubrano says. The most likely negative consequence of attempting a kiss is rejection and embarrassment, she says – which, though painful, brings valuable experience, proving it’s possible to venture beyond your comfort zone. That’s why kissing matters, separate from love, sex and relationships: “If people don’t take even the risk of kissing, we’re really not going to take bigger, more important risks.”For Spencer, the desire at least is there. The challenge is in staying open, and alive to opportunity. “I don’t care about kissing, or sex at this point,” he says. “I just want connection.”Names of all case studieshave been changedThe Kiss by Katie Barclay is out now (Reaktion Books, £20). title: Do I really need air conditioning in the UK? The best portable aircon tested – plus the pros, cons and alternatives | Summer | The Guardian
description: As hotter summers become the norm, home aircon can feel increasingly tempting. We put six units to the test for cooling power, noise and energy use – and explain what you need to know before buying
Author: Caramel Quin
Headline: As hotter summers become the norm, home aircon can feel increasingly tempting. We put six units to the test for cooling power, noise and energy use – and explain what you need to know before buying
Content: Cool dog? A portable unit can make hot, restless nights more manageable.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCool dog? A portable unit can make hot, restless nights more manageable.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianThe FilterSummerDo I really need air conditioning in the UK? The best portable aircon tested – plus the pros, cons and alternativesAs hotter summers become the norm, home aircon can feel increasingly tempting. We put six units to the test for cooling power, noise and energy use – and explain what you need to know before buyingHow to sleep in a heatwaveCan air conditioning be green?Caramel QuinThu 13 Aug 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Tell people you’re testing air conditioning, and the truth soon comes out: far more people have aircon than you’d ever imagine. It’s a guilty secret, the home improvement equivalent of Botox or weight loss jabs – everyone notices the results, but nobody admits to the method. Most portable aircons are in bedrooms, hidden away from visitors, so they’re easy to keep secret. And while friends with aircon don’t suddenly look younger or slimmer, they do look suspiciously well rested during a heatwave, while you’ve spent the night tossing and turning.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.So if you’re using an aircon unit, why have it in the bedroom? Warm air rises, so upstairs bedrooms can be the hottest by the end of the day, making for restless nights. And if your bedroom is in a loft conversion, it’s even worse: the roof absorbs the sun’s heat all day before radiating it back into the room after dark.Most UK homes are built to retain heat, not shed it. Cooling an entire home is difficult and expensive, but a single aircon unit can make at least one room – and a good night’s sleep – more achievable.So, should you get aircon? And if you do, should you feel guilty about it? Yes and no. It depends on how you power it, whether the machine is built to last, and whether you really need it.We are in aclimate crisis. This year’s hot summer hasn’t been a blip. In fact, extreme heat and flooding will worsen in the coming years. We got into this mess by burning fossil fuels, and we continue to do so, so the carbon footprint of your cooling matters. You could be making the problem worse by opting to have air conditioning. Unless you’re on a renewable tariff – or even better, producing itself yourself with solar panels – electricity use accelerates climate breakdown. (If you are looking to move to a renewable tariff, it’s worthresearching those that invest most in renewables.)Before you buy, read the “What you need to know” section at the bottom of this page on the global warming potential (GWP) of refrigerants. These are used in air-conditioning units, as well as fridges, freezers, heat pumps and other appliances that move heat. Some refrigerants have a global warming impact hundreds, or even thousands, of times greater than the same amount of CO2 if they escape into the atmosphere.We were facing our fifth heatwave of the year at the time of writing, and unsurprisingly, portable air conditioning units had been in high demand. None of the options I’ve recommended is currently in stock, with the first restock due in late November, and many more expected in March 2027. If you want a good-quality, well-recommended unit that’s built to last, bear that in mind. So take your time: these units are big investments built to last, and there’s lots to consider.How can I avoid using air conditioning?View image in fullscreenFan favourite: moving air across your skin helps sweat evaporate, making hot days more bearable.Photograph: Westend61/GettyFansThere are cheaper (and greener) alternatives to air conditioning, includingfansandevaporative air coolers, both of which I’ve tested for the Filter. Fans don’t actually lower a room’s temperature; they simply move air across your skin, helping sweat evaporate and making you feel cooler, like a breeze on a hot day.If you decide to go with a fan, buy a good one (my favourite,the Lume, is now on preorder for delivery from 31 August). Cheap models are often noisy, with much of that noise being wasted energy. A well-engineered fan is noticeably quieter and more effective.As you might have already discovered, fans and air coolers often sell out during hot weather, especially the good ones. If you find a model you like on preorder, it’s usually worth reserving it. Sadly, we’re likely to see more heatwaves.Air coolersEvaporative air coolerswork by drawing warm air through water-soaked pads. As the water evaporates, it absorbs heat, cooling the air by a degree or two, before it’s blown back into the room. The result isn’t the fridge-like chill of an air conditioner, but a gentler cooling effect – like a sea breeze on a hot day. The trade-off is that the fans built into evaporative coolers are often less powerful, so you don’t get the strong blast of air that you get from a standard fan.Importantly, evaporative coolers (sometimes known as swamp coolers) humidify your air, so aren’t a good option if you have damp and mould problems. They’re designed to be used with doors open and fresh air circulating. Many of the ones I recommend are now out of stock, but my favourite portable option, theMorphy Richards Flexi Freeze, was available at the time of writing.Keeping cool without electricityThere are natural ways to cool your home, too. The problem is that most houses in the UK have been designed to retain heat, not cope with prolonged hot weather.In countries where super-hot summers are the norm, homes are often built with high-thermal-mass walls, which warm up and cool down slowly, and external shutters that block the sun from entering through windows.We’ve written in depth aboutalternative ways to keep your home cool this summer. Closing and covering windows can keep out hot air and block solar heat by day – then opening them in the evening lets cooler air into your home, flushing out not just warm air but also the heat stored in your walls.If your home has windows on opposite sides, open both in the evening so cool air can blow through. If you live on more than one level, open windows upstairs and downstairs in the evening. Warm air will rise out of the top windows and will be replaced by cooler air that’s drawn in at the lower level.The case for air conditioningView image in fullscreenShutter speed: blocking out the sun by day can help keep indoor temperatures down before you turn to aircon.Photograph: John Keeble/GettyThere are valid reasons to own air conditioning, even during a climate crisis. Older people, young children and those with health conditions are more vulnerable to extreme heat, and some homes are simply much harder to keep cool.Like any appliance, an air conditioner has two main sources of carbon emissions: the CO2 generated from manufacturing and disposing of it (known as “embodied carbon” ) and the CO2 generated to power it over its lifetime.To reduce its overall impact, buy a unit that’s built to last, from a trusted brand with a long warranty, rather than the cheapest model you can find. A longer-lasting unit spreads its embodied carbon over many more years. Buying secondhand also reduces the impact, extending the life of an existing unit.But the biggest difference you can make is how you power your air conditioning. If you’re on a 100% renewable electricity tariff, then running it shouldn’t require burning fossil fuels (again, it pays todo your research here). Better still, if you have solar panels and a home battery, you can run aircon using electricity you’ve generated yourself. It’s a significant investment, but one that’s becoming increasingly attractive as fuel prices rise and solar panels and batteries get cheaper.Be aware that if you’re on a standard electricity tariff, the mix of fuels used to power your home will depend on the time of day. Around the middle of the day, electricity is typically supplied by a higher share of renewables. When demand peaks, typically in the early evening, gas-fired power plants are more likely to be brought online to meet it.So, if you can, run your aircon outside these evening peak hours. Use shutters, curtains, open windows and other natural cooling methods first, then use air conditioning for a short time before bed to take the edge off.I’ve tested portable air conditioners here, but for a full rundown on the types available, see the “What you need to know” section at the end of this article.Why you should trust meI’m a veteran, award-winning consumer tech journalist with decades of experience testing gadgets. I’m also a menopausal woman in her 50s, who honestly can’t recall the last time she felt cold – which may explain the appeal of wild swimming at this age. Oh, and I have a degree in engineering. Between the three, I’m well qualified to put these portable air conditioners through their paces, both from a scientific and personal perspective.How I testedView image in fullscreenTesting conditions: most units were put to work in the same room, with the exhaust hose vented through a casement window.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianUnsurprisingly, air-conditioning units have been hard to come by this summer, with many sold out, and review samples also in short supply. I focused on units that are going to be restocked and tested six, with details of stock levels and replenishment dates included, where available.Where possible, I tested units in the same 14 sq metre room with average ceiling height, and with doors and double-glazed windows closed, so it was the warmest room in the house. I opened a casement window for the hose.The only exception was the Midea PortaSplit. Its unusual design pairs an indoor unit with a rather heavy outdoor unit that remains permanently connected by refrigerant lines, so you can’t separate the two. As I couldn’t lift the outdoor unit through a window, I tested it in a larger 37 sq metre room with a sliding door – which was the only suitable space available.To test performance, I measured each unit’s power consumption at maximum draw with a plug-in energy meter, although since air conditioners cycle on and off, they don’t use that level of power all the time. The highest settings’ noise levels were recorded using a sound meter app from one metre away, and I measured each unit’s size.I also monitored room temperature with a thermometer placed on the opposite side of the room. This measured how much each unit cooled the whole room, rather than the cold air coming from the vent.Finally, I judged each air conditioner on how effective the cooling felt, how annoying I found the noise and how easy the controls were to use. I also considered the design, how easily each unit could be stored over winter and, of course, its price. Note that all models come with remote controls and on castors.All of the aircon units that weren’t collected by the manufacturers after testing were donated to charity. Some went toFurnishing Futures, a charity that creates fully furnished homes for women and children who have survived domestic abuse. And some went toLowri Housein Hackney, London, which provides safe, short-term accommodation for homeless patients leaving hospital, with support from the homeless and inclusion health charityPathway.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe best portable air conditioning units in 2026View image in fullscreenCool contenders: six portable aircon units were assessed for cooling, noise and energy use.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianBest portable air conditioner overall:Meaco MC10000MeacoMC10000£459.99£459.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveSuperb coolingWhat we don’t loveRemote is basic and there’s no appView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£459.99 at Aircon CentreCurrently out of stock; stock due 27 NovemberThis 10,000 BTU air conditioner is from the popular MeacoCool (MC) range. There are alsoProandCHmodelsthat offer a companion app and heating.It’s A-rated for energy efficiency and designed for a medium room. The controls and display sit on the top at an angle, so you can see them from a distance. This is welcome, as the remote control is pretty basic, and there’s no companion app.It uses R290 (propane) refrigerant, which has a low global warming potential of 3.3 (for more information on this, see the “What you need to know” section at the end of the page).Why we love itOn test, this was simply the best and fastest at cooling. It brought the temperature down by 3C in 15 minutes and 6C in two hours.The design is simple. For example, you have to manually open the louvres (the angled grilles on the front) and point them where you want the cold air directed. By directing them downwards, it created a cooling breeze on the floor and on my legs, which I found made everything feel cool.It also has a fan and dehumidifier. The sleep mode dimmed the display but didn’t immediately make it quieter, instead gradually increasing the target temperature by a couple of degrees throughout the night.It’s a shame that …the remote doesn’t have a display.Dimensions:32 x 32 x 74cm (WDH)Weight:26kgBTU:10,000Room size:medium (up to 28m²)Warranty:three yearsMeasured power use on top setting:890WPeak noise level on test:60dBMeacoMC10000£459.99£459.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveSuperb coolingWhat we don’t loveRemote is basic and there’s no appBest portable aircon unit for large rooms:Dimplex Eco IQDimplexEco IQ£599.99£599.99 at DimplexWhat we loveGood cooling, app and voice controlWhat we don’t loveLoud and the remote is basicView image in fullscreenCaramel Quin testing air conditioners: DimplexPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£599.99 at DimplexCurrently out of stockThe Dimplex Eco IQ has a really handy app featuring controls such as a 24-hour timer. It uses R290 (propane) refrigerant, which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.Why we love itThe unit looks classy, and is pretty compact considering it’s powerful enough for a large room. It offers 12,000 BTU, plus wifi and app control. This means you can control it from your Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant smart speaker if you want to control your aircon by voice.The cooling is impressive. It cooled the room by 1.5C in 15 minutes and 5C in two hours.I found the Dimplex a bit loud, though. It may measure the same number of decibels as others, but it has a fairly deep hum and a slight rattle, like the noise you hear from a fridge. This makes sense because, like a fridge, it uses a compressor and a refrigerant. The noise measured 60dB at its loudest (similar to a conversation – so you’ll definitely hear it, but you can learn to ignore it), and this went down to 55dB on sleep mode. However, I found the noise worth it for the cooling on a hot day.It’s a shame that …it’s loud. The remote control is also basic, to the point of looking a little cheap. It lacks a display, which is a shame because the unit’s display and controls are on top and so can’t be seen from across the room. You can always use the app, though.Dimensions:29 x 34 x 70cm (WDH)Weight:23.8kgBTU:12,000Room size:large (up to 35m²)Warranty:one year, extended to two if registered within 28 daysMeasured power use on top setting:1,400WPeak noise level on test:60dBDimplexEco IQ£599.99£599.99 at DimplexWhat we loveGood cooling, app and voice controlWhat we don’t loveLoud and the remote is basicBest split portable air conditioner:Midea PortaSplitMideaPortaSplit£1,099.99£1,099.99 at JoyBuyWhat we loveQuiet; energy efficient; great for suitable spacesWhat we don’t loveBulky; positioning limited because of the pipesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£1,099.99 at JoyBuyCurrentlyout of stockAnd now for something completely different. This “portable split” air conditioner has an indoor and outdoor unit, connected with refrigerant pipes. The pipes are 2.5 metres long and have a 6 x 2.7cm cross-section, instead of the usual 15cm diameter air hose.The units can’t be detached from each other because the pipes are full of refrigerant (R32, global warming potential 675), so it’s suitable only if you’re able to put the outdoor unit outside and close the door to leave a 2.7cm gap. Alternatively, you can mount the outdoor unit outside permanently if you’re able to accommodate space for the pipes. I found it easiest to bring it back inside when not in use: it stores neatly on top of the indoor unit. It also comes with a kit for sealing out hot air and a window lock, consisting of two fittings to stick on to the frame with Velcro to connect them, which keeps your window gap narrow.It’s large and heavy: you wouldn’t carry it up and down stairs, although it wheels around OK. If you’d struggle to get the 32.5kg indoor unit and 9.9kg outdoor unit into place, you may find JoyBuy’s £35 installation service good value; they’ll unpack it and bring it to the right room in your home. They’ll even mount it on the no-drill-required brackets if you have a suitable window.Why we love itIt’s much quieter than a “monobloc” one-piece portable aircon unit and could be a permanent fix for renters in modern flats. If you can bring it up to your flat in a lift and have a balcony on which to put the outdoor unit, you’re winning. And it offers year-round service: it’s an efficient A++-rated air conditioner and also an A+-rated heater.And despite its bulk, it’s good-looking. Controls are intuitive, and there are three displays: one on top with the controls, one on the front showing the target temperature, and one on the remote control. You can also control it via the app and add Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant voice control.It cooled the room during testing, and the dog approved of its cooling prowess, but comparing figures would be like comparing apples and oranges: the room I tested it in was considerably larger.If the Midea suits your home – a back door or a balcony really – it’s a good option.It’s a shame that …it’s only suitable for homes that can accommodate its pipes.Dimensions:indoor unit, 52 x 34 x 65cm (WDH); outdoor unit, 50 x 26 x 44cm (WDH)Weight:indoor unit, 32.5kg; outdoor unit, 9.9kgBTU:12,000Room size:large (up to 35m²)Warranty:two yearsMeasured power use on top setting:680WPeak noise level on test:40dBMideaPortaSplit£1,099.99£1,099.99 at JoyBuyWhat we loveQuiet; energy efficient; great for suitable spacesWhat we don’t loveBulky; positioning limited because of the pipesBest value air conditioner:Devola DVAC09CCBDevolaDVAC09CCB£439.99£439.99 at DevolaWhat we loveGood value for cooling a medium-sized roomWhat we don’t loveThere’s no display on the front, so use the appView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£439.99 at DevolaCurrently out of stock; stockexpected 27NovemberThis 9,000 BTU air conditioner is a good all-rounder for medium-sized rooms. It’s also a fan and dehumidifier, and Devola also offersa version with heating.It comes in black orwhite. I tested the black (known as the DVAC09CB; the white is DVAC09CW), and found the matching hose and accessories were a nice touch. It uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.The remote is simple, without a display, and the unit’s controls and display are on top, so you can’t see them from the other side of the room. The app paired easily, however, and it meant I could clearly see and control the mode and target temperature. You can also use the app to schedule and to pair with Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant for voice control.Why we love itThe unit looks good and is lightweight enough to lift. And the cooling feels powerful for its size. It reduced the room temperature only a little in the first 15 minutes, but it had dropped by 2C after an hour and 3C after two hours.I didn’t find the noise too annoying, either. The sound is reminiscent of a fan with the added deeper hum of a compressor: I could get used to it. The sleep button had no immediate impact on noise, simply dimming the display, but it gradually reduces cooling through the night to save energy.It’s a shame that …there’s no display on the front.Dimensions:35 x 35 x 70cm (WDH)Weight:24kgBTU:9,000Room size:medium (up to 28m²)Warranty:two yearsMeasured power use on top setting:895WPeak noise level on test:55dBDevolaDVAC09CCB£439.99£439.99 at DevolaWhat we loveGood value for cooling a medium-sized roomWhat we don’t loveThere’s no display on the front, so use the appThe best of the restMeaco MC12000RPROMeacoMC12000RPRO£549.99£549.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveWell-featured; powerful enough for large roomsWhat we don’t loveI found the noise annoyingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£549.99 from Aircon CentreCurrently out of stock, stock due 27 NovemberBest for:high-end air conThe 12,000 BTU capacity makes this powerful enough for large rooms, and it’s a well-featured unit too. The front display shows you the target temperature, and the remote control features a display. You can also pair it with an app for more functionality.It was immediately cooling, but performance was so-so: the temperature dropped 1C within 15 minutes and 3.5C after two hours. As with many others here, it uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s loud. It measured 60dB, like several others, but I found its deep hum annoying and had to turn up the TV.Dimensions:47 x 35 x 76cm (WDH);weight:29.5kg;BTU:12,000;room size:large (up to 35m²);warranty:three years;measured power use on top setting:1,255W;peak noise level on test:60dBMeacoMC12000RPRO£549.99£549.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveWell-featured; powerful enough for large roomsWhat we don’t loveI found the noise annoyingDreo 318SDreo318S£399.99£399.99 at DreoWhat we loveA good budget model for small roomsWhat we don’t loveThe hose was shorter than mostView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£399.99 at DreoCurrently out of stockBest for:small roomsThis has the lowest cooling capacity (7,500 BTU) on test, so it’s suitable only for small rooms up to 14 sq metre. The 1.5m hose was too short to reach my high window, too (meaning I had to test all of the monobloc air conditioners on top of a desk, to be sure of a fair test, even though most come with 1.8m hoses).It’s small but has decent features, including a front display, companion app and voice control via Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant, and the remote control features a display. Cooling was impressive considering its size: the temperature dropped 1.5C within 15 minutes and 3.5C after two hours. I liked the flat, magnetic area on top for storing the remote control, too.Sound is a deep hum, although it’s a bit quieter on sleep mode. As with others here, it uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.It didn’t make the final cut because …for only a little more, you can buy the Meaco MC10000, which offers much better cooling.Dimensions:39 x 36 x 63cm (WDH);weight:22.5kg;BTU:7,500;room size:small (up to 14m²);warranty:two years;measured power use on top setting:755W;peak noise level on test:55dBDreo318S£399.99£399.99 at DreoWhat we loveA good budget model for small roomsWhat we don’t loveThe hose was shorter than mostWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenDog days: portable aircon can cool a single room when other ways of beating the heat aren’t enough.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianWhat types of airconditioning are there?Here I’ve tested portable air conditioners. These are freestanding units with an exhaust hose that carries hot air through an open window. They’re designed to cool a single room and can be packed away at the end of summer. They need to be positioned close to an opening window and a power socket.Most are “monobloc” all-in-one designs that sit on castors and are portable, in that they can be wheeled from one room to another. However, they’re not light, so moving them between floors is another matter entirely.Another option is a “split” air-conditioning unit, which is a permanently installed system with two separate units. The indoor unit is usually mounted high on a wall and blows cool air into the room. The other unit sits outside the home (on a roof or hanging off the wall), with pipes and electrical cables connecting the two. These systems tend to be more expensive but much quieter.This test also features a portable split air conditioner, which is a hybrid between a portable aircon unit and a fixed split system. This, too, has two units, but the outdoor one is more compact, and the pipe is thin and more flexible, making it easier to move around. It works well on the ground floor, where you can safely put the external compressor unit outside on the ground, which also makes it quieter. Using it upstairs would require the use of brackets outside, which makes it rather less portable.Air conditioners use the same tech as air-sourceheat pumps. By compressing and expanding a refrigerant, they move heat from one place to another. In cooling mode, they pump heat out of your home; in heating mode, they bring heat in. If you’re installing a permanent split system, go for a reversible model so you can use it to cool your home in the summer and heat it in winter.I haven’t carried out a group test of split aircon units because they require professional installation, but I have tested theBosch Climate 3000i 3.5kW(from £2,420) fromBoxt. It cools a room quickly and also works as a heater, air purifier and dehumidifier, doing four jobs without taking up any floor space.How much does air conditioning cost to use?For each aircon unit here, I’ve measured its power use on the top setting, in watts (W). Electricity costs are in kilowatt hours (kWh). If, for example, you were using a 900W aircon for an hour, it would use 900Wh. Divide by 1,000 to convert it to kilowatt hours: 0.9kWh.The energy price cap for 1 July to 30 September 2026 is 26.11p a kWh. So that’s the price to use 1kWh of energy. Multiply 26.11p by 0.9kWh, and you’ll discover it costs 23p an hour to run a 900W portable aircon unit. It’s not a fortune if you use it sparingly, but fans are much cheaper to run: thewinner of my fans testcost less than a penny an hour.What is a BTU rating, and which one do I need?An air conditioner’s British Thermal Unit (BTU) rating indicates its cooling capacity. The higher the BTU rating, the larger the room it can cool. There areonline BTU calculatorswhere you can input your room measurements to find out the BTU you need. Above, I’ve given a maximum floor space for the models reviewed, assuming an average ceiling height of 2.5 metres.An undersized air conditioner will struggle, meaning it’s more likely to be on constantly and at higher risk of breakdown, so it’s important not to buy a unit that’s underpowered for your space. On the other hand, getting a more powerful unit than you need means it will be more expensive and larger than necessary. Make sure to measure your room and get a unit with the right BTU or only slightly more than you need on paper. For example, if you’re not sure which room it will be used in, buy a unit that suits your largest bedroom.What’s a window kit?When you poke the flexible hose out of the window to remove hot air, you’ll want to seal the rest of the window. How you do this depends on the type of window. I have hinged, casement windows, so I used sticky-backed Velcro to make a line around the window opening and then attached a fabric cover, with zips to open a hole to poke the hose through. Most air conditioners come with two window kits: the other is an adjustable solid cover for sash and other sliding windows.Howlong a warranty do I need?All the units on test have two- or three-year warranties. I’m a big fan of long product lifespans, as the “embodied carbon” used in your unit’s manufacture and shipping also matters, alongside the electricity it uses to cool you. The longer you can get your unit to last, the better. To give yours its best chance of a long life, clean or replace the air filters regularly, dry it out on the fan-only mode before winter storage, and store upright.What is GWP?Global warming potential (GWP)is a measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps in the atmosphere over time, relative to carbon dioxide – CO2 has a GWP of 1. This matters if the refrigerant leaks or is disposed of unsafely. Propane, used in many of these models, has a low GWP of 3.3 and is climate-friendly compared with refrigerants with a GWP measured in hundreds or thousands.What to do with your old air conditionerIf your old aircon works, try to find it a good home on a local swap site or street WhatsApp. If it’s not working, check your council website orRecycle Your Electricals. Electrical items don’t belong in general waste and, like fridges, air conditioners contain a refrigerant that needs to be removed by a specialist. If it’s allowed to leak into the atmosphere, it contributes to global warming as a greenhouse gas (which is where its GWP, above, comes in).For more, readreaders’ top tips for beating the heat this summerand our roundup of thebest folding fansCaramel Quin is a journalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plain language. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. Caramel is an engineering graduate who has won awards for communicating hi-tech subjects to normal people. When she’s not testing gadgets, she’s feeding pets (16 beasts at the time of writing) or pottering at the allotmentExplore more on these topicsSummerThe FilterHomesGadgetsInteriorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I spent 18 months testing the best video doorbells – here are my favourites | Technology | The Guardian
description: Whether you want to improve your home’s security or simply know who’s at the door, the latest generation of smart doorbells will help put your mind at ease
Author: Andy Shaw
Headline: Whether you want to improve your home’s security or simply know who’s at the door, the latest generation of smart doorbells will help put your mind at ease
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterTechnologyReviewI spent 18 months testing the best video doorbells – here are my favouritesWhether you want to improve your home’s security or simply know who’s at the door, the latest generation of smart doorbells will help put your mind at easeThe best robot vacuums, testedAndy ShawThu 13 Aug 2026 05.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Doorbells have evolved. Today, they watch us as we approach, let the people inside the home know we’re coming sooner than our finger can hit the button, and give them a good look at our faces before they open the door. They’re essentially security cameras with a chime function.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.If you haven’t already installed one of these handy tools, there’s a huge array available. Choosing the best video doorbell can be a bewildering task, with various factors to consider, including how much of your doorstep you want to see and whether you’re prepared to pay for a subscription. To help make the decision a little bit easier, I tested 11 popular video doorbells to find the best.At a glanceBest video doorbell overallRingBattery Doorbell Pro£219.99 at AmazonBest budget video doorbellBlinkBattery Doorbell 2K+£69.99 at AmazonBest for Google Home usersGoogleNest Doorbell (battery)£129 at ToolstationBest subscription-free video doorbellEufyVideo doorbell E340£139.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust meI’ve been testing products, including everything fromvacuum cleanersand robotlawnmowersto computers and games, for various publications for more than three decades. I’ve also owned a video doorbell for several years, so I am well aware of their strengths and weaknesses. It gives me a good understanding of what I’m likely to be looking for in the next one I buy.How I testedView image in fullscreen‘I’ve mounted 11 doorbells to various rigged-up contraptions over the past 18 months or so.’Photograph: Andy ShawThe only way to test a doorbell is to stick it next to your front door and see how well it works. To this end, I’ve mounted 11 doorbells to various rigged-up contraptions over the past 18 months or so. With these, I can compare several doorbells at once, seeing how they all react to the comings and goings of my doorstep. Delivery drivers were rightly suspicious of the number of buttons and cameras that appeared as new models were reviewed, and struggled to work out whether it was them or the doorbells that were being tested.I’m not sure whether my neighbours noticed them all or spotted the number of times I lapped my drive at various times of day and night to test the movement sensors. If they did, they were too polite to mention it.I compare the doorbells by measuring how close I can get to the door before the motion detection is triggered, how much video is recorded and how useful that footage is. I time how long it takes for notifications to reach the doorbells’ apps on a smartphone and how long it takes for the doorbell to send an alert or ring a chime (if included) when its button is pressed. I also test the apps, examine the prices and consider the additional cost of subscriptions.All the doorbells that didn’t need to be returned to the brands after testing are being donated to theBritish Heart Foundation.The best video doorbells in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: RichLegg/GettyBest video doorbell overall:Ring Battery Doorbell ProRingBattery Doorbell Profrom£219.99£219.99 at Argos£219.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat footage day and night; clever pre-roll videoWhat we don’t loveExpensive; limited without a subscriptionView image in fullscreen£219.99 at Argos£219.99 at AmazonWhen this article was first published, it included an older version of Amazon’s Ring Doorbell Pro, which has since been discontinued. I wasn’t overly impressed with it for a variety of reasons, but Ring has pulled out all the stops with this newer version, addressing most of its weaknesses and leapfrogging its rivals with a host of useful features.Why we love itMost importantly, the video and sound quality are excellent. Ring still uses a slightly odd fish-eye lens, which provides a lot of area coverage but makes things look small at a distance and distorted up close. With 4K recording, however, it offers an unparalleled ability to zoom into footage from the app. It barely matters if someone looks small from a few metres away when you can zoom in on their face and still see a remarkable amount of detail.The picture quality is crystal clear in daylight and still excellent in low light, such as at dusk or when illuminated by a doorstep lamp. The night vision also works well when the ambient light is low enough for it to kick in.It’s also faster to respond than the previous model, alerting my phone within a couple of seconds when the doorbell is pressed or movement is detected. Ring does a particularly good job of tracking visitor movements by constantly storing a few seconds of video, which it can add to the beginning of the recording when motion is detected. It means you get to see people as they arrive, rather than seeing them only once they’re already on your doorstep.It’s a shame that …it doesn’t really work well without a subscription, which costs at least £4.99 per month.Subscription:Ring Solo, £4.99/mth or £49.99/yr (one device, 180-day storage); Ring Multi, £7.99/mth or £79.99/yr (all devices at one location, 180-day storage); Ring Pro, £15.99/mth or £159.99/yr (as Multi but adds video descriptions)RingBattery Doorbell Profrom£219.99£219.99 at Argos£219.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat footage day and night; clever pre-roll videoWhat we don’t loveExpensive; limited without a subscriptionFor more, read consumer technology editor Samuel Gibbs’Ring Video Doorbell Pro (wired) reviewBest budget video doorbell:Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+BlinkBattery Doorbell 2K+£69.99£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable, even with a subscriptionWhat we don’t loveLess sharp footage; slower motion detectionView image in fullscreen£69.99 at AmazonThe latest version of Blink’s Battery Doorbell has the lowest price of all the doorbells I’ve tested. Its resolution has been improved in this version from HD to 2K (although there’s also now anHD model that costs £10 less), but other elements have been downgraded. For example, the new Sync Module Core, which needs to be plugged into a nearby wall socket, doesn’t provide the option of local storage like its predecessor did, which means the £2.50/month Blink Basic subscription is now an essential add-on.Why we love itDespite this, the Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ remains excellent value for money. You can buy an annual subscription at a slight discount (£24.99/year) and still not have spent £100 in total.Considering it’s a cheaper model, I was impressed with the video footage. Daytime footage was clear, and with night vision enabled, it was good enough to clearly make out the faces of any visitors who wandered close to my front door.The motion detection doesn’t activate as quickly as its rivals, so the captured footage tends to show people already on your doorstep rather than making their approach. But the two-way communication was reasonably clear, and the app you use to control the doorbell is intuitive and simple to operate.It’s a shame that …on average, it took six seconds for motion detection notifications to reach my mobile devices, which is a little slow.Subscription:Blink basic, £2.50/mth or £24.99/yr (one device, 60-day storage); Blink basic AI, £5.49/mth or £54.99/yr (one device, 60-day storage, includes video descriptions); Blink plus, £8/mth or £80/yr (unlimited devices, 60-day storage); Blink plus AI, £14.99/mth or £149.99/yr (unlimited devices, 60-day storage, includes video descriptions)BlinkBattery Doorbell 2K+£69.99£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable, even with a subscriptionWhat we don’t loveLess sharp footage; slower motion detectionBest for Google Home users:Google Nest Doorbell (battery)GoogleNest Doorbell (battery)from£129£129 at Toolstation£136.97 at AmazonWhat we loveGood view angle; quick to send alerts to other devicesWhat we don’t love£80 subscription to store footage; no inbuilt chimeView image in fullscreen£129 at Toolstation£136.97 at AmazonDoorbells can be inundated with features, and their apps can be amazing. But if they don’t do a good job of letting you know when someone approaches your door and capturing a video of them, there really isn’t much point. The Nest Doorbell is excellent at this.Why we love itIn my tests, the Nest was a solid all-rounder. I found the viewing angle of its lens to be about perfect, not going so wide that people appear too small, but still capturing enough of the surrounding area to catch people skirting around its periphery. The video and audio were as consistently clear as those on any of the doorbells I tested, and they were decent in daylight and at night.The Nest would sometimes detect people right at the end of my drive (about 15m away), but proved consistent at capturing movement from about three metres away. There was a little delay between the button being pressed and notifications arriving on other Nest devices and smartphones, but it averaged a fairly reasonable five seconds. While not as fast as the doorbells with dedicated local chimes, which tend to go off almost immediately, this was among the fastest for sending alerts to smartphones and smart speakers.It’s a shame that …it doesn’t come with a chime. Instead, you need to buy a separateGoogle Home smart speaker, which costs £99.99 (or a last-gen Nest Mini if you can pick one up secondhand). If you have an existing Nest or Amazon Echo speaker, you can of course use that. You also have to sign up for the Google Home Premium subscription at £8 a month or £80 a year – without it, motion events are stored for only three hours, which isn’t hugely useful.Subscription:Google Home Premium (30-day storage, records only when movement triggered), £8/mth or £80/yr; Google Home Premium Advanced (60-day storage, records 24/7 for 10 days), £16/mth or £160/yrGoogleNest Doorbell (battery)from£129£129 at Toolstation£136.97 at AmazonWhat we loveGood view angle; quick to send alerts to other devicesWhat we don’t love£80 subscription to store footage; no inbuilt chimeBest subscription-free video doorbell:Eufy video doorbell E340EufyVideo doorbell E340from£139.99£179 at Argos£139.99 at AmazonWhat we loveNo subscription; footage saved to internal storageWhat we don’t loveMotion detection can miss fast-moving visitorsView image in fullscreen£179 at Argos£139.99 at AmazonMost video doorbells provide limited features without additional costs, hiding all their best bits (such as storing video for any length of time) behind a paywall. The Eufy E340 is unusual because it ditches the paid-for subscription concept entirely.Why we love itThe Eufy uses local rather than cloud storage, with 8GB built into the device. How long that lasts before overwriting itself will depend on how busy your doorstep is. This built-in storage makes it one of the more expensive models, although that’s not its only trick. It uses two cameras, with the extra one pointed to the floor, so you can also keep an eye on parcels (and analyse your visitors’ footwear).It’s a shame that …while the stars have aligned over the Eufy’s video quality and lack of subscription costs, there were one or two occasions when movement didn’t trigger the camera early enough or at all. Ideally, I’d prefer something more reliable.Subscription:none requiredEufyVideo doorbell E340from£139.99£179 at Argos£139.99 at AmazonWhat we loveNo subscription; footage saved to internal storageWhat we don’t loveMotion detection can miss fast-moving visitorsThe best of the restEzviz EP8 UltraEzvizEP8 Ultra£139.99£139.99 at AmazonWhat we loveDual cameras; optional subscriptionWhat we don’t loveCartoon animals; clunky app; slow local playbackView image in fullscreen£139.99 at AmazonBest for:disguising who’s inIf you want to confuse visitors about who might be in when they call, pick the Ezviz EP8 Ultra. For starters, they’ll be greeted by an animated animal that appears on the device’s screen when they arrive and starts pulling faces even before they’ve pressed the button. After that, if you want to speak with whoever’s pressed the doorbell, you can use a voice-changing option on the mobile app, which can digitally shift the pitch of your voice to sound more or less deep.The doorbell has two cameras, one face on and onepointing down to the floor, so you can clearly see the face of a visitor and any packages they might leave on your doorstep. It comes with two batteries, so there’s no downtime while charging, and a wireless chime that alerts you instantly when the button is pressed.It didn’t make the final cut because …the app is clunky. It can store 32GB of video locally without a subscription, which Ezviz suggests is about 30 hours, but footage is slow to load.Subscription:Ezviz CloudPlay, £4.99/mth (event recording, seven-day history) or £9.99/mth (event recording, 30-day history)EzvizEP8 Ultra£139.99£139.99 at AmazonWhat we loveDual cameras; optional subscriptionWhat we don’t loveCartoon animals; clunky app; slow local playbackAqara G4AqaraG4from£79.99£79.99 at Aqara£84.99 at AmazonWhat we loveReplaceable batteries mean no charging downtimeWhat we don’t loveApp for reviewing footage is cumbersomeView image in fullscreen£79.99 at Aqara£84.99 at AmazonBest for:no charging timeThe big problem with rechargeable doorbell batteries is that there’s a period when they have to be removed from the door and charged up, at which point any visiting friends will have to knock, and unwanted visitors won’t be recorded. This doorbell uses six AA batteries rather than a rechargeable battery, so its only downtime is while you’re replacing them.This model also comes with the option of recording video to a microSD card (not included), which slots into the supplied chime, sitting safely inside the house. However, it only provides access to the past seven days of video recordings through the app. To view further back, you have to remove the memory card and watch the files on a computer.It didn’t make the final cut because …the app is nothing short of horrible. It has an AI chatbot. No, I don’t know why either. It was also one of the slowest to send notifications to a smartphone.Subscription:not required if using a memory card. Seven days of cloud storage included for free. This can be increased to 90 days at £4.79/mth or £47.99/yrAqaraG4from£79.99£79.99 at Aqara£84.99 at AmazonWhat we loveReplaceable batteries mean no charging downtimeWhat we don’t loveApp for reviewing footage is cumbersomeYale smart video doorbellYaleSmart video doorbellfrom£149.99£149.99 at Argos£169.98 at YaleWhat we loveResponsive to movement; good doorstep angleWhat we don’t lovePoor-quality sound; unnatural tint to footageView image in fullscreen£149.99 at Argos£169.98 at YaleBest for:field of viewThe Yale doorbell proved reasonably responsive at detecting movement, triggering when I was about 2.5 metres away. It has a medium field of view compared with its rivals. That means people are still reasonably sized in the captured videos, but it gets a fish-eye effect around the edges, making it tricky to catch people hiding or sneaking up.The app is simple to use. It has few frills, but that may suit someone who doesn’t want their doorbell to be too complicated. There’s also internal storage, but only enough for two to four days, so it’s worth the subscription if you often go away for the weekend.It didn’t make the final cut because …sound quality was the worst of the group, and the video had an unnatural colour tint.Subscription:from £3.50/mth(30-day storage)YaleSmart video doorbellfrom£149.99£149.99 at Argos£169.98 at YaleWhat we loveResponsive to movement; good doorstep angleWhat we don’t lovePoor-quality sound; unnatural tint to footageTapo D235 video doorbell cameraTapoD235 video doorbell camerafrom£116.99£119.99 at Tapo£116.99 at AmazonWhat we loveComes with a chime and local storage for a reasonable priceWhat we don’t lovePoor distance detail; short motion-detection rangeView image in fullscreen£119.99 at Tapo£116.99 at AmazonBest for:a good value camera with no subscription requiredIf our budget choice doesn’t appeal, then the Tapo D235 may suffice instead. It’s more expensive but sits comfortably in the middle of the price range of doorbells reviewed, and it can record video locally on a microSD card (not included). However, there’s still a £2.99-a-month subscription available. That lets you save captured footage to the cloud as well as or instead of a memory card and sends camera snapshots with its text alert notifications.For the price, I was impressed with the quality of the footage captured, but it uses colour night vision as it gets dark, which was a bit too grainy. It has a wide 180-degree viewing angle and comes with a chime that sounds inside when someone pushes the doorbell button.It didn’t make the final cut because …motion detection started at about 1.5 metres in my tests, which meant some movement was missed. Also, its wide-angle lens makes distant visitors appear small.Subscription:Not required if using a memory card. Otherwise:Basic seven-day video history, £2.59/mth or £25.99/yr; Premium 30-day video history, £2.99/mth or £29.49/yrTapoD235 video doorbell camerafrom£116.99£119.99 at Tapo£116.99 at AmazonWhat we loveComes with a chime and local storage for a reasonable priceWhat we don’t lovePoor distance detail; short motion-detection rangeWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenAs you may expect, buying a video doorbell isn’t (just) about whether the colour matches the paint job on your front door. Smart doorbells are crammed with features designed to make you think they sound good, luring you into choosing one over another. However, you should also take into account how good they are at alerting you when people arrive at your door, and whether you’ll be able to tell who it is when you watch a video or live feed on your smartphone, as I did in my tests.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBattery vs wired video doorbellsIf you have an existing wired doorbell, you can use its wiring to connect most video doorbells. There are two main benefits to a wired doorbell: there’s no battery, so it doesn’t need to be recharged; and it will ring the existing doorbell chime inside the house when the doorbell button is pressed. They’re a bit more complicated to install, though, so if you’re not a competent electrician, we’d suggest getting a professional to do it for you.Battery doorbells are much easier to install, but charging them can be a faff. You usually have to remove the doorbell (or at least its battery) and charge it overnight. During that time, you will have no doorbell or camera. You’ll probably have to do this every month or so, but it depends on the battery and how busy your doorstep is.Some doorbells can use a spare battery or come with regular batteries that can simply be swapped, so you don’t need to be without a doorbell while it charges. Others can be topped up using a small solar panel, either out of the box or as an additional accessory.Installing your video doorbellInstalling a new battery doorbell is simple. Most come with a mounting plate to attach wherever you want the doorbell to sit. Screwing into a wooden door frame, if your doorway has one, is easy and convenient, but the doorbell can also be mounted on to a wall if you’re prepared to drill some holes and use a wall plug to hold the screws in place. Once the battery is charged, the doorbell attaches to the mounting plate.If you’re replacing a wired doorbell, ensure you switch off the electricity first. This should be possible through your circuit breaker, and you should test it before you remove your old doorbell by ringing it – if it stops ringing, you’ve successfully shut off the power to it. The old wires should then attach to terminals on the new doorbell, but we’d strongly advise tackling this only if you know what you’re doing or getting a professional to do it for you.Subscriptions and storageOne of the hidden costs of a video doorbell is the price of a subscription, which usually costs a few pounds a month and includes some form of cloud storage. Without a subscription, most video doorbells are little more than a regular doorbell with the video equivalent of a peephole that allows you to see who is at the door right at that second. A storage subscription elevates it into an archive of visitors, with video footage of everyone who’s been on your doorstep in recent days, so you can go back and check.Having said this, some doorbells (such as the Eufy doorbell reviewed here) have their own storage, can accept a memory card or connect to a wireless hub that’s kept inside the house. This kind of doorbell can be used without a subscription and stores footage locally, though many still offer a subscription that can provide additional features, such as recognising the faces of your visitors.Do video doorbells work with voice assistants?Video doorbells integrate nicely with other smart home devices. The most useful add-on is a smart screen, such asAmazon’s Echo Show (available in various sizes from £89.99)orGoogle’s Nest Hub Max (£219). These screens can be set to alert you when your doorbell rings and immediately switch to a live video feed from the doorbell camera.Smart speakers, such asAmazon’s Echo DotandGoogle Home Speaker, can also be used in conjunction with a doorbell, though without a screen, they can’t display a live view. You can still set them to chime, which can be useful for hearing the doorbell all around your house.Video doorbells can also be controlled using Amazon’s and Google’s smart assistants. You can use voice commands to perform doorbell tasks, such as showing the view from your doorbell on your phone or smart screen.Your doorbell doesn’t have to come from the same company as your smart device or favoured voice assistant; Google’s Nest Doorbell is compatible with Amazon Alexa as well as Google Assistant devices, for example. However, you tend to get more functions with a directly compatible system – Amazon’s Echo devices, for example, with a Ring or Blink doorbell.How long do video doorbells generally last?Quoting the battery life of a video doorbell is problematic even for the manufacturers. Amazon states only that the batteries in its Ring doorbells can last for “months”, while Google quotes the battery life of the Nest Doorbell (battery) as being between one and six months. Both are too vague to be particularly useful.However, it’s hard for the manufacturers to be more specific because there are huge differences between how people use their doorbell. If you live on a busy street and have motion detection switched on, your doorbell will be activated by every passerby. Video doorbells can also be activated by movement from cars, trees and animals.Other factors can reduce the battery life too. If you often use the device to view a live picture of your doorstep even when there’s no one there (which can be very tempting, especially when the doorbell is new), then the battery will run down faster. Battery life is also reduced in cold weather, so those living in chillier parts of the country might find that their battery doesn’t last as long, particularly during winter months.When it comes to the life of the doorbell itself, manufacturers tend to offer warranties of between one and two years. We’d expect that to be a minimum lifespan, since given that the device has few moving parts, there isn’t that much that can go wrong.The first thing that’s likely to fail is the battery, because it tends to deteriorate over time. That puts doorbells with removable batteries at a slight advantage, because a failed battery in a sealed device may be impossible to replace. You can extend a battery’s life by treating it well: wait until its charge is below 20% before recharging it, and try not to let it run down completely. That way, there’s no real reason why a video doorbell shouldn’t last for years.In some cases, it’s possible that a manufacturer’s support for a doorbell will run out before the hardware dies. For most doorbells, that’s about five years after the product was launched. Support is usually withdrawn by stopping software updates, which can leave a product vulnerable to hacking, or by changing elements such as cloud storage services that can render advanced features unusable.What to do with your old video doorbellIf you’re upgrading from one video doorbell to another, there are several things you can do with your old one. The most obvious is to install it on a back or side door if you have one. Although you’re unlikely to see much action on the ringer, the camera can provide a useful extra layer of security, particularly if intruders have spotted and circumvented the doorbell on your front door by scaling a fence.You could also use the camera as a regular security camera, either indoors or out. Most devices let you switch off specific doorbell features, such as the ringer, so you won’t be disturbed by people ringing it. You could also mount it out of reach, though it’s worth considering that you might have to access it every now and then to recharge the batteries.Footage from the doorbell can be accessed and managed through the app as if it were a security camera. However, note that some subscription services might charge you more if you have multiple devices connected and want to store captured footage online.If you want to get rid of your doorbell, make sure you uninstall it from your smart home setup before you physically remove it. Also, check the manual to find out how to do a factory reset so the camera doesn’t try to connect to your accounts if it’s reinstalled by someone else.Older doorbells may still have some value, so you could try selling yours, donating it to a charity or giving it away locally. If all else fails, don’t chuck it in the bin. Check your local waste collection, as they may pick it up on bin day if it’s left in a separate plastic bag. Alternatively, take it toyour nearest recycling centreand leave it with the other electrical items so it can be properly recycled.For more, readthe bestrobot vacuums, testedand21 home organisation hacksAndy Shaw is aconsumer journalist and technology addict.As he has reviewed tech products professionally for more than 30 years, his favoured working environment is a small desk surrounded by big boxes. His greatest weakness is that he never, ever remembers how things came out of their boxes, so they rarely fit back inwhen it’s time to send them backThe article was originally published on 14 November 2024. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page.
