title: Berries with a hint of tarmac – what do we mean when we call a wine ‘fruity’?  | Wine | The Guardian
description: Bananas, peaches, strawberries – anything but ‘grapes’. What do all those volatile organic compounds really mean for your summer sipping?
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Bananas, peaches, strawberries – anything but ‘grapes’. What do all those volatile organic compounds really mean for your summer sipping?
Content: There’s no accounting for taste, so if you think you can taste felt-tip pens, then so be it.Photograph: fstop123/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThere’s no accounting for taste, so if you think you can taste felt-tip pens, then so be it.Photograph: fstop123/Getty ImagesWineBerries with a hint of tarmac – what do we mean when we call a wine ‘fruity’?Bananas, peaches, strawberries – anything but ‘grapes’. What do all those volatile organic compounds really mean for your summer sipping?Mina HollandThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.“Strawberries, cherries and an angel’s kiss in spring,”sang Nancy Sinatra. “Mysummer wineis really made from all these things …” Overlook the angel’s kiss and, if you’re a wine drinker, you might recognise some of those fruity tasting notes – strawberries and cherries, indeed, but also citrus, orchard, other stone fruits and the whole berry family. In fact, it’s common to liken a wine to almost any fruit – except grapes.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.A wine can have notes of almost anything – pencil shavings, tennis balls, cat pee – but fruit is the most obvious (clearly, wine is made from fruit) and universally recognised. If I told you I was getting, say, green apple and lime zest from a riesling, you would probably have a good sense of what that meant, and what you might be able to expect on tasting it yourself. If I described a petroleum aroma, that might sound a bit cryptic and much less appealing, unless you were familiar with this tasting note commonly found in riesling. In other words, a wine’s fruit profile is often leveraged as a marketing tool. What better example of this than the “strawberries and cream” of Provence rosé? It’s a tasting note that underpins our collective sense that rosé is a summer drop, perfect for sun-drenched days filled with watching tennis, ocean views and seasonal produce.But that probably sounds more cynical than I intended.Fruitnotes in wine are very much a real thing. When we talk about a wine having notes of tart cherry or candied orange, we’re describing what we find in its aroma – smell being, of course, a factor in how we taste. Wines contain aromatic compounds that are similar to or the same as those found in other fruits – for example, esters (made by yeasts during fermentation, bringing notes of banana, pear, pineapple), or compounds originating in grapes, including thiols (tropical fruit), norisoprenoids (dried fruit and honeyed notes) and terpenes (citrus and floral aromas).To deconstruct a wine in this way can feel pedantic – a wine is so much more than a collection of aromatic compounds, after all. Something of its magic lies in Sinatra’s ineffable “angel’s kiss in spring” – often, I find, this is the time or place in which you drink it, or the people with whom you do so – but today’s picks showcase some of the different fruit aromas you might find in grapes, styles and regions, from the apricots and orange blossom of the moscatel and torrontes blend from southern Chile to a simple, peachy Roussillon orange, to the damsons and dark cherries of a Georgian saperavi. Your summer wine really can have aromas of all these things.Six fruity little numbers to splash out onPipeño Blanco 2024, A Los Vinateros Bravos£20.90 Monty Wines, 12.5%. Apricot, peach and citrus peel in this skin-contact white made from aromatic, old bush vines in Chile.W/O Organic Nero d’Avola Rosato 2024£14.99Laithwaites, 12%. You’ll find all the summer berries in this volcanic and organic Sicilian rosé from Etna.Cote Mas Orange£10.25 Waitrose, 13%. Any orange notes in this orange wine are zesty and a little cooked; a peachy introduction to the genre.M&S Found Saperavi£12 Ocado, 13%. Saperavi means “dyed” – its skins bring deep colour and rich, grippy dark red fruit aromas. Great for a barbecue.Alain Grignon Reserve Carignan Vieilles Vignes2023/24£12.50, Majestic, 12.5%. A spicy, old vine carignan with lots of cherry and dried cranberry – a proper bargain crowdpleaser.Flavia Catarratto Zibibbo£33 Ocado, 12.5%. A delicious, tropical fruit bomb from Sicily – expect pineapple and grapefruit. I almost wanted a cocktail umbrella.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodFruitSummer food and drinkItalian food and drinkFrench food and drinkEastern European food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Escaping the ​heat​ and rediscovering the ​joy of ​cooking | Food | The Guardian
description: Parts of the UK are roasting but some of us are glad to turn the oven on. Bring on the​ ​curries and pasta pies
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Parts of the UK are roasting but some of us are glad to turn the oven on. Bring on the​ ​curries and pasta pies
Content: From aubergines to berries, there is still plenty cook with this summer, including Yotam Ottolenghi’s stuffed courgettes with oregano and pine nut salsa.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFrom aubergines to berries, there is still plenty cook with this summer, including Yotam Ottolenghi’s stuffed courgettes with oregano and pine nut salsa.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianFeastFoodEscaping the ​heat​ and rediscovering the ​joy of ​cookingParts of the UK are roasting but some of us are glad to turn the oven on. Bring on the​ ​curries and pasta piesSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastFelicity CloakeThu 13 Aug 2026 07.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t wish to boast, but I’m typing this with a jumper on. Not because my flat has air-conditioning, but because it doesn’t – and the relentless heat of south-east England was having a seriously detrimental effect on my productivity and the health of my elderly dog (NB: the two are not mutually exclusive). So, witha second novel to write, I decided to rent a studio as far north, and as far west, as I could reasonably drive in a day. And, so far, I have no regrets. Driving through North Yorkshire, I had to put on a sweatshirt – the weather in the Pennines gave my car the first good wash it’s had in months – and now, in Scotland, the dog and I feast on hot porridge in the mornings. I’d genuinely forgotten what it’s like to be cold – and what it’s like to cook for pleasure.This newsletter isn’t just for those parts of the country enjoying, rather than suffering, the sunshine; yesterday it was raining and tonight the temperatures will drop to almost single digits. It’s also for anyone, wherever you are, who’s eaten enough cool, crunchy salads and chilled soups to last a lifetime, or at least until next summer. (You’re not alone: last month,Waitrose reported a spikein sales of cottage pie and robust South African red wine.)Much as I enjoy those things, I’m not craving winter food just yet; there will be time enough for that, and I’m keen to make the most of summer produce while we have it. I would have no issue turning on the oven for Yotam Ottolenghi’sMexican-inspired prawn-stuffed peppers, for example, or Sami Tamimi’sPalestinian versionwith freekeh, lamb and spicy tomato sauce. Unsurprisingly, I also have a soft spot for my ownProvençal-style stuffed courgettes.View image in fullscreenAn all-weather treat … berries with raw cream.Photograph: Matt Russell/The GuardianStaying with baked vegetables, now is the perfect time of year for an aubergine parmigiana –in her recipefor a slightly lighter take, Rachel Roddy recalls her partner informing her that his Sicilian grandmother always did any frying or baking early in the morning, so the hot work was finished for the day by 10am, an approach familiar to me from recent weeks of recipe testing in London. On the aubergine front, I’m afraid I couldn’t choose between highlighting Atul Kochhar’s Chettiar aubergine curry, Arto Der Haroutunian’s aubergine tagine and Anna Del Conte’s showstopping aubergine pasta pie inthis selection of recipesfrom 2013, so please have at them with my blessing.I must confess, however, that I brought tomatoes up to Scotland with me, which I’ve mostly been eating on toast (would that I had the right ingredients for Joe Woodhouse’s luxuriant take withcreme fraiche and mint). But if I happen upon any less worthy candidates, they’re going straight into Nigel Slater’ssausage, tomato and lentil bake gilded with chilli oil, or perhaps Jessica B Harris’fried green tomatoes, a dish that, I was strictly informed by a lady from Alabama a few years ago, needs no accompaniment.Although I suspect there must be great tomatoes available on the Scottish west coast, I know there to be fantastic berries and, thanks to the long, light days at this time of year, far better ones than most of those grown down south. You might fancy Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’sraspberry and almond streusel cake, or Anna Jones’sroast strawberries with lemon and black pepper, though, whatever the weather, I still prefer my berries raw with cream in afruit foolor anEton mess; the most complex I might get is Nigel’sloganberry cream with flapjack.When I find some really good ones, however, I’m more likely to eat them straight from the punnet. If you’re reading this somewhere hot, I very much suggest you do the same. Alternatively, take the day off cooking, and go and buy an ice lolly instead. I would.My week in foodView image in fullscreenTaste wars … Japanese katsu curry.Photograph: Saowaluck Voraprukpisut/Getty/iStockphoto‘The worst curry in the world’|According to a British-born Australian journalist witha column in the Canberra Times, this is Japanese katsu. Don’t click on it for his opinions on sashimi, or seaweed, or Indian food (“arguably overcooked”), but do readEmiko Davies’ rebuttal, which will teach you far more about Japanese cuisine, seaweed and nuanced, well-researched, thoughtful writing. And then try makingkatsu curry riceand decide for yourself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland’s best service station|I haven’t visited every service station in Scotland – in fact, I’ve visited very few of them, because I usually bring sandwiches – but having stopped at Cairn Lodge Services on the M74, I think it must be a strong contender for this crown. Newly refurbished by the same group asTebayandGloucesterservices, it boasts a farm shop and a cafe offering homemade food, canteen-style, on china plates. I had a bowl of courgette, pea and mint soup with an excellent cheese scone, and I will certainly be stopping there for breakfast on the way home. Why can’t we have more options such as this alongside the hamburgers?Great Taste awards results|The results of the Guild of Fine Food’s annual taste tests came out a couple of weeks ago, and it’s well worth having alook at the directoryto see what has scooped those coveted three stars. Having helped to judge the awards for the past decade or so, I can promise you that the process is as fair and as rigorous as possible, and a starred sticker is often all the sales pitch I need. My takeaway from my stint this year: Irish readers, if you’re not familiar with sour cream from Green Pastures, I’d suggest rectifying that. We ate it straight from the spoon with no embellishment.Best breakfast in Cornwall|I had the pleasure of spending a couple of nights in Penzance last month during the town’s literary festival, and thus of revisitingChapel House (boutique) B&B. The menu included, among other delights, fry-ups with both black and hog’s pudding (a creamy white pudding that deserves to be better known outside the West Country), and an amazingly light-green omelette with spinach, tarragon and cheese, cooked in plenty of butter. Wish I’d asked for the recipe now. Sue, are you reading?If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastSummer food and drinkBritish food and drinkTomatoesFruitnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuits | Food | The Guardian
description: Combine these simple Italian baked treats with chilled fruit and thick cream for a playful summer pudding
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Combine these simple Italian baked treats with chilled fruit and thick cream for a playful summer pudding
Content: Rachel Roddy’s figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuits.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuits.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuitsCombine these simple Italian baked treats with chilled fruit and thick cream for a playful summer puddingRachel RoddyThu 13 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his exquisiteThe French Menu Cookbook, Richard Olney has clear ideas and strong opinions about everything, including dessert. He believed that rich desserts should follow only the simplest of meals, whereas with most menus (meaning all the sophisticated menus in his book), something light, airy and playful is best. His suggestions read like a summer fruit poem: peach melba, apple mousse with peaches, apricot fritters dusted with icing sugar, strawberries in sweetened orange juice, strawberries in beaujolais, strawberry mousse with raspberry puree, iced cherries and fresh almonds. One of his late summer/early autumn menus also suggests fresh figs with raspberry cream (figues à la crème framboise), which is both fun to make (the red puree streaking through the cream for a raspberry ripple) and to eat.An airy and playful pudding calls for an airy and playful biscuit. What better thanlingue di gatto,or cat tongues, so called because of their flat, elongated shape. Made from butter, sugar, flour, and egg whites,lingue di gattoare not complicated to make, but do require a piping bag, which can be mimicked by a zip-lock bag – just remember to scrape the mixture into the bag first, and only snip the end off when you are ready to pipe.This recipe is from Italian pastry chef Iginio Massari’s Non solo zucchero [Not Only Sugar] Volume 1, an invaluable step-by-step guide to short pastry, sponge cakes, butter masses, creams, cream puffs and meringues aimed at professional pastry chefs, but just as suitable (and revelatory) for enthusiastic but chaotic pastry cooks like me.There are various ways to serve this pudding. Olney suggests a large serving dish, which, considering his warning never to put tomato dishes on a red plate or those including spinach on a green one, shouldnotbe pink. Olney arranges the chilled fig slices first, then pours the raspberry cream over the top, which baffles me slightly, because the cream is so thick. An alternative is serving in individual bowls, saucers or glasses: a spoonful of the raspberry cream first, then topping it with a small pile of fruit (figs, the whole raspberries you’ve set aside, plus redcurrants and mint leaves). The cat tongue biscuits can be stuck in the cream like fairy wings, put on the side of the plate, or passed around the table on a separate plate so everyone can help themselves.Figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuitsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appServes84-6 ripe figs(pale green or dark purple)250g raspberries,washed250ml whipping cream1-2 tbspicing sugarA few redcurrantsA few mint leavesFor the biscuits50gsoft butter60gicing sugar3 egg whites(50g)60gplain flour, sifted30g flaked almondsPut the softened butter and icing sugar in a bowl, and use a spatula to mix them together. Fold in the egg whites, before adding the sifted flour and mixing again.Scrape the mixture into a pastry bag with a smooth 10mm nozzle (or a zip-lock bag you can snip the corner from). On a baking tray lined with baking paper, squeeze out lines that are 10cm long, ensuring you leave 4cm between each one. Top each one with three or four almonds, then bake at 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 for about eight minutes, until golden. Leave to cool a little before lifting on to a cooling rack.It is up to you whether you peel the figs before you slice each one into four; chill. Set aside half of the raspberries, then press the rest through a fine sieve for a smooth, bright-red puree. Whip the cream until stiff, then stir in the icing sugar to taste and the raspberry puree for a mottled effect.Divide the cream between four individual bowls or glasses, top with wedges of fig and a few raspberries, plus some redcurrants and mint leaves. Serve with the biscuits.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkDessertBiscuitsFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra review: the top dog of folding Androids | Samsung | The Guardian
description: With great software and battery for two days, the pricey svelte folder strikes best balance between phone and tablet
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: With great software and battery for two days, the pricey svelte folder strikes best balance between phone and tablet
Content: The slim and light Fold 8 Ultra is a great phone that squeezes a quality tablet in your pocket.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe slim and light Fold 8 Ultra is a great phone that squeezes a quality tablet in your pocket.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSamsungReviewSamsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra review: the top dog of folding AndroidsWith great software and battery for two days, the pricey svelte folder strikes best balance between phone and tabletSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorThu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Samsung’s top folding phone for 2026 is its first to carry the “Ultra” moniker in its name, packing a much bigger battery and better cameras into the thin and light body of a book-style foldable.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra continues from where theexquisite Z Fold 7left off last year. With its svelte chocolate bar dimensions opening into a square tablet, the Ultra sits above the newpassport-shaped Z Fold 8as Samsung’s top model. Costing £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), it is a lot of money to pay for a phone, regardless of how many other devices it can theoretically replace in your pocket.The Ultra sticks with the tried and tested form of its many Z Fold predecessors, and is almost identical to the Fold 7 physically. Weighing 215g and being only 8.9mm thick when closed, it is about the same as a large normal slab phone. The tall and super-bright outside screen makes easy work of phone-type tasks such as messaging, calls and mapping.View image in fullscreenThe chocolate bar dimensions of the Ultra (right) provide plenty of space for messaging and other activities while being easier to use one-handed than the squat shape of the Fold 8 (left).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOpen up the Ultra like a book to reveal the 8in OLED tablet screen, which is notably crisper and brighter than previous models, with a new anti-reflective coating that makes it easy to see in direct sunlight.Browsing or reading books is particularly satisfying, while videos look great but have large letterboxing black bars top and bottom. The stereo speakers, when held in landscape, are good for watching TV without headphones.The crease is less visible where the display folds but is still noticeable when the screen is off or you run your finger over it, and the necessarily softer material picks up fingerprints easily and needs more care than a traditional hardened glass smartphone.View image in fullscreenReading books, comics and websites on the tablet screen is a joy on the go.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSpecificationsMain screen:8in QXGA+ 120Hz (422ppi) Amoled flexible displayCover screen:6.5in FHD+ 120Hz (422ppi) AmoledProcessor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for GalaxyRAM:12 or 16GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:One UI 9 based onAndroid17Camera:200+50+10MP rear with 3x telephoto; 10MP+10MP selfie camerasConnectivity:5G, dual sim, esim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, GNSSWater resistance:IP48 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)Dimensions folded:158.4 x 72.8 x 8.9mmDimensions unfolded:158.4 x 143.2 x 4.1mmWeight:215gTwo-day battery life and plenty of power for multitaskingView image in fullscreenThe Ultra fully charges in 60 minutes and hits 70% in half an hour using a 45W or greater USB-C power adaptor (not included). It also supports 20W wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Ultra has two meaningful upgrades on the inside. The latestQualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5chip has plenty of power for multitasking and demanding tasks, while a 13.6% larger capacity battery powers the phone through about two days of use. That is with the screens used for more than four hours each across a mix of wifi and 5G for browsing, messaging, taking notes, work and shooting photos, matching some of the longest-lasting folders available.Gaming and more intensive tasks hit the battery harder, but most people will only need to charge the Ultra every other day.One UI 9 (Android 17)View image in fullscreenThe tablet display is big enough to allow two apps to be run at full phone size when side by side for easy multitasking.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Ultra runs the same One UI 9 software built on the latest Android 17 as theFold 8. It is the best available for folding screens, allowing you to do more with the form while remaining a polished, customisable and refined experience.The Ultra can run up to three apps in a split-screen grid at once, plus more as floating windows, which can be handy for messaging while watching videos. Flex mode pushes the app or video to the top half of the screen when partly folded like a tiny laptop. You can have separate home screens for the phone and tablet displays, and choose whether or not to continue using apps on the outside when you shut the phone.TheNow Barworks great for putting live scores, music controls and other ongoing tasks on the bottom of the lock screen or in the status bar. The Ultra also has some of the better AI tools available, including Google’s Gemini and a proactive suggestion tool calledNow Nudgefromthe S26, which has been expanded for One UI 9.The Ultra will receive Android and security updates until 31 July 2033.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app can be used open or closed and has plenty of modes to get creative, including the downloadable Expert RAW for manual control.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Ultra has five cameras: a 10-megapixel selfie camera in each screen that is great for video calls; and three cameras on the back.The main 200MP rear camera is little changed from last year’s model and remains the best of the bunch, capable of shooting fantastic photos across a range of lighting conditions. By default it captures photos at 12MP but can shoot at 50MP or the full 200MP with a quick tap of button. It also manages a very good 2x crop zoom for a bit of magnification.The new 50MP ultra-wide camera is a big improvement on previous models, capturing brighter, more detailed photos, particularly in lower light settings. It also handles macrophotography well, producing excellent, highly detailed closeup shots.The 10MP 3x telephoto camera is the weakest of the bunch. It can shoot good photos with a bit of work, but it falls far short of modern rivals on zoom and quality, particularly with indoor lighting. Digital zoom takes over for further magnification up to 30x, which starts to fall apart beyond 10x.The cameras shoot great video, too, with a range of modes available including the impressive horizontal lock stabilisation featurefrom the S26 Ultra.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe rear cameras protrude prominently from the back of the phone causing it to wobble when in use on a desk or table.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe battery has an expected lifespan of at least 1,200 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone isgenerally repairable. Inside screenrepairs cost about £600. Samsung offers aself-repair programme, as well as Care+accidental damage insurancethat reduces the cost of repairs to £50.The Fold 8 is made from 14.4% recycled materials by weight. Samsung offerstrade-inandrecycling schemesfor old devices, and publishesenvironmental impact in its reports.PriceThe Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs from£1,899(€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999).For comparison, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 costs£1,699, theS26 Ultracosts£1,279, theHonor Magic V6costs£1,999.99and theGoogle Pixel 10 Pro Foldcosts£1,299.VerdictThe Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the best folding phone available. It is not a radical upgrade on last year’s excellent Z Fold 7 and does not really deserve the “Ultra” branding, but the longer, two-day battery life is very welcome.The form factor is great: easy to use as a regular phone when closed, plus an 8in internal screen that is brighter, crisper and much easier to use outdoors than before. The square tablet screen is great for multitasking, browsing and apps while being big enough to make watching video a good experience despite needing large letterboxing black bars.The triple camera on the back is generally capable and does not feel like a large downgrade from normal flagship phones, even if the 3x telephoto camera is a bit weak. The Ultra has the top Android processor from Qualcomm with plenty of performance for anything you would want to do.While you can get similar performance and battery life with better cameras and a less visible crease from some rivals, the Fold Ultra’s excellent, adaptable software is simply better and will be kept up to date until at least 31 July 2033.Samsung has given wealthy buyers a choice of shape for its book-style foldable phones this year, but while the squatter Fold 8 seems better for video on paper, the Fold 8 Ultra is the one to get.Pros:super thin and light, just like a regular phone when closed, great tablet screen, powerful multitasking with top performance, two-day battery life, water resistance, good set of cameras.Cons:extremely expensive, no dust resistance, more fragile than a regular device and costly to repair, weak zoom camera compared with the very best normal phones, not a big upgrade on last year’s Z Fold 7.View image in fullscreenThe Fold 8 Ultra is the most complete folding phone from Samsung yet, but comes at a very high cost.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsSamsungSmartphonesMobile phonesTablet computersAndroidreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Living proof damaged landscapes can recover’: exploring a vast restored forest in southern Sweden | Sweden holidays | The Guardian
description: Söderåsen national park is one of Europe’s largest protected broadleaf woods, offering wild swimming, spectacular hiking trails and an inspiring story of regeneration
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Söderåsen national park is one of Europe’s largest protected broadleaf woods, offering wild swimming, spectacular hiking trails and an inspiring story of regeneration
Content: Sunrise over Söderåsen national park, Sweden.Photograph: Anders Tukler/AlamyView image in fullscreenSunrise over Söderåsen national park, Sweden.Photograph: Anders Tukler/AlamySweden holidays‘Living proof damaged landscapes can recover’: exploring a vast restored forest in southern SwedenSöderåsen national park is one of Europe’s largest protected broadleaf woods, offering wild swimming, spectacular hiking trails and an inspiring story of regenerationCoco Lone NealThu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the bus window, the ridge looks like a giant slumbering beast stretched deep green across the flat farmland. “It feels alive,” I say to the woman beside me. “Yes,” she answers. “It is where you would run for safety, don’t you think?”I am in southern Sweden to exploreSöderåsen national park, established in 2001 to protect more than 1,600 hectares (4,000 acres) of the larger Söderåsen ridgeline. Shaped over millennia by immense geological collisions, fractures, volcanic eruptions and ice ages, today it is one of northern Europe’s largest continuous protected broadleaf forests, and only 90 minutes by car from Copenhagen or, in my case, two hours bypublic transport.The little village of Röstånga at the gateway to the park is where travellers stop for supplies from the supermarket before disappearing into the forest on foot, bike or horseback, and people gather for food, live music and art.My room for the first night is inVilla Söderåsen, a grand timber-framed yellow and white guesthouse, which has stood at the park’s entrance since 1904. It was built for tourists arriving via the new railway in search of connection to nature. Sebastian and Åsa, the owners, want to continue that tradition. “We humans are as loud as elephants in the wood,” says Sebastian. “Sit quietly for half an hour and see what happens.”That evening, I eat with strangers at long wooden tables outside the hip restaurant and live music venueStationen. Music drifts out of open doors, adults chat around the fire, children run circles around us.View image in fullscreenPool of mystery … the ‘bottomless’ lake of Odensjön (Odin’s Eye).Photograph: Coco NealThe next morning, Åsa recommends I take a dip inOdensjön (Odin’s Lake). “Some say it is bottomless,” she says. It’s almost perfectly round, edged by steep beech-covered slopes, and fed by underground springs. Fifteen minutes into the forest and I am there.A woman making her way back to the village says: “There is a rock in the water, heated by the sun, sit there, let your body adjust.”Grasshoppers trill, spider silk trails from branches, noble chafer beetles glimmer like the aurora borealis, a dragonfly rests electric-blue on my now empty walking boots. I swim, the circle of blue sky rippling, and emerge ready for anything.A few years ago, scientists obtained a sediment core from the bottom of the lake, providing detailed information from the past 600 years of land-use history. This showed that in the 18th and 19th centuries the plateau was largely deforested. I would have been walking across a heath, repeatedly burned to improve grazing grounds. It is difficult to imagine as I move through endless layers of beech, mossy trunks, roots like octopus arms. Dead wood is left to rot, creating a rich habitat, that is the magic.Once I start searching, the signs of human history are everywhere too, from hollow ways to clearance cairns and dry-stone walls.Two hours of hiking later, I arrive at the second entrance to the park: Skäralid, a rift valley. The visitor centreNaturum, packed with information and playful exhibits, shares its premises withCafé Italia.Both look out onto a picturesque dam. A ranger explains that much of the initial conservation efforts since designation as a national park involved the felling of non-native Norway spruce and the planting of broadleaved trees in its stead.View image in fullscreenGreen idyll … several hiking trails weave through the woodlands of Söderåsen national park.Photograph: Nick Gregory/AlamyIn search of solitude, I choose the wilder three-hour Hjortsprångsrundan or Deer Leap circular, a trail named after a prehistoric hunting method where people drove game over a narrow cliff shelf. I pick my way along it, across heather and bilberry, to perch on the hard gneiss bedrock that blushes a startling mineral pink. A buzzard swoops down from the branch of a gnarled oak.The descent is like scrambling and slipping back through time into an entirely other world. Many of these slopes managed to escape the historical land clearances and thus are the closest to ancient woodland. But all around this area, ferns, lichen, fungi, seeds and spores are recolonising the land.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markThere’s a sudden crashing through the undergrowth. A young stag steps from a pocket of alder trees, pawing the groundThe scree slopes are dotted with springs pushed up from a subterranean lake and laced with streams that feed into the Skärån river. The scent in the bottom of the valley is heady, sweet and damp, bringing with it a keen awareness of how much is always happening just out of sight.I rest on a wooden walkway, pop a wild raspberry in my mouth and watch a slowworm the length of my forearm slither past. Then, a sudden crashing through undergrowth. Wolf? Wild boar? Moose? A young stag steps from a pocket of alder trees, pawing the ground. We look at one another. The sun drops, and as it does its light rises up the walls of the ravine.View image in fullscreenRooted … broadleaved woodland has replaced earlier spruce plantations.Photograph: Coco NealMy room for the second night is inSöderåsens Skafferi,avandrarhem, or wanderer’s home. The house glows like a lantern on the edge of the dark wood. The owner Elisabeth, who spent her childhood exploring Söderåsen on horseback, says the house was once the first nature school in Sweden.On my final morning I climb to Kopparhatten, the park’s highest viewpoint at 212 metres, and hold up a booklet with an image of a painting from 1840 of this same vista, almost bare of trees. “We used to holiday in the south,” a couple tell me. “But we’re searching for cooler climates now.” I wonder what stories they will bring home.Summer, all green infusion; autumn, rust and gold; winter, snow and stone; spring, wood anemones and paper-thin leaves. The national park feels like living proof that damaged landscapes can recover if nature, and humans, are given half a chance.Accommodationwas provided byVilla Söderåsen(doubles from1,095 Swedish Kronor,about £85,B&B). Coco also stayed atSöderåsens Skafferi(doubles fromaround £78).Söderåsen national parkhas multiple wild campsites with wind shelters and barbecue areas.For information on public transport access, visitskanetrafiken.seExplore more on these topicsSweden holidaysScandinavia holidaysEurope holidaysWalking holidaysRewildingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: This is how bad the heatwave has got for us arable farmers – I’m going on holiday | Environment | The Guardian
description: Brigg, Lincolnshire: I should be busy, but the boom-bust climate has upset all my usual routines
Author: Colin Chappell
Headline: Brigg, Lincolnshire: I should be busy, but the boom-bust climate has upset all my usual routines
Content: Huge cracks in the fields.Photograph: Colin ChappellView image in fullscreenHuge cracks in the fields.Photograph: Colin ChappellCountry diaryEnvironmentCountry diary: This is how bad the heatwave has got for us arable farmers – I’m going on holidayBrigg, Lincolnshire:I should be busy, but the boom-bust climate has upset all my usual routinesColin ChappellThu 13 Aug 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 00.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time you read this, I will be away in the Scottish Borders – a British arable farmer on holiday in August? This is unheard of. I’ve never done it myself in 30 years of farming. The reason I’m going away is that, remarkably, I have very little to do, and it’s all down to this destructive modern climate.We have finished the harvest, all done in almost entirely the month of July. Overall our farm will be 20% down on our long-term average yield, with winter cropping 2 tonnes per hectare and spring cropping 1 tonne per hectare below normal. Winter barley will be the only crop close to normal yields due to its natural maturity at the time of the first heatwave in late May. Beans finished five weeks ahead of schedule, and are almost 50% down on expectations.View image in fullscreenThe bean yield, which is half of expectations.Photograph: Colin ChappellSo, what to do? Normally I would be drilling cover crops and soon oilseed rape, but there is no point – the soil is just too dry. Instead, I’m doing odd jobs like digging up “blown” land drains (bursts in the piping deep underground that is the backbone of our healthy soils).Meanwhile, traditional hedgerow plants such as blackberries have appeared early, and I worry for the wildlife (which seem to have a decent number of young this year) if winter is prolonged.The heat will make the headlines, but only a few months ago the farm was suffering from excess rainfall. This, I feel, has done more harm to our crops than the high temperatures, as the clay loam here can tolerate dryness to some extent.The new normal is all boom and bust: long spells of either extreme, with little in the way of typical seasonal weather, making growing any form of food challenging. Some think we can import our way out of this problem, yet the UK is not alone in having such issues.So for now it is a bit of rest, but as the season changes I will be back to do what we do best: grow the nation’s food. If the climate lets us.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentCountry diaryRural affairsFarmingExtreme heatClimate crisisAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thursday news quiz: A speeding car, a police faux pas and an app that’s gone too far? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?
Content: This little dormouse has some questions for you.Photograph: Ovia Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThis little dormouse has some questions for you.Photograph: Ovia Images/AlamyThursday quizLife and styleThursday news quiz: A speeding car, a police faux pas and an app that’s gone too far?Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?Martin BelamThu 13 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn this day in 1888, the mechanical mastermind John Logie Baird was born in Dunbartonshire. He was the pioneering inventor who first beamed a recognisable image across a room, giving the world the very first working television. Without his early experiments with biscuit tins, darning needles and bicycle lenses, half of the questions the Thursday quiz has asked would never have been possible. So tune in, turn up your mental brightness, and test your frequency with these 15 questions.Allons-y!The Thursday news quiz, No 2601.Unfortunately, the invention of the television also gave us Donald Trump (not pictured). His media company – which owns the Truth Social platform the US president uses – posted a loss of how much in the second quarter of this year?$38m$138m$238m$338mReveal2.What is the name of the typhoon that has been causing havoc in China?Typhoon DragonfishTyphoon DolphinTyphoon DugongTyphoon DerekReveal3.Which dating app is dropping its famous feature that only women can initiate a conversation on it?BumbleFeeldHingeGhosterReveal4.The British driver Andy Green reached 406.320mph (653.908km/h) in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines (not pictured, that's Herbie), setting a new land speed record. Where?Hakskeen Pan, South AfricaBlack Rock Desert, NevadaBonneville Salt Flats, UtahPendine Sands, WalesReveal5.Send Derren Brown today's collective noun. Use your psychic powers to let him know what, according to Grammar Monster, is the collective noun for herons?A settlementA scytheA stealthA siegeReveal6.Revelations that a "body" found inside a suitcase was actually a sex doll were rather embarrassing for police where?New South Wales, AustraliaNew England, USCanterbury, New ZealandKlow, SyldaviaReveal7.Back to the president of the US (not pictured). Donald Trump was apparently snuck off Air Force One because of a security threat, leaving White House staff and the press pack somewhat uncomfortably ignorant that they were on a flight subject to a "credible" threat. Where was Air Force One flying from?BudapestAthensRomeAnkaraReveal8.This week's actual guest canines are, from left to right, Cranachan, Poppy and Fergus, courtesy of Thursday quizzer John Christiansen. Tell them who won the Tour de France Femmes.Antonia Niedermaier (Ger)Tegan Jovanka (Aus)Demi Vollering (Ned)Dominika Włodarczyk (Pol)Reveal9.What is the name of the Game of Thrones play being performed at the Royal Shakespeare Company’s Stratford theatre in England?Game of Thrones: Winter's PromiseGame of Thrones: The Mad KingGame of Thrones: The Dragon's FallGame of Thrones: The One With the Swords, Horses and the BonkingReveal10.Which music service has said it will add a label "AI persona" to distinguish AI artists from real people?SpotifyApple MusicDeezerNapsterReveal11.The Brazilian footballer Jacy Maranhão went viral last week after what happened when he scored a goal?He got tangled in the net after sliding into the goal to celebrate and had to be cut freeHe dropped his shorts to reveal a sponsor's advertising slogan inked on to his buttocksHe jumped excitedly into the crowd to celebrate only to realise he'd jumped into the other team's fansHe jumped over the advertising boards only to fall down a hole in the groundReveal12.It is Janet Yellen's birthday today. Happy birthday Janet! Money, money, money. In 2014 she became the first woman to hold which position?President of the European Central BankChair of the Federal ReserveManaging director of the International Monetary FundPresident of the World BankReveal13.The Thursday quiz remembers Keith Chegwin fondly, so here is Cheggers plays population! According to the 2026 CIA World Factbook, what is the population of Poland?28.7 million people38.7 million people48.7 million people58.7 million peopleReveal14.On this day with Brian May! And his badger! 13 August is the anniversary of the French king Louis XIII appointing Cardinal Richelieu as prime minister. The Thursday quiz imagines Queen's legendary guitarist wants you to tell him – and his badger – in which year …1324142415241624Reveal15.And finally … a high school football player in Arkansas discovered what in his helmet during practice?A small swarm of increasingly annoyed fire antsA striped bark scorpion with a nasty stingA 2ft venomous cottonmouth viperA very naughty miniature dachshundRevealIf you really do think there has been an egregious error in one of the questions or answers – and can show your working and are absolutely 100% positive you aren’t attempting to factcheck a joke – you can complain about it in the comments below.
