title: DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever
Content: People in protective clothing lower the coffin of an Ebola victim into a grave in Bunia, Ituri province, on Tuesday.Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/APView image in fullscreenPeople in protective clothing lower the coffin of an Ebola victim into a grave in Bunia, Ituri province, on Tuesday.Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/APEbolaDRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth provinceMan dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest everRachel Savageand agenciesThu 13 Aug 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ebola outbreak in theDemocratic Republic of the Congohas spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago.The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in westAfrica, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data.Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said.There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak.The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace.Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded.The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming thatEbolais not real.Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials sayRead moreHealth workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months.The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February.Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate.Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”.Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months.Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time.This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in apaper published this weekin the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola.Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the viruscould be mutatingand that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate.Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.Explore more on these topicsEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaWorld Health OrganizationGlobal healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: French ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of women  | Central African Republic | The Guardian
description: Disciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residence
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Disciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residence
Content: Foucher, pictured in 2018 during his posting to Lebanon, has served as France’s ambassador to Central African Republic since 2023.Photograph: Wael Hamzeh/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFoucher, pictured in 2018 during his posting to Lebanon, has served as France’s ambassador to Central African Republic since 2023.Photograph: Wael Hamzeh/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockCentral African RepublicFrench ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of womenDisciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residenceAgence France-PresseThu 13 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance has opened disciplinary proceedings against its ambassador toCentral African Republicover allegations of misconduct, after claims he brought dozens of women into his official residence, raising potential security concerns.The investigation comes as Paris seeks to rebuild relations with CAR after their sharp deterioration in recent years amid Russia’s expanding influence in the former French colony.The French weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported that the ambassador, Bruno Foucher, 65, brought about 30 women between the ages of 20 and 30 into his residence during the period of January 2024 to March 2026, with some of them staying overnight. The visits prompted officials to report a security breach.The ambassador acknowledged having had sexual relations with two young women, the weekly said.The French foreign ministry said: “At the initiative of the ministry, an administrative investigation was carried out in Bangui in 2026. Upon receipt of the findings of this mission, and at the request of the minister, the ministry initiated disciplinary proceedings against the ambassador. These proceedings are ongoing.”The ministry conducted an on-site inspection in April, which led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings.Foucher is a career diplomat who has served as ambassador to CAR since 2023. He was ambassador to Lebanon from 2017 to 2020, to Iran from 2011 to 2016, and to Chad between 2006 and 2011.According to Le Canard enchaîné, which said it obtained the inspection report, the ambassador received about 15 visits a month.He also allegedly instructed staff to allow one of the young women to stay at the residence during his absence.Russia maintains a strong foothold in CAR, primarily through the Wagner paramilitary group, which plays a key role in providing security for the country’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra.French officials have accused Russians of fostering anti-French sentiment in a number of African countries.The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, praised the “complete restoration of relations” betweenFranceand CAR when he visited Bangui in March.Explore more on these topicsCentral African RepublicFranceAfricaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Zambia elections haunted by ghost of incumbent president’s arch-rival | Zambia | The Guardian
description: Hakainde Hichilema is bidding for second term, but feud between him and family of Edgar Lungu, who died in 2025, continues
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Hakainde Hichilema is bidding for second term, but feud between him and family of Edgar Lungu, who died in 2025, continues
Content: Supporters of the president, Hakainde Hichilema, campaign in Lusaka, Zambia.Photograph: Anita Reed/APView image in fullscreenSupporters of the president, Hakainde Hichilema, campaign in Lusaka, Zambia.Photograph: Anita Reed/APZambiaZambia elections haunted by ghost of incumbent president’s arch-rivalHakainde Hichilema is bidding for second term, but feud between him and family of Edgar Lungu, who died in 2025, continuesRachel Savagein JohannesburgThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 04.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Zambians go to the polls on Thursday, the ghost of the current president’s predecessor hangs over the elections.Hakainde Hichilema, 64, is bidding for a second term leading the southern African country after defeating his arch-rival Edgar Lungu by a landslide in 2021.A feud between the two men, their families and supporters has dominated Zambian politics, to the extent that the quarrel has continued even after Lungudied in South Africain June 2025.Zambia’s government went to court to try tostop the burial of Lunguby his family, who did not want Hichilema presiding over a state funeral. In June, South Africa’s supreme court of appeal ruled in favour of Lungu’s family, overturning a previous high court decision in favour of the government.View image in fullscreenEdgar Lungu and his wife at a rally in Lusaka in 2015.Photograph: Rogan Ward/ReutersIn this election, Hichilema is facing the Tonse Alliance of opposition parties led by Brian Mundubile, 55, who was a government chief whip under Lungu. Mundubile’s running mate Makebi Zulu acted as the Lungu family’s spokesperson during the burial row, and on the campaign trail the two men have promised to bring Lungu’s body back to Zambia for a dignified burial.The way death is dealt with is very important in Zambia, said Christopher Vandome, a senior research fellow at the thinktank Chatham House. “Even Hichilema supporters want to see due respect given to those that have died,” he said. “When it appears things get messy, it just makes the incumbent look disrespectful.”The shadow of Lungu has also hung over allegations by the Tonse Alliance that Hichilema has deployed authoritarian tactics during the election campaign, including raiding its offices and detaining 36 members of Mundubile’s team.Hichilema’s team furiously denied the claims, invoking Lungu’s treatment of Hichilema during the last election. “Zambians know what repression looks like. In 2021, the opposition leader [Hichilema] had been arrested 15 times, Prime TV [a private station] and the Post [a newspaper] had been shut down, and on election day the internet was switched off,” said a spokesperson for the ruling United Party for National Development. “Today the opposition campaigns freely across all 10 provinces, no media house has been closed and the airwaves are open.”View image in fullscreenBrian Mundubile, the main opposition challenger, waves to supporters as he leaves a radio station in Lusaka.Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/GettyTransparency International Zambia monitors have recorded incidents of police interrupting opposition rallies, said Tamika Halwiindi, a coordinator at the organisation. “Disruptions from the police citing issues to do with safety have been noted to be more biased against the opposition and independents, as opposed to … the ruling party,” she said.During Hichilema’s term, activists have also reported having peaceful demonstrations shut down. Mputa Ngalande of the Fight Inequality Alliance said he was among a group detained for more than 12 hours in July 2024 when they were protesting against the state power company during a period of 22-hour-a-day blackouts.Vandome said: “[Hichilema’s] prospects of winning are very high. But his … personal lived experience of how complicated Zambian elections can be has given him this insecurity which is actually counting against him … denting his image in a way he doesn’t have to.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionZambia’s economy has stabilised since an economic crisis, which was triggered when it defaulted on its debts in 2020 under Lungu. Annual inflation is now 6.5%, compared with 24.6% in July 2021. The government made primary and secondary education free in 2022.View image in fullscreenSupporters of Hakainde Hichilema and the United Party for National Development gather at a campaign rally in Lusaka.Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/GettyMeanwhile, Zambia has attracted more international investment in recent years due to its huge deposits of copper, a key material in green technologies.At the start of the month, in a giveaway to young voters, Hichilema, also known by his initials HH and nickname Bally (a slang word for an elder),tolda crowd of jubilant university students that he was increasing their accommodation allowance by 50% with immediate effect.However, the cost of living could still count against Hichilema in the elections, in which almost 8.8 million registered voters will also choose MPs and local councillors. The average annual income rose from $1,127 to $1,318 between 2021 and 2025, according toWorld Bank data. But pricesalmost doubledover the same period.“What people are asking is: ‘If we are doing well economically, why are we not feeling impact on the ground?’” said Ngalende. “Because you will find on the ground that it is very difficult to access three meals a day.”Explore more on these topicsZambiaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Absolutely unacceptable’: Japan condemns visit by Vladimir Putin to disputed Kuril Islands | Japan | The Guardian
description: Japanese PM says islands seized by Soviets late in second world war are part of her country under international law
Author: Gavin Blair
Headline: Japanese PM says islands seized by Soviets late in second world war are part of her country under international law
Content: Vladimir Putin at a fish processing plant on the disputed Kuril Islands.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/ReutersView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin at a fish processing plant on the disputed Kuril Islands.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/ReutersJapan‘Absolutely unacceptable’: Japan condemns visit by Vladimir Putin to disputed Kuril IslandsJapanese PM says islands seized by Soviets late in second world war are part of her country under international lawGavin Blairin TokyoThu 13 Aug 2026 08.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Japanese government has reacted angrily to Vladimir Putin’s first visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, which are claimed by both Tokyo and Moscow.Japan’s foreign minister, Toshimitsu Motegi, summoned the Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev, while the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, called Putin’s actions “absolutely unacceptable”.Known inJapanas the Northern Territories and by Russia as the Southern Kurils, the islands were seized by the then Soviet Union in the closing stages of the second world war and have been a source of contention ever since.The Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945 as Tokyo was about to surrender, and the dispute has prevented the two nations from signing a formal peace treaty.View image in fullscreenPutin visits a hospital.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL/EPATakaichi told reporters in Tokyo that the islands, which are just off Hokkaido, were “both historically and under international law” a part of Japan and called the visit by the Russian leader “incompatible with Japan’s consistent position” on the territory.Japanese television showed footage of Putin on the island of Etorofu, or Iturup in Russian, visiting a hospital, meeting residents and trying caviar at a processing plant, as well as comments condemning the visit by former Japanese residents who were deported when Russia took control of the islands.About 17,000 Japanese formerly lived on the islands, which today are occupied by about 20,000 Russian citizens.As well as its strategic significance, the island chain – consisting of Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group – provides access to rich fishing grounds and valuable mineral deposits.On Wednesday, Putin travelled to the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where he inspected navy drills and declared that the four disputed islands were recognised as Russian in international documents.Shinzo Abe, the late Japanese prime minister, had reached an entente with Putin over the territory, with visits by Japanese citizens to family graves resuming and talk of a future peace treaty. However, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine prompted Japan to impose sanctions on personnel and entities linked to Moscow, souring bilateral relations.The Russian president acknowledged Abe’s actions in his remarks on Wednesday and went to call the recent sanctions “unprovoked”. He said: “Japan has identified Russia as a major source of threats. I would like to point out that we are not threatening Japan. On the contrary, it has territorial claims against our country.”Though it is Putin’s first visit to the islands, Dmitry Medvedev went to Kunashiri in 2010 when he was president. Medvedev was widely seen as loyal to Putin, who was prime minister at the time.Explore more on these topicsJapanRussiaVladimir PutinAsia PacificEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs
Content: It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001.Photograph: LegoCamera/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIt is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001.Photograph: LegoCamera/ShutterstockAir transportSouth Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran warIncheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubsRaphael Rashidin SeoulThu 13 Aug 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for international passengers, in part owing to disruption in the Middle East caused by the Iran war.The airport, South Korea’s main gateway, about 30 miles (48km) west of Seoul, handled 38.39 million international passengers in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Airports Council International (ACI), the global trade body for airports.Heathrow in the UK was second, with 37.79 million, followed by Changi airport in Singapore with 34.53 million.It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. The airport was 10th in the world in 2002, rising to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024 and 2025.Part of the increase was attributed to disruption caused by theUS-Iran conflict, which weakened the role of Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and diverted some transfer traffic to alternative routes through east Asia, Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC) wasquoted as sayingby the Yonhap news agency.Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airportRead moreIncheon’s international passenger traffic was up 6.3% year on year overall, with rising numbers of foreign visitors also contributing to the increase.Foreigners accounted for 39.3% of Incheon’s passengers in the first half of the year, up from 35.2% for the whole of 2025. The proportion reached a record 44.4% in the second quarter, with IIAC attributing the increase largely to growing numbers of visitors from China and Japan, according to local media.Heathrow, in west London,recorded 40 million passengersin total in the first half of the year, including both domestic and international travellers, its busiest first half on record. Passenger traffic to Asia-Pacific rose 7.9%, while capacity to the Middle Eastreportedly fell16.5% owing to the regional conflict.Earlier this weekIstanbul overtook Heathrowas Europe’s busiest airport by total passenger numbers. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.Incheon has also expanded its role as an international hub. It serves 101 airlines flying to 183 cities, including 158 international passenger destinations.A four-phase expansion completed in late 2024 increased the airport’s annual capacity to 106 million passengers.Kim Beom-ho, the acting president of IIAC, said the ranking reflected “the support of the government, the public’s encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport”.South Korea also lays claim to theworld’s busiest air route. The domestic corridor between Gimpo airport and Jeju island had 14.4 million seats scheduled in 2025, according to the aviation data provider OAG, more than any other route in the world.Explore more on these topicsAir transportSouth KoreaMiddle East and north AfricaUS-Israel war on IranAirline industryAsia PacificHeathrow airportnewsShareReuse this content

title: One Nation staffer accused of posing as leftwing content creator in ‘undercover’ videos | One Nation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: The videos, filmed at anti-One Nation rallies, were posted to party’s social pages and appear to be endorsed by Pauline Hanson
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Exclusive: The videos, filmed at anti-One Nation rallies, were posted to party’s social pages and appear to be endorsed by Pauline Hanson
Content: A TikTok screenshot of Pauline Hanson with the staffer who has appeared in videos taken at anti-One Nation protests.Photograph: One Nation/TikTokView image in fullscreenA TikTok screenshot of Pauline Hanson with the staffer who has appeared in videos taken at anti-One Nation protests.Photograph: One Nation/TikTokOne NationOne Nation staffer accused of posing as leftwing content creator in ‘undercover’ videosExclusive: The videos, filmed at anti-One Nation rallies, were posted to party’s social pages and appear to be endorsed by Pauline HansonFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerThu 13 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe owners of a progressive social media page have accused One Nation of impersonating them at anti-Pauline Hanson rallies while shooting a series of “undercover” videos.Hanson’s party has recently published a string of videos with a young male host attending leftwing protests. In the clips – published on pages owned byOne Nationand Hanson on Instagram, TikTok and X – a party staffer seeks to embarrass protesters in filmed interviews.He asks people questions that appear designed to catch them out, such as: “We’re going to fight [racism] by uniting under one nation, right?”Inside a meme factory: meet one of thousands of Indonesians trading political outrage clicks for Facebook cashRead moreIn one video, he says: “I’m going undercover to protest against my boss, Pauline Hanson.” In another, Hanson herself appears, joking with the host as she asks: “Who have you been hanging around with?”The founders of Toilet Paper Australia, a political meme and commentary page with 128,000 Instagram followers, told Guardian Australia they have received reports from followers that a One Nation representative has been attending rallies inBrisbaneand other cities, alleging to be “from Toilet Paper Australia” when seeking interviews.Toilet Paper Australia regularly criticises One Nation and promotes critical news stories about the rightwing populist party.“We want to make abundantly clear: this person is not from Toilet Paper Australia. They are not affiliated with us, and they do not represent us in any capacity,” a spokesperson for the page said in a statement.View image in fullscreenA post on X by One Nation features protester Che Janz at a rally in Brisbane.Photograph: One Nation/XGuardian Australia has spoken to three attendees of a Brisbane rally against Hanson in June – organised by the organisation Campaign Against Racism and Fascism – who alleged they were approached by the host in the One Nation videos and that he claimed to be from Toilet Paper Australia.In the videos, the host films protesters chanting slogans or making speeches that strongly criticise Hanson, as well as interviewing people wearing Greens merchandise, with communist or socialist T-shirts and flags, or holding colourful signs.One participant is asked: “Did you come here stoned?” To which they say yes.The host asks a man wearing a pirate outfit: “When was the last time you showered?”“I hope I’m not going to become trans tomorrow,” the host says in another while speaking to a participant. He yells along with the chant: “Hanson is not welcome here.”The Brisbane rally attendees said they had no suspicions that the host was from One Nation.Che Janz, who was featured in one video, claimed the host approached him and friends at the event.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I think he saw us from afar and then wandered over. He said ‘how are you going, I’m from Toilet Paper Australia and I’m doing some interviews here’,” Janz said.He said he “didn’t suspect anything”, noting there were often people filming at such rallies for social media, but said he was aware of political opponents filming “undercover” content at social rallies in Australia and overseas.“It wasn’t out of the ordinary … but I always know there’s a risk involved going to something like that, know that could happen,” Janz said.Two other attendees, who requested to not be named and were ultimately not featured in videos published by One Nation, claimed the host asked them “leading questions” at the rally, giving them an opportunity to criticise Hanson’s party.Students shun calls to stay in school as anti-Hanson protesters gather across AustraliaRead more“It was just the one guy with a phone and lapel microphone, nothing seemed suss at all,” one said. “He wasn’t rude, he looked perfectly normal, just a guy doing some media.”Toilet Paper Australia’s Instagram page describes the group as “Proudly Union. Proudly Biased”, adding: “Fighting Murdoch, the Liberals and One Nation.” It regularly features criticism and news stories about conservative politicians, and has in recent weeks strongly focused on One Nation.Toilet Paper Australia last week posted links to One Nation’s volunteer sign-up website, writing: “I’m sure you’d all love to *definitely* show up and *definitely* not miss out and no-show.”One Nation did not respond to request for comment. Guardian Australia contacted the host on several social media platforms but did not receive a reply.Explore more on these topicsOne NationAustralian politicsPauline HansonBrisbanenewsShareReuse this content

title: Is Australia’s buy now, pay later boom at an end?  | Buy now, pay later | The Guardian
description: Several firms promised to disrupt the consumer credit market by offering consumers their purchases instantly and the bill later. Did it work?
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Several firms promised to disrupt the consumer credit market by offering consumers their purchases instantly and the bill later. Did it work?
Content: Sydney SuperDome is now known as Afterpay Arena under a multimillion-dollar naming rights deal.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenSydney SuperDome is now known as Afterpay Arena under a multimillion-dollar naming rights deal.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPBuy now, pay laterIs Australia’s buy now, pay later boom at an end?Several firms promised to disrupt the consumer credit market by offering consumers their purchases instantly and the bill later. Did it work?Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniThu 13 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 17.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfterpay has never turned a profit in Australia. Last month, it spent millions to take over a Sydney Olympic Park arena.The company says Afterpay Arena will be the first venue where Australians can “buy now, pay later” for their event tickets, merchandise, dinner and even alcohol.The deal to take the naming rights from a traditional lender, Qudos Bank, is the latest evolution for a sector that has rapidly expanded over the past decade. But as growth slows and players leave the market, is the buy now, pay later (BNPL) boom over?Will AI take Australian jobs, or is it just an excuse for corporate restructure?Read moreAustralians’ yearly spending through buy BNPL platforms grew $3bn a year in the late 2010s but slowed to growth of $1.5bn in 2025, according to the Reserve Bank.And while BNPL arrived promising to one day replace credit cards, Australians spent 20 times more via credit cards last year than through BNPL ($22bn).BNPL spending graphAt least eight BNPL platforms have left Australia since 2022, including the National Australia Bank withdrawing its product earlier this year, leaving four major operators: PayPal, Klarna and Zip (each with about 2 million customers) and Afterpay, with 4.5 million.Afterpay and Klarna report that they are growing, while PayPal’s Pay-in-4 service customers have not grown since 2023 and Zip has seen a 7% year-on-year fall in users. Zip will leave the New Zealand market on Monday.Credit agency Equifax has found new BNPL account applications in the three months to June 2026 were down 35% from the previous year.Experts attribute the slowdown in part to 2025 laws that aimed to stop companiesapproving customers for fundsthey couldn’t afford to repay. The reforms defined BNPL as a form of credit, forcing companies to perform credit checks and report new accounts to credit agencies, potentially affecting future activities like mortgage applications.Kevin James, analyst at Equifax, says the reforms have stopped platforms from offering instant approvals, detracting from their unique appeal. Some customers have turned to other forms of lending like credit cardsand personal loans, he says.“If I wanted to go for a BNPL product in 2022, I would have found it relatively easy,” James says. “Once it became more regulated and had more friction, then I think people changed.”Before the reforms, younger shoppers had piled into BNPL’s promise of getting goods and services immediately and spreading out the interest-free payments over time.Users were instead lumped with late payment fees, or cut off from platforms, if they failed to repay.Afterpay has reported 2.9% of customers were three months late on repayments inJune 2025, compared with 2.1% for credit cards. Contacted for comment, the company said 2% of purchases in the last three months 2025 attracted late fees.The company earned $123m in late fee revenue annually in 2024 and 2025, according to its Australian accounts.More options and ‘significant wins’With uptake slowing, companies have been working to expand the range of outlets that accept BNPL and to encourage existing customers to spend heavily on more types of products.Businesses pay the platforms a fee of 3% of a transaction’s value when customers use BNPL, on average. In comparison, credit card fees are 1% and debit card fees a fraction of that. In exchange, those businesses hope BNPL users will spend more.Fees from merchants make up the majority of Afterpay’s local revenue, at $625m in 2025. The company, owned by the US-based business Block, recorded a $741m pre-tax loss in Australia as it has repeatedly slashed estimates of the value of its local business.Afterpay’s Asia-Pacific vice-president, Mike Ryan, says the company is giving users a greater range of businesses at which to use its services so it can become their first choice of payment method.Afterpay had been adopted by 290,000 Australian businesses by 2024, adding Uber and Amazon in Australia in 2025.He says Afterpay is seeing “significant wins” in spending on petrol, convenience and groceries and plans to expand into insurance, travel and telecommunication. The company declined to share supporting data, but advocates have long warned the rising cost of living has pushedcustomers to BNPL for essentials.Angel Zhong, a professor of finance at RMIT, says it will soon be harder for platforms to sign up new businesses. The Reserve Bank’s ban on card surcharging is set to make card transactions even cheaper, meaning businesses could find higher BNPL fees less palatable.“Merchants would likely stay away, unless they can see that while using BNPL, they can attract a strong customer base,” Zhong says.Michael Ebstein, from MWE Consulting, says the industry can survive at a slower pace as consumers will still want to spread out their spending.“I think there’ll still be attractive growth for the next couple of years, but that’s all,” Ebstein says.Ignore the doomsdayers – property investing in Australia is far from brokenRead moreBut Grant Halverson, from McLean Roche, says the sector has been “dying slowly”.Halverson believesthe remaining operators will have to abandon the fee-free, interest-free model that made BNPL’s name, by adding fees or introducing new products to raise revenue from a stagnating base of users.Zip, for example, charges monthly fees and interest on some products unless customers meet certain conditions. The trade-off is that Zip cards can be used anywhere. Afterpay offers a similar product, “Afterpay Plus”, which charges users $9.99 a month to pay in instalments anywhere that accepts mobile phone payments. Its accounts show revenue from the product’s fees surged from $22.8m in 2024 to $42.5m in 2025.Afterpay’s co-founder, Anthony Eisen, says the entire platform is still growing rapidly and its customers are using it more frequently.“If you’re a product that doesn’t deliver what customers want, obviously things stagnate,” Eisen says, speaking at the Arena launch in late July.Zhong says the arena’s renaming, replacing a traditional bank, shows that BNPL has become part of the establishment.“It is now becoming a more mature and regulated industry … [and] once you reach that saturation, it’s really hard to attract new customers,” Zhong says.Explore more on these topicsBuy now, pay laterBusinessConsumer affairsBankingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian plot to kill Ukrainian American thwarted in Warsaw, says Polish PM | Poland | The Guardian
description: Donald Tusk says it is first time ‘someone on the order of Russia’ has sought to attack US citizen in Nato country
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Donald Tusk says it is first time ‘someone on the order of Russia’ has sought to attack US citizen in Nato country
Content: Donald Tusk said Poland and other Nato countries had to be ready to counter other Russian attacks.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Tusk said Poland and other Nato countries had to be ready to counter other Russian attacks.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersPolandRussian plot to kill Ukrainian American thwarted in Warsaw, says Polish PMDonald Tusk says it is first time ‘someone on the order of Russia’ has sought to attack US citizen in Nato countryAssociated PressThu 13 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Russian plan to kill a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted by Poland before it could be carried out, the Polish prime minister has said.Donald Tusk said it was the first time that “someone on the order of Russia” had sought to attack a US citizen on the territory of another Nato country.Western officials have previously warned that Russia stepped up a campaign of targeted killings since Vladimir Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, saying they had disrupted several plots across Europe. But Tusk said this incident was unprecedented.The suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Russia’s secret services, was detained by Polish authorities on 7 August. He will be held in custody for three months, the Warsaw police said in a statement.The American Ukrainian citizen “was uncomfortable for the Putin regime”, Tusk said in a news conference, without elaborating.The operation was carried out in cooperation with US services, said Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland’s minister overseeing intelligence services. He said the targeted victim was a US citizen “of Ukrainian origin”. Officials did not immediately provide further details.The Russian foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The US state department said it was aware of the reports but said it had no additional information.Russia has long been accused of targeting its enemies abroad, including by using rare poisons. But intelligence officials previously told the Associated Press that Russia’s security services are now more brazen in their choice of targets, going after Russian activists and foreign supporters ofUkraineas well as military defectors.Tusk said: “We must assume that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons, in various places around the world.” He added that Poland and other countries must be prepared to counter such actions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA bungled bomb plot in Poland exposed a spy – but whose spy was he?Read moreWestern officials see the campaign as connected to Russia’s broader efforts to undermine European countries that support Ukraine. The AP has mapped about 200 acts of sabotage, arson and other disruption acrossEuropesince the start of the war in Ukraine that officials have linked to Russia. Putin told the AP in June that Russia was not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe.In 2006, British authorities accused Russia of being behindthe killing in London of the former FSB officerAlexander Litvinenko with radioactive polonium. The UK also blames Russia for theattempted killingof the former Russian military intelligence officer Sergei Skripal in Salisbury in 2018 with the nerve agent novichok.German authorities said Russia had organised the 2019 killing ofZelimkhan Khangoshvili, a former Chechen rebel commander who was shot in a Berlin park by Vadim Krasikov, a hitman who was later greeted by Putin after he was exchanged in a spy swap.In June, a Russian artist who was critical of Putin was shot and killed at close range near his home in eastern Poland. Tusk said at the time thatthe killing of Robert Kuzovkov, known by the pseudonym Semyon Skrepetsky, had the hallmarks of a political assassination. He suggested it was possible Russia was behind it but Polish officials have not yet attributed it to Moscow.Last year French officials disrupted a plot that they believe was aimed at killing Vladimir Osechkin, a Russian exile who lives under police protection and works to help military defectors flee Putin’s war. Lithuanian officials also disrupted a plot last year to kill a Lithuanian supporter of Ukraine and another against a Russian activist. Officials in Germany have similarly broken up two plots: one to target the head of a German weapons company supplying Ukraine, the other against a Ukrainian military official.Polish authorities arrested a man in 2024 in what they said was a plot to assassinate the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. That year, a Russian helicopter pilot who defected was killed in Spain – Russian operatives were the prime suspects.“This campaign is not by accident or chance,” a senior European intelligence official previously told the AP. “There is political authorisation.”Explore more on these topicsPolandRussiaVladimir PutinDonald TuskEuropeNatoUkrainenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nearly 100 children detained as adults under UK-France migration deal | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Figures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilities
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Figures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilities
Content: People thought to be migrants attempt to board a small boat off the coast of Neufchâtel-Hardelot, France, in July.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenPeople thought to be migrants attempt to board a small boat off the coast of Neufchâtel-Hardelot, France, in July.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAImmigration and asylumNearly 100 children detained as adults under UK-France migration dealFigures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilitiesRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 13 Aug 2026 14.13 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly 100 children have been wrongly identified and detained as adults under Shabana Mahmood’s “one in, one out” deal withFrance, the Guardian can disclose.Home Office staff said that of 304 age-disputed cases arising from the scheme over nine months, 94 (31%) – were ultimately found to be minors. Children are supposed to be excluded from the scheme, while government policy limits immigration detention of unaccompanied children to 24 hours.The figures have emerged in a letter sent to the Home Office minister Anna Turley from Jane Leech, the interim chair of independent monitoring boards (IMBs), which scrutinise prisons and immigration detention facilities.In the highly critical letter, Leech also said some people detained under the scheme:Had been awaiting deportation for more than six months, despite being supposed be held for up to 28 days only “in exceptional cases”.Were being readied for removal to France despite having TB or requiring hospital treatment.Faced removal after being separated from family members with whom they had travelled, which she said had a “particularly damaging impact”.French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since springRead moreThe “one in, one out” initiative, launched last August, allows the UK to send somepeople who arrive by small boat back to France while agreeing to take the same number of people from France if they are judged to have a legitimate claim.Leech said the deal was “placing highly vulnerable, newly arrived individuals, including children and survivors of abuse, in detention”.In the letter to Turley, she wrote: “Your officials have informed the IMB that 304 age disputes have taken place between 15 August 2025 and 1 May 2026, of which 94 (31%) were assessed to be children.“The IMB is therefore concerned that child safeguarding mechanisms are ineffective, and believes more should be done to ensure that those whose age is under dispute are not detained in the first place.”Leech criticised the length of time it took for officials to complete age assessments. “In two cases observed by the Heathrow Board, it took 40 days or more from arrival at the IRC [immigration removal centre]to age assessment,” she wrote.Referring to the deal as Operation Hillmore, its official name within the Home Office, Leech said she had “significant concerns” about the vulnerabilities of those detained under the scheme.She wrote: “Many of those who have recently arrived present as psychologically distressed, and Boards have observed records and heard testimonies showing that many are survivors of torture and abuse.”There was evidence of poor health screening at Manston among the Hillmore detainees, Leech wrote. “Gatwick IRC recently received one individual from Manston with tuberculosis, while a second was refused admission to Brook House because of the critical state of their health, and referred directly to hospital.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe said people were being held for lengthy periods despite the scheme being intended to operate at pace, with one man detained for 27 weeks.Government figures covering 4 August 2025 to 30 June 2026 show that1,087 people were returned to Franceunder the deal. During the same period, 27,920 people arrived in the UK on small boats.Imran Hussain, the executive director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, described the figures as “disturbing” and said they were the latest example of children being wrongly treated as adults by the Home Office.“Too often refugee children are being treated as adults and put into unsafe situations, at risk of abuse and neglect, and exposed to significant safeguarding risks,” he said.“We call on the government to prioritise professional assessments led by trained social workers, which has been found to be the most accurate way to determine age and therefore avoid these risks.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “Robust age assessments are essential to maintaining the integrity of our border and ensuring migrants receive appropriate safeguarding and access to services.“We will continue to strengthen and modernise this process, including through the rollout of cutting-edge AI technology from next year to support age assessment.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeFranceEuropeMigrationForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine ‘offering Russia deal to halt attacks on civilian ships in Black Sea’ | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Kyiv reportedly suggested mutual agreement in attempt to reopen crucial grain corridor
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Kyiv reportedly suggested mutual agreement in attempt to reopen crucial grain corridor
Content: The ‘Nadezhda’ was brought into Samsun, a seaport on Turkey’s northern coast, last week after it was attacked by a drone in the Black Sea.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe ‘Nadezhda’ was brought into Samsun, a seaport on Turkey’s northern coast, last week after it was attacked by a drone in the Black Sea.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesUkraineUkraine ‘offering Russia deal to halt attacks on civilian ships in Black Sea’Kyiv reportedly suggested mutual agreement in attempt to reopen crucial grain corridorLuke Harding,Andrew Rothin Washington and agenciesThu 13 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine has proposed a deal with Russia for both sides to halt their attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea in an apparent attempt to reopen a crucial grain corridor, Reuters reports.Kyiv is said to have made the offer through a third party. Moscow has yet to respond, the news agency added. The busy waterway is a key export route for bothRussiaand Ukraine, used to transport grain and other vital foodstuffs worldwide.Since July Ukraine has effectively closed the route for commercial Russian shipping. Its drones havehit nearly 220 vessels in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea, including oil tankers, grain cargo ships and passenger ferries.The campaign has forced Russia to suspend shipping through a canal that connects the Caspian Sea with the Sea of Azov via a Russian river network. The route goes through the Kerch strait between occupied Crimea and Russia, and leads on to the Bosphorus strait in Turkey.During the same period, Russia has escalated its attacks on Ukraine’s southern ports, dealing a severe blow to the country’s agricultural sector. About 90% of grain and sunflower shipments leave from Odesa, and the neighbouring harbours of Chornomorsk and Pivdenne.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises from a ship damaged by a purported Russian attack in the Black Sea last month.Photograph: Ukrinform/ShutterstockIn July Russian droneskilled 10 sailors soon after their Turkish-owned grain carrier, the Golden Leo, set off from Odesa. Many of the victims were from Syria and India. Another 16 port workers and sailors have died in other recent strikes.Kyiv’s reported overture appears to be pragmatic, allowing both sides to resume shipments that are crucial to international food security. It comes as the country’s harvest season begins and with shipping from Ukrainian ports at a virtual standstill.The offer also followsa report in the FTthat the US vice-president, JD Vance, had asked Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to cease some attacks on the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.Ukrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human history | Simon JenkinsRead moreIn a phone call on 31 July, Vance complained that Ukrainian strikes on tankers carrying oil from Kazakhstan were hurting US companies and destabilising oil prices. He told Zelenskyy to stop them, the newspaper said, citing unnamed Ukrainian officials.Zelenskyy’s office has not commented, but Kyiv is in the middle of delicate negotiations with the Trump administration. It is seekingUS-manufactured Patriot interceptorsto defend Ukrainian cities from rampant Russian ballistic missile and drone swarms.Since the phone call, Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces have not attacked ships carrying oil from Kazakhstan via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal. But they have continued to pound other targets in Novorossiysk, which is home to Russia’s Black Sea naval fleet.On Wednesday Zelenskyy hailed a “massive” combined attack on the port, featuring rockets, jets and sea drones. He said Ukraine had taken out Russian warships, including two frigates, a large landing ship, a corvette and other vessels. They had been “hiding” in Novorossiysk Bay, he wrote on Telegram.Other targets included two major grain export terminals, it was reported. Russian officials said three people, including a child, were killed. “It is entirely justified that Ukraine is responding to Russia’s war, and it is Russia that can and must bring this war to an end,” Zelenskyy posted.The two sides have previously signed an agreement, brokered by Turkey and the UN, to stop maritime attacks. The Black Sea grain initiativelasted from July 2022 to July 2023. It ended when the Kremlin refused to renew it, complaining that western sanctions were damaging Russia’s agricultural sector.Ukraine subsequentlyreopened the route unilaterally, using sea drones to sink Russian ships using the north-west part of the Black Sea. Most vessels in Russia’s Black Sea fleet were forced to relocate from the exposed occupied Crimean port of Sevastopol to Novorossiysk.Explore more on these topicsUkraineShipping industryRussiaOceansEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli troops force families from homes amid settler terror campaign in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Former PM of Israel calls events ‘concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing’ against Palestinians
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Former PM of Israel calls events ‘concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing’ against Palestinians
Content: The Israeli army entered Qusra after days of a settler siege on Palestinian homes in the area.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Israeli army entered Qusra after days of a settler siege on Palestinian homes in the area.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAWest BankIsraeli troops force families from homes amid settler terror campaign in West BankFormer PM of Israel calls events ‘concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing’ against PalestiniansEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemThu 13 Aug 2026 14.54 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli troops have forced two Palestinian families to leave their besiegedWest Bankhomes, the day after a top Israeli commander personally promised he would end a violent settler campaign to drive them out.Israeli soldiers also took over eight other homes in Qusra early on Thursday, telling the village’s mayor, Abdul Azim Wadi, that the buildings were needed for a days-long operation to remove the settlers. They later relinquished six. Settlers still roam the village.The Palestinians’ ordeal began on Sunday when Israeli settlers and soldiers set up a tent blocking the entrance to three homes on the edge of the village. They severed water and electricity supplies and prevented an ambulance from reaching a sick toddler.Amid mounting international pressure over the siege, Maj Gen Avi Bluth, who commands all Israeli troops in the occupied West Bank, visited Qusra on Wednesday to meet the trapped Palestinians andcommittedto “evacuate” the settlers from the village.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers stand guard next to settlers in front of Palestinian houses in the village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/GettyBluth’s troops later removed the tent but left the militants, their bedding and other equipment. Soldiers retreated after a failed attempt to drive out the Israeli settler group with riot control techniques. The siege continued into a fifth day on Thursday, with the impact on the village only expanding after Bluth’s visit.“The army arrived at around 10am and asked us to evacuate the houses because of a military operation in the area that would last for three days. We refused to leave,” said Qusai Ridi, one of the besieged Palestinians. “The army then moved us all into one house.”He was allowed to return home in the afternoon, where he found Israeli soldiers had damaged a security camera system and stolen some equipment. They are still occupying the home of his neighbour Yousef Hassan, who is staying with Ridi.Settlers are still patrolling outside in the area where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh waskilledby a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault.“I am afraid and do not trust that the army will actually evacuate the settlers. But I sincerely hope they do,” Ridi said.View image in fullscreenCritics in Israel say a lack of will on the part of soldiers in Qusra has led to the siege continuing.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyHis brother is an American citizen, and the US ambassador to Israel,Mike Huckabee, who is generally supportive of Israel’s settlement project, described the siege as a “horrific act of terror” carried out by Israeli terrorists.On Thursday afternoon, Israeli soldiers left six homes they had taken over in the morning. The returning Palestinian families reported damage including a Qur’an with pages torn out and destroyed decorations.Israel’s former prime ministerEhud Olmertsaid the siege was a “concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing”, which left him disgusted and ashamed.“These are crimes against humanity which are actively supported by the Israeli government and are assisted by the indifference and total lack of action by the IDF and the Israeli police. It’s unforgettable and unforgivable.”The same terrortacticswere used to force another Palestinian family out of their home in the neighbouring village of Jalud in July. Soldiers and settlers were filmed playing with a football together on the terrace of that house on Thursday.An Israeli military spokesperson said soldiers had been ordered not to displace Palestinian residents of Qusra and would not operate inside the besieged homes.“The soldiers were instructed that the Qusra residents will remain in their homes,” the military said in a statement. The spokesperson declined to comment on why those orders were being violated.The chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), Eyal Zamir, has ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank. Domestic critics said the army’s failures in Qusra were more the result of a lack of will than shortage of forces.Abandoned by the US: Palestinian Americans trapped in a surge of Israeli settler violenceRead more“Yesterday’s events in Qusra illustrate the impotence of the IDF, the police, the GSS [Shin Bet] and other security organizations in the face of a group of bullies,” the commentator Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Israeli newspaper Ma’ariv.“Instead of bringing a police van [and] arresting the criminals … [security forces] have been trying to negotiate with them. They are thugs. They believe themselves to be the lords of the land.”Israeli militants target Palestinians with neartotal impunityin the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only oneindictmentover those deaths.Violence isdeployedas part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, the rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes.Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineMike HuckabeeEhud OlmertnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror
Content: Refqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAView image in fullscreenRefqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAWest BankIsraeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homesSettlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terrorEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemThu 13 Aug 2026 02.45 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in theWest Bankvillage of Qusra through a campaign of terror.A group of settlers and soldiers set up a tent outside the home of Yousef Hassan’s family on Sunday afternoon, trapping him inside with his wife and two young daughters.The Israeli men gathered just metres away from the spot where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh waskilledby a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault.“Every night, the settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night. We are living in a state of terror,” Hassan said. His mother, brother and sister, and three neighbours have also been blockaded inside, and their power and water have been cut off.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers stand guard next to settlers in front of Palestinian homes that they have blockaded in the village of Qusra.Photograph: Nidal Eshtayeh/APSettlers used thesame tacticsto steal another Palestinian home in neighbouring Jalud village, driving the al Tubasi family out in July after a months-long siege.They cut off water and electricity to the homes, although a solar panel allows Hassan to keep some devices charged in Qusra. They have also blocked medical care.When his younger daughter, aged two, fell ill with vomiting and a high fever on Monday, settlers blocked an ambulance from reaching the house. The girls and their mother were eventually evacuated on Tuesday.Hassan said those in the house were short on food and were drinking water and juice delivered by the ambulance that came to collect his daughter. “The situation is extremely dire.”On Wednesday morning, the commander of Israeli forces in the region, Gen Avi Bluth, visited the families and promised to lift the siege, an Israeli military spokesperson said. Hassan confirmed the visit.“Today, the area commander came and spoke with us and assured us that he would evacuate the settlers. For the first time, I feel that there is some seriousness on the part of the army in dealing with the settlers,” Hassan said, but added that it had not yet produced tangible results.Soldiers removed the tent but not the bedding and other possessions and, after brief clashes with the settlers, withdrew. “The settlers are still there in front of the house, and we are still unable to leave.”View image in fullscreenYousef Hassan said Israeli settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAAn Israeli military spokesperson said commanders were “gravely concerned” about the settlers’ actions and that soldiers who supported them would face disciplinary action, but declined to give a timeline for lifting the siege.On Wednesday evening, the chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Eyal Zamir, met other senior commanders to discuss the situation in Qusra. He ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank.“The battalion, which is currently undergoing a period of refreshment and training, will be deployed to the sector in order to strengthen operational control. Furthermore, additional soldiers will remain on standby for deployment as necessary,” a military spokesperson said.The military was working with the police to bring “those responsible for the disturbances to justice”, the spokesperson added.The incident has become an international issue for Israel. On Thursday, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, whosupportsthe wider settler movement,calledthe group who surrounded the homes “Israeli terrorists”.Israeli militants target Palestinians with neartotal impunityin the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only oneindictmentover those deaths.Violence isdeployedas part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, the rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes.View image in fullscreenAn Israeli settler tends to his animals as settlers besiege a Palestinian home.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA“What is happening in Qusra is not an isolated incident,” said B’Tselem’s executive director, Yuli Novak.“Settler militias, backed by the Israeli military, are expanding their attacks into Palestinian villages and towns – seizing land, attacking homes and forcing families out. Israel’s ethnic cleansing of the West Bank is accelerating and expanding in plain sight.”Dozens of Israelis from the country’s security, political and cultural elite havethreatenedlegal action against their government over its failure to tackle “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank.As the occupying power in the West Bank, Israel is responsible under international law for ensuring the safety of Palestinian civilians and meeting their basic needs.The Israeli military has declared the area a closed military zone and blocked journalists from approaching the Palestinian homes. Israeli settlers are subject to the same orders but have not been removed.Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: CPS director apologises for failings in case of rapist-murderer Simon Levy | Crown Prosecution Service | The Guardian
description: Stephen Parkinson says court should have been told that sex offender was being investigated for even more serious offences
Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: Stephen Parkinson says court should have been told that sex offender was being investigated for even more serious offences
Content: Stephen Parkinson, pictured in 2023, said he was ‘very sorry indeed’ that the court was not given information about the investigation into Levy.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenStephen Parkinson, pictured in 2023, said he was ‘very sorry indeed’ that the court was not given information about the investigation into Levy.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PACrown Prosecution ServiceCPS director apologises for failings in case of rapist-murderer Simon LevyStephen Parkinson says court should have been told that sex offender was being investigated for even more serious offencesAngus ThomsonThu 13 Aug 2026 19.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe director of theCrown Prosecution Servicehas apologised and vowed to increase staff numbers after conceding that the court deciding whether to release Simon Levy on bail should have known the serial sex offender was being investigated for rape and murder.Levy, 40, was this week given arare whole-life sentencefor the murders of Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins, and the rape of another woman.He was on bail and being monitored by police when he murdered Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and Wilkins five months later. Wilkins was murdered the day before what would have been her 40th birthday. She was found with 83 injuries or marks on her body.In an interview with LBC on Thursday, the director of public prosecutions for England and Wales, Stephen Parkinson, said his agency should have told the court it was investigating Levy for rape and murder before he was released on bail.“I absolutely accept that the court should have had that information, and I’m very sorry indeed,” he said.Parkinson said that Levy’s two bail hearings, which followed the murder of Valencia-Trujillo, were both held on a Saturday, when prosecutors were dealing with “an incredibly busy list”.View image in fullscreenSimon Levy was given a whole-life sentence for the murders.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAThe details of the ongoing investigations into Levy were in the system but prosecutors were not “aware of that information” and did not present it to the court, he said.“I don’t know whether that would have made a difference, but the point is the courts should have had it,” Parkinson said.Asked whether he thought Wilkins might still be alive if Levy had been denied bail, Parkinson said: “Clearly, if he had been remanded in custody, then he would not have had the opportunity to commit the crime that he did.”Parkinson said the service was providing extra resources to prosecutors to “minimise the risk” of such a case being repeated. Offer letters would be sent out this week to employ more staff, he said.After the Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley,questioned why Levy was released from jail despite sexually assaulting a female prison officer, Parkinson said the public did not want to see different parts of the criminal justice system “taking shots at each other”.“I think what they want to know is that lessons have been learned and that action is being taken,” he said.Levy was not charged with the prison assault until October 2025, by which time he had attacked 13 more women – killing two of them.Explore more on these topicsCrown Prosecution ServiceCrimeRape and sexual assaultnewsShareReuse this content

title: Unemployed young people to join AI boot camps to get job-ready | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Pilot scheme will provide three weeks of training as part of UK government’s latest attempt to address Neets crisis
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Pilot scheme will provide three weeks of training as part of UK government’s latest attempt to address Neets crisis
Content: The government wants the majority of attenders at the boot camp to gain an apprenticeship.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe government wants the majority of attenders at the boot camp to gain an apprenticeship.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianYouth unemploymentUnemployed young people to join AI boot camps to get job-readyPilot scheme will provide three weeks of training as part of UK government’s latest attempt to address Neets crisisDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 13 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYoung peopleout of work or at risk of unemployment in the UKare to join “AI boot camps” where they harness the technology to get a foothold in the workplace.The government’s latest attempt to address the crisis in Neets – young people not in work or education – involves turning to a technology that many view as a potential threat to employment.A pilot in north-westEnglandwill provide up to 70 people aged 16 to 21 with three weeks of AI training, including learning to build AI tools, understanding how businesses use AI and learning to use the technology responsibly. There will also be workplace skills training such as in using office IT systems and timekeeping.The government wants the majority of attenders at the boot camp to gain an apprenticeship at local businesses that have signed up, including the defence firm BAE Systems and the food company Heinz.Lisa Nandy, the digital, culture, media and sport secretary, said the scheme would “support young people at a crucial juncture in their lives”. The pilot will be used to refine an England-wide AI skills scheme due to roll out next summer.The boot camp will use AI tools from US tech firms including Microsoft, the ChatGPT developer OpenAI and Anthropic, the startup behind the Claude chatbot.Bouke Klein Teeselink, an academic at King’s College London and an expert on the impact of AI on work, said the boot camp was a “good idea in principle”.“What we need to do is make juniors more attractive to companies and one way to do that is make them more productive by teaching them how to do AI well,” he said.However, Teeselink said he was sceptical that a three-week programme would be enough to make teens “AI-ready”, because AI readiness required continuous learning and updating of skills.Fears of AI’s impact on jobs have focused heavily on school leavers and graduates because AI tools are viewed as capable of performing the “grunt work” that is typically set aside for workforce newcomers, with white-collar industries such as law, finance and marketing among the most vulnerable.This weekStanford University in the USflagged a decline in the employment of young workers in AI-exposed occupations such as software engineering and customer service.The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said the programme would give young people “the skills they need to thrive in the AI workplace”, amid signs of growing pressure on youth employment.The latest data, published in May, showed the number of young people aged 16 to 24 neither working nor learning surpassed 1 million for the first time since 2013, reaching 1.01 million in the three months from January to March.Aninterim report by the former Labour minister Alan Milburn, also published in May, warned that the figure could rise to one in six by 2031 and that Britain risked leaving behind a “lost generation” of young people ill-prepared for work.Last month Andy Burnham committed to cutting the number of Neets but declined to set a target deadline.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentUnemploymentYoung peopleAI (artificial intelligence)Work & careersEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage set for decisive but arguably empty victory in Clacton | Politics | The Guardian
description: Leader of Reform UK on course to defeat Count Binface and an assortment of fringe candidates as polls close in Essex
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Leader of Reform UK on course to defeat Count Binface and an assortment of fringe candidates as polls close in Essex
Content: Count Binface graffiti seen on Clacton pier on 13 August.Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCount Binface graffiti seen on Clacton pier on 13 August.Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesPoliticsNigel Farage set for decisive but arguably empty victory in ClactonLeader of Reform UK on course to defeat Count Binface and an assortment of fringe candidates as polls close in EssexPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentThu 13 Aug 2026 17.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVoting has closed in one of the UK’s more unusual and least tense byelections, withNigel Farageset for a decisive if arguably empty victory against dozens of independent, fringe, extreme or otherwise oddball opponents.The Reform UK leadersought re-electionto his Clacton seat in early July in an attempt to regain the political initiative following weeks of scrutiny over gifts he received and other aspects of his financial affairs.He framed the byelection as a chance for local voters to show their disdain for mainstream politics in a “people versus the establishment” contest, but was caught out after all the other main parties declined to stand candidates.Farage, 62, was instead left competing against a vast if decidedly niche field of 33 other hopefuls, including 20 independents, several representatives from tiny parties and no fewer than three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony party.The result, due to be announced from around 6am on Friday, will inevitably be a clear Farage win, with the only question being his margin of victoryover Count Binface, the self-styled campaigning alien who is the most prominent of his opponents.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage poses with a pint in a Clacton pub beer garden.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockWhile Reform will necessarily style the result as a clear endorsement of Farage’s record in the Essex seat, and of his tactic in calling the byelection, opponents will seize on any signs of a lower-than-expected majority or a slim turnout.Farageis being investigatedby the parliamentary standards watchdog over allegations he failed to declare gifts and donations, including a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne,first revealedby the Guardian.The process was paused when he resigned as an MP, but will resume once he is re-elected. If he is found to have breached declaration rules and suspended from the House of Commons, this could trigger a second byelection, which the other main parties would contest.While Farage insists he has relished a summer of knocking on doors in his constituency, he has been less visible on the national political stage – in part because of rules connected to how broadcasters must ensure balance during elections.Farage has insisted he did not need to declare the £5m from Harborne as it was given in advance of his return as Reform leader before the 2024 election. He has, however, given a series of explanations for the gift, including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit.The parliamentary inquiry is also looking into allegations that Farage wasfinancially supported by the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell, a close friend, afterthe Sunday Timesreported that Cottrell’s support included security and social media staff who worked on Farage’s online content in the year before he was elected.The 34-candidate field in the Clacton byelection is a UK record, beating the July 2008 contest in Haltemprice and Howden, East Yorkshire, regained by the Conservative MP David Davis after he resigned his seat and stood again as a protest over civil liberties.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsNigel FarageCount BinfacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Polls close in Clacton byelection where Nigel Farage faces slew of fringe candidates | Clacton byelection August 2026 | The Guardian
description: Longest ballot in UK voting history features likes of Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope alongside Reform leader
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Longest ballot in UK voting history features likes of Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope alongside Reform leader
Content: Count Binface (left) and Nigel Farage are among the candidates on the ballot.Composite: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCount Binface (left) and Nigel Farage are among the candidates on the ballot.Composite: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesClacton byelection August 2026Polls close in Clacton byelection where Nigel Farage faces slew of fringe candidatesLongest ballot in UK voting history features likes of Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope alongside Reform leaderAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentThu 13 Aug 2026 17.37 EDTFirst published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolls have closed in Clacton, where thousands of residents in the Essex seat voted in a ballot featuring Nigel Farage and a range of novelty and fringe candidates led byCount Binface.TheReform UKleader resigned as the MP for Clacton at the start of July and forced a byelection in an attempt to address complaints over a deepening scandal about gifts he received.He is expected to face aformal investigationby theparliamentary standards watchdog, which was opened in May after the Guardian revealed he had receiveda £5m personal giftfrom Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, in April 2024.Farage has denied the gift amounted to an inducement to run for office, insisting it was personal in nature. He has given a series of explanations for the gift, including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit.The inquiry will look into allegations Farage wasfinancially supported by the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell, a close friend, afterthe Sunday Timesreported that Cottrell’s support included security and social media staff who worked on Farage’s online content in the year before he was elected.Reform UK claimed that was a “baseless and contrived story” and that no parliamentary rules had been broken.The inquiry, which was suspended on 8 July after Farage’s decision to force a byelection, could restart as soon as Friday if he is re-elected.If parliament imposes sanctions for failing to declare the gifts, he may be removed from the House of Commons and face a second byelection.All of the main parties have boycotted the byelection, announcing they would not stand candidates for a “media circus” and a “vanity project”.
