It is also working with the Frankfurt Public Prosecutor’s Office to identify, delete and prosecute hate speech.At the 2024 Olympics, the German Olympics Sports Confederation also said it would take legal action against hate speech to protect athletes, and used AI software to automatically delete nearly 4,000 messages that were threatening, abusive, racist or sexist.Hodgkinson has herself sometimes deleted X, formerly known as Twitter, around major championships, describing the app as “awful”, and World Athletics have also made it a priority to tackle online abuse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt the end of 2024, the World Athletics president, Sebastian Coe, concluded a study that looked at 1.4m messages sent to athletes by saying that the governing bodywas giving athletes toolsto “proactively protect themselves against online abuse”.“Athlete welfare is at the very top of our priority list, and we will continue to put measures in place to ensure that athletes can confidently and safely engage with social media platforms,” he added.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsRaceGermanynewsShareReuse this content

title: This week’s soccer questions: is the Premier League wide open and should Barça avoid Rodri? | Soccer | The Guardian
description: We look at the many contenders for the English title this season, one of the big potential moves of the summer and chaos at Fifa
Author: Graham Ruthven
Headline: We look at the many contenders for the English title this season, one of the big potential moves of the summer and chaos at Fifa
Content: Declan Rice and Eberechi Eze celebrate last season’s title triumph.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeclan Rice and Eberechi Eze celebrate last season’s title triumph.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesSoccerThis week’s soccer questions: is the Premier League wide open and should Barça avoid Rodri?We look at the many contenders for the English title this season, one of the big potential moves of the summer and chaos at FifaGraham RuthvenThu 13 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 06.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCould this be the most open Premier League season ever?It’s difficult to recall a Premier League season starting amid such widespread uncertainty as this one. Half the division, including Chelsea, Liverpool and Manchester City, is under new management. The Pep Guardiola era is over and,as Jonathan Wilson put it, the Premier League has no alpha manager possibly for the first time ever.Mikel Arteta may be the new alpha. His Arsenal team the new dominant force. The Gunners, however, haven’t been great in preseason, conceding six goals in back-to-back defeats to Real Betis and Borussia Dortmund. Arsenal were still missing many of their best players after the World Cup, but what condition will they return in? William Saliba is sidelined with a back injury. Declan Rice played over 5,000 minutes for club and country last season. How fresh will thePremier Leaguechampions be?Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur have kept their managers over the summer, yet Michael Carrick and Roberto De Zerbi find themselves in a very difficult situation. Can Carrick prove he has a long-term vision for United? Will De Zerbi be afforded the freedom to reshape Spurs in his own image after saving them from relegation last season?It’s tempting to suggest this season could be ripe for a Leicester City-esque outsider to emerge as a shock challenger. Stability, however, is difficult to find anywhere in the league right now. Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham, Ipswich Town and Nottingham Forest all have new managers. Many of them have lost key players. Uncertainty is rife up and down the table.City may hit the ground running under Enzo Maresca. The same may happen for Chelsea under Xabi Alonso and Liverpool under Andoni Iraola. Equally, they could each require time to impose their own ideas on a new group of players. The Premier League’s established order doesn’t currently look so established. Someone could take advantage. But who?View image in fullscreenThere is no doubting Rodri’s ability, but is he the right fit for Barcelona?Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesAre Barcelona repeating mistakes by targeting Rodri?For a player with no previous links to the club, Rodri is about asBarcelonaas they come. Nobody had more touches of the ball at the 2026 World Cup. Nor did any other player complete more passes than the metronome at the base of Spain’s midfield. It makes sense that the Catalans want the 30-year-old this summer.Rodri is the closest thing to Sergio Busquets since Sergio Busquets. It’s easy to envisage how he will fit into Barcelona’s midfield. He will give Hansi Flick the sort of structure his team has lacked in the biggest games over the last two seasons. Barça will be a bigger threat in the Champions League with Rodri controlling things from deep.Something, however, about Barcelona’s move for the World Cup winner harks back to the club’s darkest days, when their recklessness in the transfer market nearly sank the whole club. The Catalans have only recovered in recent years thanks to the unmatched output of their youth academy, so would Rodri’s signing indicate another change in approach?Barcelona have done a good job of supplementing their squad with an experienced head or two. Robert Lewandowski spent four years at the club while Marcus Rashford enjoyed a moderately successful season on loan there last term. These signings, however, plugged a hole in Barça’s squad that La Masia couldn’t fill.The Rodri signing is different because Barcelona already boast one of the strongest midfields anywhere in the world. At least one of Marc Bernal, Marc Casado, Gavi or Pedri will be impacted by the arrival of the Ballon d’Or winner and the last time Barça put up barriers between their famed youth academy and the first team, things didn’t work out so well.Is Gianni Infantino causing an irreparable divide?Two weeks on from Gianni Infantino’s failed attempt to sell off the World Cup like a cartoon villain trying to steal a giant diamond from a museum, the soccer landscape shows no sign of healing. If anything, divisions are now even deeper as confederations have lined up to either oust the embattled Fifa president or back him.The past few days have made clearer where exactly the divides are. While AFC, Concacaf and Uefa co-signed an open letter calling for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it,” confirming preliminary discussions about the hosting of alternative tournaments, Infantino has received support from Caf and Conmebol. The battle lines have been drawn.It’s difficult to envisage how the sport will ever come together again with Infantino still in place. Even if he is ultimately ousted or defeated in March’s presidential election, the political divisions that have opened up could take a long time to mend. Infantino may have broken international soccer for the foreseeable future.Nobody really knows how serious AFC, Concacaf and Uefa are in their threat to boycott future World Cups and organise their own tournaments. That in itself, however, is proof of how the sport is fracturing. If trust in soccer’s governing body is so low that this is a viable option, how can there possibly be a way forward without further fragmentation?Only a few weeks ago, Infantino appeared untouchable. That may still be the case. The rebels may not have the numbers to get rid of him in a vote. The pertinent question, though, concerns the position of Fifa president itself and what power it will still hold once all this is over.Explore more on these topicsFootballLionel MessiMLSBarcelonaPremier LeagueUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carrick rules out £100m signing for Manchester United as Rashford rejoins squad | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick has stated that Manchester United will not make a £100m signing due to finances as Marcus Rashford joined up with the squad again
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Michael Carrick has stated that Manchester United will not make a £100m signing due to finances as Marcus Rashford joined up with the squad again
Content: Marcus Rashford did not play for Manchester United in their friendly against Leeds.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarcus Rashford did not play for Manchester United in their friendly against Leeds.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedCarrick rules out £100m signing for Manchester United as Rashford rejoins squadUnited unable to financially compete with rivalsRashford back after Barcelona loan but could leaveJamie Jacksonin County KildareThu 13 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick has stated thatManchester Unitedwill not make a £100m signing this summer due to their finances, with the manager also insisting that Marcus Rashford “is our player” despite the forward and club preferring him to depart.In the current window United have invested a total of £85mon Youri Tielemansand Andrey Santos but have never spent £100m on a single transfer.Chelsea set Friday deadline for Fernández suitors as City reject new £51m Barça bid for RodriRead moreThis is in contrast to Manchester City, Tottenham, Liverpool, Arsenal, and Chelsea, the rest of the traditional big six, who have all spent £100m-plus on a player in recent years.Carrick was asked how United can compete. “Money’s money. I get that,” said the manager. “It’s still about football and that’s where the competition lies. What we feel naturally as a group is to try and win games. So there’s a lot that goes into that, but certainly the situation is what it is as well, whether that’s finances or whatever.”Carrick guided United to third last season and was asked why the money from Champions League qualification cannot be invested in expensive elite players.“To be honest, I haven’t got the answers for that. We’re working with pushing everything that we can to make the best of it,” he said. “For now, we’ve got to make the most of it, push everything in every boundary that we can to be able to win again, basically.”Quick GuideTielemans apologises for offending Villa fans with United boastShowYouri Tielemans has apologised to Aston Villa after saying he joined Manchester United because they are a bigger club than his former team.Tielemans made a £35m move to Old Trafford in July, when United triggered a release clause in his Villa contract. The Belgium midfielder helped Villa end their 30-year trophy drought by winning the Europa League last season, but Tielemans had no qualms about joining United, who finished one spot above fourth-placed Villa in the Premier League last season."There are clubs above Villa, and Manchester United is one of them," he said on Wednesday – before taking to social media on Thursday to make peace with his former club."Never meant for my words in the press yesterday to offend anyone or the institution of Aston Villa Football Club, which I massively respect and I’m grateful for the past three years," the 29-year-old wrote on Instagram."I must however admit my mistake and apologise for my choice of words, will be more careful in the future. Wishing the club the best in the future."AFPWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The 45-year-old was asked whether United can win the title without any players worth £100m or more in the squad.Carrick said: “A little bit depends on what position that is and what you’ve got and the dynamics you need at certain points. Sometimes you do need that if it’s the right player. Again, it’s not purely on money. Obviously over time we need to be pushing to look to enhance the squad. So, yeah, 100% we need to do that.“We’ve done really good business. So we’re delighted with that [but] we want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that, so that never stops.”View image in fullscreenYouri Tielemans, who arrived from Aston Villa, was one of United’s big summer signings.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesRashford joined the squad at their County Kildare training camp base on Sunday following a post-World Cup break. The 28-year-old has been on loan the past season and a half at Barcelona and Aston Villa respectively, due to a breakdown in his relationship with the club’s executive and the former United head coach Ruben Amorim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRelations have eased andRashford is focused on workingunder Carrick, though the player’s preference is to depart. The club want the same as they seek to reduce the wage bill. The forward’s final two years of his deal are worth £35m.Disney+ secures rights to Gary Neville’s Overlap content in riposte to Lineker’s Netflix dealRead moreCarrick was asked if Rashford will stay beyond the 1 September deadline. “He’s our player and has trained really well,” said Carrick. “It’s been good to have him around the group again.”The manager was asked if he wants Rashford to remain. “He’s a very good player, Marcus, and if you’re going to have a career over 10 or 15 years, there’s going to be times when things go in a direction and maybe a different direction. All right, that happens,” he said. “There’s ups and downs, and that doesn’t judge you as a one-off kind of [state]. It’s what happens over time, and now we’re in a positive place as a group, and Marcus can offer us so much. He has done, and he can do again, so it’s quite exciting.”Asked if Carrick views Rashford as not for sale, he said: “No, he’s our player and he gives something a little bit different in the group.”Harry Maguire, Noussair Mazraoui and Tielemans have all indicated United can win the title. “We’ve definitely got the potential to achieve something really special,” said Carrick. “I’m not hiding from the fact, and we should aim to do that, but I can’t give you a definite answer on that – it’s certainly what we’re pushing to do because that’s the club we are.”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMarcus RashfordMichael CarricknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Boxing is in the blood’: Sherlock Holmes, Arthur Conan Doyle and the prize ring | Boxing | The Guardian
description: The author of a new novel about the famed detective explores a little-known facet of Holmes’s creator
Author: Thomas Hauser
Headline: The author of a new novel about the famed detective explores a little-known facet of Holmes’s creator
Content: The Sherlock Holmes statue at Baker Street in London.Photograph: Alex Segre/Moment Editorial/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Sherlock Holmes statue at Baker Street in London.Photograph: Alex Segre/Moment Editorial/Getty ImagesBoxing‘Boxing is in the blood’: Sherlock Holmes, Arthur Conan Doyle and the prize ringThe author of a new novel about the famed detective explores a little-known facet of Holmes’s creatorThomas HauserThu 13 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat do Sherlock Holmes andArthur Conan Doylehave to do with boxing? More than you may think. Doyle, who created Holmes, was a boxing enthusiast who boxed a bit and wrote extensively about the sport.Doyle stood 6ft tall and weighed in the neighborhood of 200lb. He began sparring while a medical student at the University of Edinburgh and described himself as “a fair average amateur”.“One can compress more exercise into a short time in this way than in any other,” Doyle advocated. He also wrote, “Boxing is the finest single man sport” and added, “I have seen nearly all the great boxers of my time from JL Sullivan down to Tommy Burns and Jack Johnson.”Indeed, Doyle claimed in 1920 that he’d been asked to referee the 1910 championship fight between Johnson and James Jeffries. “I considered the proposal carefully,” he wrote. “But I did not feel inclined to travel thousands of miles and possibly to have to face a hostile demonstration from the supporters of the beaten man, whichever it might be.”In reality, it’s unlikely that the offer to referee Jeffries-Johnson was a serious one. At one point, the publicity machine that promoter Tex Rickard put in place to heighten interest in the fight had turned to the choice of a referee, and the editor of the New York Morning Telegraph suggested that Doyle officiate. Johnson thought that former US president Theodore Roosevelt would be a better choice.Doyle revered boxing tradition but acknowledged there were times when the sport had fallen low. Writing in 1921, he looked back a half-century and declared, “They were the bad old days, those, in the prize-ring. The old knuckle-fighting had died out in scandal and disgrace, smothered by the pestilent crowd of betting men and ruffians of all sorts who brought disgrace and ruin upon the decent fighting men. An honest sportsman who desired to see a fight was usually set upon by villains against whom he had no redress, since he himself was engaged on what was technically an illegal action. He was stripped in the open street, his purse taken, and his head split open if he ventured to resist. No wonder that the classic sport was attended by those only who had nothing to lose. The legal glove fight had not yet arisen, and the cult was in a strange intermediate condition. It was impossible to regulate it and equally impossible to abolish it, since nothing appeals more directly and powerfully to the average Briton.”But Doyle took joy in the spread of boxing through the general population in the early-20th century and wrote, “I rejoice to think that boxing is taken up by most of our public schools and in the Army. That a weaker man should be beaten by a stronger man would indeed be intolerable. But when we have two men of equal weight and equal experience, either of whom can surrender of his own free will, I see no reason why we should raise any cry of brutality.”And he vigorously opposed reformers who sought to abolish the sport, stating, “Of one thing I am certain. The present course of action will never succeed in exterminating boxing in England. You can drive it underground, but you cannot stop it. Instead of having contests in the presence of the public, the press, and the police, you will have it underground. You can have it in the back parlour of a public-house. But you are going to have it somehow. It is certain you will not stop it. That is absolutely impossible. Boxing - the love of boxing - is in the blood of the people.”That brings us to Sherlock Holmes, one of literature’s most beloved characters. The original Holmes canon consists of four novels and 56 short stories written by Doyle and published between 1887 and 1927. In the first – a novel titled A Study in Scarlet – Dr Watson lists Holmes’s areas of expertise and says he was an “expert boxer” while noting that the detective knew “next to nothing” about the contemporary boxing scene.Boxing surfaces again in The Sign of Four (the second Holmes novel) when Holmes encounters an ex-prizefighter named McMurdo who is working as a porter:“McMurdo,” cried Sherlock Holmes genially. “I don’t think you can have forgotten me. Don’t you remember the amateur who fought three rounds with you at Alison’s rooms on the night of your benefit four years back?”“Not Mr Sherlock Holmes!” roared the prize-fighter. “God’s truth! How could I have mistook you? If instead o’ standin’ there so quiet, you had just stepped up and given me that cross-hit of yours under the jaw, I’d ha’ known you without a question. Ah, you’re one that has wasted your gifts, you have! You might have aimed high, if you had joined the fancy.”Holmes’s skill as a boxer is also cited in several short stories – The Gloria Scott, The Yellow Face, and The Solitary Cyclist. But in truth, the references to boxing in the Holmes canon are simplistic. Doyle’s best writing about boxing was elsewhere.The Croxley Master: A Great Tale of the Prize Ring is a novella that tells the story of Robert Montgomery, a young medical student with a background in amateur boxing who enters the prize ring out of desperation to compete for a £100 purse that he needs to finance the final year of his medical education.Doyle described Montgomery’s first sighting of his opponent on the day of the fight as follows: “The prize-fighter had come out from his curtain, a squat formidable figure, monstrous in chest and arms, limping slightly on his distorted leg. His skin had none of the freshness and clearness of Montgomery’s, but was dusky and mottled with one huge mole amid the mat of tangled black hair which thatched his mighty breast. His huge shoulders and great arms with brown sledge-hammer fists would have fitted the heaviest man that ever threw his cap into a ring.”Montgomery is on the brink of defeat during the fight but rallies to turn the tide.“It was a magnificent blow,” Doyle wrote. “Straight, clean, crisp with the force of the loins and the back behind it. And it landed where he had meant it to – upon the exact point of that blue-grained chin. The Master fell backwards, flat, prostrate, striking the ground with so simultaneous a clap that it was like a shutter falling from a wall. A yell broke from the crowded benches as the giant went down. He lay upon his back, his knees a little drawn up, his huge chest panting. He twitched and shook, but could not move. His feet pawed convulsively once or twice. It was no use. He was done. ‘Eight – nine – ten!’ said the timekeeper. And the roar of a thousand voices with a deafening clap like the broadside of a ship told that the Master of Croxley was the Master no more. Montgomery stood half dazed, looking down at the huge, prostrate figure. He could hardly realize that it was indeed all over.”Doyle’s love of boxing is also on display in three short stories.The Lord of Falconbridge is set in the early days of prize fighting with an overly contrived plot but a dramatically-told prizefight at the end. The Fall of Lord Barrymore has an unusual boxing scene in which an elite boxer dressed as a woman throttles a bully to humiliate the bully and his patron. The Bully of Brocas Court draws on Doyle’s love of the paranormal.Unfortunately, Doyle came down on the wrong side of history in a controversy that involved boxing. In 1922, the British Home Office banned a proposed fight in England between world light-heavyweight champion Battling Siki and British heavyweight champion Joe Beckett and issued a statement that read, “In contests between men of colour and white men, the temperaments of the contestants are not compatible. Moreover, all sorts of passions are aroused. Such contests, considering there are a very large number of men of colour in the British empire, are considered against the higher national interest and they tend to arouse passions which it is inadvisable to stimulate.”Doyle supported the ban, writing, “Let black and white keep separate and fight among themselves. Some of the greatest fights in the history of the ring have been between white and coloured men, as when Cribb and Molyneaux met last century. But conditions were not so complex then. The British Empire did not contain so many black people. Nowadays a mixed fight gets beyond sport and enters the region of interracial politics.”Putting that statement in context of its time, it should be noted that the Times also supported the ban, editorializing, “Boxing matches between white men and blacks, to be photographed for the delectation of coloured races all over the world, have become a dangerous anachronism. To allow them to take place on English soil would in these days be an act of suicidal folly.”But let’s return to boxing at its core and close with Rodney Stone – a novel Doyle wrote in 1896 that builds to a fight between an honorable former champion turned blacksmith named Jack Harrison and Crab Wilson (an elite fighter with a dastardly patron).Reflecting back on that battle, the narrator who tells the tale declares, “Many a time in my life, I have braced myself to a hard task by the remembrance of that morning, asking myself if my manhood were so weak that I would not do for my country, or for those whom I loved, as much as these two would endure for a paltry stake and for their own credit amongst their fellows. Such a spectacle may brutalize those who are brutal. But I say that there is a spiritual side to it also, and that the sight of the utmost human limit of endurance and courage is one which bears a lesson of its own.”Doyle wrote those words more than a century ago. But they could have been written about Muhammad Ali fighting Joe Frazier in Manila, Arturo Gatti v Micky Ward, or any number of other fights that have enthralled boxing fans over the years.The essence of boxing remains unchanged.Thomas Hauser’s email address isthomashauserwriter@gmail.com. His next book – Sherlock Holmes and Mrs. Rutledge – will be published later this month and is available for preorder onAmazon.comandAmazon.co.ukas well as other platforms. In 2019, Hauser was selected for boxing’s highest honor - induction into the International Boxing Hall of Fame.Explore more on these topicsBoxingArthur Conan DoyleUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Empty seats and faded aura show how Springboks outgrew the All Blacks | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: The Springboks can use Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry to establish themselves as one of the greatest teams of all time
Author: Daniel Gallan
Headline: The Springboks can use Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry to establish themselves as one of the greatest teams of all time
Content: New Zealand looked like the team the marketing promised against the Sharks in Durban.Photograph: Phill Magakoe/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNew Zealand looked like the team the marketing promised against the Sharks in Durban.Photograph: Phill Magakoe/AFP/Getty ImagesRugby unionAnalysisEmpty seats and faded aura show how Springboks outgrew the All BlacksDaniel GallanBack-to-back world champions can use Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry to establish themselves as one of the greatest teams of all timeThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTShareSouth Africans are supposed to care about the All Blacks more than this. On Tuesday night 14,759 people dotted the 52,000-seat Kings Park Stadium to watch New Zealand dismantle the Sharks 54-0. Durban was cold and soaked, with snow falling elsewhere in KwaZulu-Natal, but even allowing for the weather it made for an awkward advertisement for a grand new project.Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry– the eight-match tour by New Zealand, culminating in four Tests, including one in the US – is an attempt to turn more than a century of history into a modern commercial property. The unions have formed a 50-50 venture, sharing commercial income, while taking the final Test to Baltimore is expected to generate $4m-$6m more than another game in South Africa. Both unions need the money and professional sport is supposed to generate revenue. But a rivalry cannot live on branding alone.Springboks and All Blacks flex financial muscles with ‘Greatest Rivalry’ tourRead moreThe early South African response to these All Blacks has been respectful without being reverential. More than 47,000 watched their opening 38-21 win against the Stormers in Cape Town, but there was little sense that an irresistible force had arrived. The contest was level after 65 minutes, New Zealand’s scrum and maul were troubled and four late tries gave the score an emphatic gloss.Tuesday offered a different picture. The Sharks were desperately depleted, but the scale of their defeat still carried a thud. New Zealand scored eight tries and added 40 points after half-time in conditions that ought to have made handling difficult. South Africa’s Daily Maverick called it “vintage class”. For the first time, the All Blacks looked like the team the marketing promised.Yet it is difficult to imagine Rassie Erasmus losing much sleep. For generations, the arrival of the All Blacks in South Africa came with a particular menace. Between the 1995 World Cup final and Erasmus taking charge, in 2018, New Zealand’s win-rate in the Republic was 68.2%. They claimed a 2-1 series win in 1996, won by 36 points in Pretoria in 2003 and by a record 42 points in Durban in 2016.That deference has gone. South Africa have won four of the past five meetings, including the2023 World Cup final, and last year handed the All Blacksa 43-10 hiding in Wellington. The Springboks are back-to-back world champions. The question is no longer whether they can live with the All Blacks. It is how much further they can pull away.View image in fullscreenNew Zealand showed plenty of enterprise at a wet Kings Park Stadium, but the attendance was poor.Photograph: Rogan Ward/ReutersPerhaps there is some insecurity buried in all this. South Africa and New Zealand sit far from the traditional centres of global power, two countries shaped differently by an empire that has long since receded. Rugby offers a rare chance to look at the rest of the world from above.In South Africa, the All Blacks are woven into the national mythology: Nelson Mandela in the No 6 jersey means more because Jonah Lomu and New Zealand were standing on the other side. Remove the All Blacks and something in the Springbok mythology loses its meaning. Being the best matters. Being better than the All Blacks matters more.This is where Erasmus has excelled. He keeps moving the finish line. Eight years ago, his job was simply to make the Springboks competitive again. Then came the boxes. Beat the All Blacks in New Zealand. Tick. Win the Rugby Championship. Tick. Win the World Cup. Tick. Beat the British & Irish Lions. Tick. Defend the World Cup. Another tick. Complete one checklist and Erasmus simply finds another.Since 2023, that has meant proving South Africa are more than a team built to peak at World Cups. Theywon the 2024 Rugby Championshipand have broadened their rugby without surrendering the violence that made them champions. Damian Willemse can shift between full-back and first receiver, Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu threatens the line and Cheslin Kolbe goes looking for work. Two Test-class front rows allow Erasmus to replace almost an entire pack without surrendering scrum pressure. They can cut teams apart as readily as bludgeon them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll Blacks great Ma’a Nonu performs solo haka against New Zealand in South Africa tour matchRead moreWhich invites comparison with the last great dynasty. Richie McCaw’s All Blacks won the2011and2015 World Cups and lost only three Tests between them. Their greatness lay not merely in winning twice when it mattered most, but in dominating the years in between. The Springboks have matched their two World Cups and next year will attempt to go one better. What they have not yet matched is the sustained supremacy over their greatest rival that made those All Blacks feel untouchable. The next four Tests offer the chance.Which is why South Africa should want these All Blacks to find another gear. This series, due to return in New Zealand in four years’ time, needs a contest worthy of its name. So does South Africa’s idea of itself as rugby’s dominant power. Sweeping aside a faded force proves rather less.For decades the Springboks chased New Zealand. Erasmus has caught them and passed them. One box remains. Tick it and this team may have the strongest claim yet to being the greatest of all time.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teamanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 9: Everton | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: Modest but sensible-looking recruitment befits the club’s new air of stability but a continuation of their spring slump could test David Moyes’s appetite for the fight
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Modest but sensible-looking recruitment befits the club’s new air of stability but a continuation of their spring slump could test David Moyes’s appetite for the fight
Content: Thierno Barry has shown promising signs during Everton’s pre-season matches. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersModest but sensible-looking recruitment befits the club’s new air of stability but a continuation of their spring slump could test David Moyes’s appetite for the fightByAndy HunterThu 13 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:10th (NB: this is not necessarily Andy Hunter’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:13thProspectsA season stripped of the fear of relegation, featuring more proactive, front-footed football and the return of some hope: hadEvertonbeen offered that package before their relocation to Hill Dickinson Stadium last summer it would have been accepted gratefully given the turmoil of the previous four years. For four fifths of last season it was accepted gratefully, but then came a collapse that transformed perceptions of David Moyes’s first full season back in charge. Talk of progress requires more supporting evidence this time around.Everton were three points off the fifth and final Champions League qualification spot on 21 Marchhaving dismantled Chelseain their finest performance at the club’s new stadium. They did not win another game all season and slumped to 13th on the final day – the same position as the previous campaign under Sean Dyche and Moyes, with only one point more but an inferior goal difference. European football may well have been an ambitious target for a club adjusting to a new home and the loss of 10 players following the expiry of their contracts, loans included. But the opportunity presented itself to Moyes’s team and they blew it.Without the upheaval of last summer, with midfield resources improved and young players having had the benefit of a year’s experience of thePremier League, European qualification could be a more realistic proposition this season. Provided a few glaring holes in Moyes’s squad are finally filled. An upgrade on the limited centre-forward options of Beto and Thierno Barry is essential, although the latter has shown more promising signs in pre-season. Likewise a successor to Séamus Coleman – one of several big Evertonian losses behind the scenes recently. Everton’s quest for a new right-back is their very own Odyssey, while central defence was another area of concern last season. Genuine progress, the measure of which is not open to debate, rests on the final moves of the window.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureThe consequences of Farhad Moshiri’s calamitous ownership are still being felt with Evertonordered to pay almost £40m in compensationto Burnley over the latter’s relegation in 2021-22. Everton are appealing against the can-of-worms verdict by a Premier League independent disciplinary commission, along with the biggest financial penalty ever imposed on a Premier League club, but claim their latest punishment has not affected this summer’s transfer plans. Many season ticket holders have been hit by above-inflation price increases – in some instances of almost 10% – and the club have extended a sponsorship deal with Stake, despite the UK governmentpledging to crack downon unlicensed gambling operators sponsoring British sports teams.Owner-fan relationshipThe Friedkin Group (TFG) has brought the financial stability that Everton desperately needed but it would be a stretch to suggest fans have connected with a low-key ownership group that rarely attend games. The man they appointed to run the club, chief executive, Angus Kinnear, annoyed supporters at the end of last season by claiming the hierarchy was “happily dissatisfied” with the first campaign at Hill Dickinson Stadium. The comment was portrayed as fresh evidence of Everton accepting mediocrity but in fairness to Kinnear, who was writing about TFG’s determination to banish the threats of financial instability, relegation and regulatory sanction, he did add: “The progress is clear but we have not achieved anything yet.”The managerDavid Moyes turns 64 in April and, while the Premier League’s oldest manager clearly retains the hunger and ambition to rebuild Everton on a stronger footing, it will be interesting to see whether he retains the appetite for a fight with his critics in the event of a poor start. Particularly as the Scotland job remains available and he would appear the ideal candidate to succeed Steve Clarke. Moyes was exceeding his brief until the dismal end to last season cost Everton a shot at Europe and placed his team selections under an unforgiving spotlight. Talk of a contract extension has since gone quiet.Star signingView image in fullscreenBrennan Johnson struggled at Crystal Palace but could have just the attacking qualities Everton need.Photograph: Everton FCIt has been a sensible window rather than a sexy one from Everton so far – see replacing Idrissa Gana Gueye with the £7m Christian Nørgaard – but they might have delivered in swapping Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. No one would dispute that the Wales’ international’s move from Tottenham to Crystal Palace in January fell flat, least of all Palace who were willing to take a significant hit on their £35m, one-time record investment only seven months later. But if the 25-year-old recaptures the form he showed at Nottingham Forest, or when scoring 18 goals for Spurs in 2024-25, he could prove a steal who addresses several problems in the Everton frontline.Stat attackDavid Moyes loves to keep a settled side. Everton averaged the fewest changes to their starting XI of any team in the 2025-26 Premier League. With the squad looking largely the same as last season, this trend should continue. But what if injuries bite?StatSet for a breakthroughTyler Dibling would have been a strong candidate for this category last summer following his arrival from Southampton for an initial £35m. It reflects a nonevent of a debut season on Merseyside that he can be nominated 12 months on. Everton invested a lot of time and money into their pursuit of the England Under-21 international, who remains the most expensive signing of Moyes’s second spell in charge, but the return was a huge disappointment. The attacking midfielder started only four league games and was not given a single minute after the 2-0 win over Burnley on 3 March. The manager did not hide his frustration with what he was seeing on the training ground.World Cup impactThe longest World Cup in history should not have too onerous an impact on Moyes’s squad. Only three of his players were involved and, of those, only Jordan Pickford was in action after 1 July. Pickford came in for familiar criticism following his performances against Ghana and Argentina despite reinforcing his status as England’s undisputed No 1 goalkeeper across the tournament. Iliman Ndiaye started once for Senegal and was subbed in the 73rd minute with his country leading Belgium 2-0 in the last-32 tie. They ultimately lost 3-2. Nathan Patterson, whose Everton future is uncertain, featured in all three of Scotland’s forgettable group campaign.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27EvertonPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rangers crash out of Europa League as Derek McInnes’s winless start goes on | Europa League | The Guardian
description: Rangers drew 1-1 with Jagiellonia Bialystok but lost 3-2 on aggregate, while Hearts held Benfica but also went out of the competition, having lost the first leg 6-1
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rangers drew 1-1 with Jagiellonia Bialystok but lost 3-2 on aggregate, while Hearts held Benfica but also went out of the competition, having lost the first leg 6-1
Content: Ross McCrorie (centre) and his Rangers teammates trudge off the field after the match.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoss McCrorie (centre) and his Rangers teammates trudge off the field after the match.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersEuropa LeagueRangers crash out of Europa League as Derek McInnes’s winless start goes onRangers 1-1 Jagiellonia Bialystok (2-3 agg)Spirited Hearts hold Benfica but also out of competitionPA MediaThu 13 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDerek McInnes’s fledgling tenure as Rangers manager is in disarray after his side exited theEuropa Leaguequalifiers with a 3-2 aggregate defeat to Jagiellonia Bialystok after drawing 1-1 at Ibrox.Fog and on time (nearly): Lech Poznan reach Faroe Islands for fixture after two-day tripRead moreRangers had lost 2-1 in the first leg in Poland last week but there was optimism when the captain, Lawrence Shankland, levelled the tie on aggregate with a penalty on 19 minutes.However, in the 65th minute, the visitors deservedly equalised through the attacker Nik Prelec and the disjointed home side could not get a foothold in the game again despite changes in formation and personnel, with the boos ringing out around the ground at full time from fans frustrated atthe dismal start to the season.McInnes has failed to register a win in four competitive matchessince moving from Hearts in the summerand the dispiriting performance means Rangers will take on Jablonec, from Czechia, in the Conference League playoff round.Hearts, meanwhile, restored some pride in a 1-1 draw withBenficaas they too dropped out of the Europa League.Tómas Magnússon had the home fans dreaming of a famous win over their illustrious opponents after firing in the opener in the 77th minute. But the Portuguese giants, cruising from a 6-1 first leg win a week earlier, levelled less than a minute later through Dodi Lukébakio to wrap up a 7-2 aggregate triumph.View image in fullscreenTómas Magnússon (left) is congratulated by his teammates after scoring for Hearts against Benfica.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAIt was nevertheless an encouraging display from Wouter Vrancken’s side against a team who made seven changes from the first leg.The consolation for Hearts is a place in theConference Leagueplayoffs, where they will face Rapid Vienna of Austria.David Gray revealed hisHibernianplayers had their heads in ice buckets as he lauded them for “an incredible achievement” after closing out a 2-1 aggregate victory over Shkendija to set up a Conference League playoff round showdown with the Belgian side Gent. The two teams played out a tightly contested 0-0 draw in the second leg in the searing heat of the Todor Proeski National Arena.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHibernian fans in the stands at the Todor Proeski National Arena.Photograph: Nikola Krstic/Shutterstock“I’m delighted for the players,” the Hibs manager told BBC Sport. “It’s a brilliant time to get your first clean sheet of the season.“I just said to the players, don’t underestimate how big an achievement that is against a really good side who made it to the knockout stages of the competition last season.“Added to that, the conditions, the heat, we had to deal with all these things. I don’t think it was a brilliant game, but we put our bodies on the line and the attitude was there.”Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueRangersHeartsBenficaConference LeagueHiberniannewsShareReuse this content

title: Championship spending hits record levels and likely to go higher as playoffs expand | Championship | The Guardian
description: With a top-eight finish offering at least a playoff place, the temptation to spend big in pursuit of the Premier League will grow – but so will the risks
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: With a top-eight finish offering at least a playoff place, the temptation to spend big in pursuit of the Premier League will grow – but so will the risks
Content: Ollie McBurnie celebrates Hull’s lucrative playoff final winner with Matt Crooks. The Tigers spent 142% of their revenue on wages in 2024-25.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenOllie McBurnie celebrates Hull’s lucrative playoff final winner with Matt Crooks. The Tigers spent 142% of their revenue on wages in 2024-25.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersChampionshipChampionship spending hits record levels and likely to go higher as playoffs expandWith a top-eight finish offering at least a playoff place, the temptation to spend big in pursuit of the Premier League will grow – but so will the risksAndrew BeasleyThu 13 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Championship’s collective wage bill grew to a record £903m in 2024-25, according to Deloitte’s latest Annual Review of Football Finance. Clubs are paying players enormous sums in their pursuit of Premier League football. With the playoffsexpanding this season, the number of owners willing to risk even more money in the hope of securing promotion is only likely to increase.In isolation, the figure of £903m does not signify much. Compared to the Premier League’s £4.4bn salary outlay, it almost looks small. But England’s top division can afford that gargantuan commitment to wages whereas the second tier cannot. The 24 clubs in theChampionshipearned £942m, meaning salaries consumed 96% of revenue. If there was any surprise in their collective net debt being £1.4bn at the end of 2024-25, it was only that it had reduced from the £1.5bn it was a year earlier.While qualifying for European competitions is not on the immediate agenda for clubs at that level, Uefa’s financial sustainability regulations restrict spending on wages, transfers and agent fees to 70% of club revenues. Luton and Sheffield United spent about 59% of their income on salaries in 2024-25, with the parachute payments they received for being relegated from the Premier League the previous season helping them keep a grip on their finances.Chart showing percentage of income spent on wages by clubs in the 2024-25 ChampionshipBut only four other clubs were below 80%, with 13 – more than half the division – spending more on wages than they earned. Cardiff spent £39m on salaries against £26m income, giving them the worst wages to revenue percentage in the division (150%). The reward for their ambition was to finish bottom of the table.The reason for such risk-taking is obvious. Deloitte estimates that the newly promoted Coventry and Hull will see their revenue rise by at least £210m over the next three seasons, with the windfall potentially reaching £365m if they can retain their Premier League status into 2027-28. Ipswich’s figures are lower thanks to receiving parachute payments last season, but they are still thought to be around £170m and £325m respectively.These sums are helping to form a strata of clubs that regularly flit between the top two tiers of English football. Burnley have either enjoyed promotion from the Championship or suffered Premier League relegation for five consecutive seasons. The Clarets are fourth favourites with bookmakers to go up once again next May, with their fellow relegated sides West Ham and Wolves leading the Championship promotion market.Their advantage is obvious. Capology estimates West Ham have the 15th highest wage bill in the world outside the Premier League and Saudi Pro League. Wolves are only two spots behind them in these amended standings, with Burnley a further six places back.The majority of top division teams in France, Germany, Italy and Spain can’t keep pace with the salary spend of these clubs so how can most Championship teams expect to compete? Jarrod Bowen alone is thought to earn £7.8m per year at West Ham, more than the entire squads of Lincoln (£5.8m) or Bolton (£6.3m).Chart showing the top 10 club wage bills in the 2026-27 ChampionshipThe new playoff system in the Championship at least offers more clubs the chance of a Premier League golden ticket. The teams that finish between third and eighth will qualify, with third and fourth going straight through to the traditional two-legged semi-finals. Their opponents in those ties will be decided by one-legged quarter-finals that feature the teams in fifth and sixth at home to those in eighth and seventh respectively.This will leave the tantalising possibility of a playoff berth open to plenty of clubs until very late in the season. Few will be entirely out of the running in January, when the transfer window offers an opportunity for squad investment. The fate of Leicester highlights the possible risks though. When the winter window closed earlier this year, they were six points from eighth, nine above the bottom three. Clubs in a similar position next January may gamble on going for a playoff spot but could end up being relegatedas Leicester were.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChart showing National League playoff wins by position in the final table since 2017-18The National League also highlights how unlikely it is that teams that take the additional playoff spots go up. The highest tier of non-league football has employed a six-team playoff format since 2017-18, with only the division winner earning automatic promotion. The club finishing seventh have yet to win the playoffs, with the side in sixth succeeding only once. Even then, the team in question (Grimsby in 2022) were in their only season outside League Two in the past 10. They were below their regular level, not climbing up to reach sixth.The Championship has a similar theme for playoff success. No team finishing sixth have gone up since 2010, with Aston Villa the most recent fifth-placed side to earn promotion,in 2019. None of the previous seven teams that finished eighth in the second flight averaged more than 1.5 points-per-game or won more than 43.4% of their matches. If they can’t win every other game at that level, how can they hope to compete in the Premier League in the unlikely event they go up?No one cares about that when there’s a reward in the region of £200m simply for getting there. Supporters might care if the owner drives their club’s finances further into the red chasing an unlikely playoff dream though.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kieran Trippier: ‘The Championship is relentless … it’s totally different to the Premier League’ | Wolverhampton Wanderers | The Guardian
description: The former England full-back is back in the Championship after 12 years away, hoping to lead Wolves out of it
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: The former England full-back is back in the Championship after 12 years away, hoping to lead Wolves out of it
Content: Kieran Trippier has played under some of the biggest names in football and won La Liga at Atlético Madrid.Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFCView image in fullscreenKieran Trippier has played under some of the biggest names in football and won La Liga at Atlético Madrid.Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFCWolverhampton WanderersInterviewKieran Trippier: ‘The Championship is relentless … it’s totally different to the Premier League’Ben FisherThe former England full-back is back in the Championship after 12 years away, hoping to lead Wolves out of itThu 13 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the question inevitably comes, Kieran Trippier is happy to set the record straight. Fresh from training, head to toe in Wolves kit – vest, shorts and club-branded sliders – he walks into a suite at their Compton Park base, conversation soon shifting to an episode that rocked supporters and stopped outsiders in their tracks: three days after signing, the manager Trippier cited as a significant driver behind his decision to drop into the second tier, Rob Edwards,was sacked. All the while, a deal for his replacement, César Peixoto, was being accelerated.“I’m not going to sit here and lie, I wasn’t expecting it,” Trippier says. “But it’s the club’s decision. I had good chats with Rob, of course, but I’m here to play for Wolves. There are many surprises in football and that certainly was a surprise, I’m not going to deny that. But I just cracked on, I was with my kids on holiday, training in Mallorca and just looking forward to day one in pre-season.”David Squires on … the masochistic life of a Football League fanRead moreOther reports followed the bombshell news. “I’ve read it all: that I was looking to rip my contract up, and all this nonsense. I was just looking forward to reporting back to Wolves. I don’t know where it even came from to be honest, that I was looking to rip my contract up – it certainly didn’t come from me, otherwise you would have heard it from me, that’s just the player that I am.”It is a line in keeping with Trippier’s endearing straight-talking character that has made him a big hit everywhere he has been. He left Newcastle at the end of last season after playing an instrumental part in their rise under Eddie Howe, the crowning glory the Carabao Cup win last year. He spent three seasons at Atlético Madrid under Diego Simeone, where he won La Liga, after four at Tottenham under Mauricio Pochettino, culminating in a Champions League final appearance. He represented England at four major tournaments, playing every game en route to the Euro 2024 final.Now he is back in the second tier for the first time since promotion with Burnley 12 years ago, poised to start Wolves’Championshipopener against Blackburn on Friday. He accepts it is not a natural segue. Instead of entertaining Barcelona at St James’ Park last September, here comes Bolton at Molineux in October.View image in fullscreenKieran Trippier in a huddle with his new teammates during Wolves’ 3-0 friendly win against Racing Santander.Photograph: WWFC“I’m not ashamed to go to the Championship because I played in it for many years,” Trippier says, recalling his first taste of the division: defending alongside Darren Moore while a teenager at Barnsley. “I had a good chat with Eddie Howe and Ross Wilson [Newcastle’s sporting director] and made my decision at the end of the season that I wanted to try something new. There were a few [interested] clubs but it was important for me that I was close to my children.”Trippier, who calls Manchester home, knows what to expect from an unforgiving league. He recalls being part of a Burnley side that triumphed 2-1 at Wolves in the penultimate game of 2012-13, to extinguish lingering fears of relegation and all but condemn Wolves to League One. “I’ve been speaking to my teammates because the majority of them have never played in the Championship, so it’s important for myself and the lads who have to help them and try and make them understand that it’s going to be difficult.“I’ve just said: it’s relentless, because it is … and it’s totally different to the Premier League. Going to Lincoln away is going to be a difficult game, but they’re good lads who have listened to me, Tommy [Doyle], Adam [Armstrong]. The lads will be ready.”This is Trippier’s first external interview since joining Wolves on a two-year contract with the option of a further 12 months. He canvassed the opinions of Doyle, Conor Coady, John Ruddy and Sam Johnstone, with whom he was on holiday in Turkey before signing, to tap into “the insides of the club”. Edwards’ sudden departure – a month after André committed his future to the club and 48 hours after Raúl Jiménez returned to enhance the feelgood factor generated by Trippier’s arrival – warrants discussion, but the full-back is well placed to talk on numerous fronts, including Howe’s exit after four and a half years.“He helped the club stay in the Premier League, twice qualified for the Champions League, won a trophy, but the most important thing he did was reconnecting the supporters with the team. I was told before the [Saudi Arabia-led] takeover that it was not a good place to be – the fans were against the owners, the board etc – but when the new owners came in, and the manager, he [Howe] connected everyone, just like Gareth Southgate did with England.”Is Howe’s legacy deserving of a statue? “He’s won a trophy, hasn’t he?” Trippier says with a smile, “but that’s not for me to decide … the parade was incredible, the big banner of the manager showed the love the supporters had for him and still have now. When I first went there, it was a tough place [to play], especially after gettingbeat by Cambridge[in the FA Cup third round], but maybe that was a blessing, really, so we could just focus on [staying in] the Premier League … he will go down in history there, for sure. I’m gutted to see him go.”View image in fullscreenKieran Trippier holds the Carabao Cup trophy aloft with Alexander Isak on board the open-top bus with their teammates and manager Eddie Howe (front row, left) as they pass St James’ Park.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesThen there is England’sWorld Cup semi-final collapse against Argentina, when their low block crumbled late on. “I’ve been in that position many, many times with Simeone – I could name 30 games when he’s done it and we’ve managed to see it out, typical Simeone for you. He’s the master of the dark arts and seeing out games. Thomas Tuchel has been in that position many, many times, won a Champions League trophy with Chelsea, did unbelievably with Bayern Munich … it just didn’t happen. We were against one of the greatest players ever who can flick a switch,” Trippier says of Lionel Messi, clicking his fingers. “I’ve played against him many times where he just walks for 60 minutes, but then he can score a hat-trick. That’s just the magic of him.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPeixoto is unknown to most but Trippier says he was aware of the Portuguese’s pedigree before the 46-year-old, who spent last season in charge of Gil Vicente, succeeded Edwards. Peixoto’s command of English has meant Trippier has not needed to dip into his Spanish to converse. “When the postman used to come in Madrid, I used to get my son to answer because he was fluent,” Trippier says, smiling.So, what’s Peixoto like? “Really demanding. Honest. On the training field he is 100mph, nuts – in a good way – but he’s really, really demanding and I think that’s what we need as players if we want to be successful. He’s very demanding, like Pochettino and Simeone. He has his own rules: don’t break his trust, don’t be late. I wouldn’t like to be on his bad side, let’s put it that way.”View image in fullscreenThe Wolves manager, César Peixoto (second right), slows down from his 100mph on the training pitch to speak with Kieran Trippier (left), Andre (centre) and Toti Gomes at a pre-season training in Faro, Portugal.Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Getty ImagesTrippier turns 36 in September, twice the age of Mateus Mané, an exciting talent who Trippier witnessed first-hand when marking him with Newcastle last season and one of those Wolves hope will illuminate a positive season. “I feel good, I feel probably in the best shape I’ve been in for many, many years. I’m not as fast as I used to be but I always believe I am clever and fast up here,” Trippier says, tapping his temples. “I feel like I’ve still got many years left in the tank.”For Wolves, his signing was a coup. “It’s similar to when I went to Newcastle, when I left Atlético Madrid … There were a lot of eyebrows raised, but throughout my whole career I’ve had no regrets.”Trippier, who is part of Peixoto’s leadership group, acknowledges he and his teammates will begin the campaign with a target on their backs. “Going into the Blackburn game, the first game of the Championship season, all eyes will be on us,” he says.“When teams get relegated from the Premier League, everybody wants to beat them. It was a tough year for Wolves last year, but this season is a new season, like a reset. The reality is now we’re in the Championship, so you have to forget what happened and look forward, be positive. Our goal has to be to go straight back up to the Premier League.”Explore more on these topicsWolverhampton WanderersChampionshipinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea set Friday deadline for Fernández suitors as City reject new £51m Barça bid for Rodri | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City have rejected Barcelona’s second bid of around €60m for Rodri, while Chelsea have set a 5pm Friday deadline for the club to bid for Enzo Fernández
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manchester City have rejected Barcelona’s second bid of around €60m for Rodri, while Chelsea have set a 5pm Friday deadline for the club to bid for Enzo Fernández
Content: Enzo Fernández in Chelsea training on Wednesday. The Argentina international has been heavily linked with a move to Manchester City.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEnzo Fernández in Chelsea training on Wednesday. The Argentina international has been heavily linked with a move to Manchester City.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesManchester CityChelsea set Friday deadline for Fernández suitors as City reject new £51m Barça bid for RodriManchester City want around £65m for Spain midfielderAl-Qadsiah agree deal for City’s Tijjani ReijndersJamie JacksonThu 13 Aug 2026 05.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City have rejected Barcelona’ssecond bid of around €60m (£51m)for Rodri, while Chelsea have set a 5pm (BST) Friday deadline for the club to bid £120m for the midfielder’s potential replacement, Enzo Fernández.On Tuesday Barça improved on theirinitial offer of €45mbut this has been turned down. City, it is thought, want between £60m and £65m for Rodri, who captained Spain to victory at the World Cup and is a former Ballon d’Or winner.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreAs the 30-year has expressed a preference for Barça, City accept it is all but inevitable he will head to the Camp Nou so Fernández has been identified to take his place in Enzo Maresca’s squad.As Chelsea’s captain and a World Cup winner at Qatar 2022, Fernández would add seniority and leadership. However Chelsea’s stance is that as City and other suitors have already had two months of the transfer window to firm up interest in Fernández, if the £120m valuation is not met by an official bid for this sum by 5pm on Friday, the 25-year-old will remain their player.To generate some of the finance required Tijjani Reijnders may be sold to Al-Qadsiah. A deal has been agreed between City and the Saudi Arabian club for a package worth around €60m for the 28-year-old Dutchman who joined last summer. It is understood that Reijnders has agreed personal terms.Jérémy Doku has signed a contract extension that will keep him at City until 2031. The 24-year-old winger said: “With Enzo [Maresca] here now I am really excited about the new season. His style of football is the kind we love, so that’s exciting for the players.“The City fans are also a huge reason I have signed this new contract. I feel their love and support, and it means the world to me. I want to focus on bringing them the success they deserve.”Tottenham retain an interest in Savinho, with Maresca prepared to sell the winger if a replacement can be found. Chelsea’s Pedro Neto is an option attractive to City’s manager after the Portuguese wide player impressed him while in charge at the west London club.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityBarcelonaChelseaTransfer windowLa LigaEuropean club footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was horrendous’: Durham captain relieved WSL2 club survived after fears of folding  | Women's football | The Guardian
description: The captain, Sarah Wilson, said she is delighted that fresh investment was found, adding: ‘It honestly feels now that nothing’s ever happened’
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The captain, Sarah Wilson, said she is delighted that fresh investment was found, adding: ‘It honestly feels now that nothing’s ever happened’
Content: Durham’s captain, Sarah Wilson (No 5), leads her side out before last September’s WSL2 match against Crystal Palace.Photograph: Ed Sykes/WSL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDurham’s captain, Sarah Wilson (No 5), leads her side out before last September’s WSL2 match against Crystal Palace.Photograph: Ed Sykes/WSL/Getty ImagesWomen's football‘It was horrendous’: Durham captain relieved WSL2 club survived after fears of foldingSarah Wilson delighted fresh investment was found‘It honestly feels now that nothing’s ever happened’Tom GarryThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 06.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Durham captain, Sarah Wilson, has spoken of her relief over the fresh investment that saved the club this summer, after what she recalled as a “horrendous” period worrying that the Women’s Super League 2 club could fold.Durham finished 10th in England’s second tier last term and have been ever-present in WSL2 since 2014 but their ability to remain in the division was in major doubt when the club released a statement on 8 June warning that they would have to “cease operations” if they could not find fresh investment within 21 days. Later in June they were rescued when the local businessman and South Shields FC co-owner Geoff Thompson, together with his co-investor, agreed to acquire a majority stake in the club.‘It’s a nice hobby’: Manchester United’s Janina Leitzig on goalkeeping and gardeningRead moreWilson has played for Durham for 12 years and, recalling that mid-June period of uncertainty, she said: “There’s no way to sugarcoat it. It was horrendous. [For] a couple of weeks we didn’t know if we were coming or going or what was going on. And then all of a sudden we got the news that we had been saved and then within a couple of weeks we’ve got a new manager coming in so it’s just really exciting and it honestly feels now like nothing’s ever happened. It’s a breath of fresh air. It’s incredible.“Going from a really difficult time to where we are now in such a short space of time is an absolute credit to the club. We all kind of found ourselves in a really difficult position, waiting for answers. I was trying to support the team as much as I could [as captain], just reassuring [teammates] and keeping in contact with everyone. And I must say, we were well looked after and information was shared when it could be shared. [But] it was just such an awful time. So when we found out the really good news, it was just like a huge weight lifted off our shoulders.“There are so many jobs and young kids coming through that would have been massively affected and it would have been a massive shame for the north-east and for the club. Now it’s just really, really positive and really exciting to move forward with everything.”Durham begin the new campaign at home to Southampton on 6 September, with what will be Durham’s new head coach Willie Kirk’s first match in charge, following his appointment in July.It is the former Bristol City, Everton and Leicester manager’s first managerial job in English football since he wassacked by Leicesterin March 2024. In the intervening years he has managed the Swedish sides Linköping and Djurgårdens IF.Wilson has nothing but praise for the former Manchester United assistant manager, saying of Kirk: “[He’s been] brilliant, he’s just brought the club to a completely different new standard. When you’ve got someone who comes from that elite background, they bring all of those experiences.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As soon as we found the news, it was like: ‘Right, OK, when do we start?’ He’s got some incredible experience working with some really top players. So he’s been fantastic.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ingebrigtsen claims Kerr ‘ruining’ athletics by missing Europeans after breaking mile record | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen said Britain’s Josh Kerr was ‘ruining the sport’ by sitting out of. the European Athletics Championships
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jakob Ingebrigtsen said Britain’s Josh Kerr was ‘ruining the sport’ by sitting out of. the European Athletics Championships
Content: Jakob Ingebrigtsen (right) and Josh Kerr, pictured racing at the 2024 Olympics, have traded barbs in the past.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJakob Ingebrigtsen (right) and Josh Kerr, pictured racing at the 2024 Olympics, have traded barbs in the past.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsIngebrigtsen claims Kerr ‘ruining’ athletics by missing Europeans after breaking mile recordJosh Kerr broke longstanding world mile record in JulyNorwegian says championships are ‘for the best athletes’Sean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamThu 13 Aug 2026 18.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheEuropean 5,000m champion Jakob Ingebrigtsenhas criticised Britain’s Josh Kerr for being one of the athletes “ruining” the sport by missing the event in Birmingham.Ingebrigtsen, who won a brilliant gold medal in his first race after 11 months out of the sport due to an achilles injury, also told the BBC that he “could never” prioritise a time over a title.Quicksilver Amy Hunt flies to glorious golden double with 200m triumphRead moreAsked if he was disappointed Kerr,who broke the world mile record last month, is not racing in Birmingham, the Norwegian added: “Very – and I think a lot of people should be, because that is what championships are all about.“It’s not for us as athletes to choose almost where to participate. We have these championships for a reason, and that is for the best athletes to compete – that is the whole point.“So I definitely think it is ruining the sport if we are not participating. We all have different plans, but I could never see myself in that position.”Kerr ran a stunning 3:42.66 to break the world mile mark at the London Diamond League in July before a dominant display to take the Commonwealth title a fortnight later. However he opted out of the European championships saying he was “flying close to the sun” of injury.Ingebrigtsen did, however, praise Kerr’s world mile record performance as an “extremely good race” and “a very strong performance”.But he also questioned Kerr’s explanation for his absence in Birmingham. “Everything comes down to what you want to do. People go to work every day. It is not like because you are a professional runner you can’t work every day.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is not the first time Ingebrigtsen and Kerr have traded barbs. In 2023, Kerr accused Ingebrigtsen of “some flaws in the manners realm” after the Norwegian had said that he was ill when Kerr beat him to the world 1500m title.Then in 2024, Ingebrigsten raised his eyebrows after Kerr had broken the two-mile world record. “I would have beaten him in that race, blindfolded,” the Norwegian said. “But it’s good that people run better than they have done before.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: European Athletics Championship 2026: Hunt beats Adeleke and Asher-Smith to win women’s 200m gold – as it happened | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Amy Hunt won a second gold of the week, while Mark English won gold and Rhasidat Adeleke silver for Ireland
Author: Luke McLaughlin
Headline: Amy Hunt won a second gold of the week, while Mark English won gold and Rhasidat Adeleke silver for Ireland
Content: 5h ago17.25 EDTSean IngleTwo down. Two to go.Amy Hunt’s dream of winning a record four gold medals at a single European championships gathered further momentum with a bravura performance in front of a raucous Alexander Stadium crowd.Hunt was given a huge cheer by the 20,082 in attendance, by far the biggest of the championships so far, when she was introduced in lane seven. But she had to work hard to get past her domestic rival Dina Asher-Smith, in lane eight.She then began to tie up. But Hunt had enough to take gold in 22.19 sec, just ahead of Ireland’s fast-finishing Rhasidat Adeleke, who ran 22.28 to win silver, with Asher-Smith winning bronze a hundredth of a second further back.Quicksilver Amy Hunt flies to glorious golden double in 200mRead moreShare

title: Quicksilver Amy Hunt flies to glorious golden double with 200m triumph | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Britain’s Amy Hunt struck gold in the 200m to complete the sprint double, while Mark English became Ireland’s first European Championship men’s gold medallist by winning the 800m
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Britain’s Amy Hunt struck gold in the 200m to complete the sprint double, while Mark English became Ireland’s first European Championship men’s gold medallist by winning the 800m
Content: Amy Hunt hopes to add to her medal collection in the relays.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAmy Hunt hopes to add to her medal collection in the relays.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsQuicksilver Amy Hunt flies to glorious golden double with 200m triumphHunt had won 100m already; Asher-Smith wins bronzeMark English wins 800m for Ireland’s first men’s goldSean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamThu 13 Aug 2026 17.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid the adrenalised delirium of her second European title in three days, Amy Hunt walked to the nearest TV camera, held up her hands and, in homage to Russell Crowe’s character in Gladiator screamed: “Are you not entertained?”It quickly transpired that the 24-year-old Cambridge graduate had been quite the warrior off the track too. Because, as she revealed after collecting a 200m gold medal to go alongsideMonday’s 100m title, she has been nearly fainting this year when running over the longer distance.European Athletics Championship 2026: Hunt beats Adeleke and Asher-Smith to win women’s 200m gold – as it happenedRead more“I have had a lot of health things going on this year – some really, really low pressure,” Hunt explained. “The 200s have been really scary. I have been nearly fainting after a lot of my 200s this year. I had just to go into that one and get on the bend and be really brave.”Hunt had entered the 200m final as the overwhelming favourite, but she had to work to chase down the two-time champion, Dina Asher-Smith, one lane outside her, around the bend.Having done that, the raucous 20,000 crowd at the Alexander Stadium expected to see a coronation. Instead it turned into a struggle, and Hunt only just had enough in the tank to cross the line in 22.19sec, ahead of Ireland’s fast-finishing Rhasidat Adeleke, who ran a national record of 22.28. Britain’s Asher-Smith took bronze a further 0.01 further back.It means that Hunt’s dream of winning an historic quadruple of gold medals at these European Championships is alive – as she made clear afterwards by holding two fingers up in her right hand, before flipping the hand to show four fingers.“Two out of four,” she said. “Honestly, I think the 100 is the hardest mentally. And the 200 is the hardest physically.“I was thinking about my coach,” he said before I went in: ‘Just imagine me in lane 10 with a stopwatch and a whistle. Just keep those thighs up, girl.’“But there’s no celebrating, no champagne until Sunday night because I have a debt to the ladies,” Hunt explained, as she set her sights on the 4x100m and mixed relays over the weekend. “We have to make sure we come here and make sure we show them who is the best sprint nation in Europe.After 92 years, Ireland finally has a male European championship gold medallist. And his name is English – Mark English. The 33-year-old doctor from Donegal, produced a surgical performance to take gold, tracking and then overtaking Croatian Marino Bloudek in the home straight to win in 1:45.26.“Just relief,” said English. “I have been trying for a lifetime to get a title. I had planned to go to Sierra Nevada at 6am tomorrow, so I’m going to have to try to rebook that flight. These moments don’t come around often. I have a life that’s never come around for me before, so I’ll have to try to celebrate it somehow.”Bloudek clung on to take silver with Spain’s Mohamed Attaoui winning bronze. As the huge Irish contingent celebrated, the heart also went out to Britain’s Max Burgin, who was forced to pull out minutes before the race after suffering an injury in the warmup.View image in fullscreenMark English crosses the line to become the first Irishman to win European gold.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAIt caps a summer of woe for Burgin, who also picked up a virus at the Commonwealth Games and didn’t make it out of the semi-finals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was also no medal for another British contender, Elise Thorner, in the 3,000m steeplechase. The 25-year-old had entered the race as the fastest European over the distance in 2026 but she could only finish fifth behind Germany’s Gesa Felicitas Krause.The race was also notable for a faceplant by another German, Lea Meyer, into the water jump while running in the medal positions. While Meyer got up, she could only finish fourth.“It was gutting to see Lea actually fall, because I know her quite well,” said Thorner. “She is an amazing athlete. Shocking to see and trying to get over was a bit mad. But I was pretty spent with 200m so I was hanging on anyway.”View image in fullscreenElise Thorner (right) could finish only fifth in the women’s 3000m steeplechase final.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAFurther success Germany as Leo Neugebauer hung on to win the men’s decathlon from his compatriot Niklas Kaul after collapsing over the line. His score of 8,611 points proved enough by 38 points, even though the 6ft 7in Neugebauer looked to be wading through treacle over the last 50 metres before collapsing over the line.But the event was marred by extraordinary scenes earlier on day two in the pole vault, after officials forgot to raise the bar from 4.70m to 4.80m.
