As a result athletes were under the impression that they were attempting 4.80m, while the bar was in fact still at 4.70m.A EuropeanAthleticsstatement said that the “results of this additional 4.70m round were cancelled, and the competition was resumed at 4.80m, with all athletes given the opportunity to attempt the height.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jack Draper ‘in difficult place’ after defeat by Martín Landaluce at Cincinnati Open | Jack Draper | The Guardian
description: Former world No 4 Jack Draper slumped to a 6-3, 7-5 defeat against Martín Landaluce in the first round of the Cincinnati Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Former world No 4 Jack Draper slumped to a 6-3, 7-5 defeat against Martín Landaluce in the first round of the Cincinnati Open
Content: Jack Draper never recovered from a poor start against Martín Landaluce.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJack Draper never recovered from a poor start against Martín Landaluce.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesJack DraperJack Draper ‘in difficult place’ after defeat by Martín Landaluce at Cincinnati OpenFormer world No 4 slumps to 6-3, 7-5 first-round lossDraper still recovering from long-term arm injuryTumaini Carayolin CincinnatiThu 13 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe minuscule amount of confidence and self-beliefJack Drapercurrently has to call upon in the most difficult period of his career was underscored in the first game of his opening match in Cincinnati. Draper began his service game by shanking a forehand into the back fence, which he followed up with two double faults. He immediately fell down a break and never recovered.A few fleeting positive moments followed, but this miserable start set the tone for another excruciating day for the former world No 4 as he could not escape the mental fatigue borne out of battling serious injury for 15 months and counting. Draper fell 6-3, 7-5 to Martín Landaluce, the world No 64.Jack Draper: ‘When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again’Read more“It’s the same as last week, the way I’m usually able to fight for every ball and conduct myself, it’s just missing,” Draper said. “After last week, I put in a lot of hard work to play a bit better this week. Obviously, the conditions and all the things that I’m changing is very hard to manage, but I think from just an internal point of view, it’s a difficult place to be right now.”Draper spent the final stretch of his first-round loss at the Canadian Openlast week in tears. On Wednesday, as he tried to put on a brave face and remain positive, the 24-year-old described his emotions as a reaction to the mental toll of both his injury – bone bruising in his left arm – and the disruptive changes he has made in order to lessen the strain on it. There were no tears this time, but between a poor first set and the way he squandered six set points in set two after leading with a double break at 5-2, Draper was a shadow of himself.He said: “From the start of the match, you’re battling it a lot and you’re trying to keep going with it and moving forwards throughout the match and trying to … pump stuff up and give you energy, but it just suppresses you down. It’s got to a point with me where it’s taken probably one of my biggest qualities, my fighting spirit.”Since Wimbledon, Draper has changed his strings, his racket and he continues to adjust to his service motion. Thesechanges have all been madein service of reducing the strain on his arm and at the expense of optimising his performance. Although Draper said his injury did not directly contribute to the loss, the great uncertainty surrounding the condition of his arm remains the defining problem.View image in fullscreenJack Draper is likely to need to progress through qualifying to compete at the US Open.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesUnlike most injuries, this is not a case of resting for some time and coming back. “I think that’s the toughest part,” he said. “It’s like there are no right answers. You have to figure it out. A lot of it’s probably, I found out in the end, biomechanics and changing rackets. It’s a tough injury because you have to start again with what you do.“There’s a level of chronic pain that’s always with you. That starts to go away, but obviously the arm is linked to the elbow. It’s linked to bicep tendinitis, it’s linked to so many nerves around that area. So when you have an injury to that area, the whole arm is kind of lit up. It’s like someone taking blood pressure. And your arm’s just [struggling].“When you’ve got that on your playing arm – this is my life, this is my career, you know? It’s tough enough as it is to play such an intense sport and the amount we have to give to it. And when you’ve got an injury that is tough to come past and tough to understand, there’s many challenges, there’s many obstacles. For a normal person, they’d go and probably have six months off and it might recover and heal. Truth is, I’m playing tennis and so it’s not as simple as taking time off and it’s going to go because it doesn’t [work]. I’ve tried it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is more uncertainty on the horizon. Since he is ranked No 143 and does not have a protected ranking, Draper has been reliant on wildcards to enter ATP events.He does not expect to receive a wildcard for the US Open, meaning he will have to play in the qualifying draw in order to compete in New York. “I think it’s the fatigue in my mind and my body from a long period of setback and struggle and isolation and just trying to get back all the time. The level of my fall almost from where I was last year and the amount of things that I’m having to change in my tennis. Yeah, the mountain seems very, very big.”Cameron Norrie, the British No 2, set up an intriguing second-round match against the top seed, Alexander Zverev, after he recovered from a set down to defeat Dino Prizmic 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. Norrie, who missed out on being seeded by one ranking spot, has begun to find his form during the hard court swing after a rib injury hurt his momentum during the clay and grass court seasons. His meeting on Saturday with the French Open champion will provide him with a clear measure of his level.Explore more on these topicsJack DraperTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hodgkinson’s key rival Werro reinstated after shock fall to set up dream Euro 800m final | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Audrey Werro finished last but was advanced after a review while Keely Hodgkinson and Femke Broeders-Bol eased through in their semi-final
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Audrey Werro finished last but was advanced after a review while Keely Hodgkinson and Femke Broeders-Bol eased through in their semi-final
Content: Audrey Werro (right, on the floor) falls after accidental contact with Anaïs Bourgoin (second from left).Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenAudrey Werro (right, on the floor) falls after accidental contact with Anaïs Bourgoin (second from left).Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsHodgkinson’s key rival Werro reinstated after shock fall to set up dream Euro 800m finalWerro makes final after review reveals accidental tripHodgkinson and Broeders-Bol ease into final togetherSean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamThu 13 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeely Hodgkinson’s biggest rival for European 800m gold has been dramatically put through into Friday’s final after being tripped and sent sprawling during Thursday’s first semi-final.It means thatthe hugely anticipated showdownis still on between Hodgkinson, the Olympic gold medallist; Audrey Werro, the 22-year-old Swiss superstar who ran thethird fastest time in historyin June; and the Netherlands’ Femke Broeders-Bol, the 400m hurdles world champion who has moved up this season.Keely Hodgkinson puts on shades and breezes into European 800m semi-finals in styleRead moreBut for 50 minutes or so after Werro’s huge tumble, her part in the final was in doubt as she trudged home in last place and the official results showed she was out.However, she was reinstated into a 10-strong final after a video review showed that the back of her right foot made contact with the left hand of the French athlete Anaïs Bourgoin with 120m to go.The effect of Bourgoin’s hand was like a rugby tap-tackle and it sparked an extraordinary chain of events. First Werro was unable to get her back leg through and ended up crashing face-down on to the curb. Then her back legs clipped the Lithuanian Gabija Galvydyte, who also fell to the floor.“I made a conscious choice to try and manage the race at a moderate pace,” said Werro. “It’s always safer to run at the front, but today there were risks; I could sense things were hectic behind me. A fall can happen in an instant. I’ve only got a few scrapes. It knocked the wind out of me at the time.”As Werro crossed the line last in 2min 35.35sec it looked as if she was out – only for her and Galvydyte to be reinstated on appeal. Far in front of her was Britain’s Jemma Reekie who crossed the line first in 1:58.61, and was quick to comfort Werro when she slowly trudged over the line holding her chest.There were no such problems for Hodgkinson, who won the other semi-final in 1:57.38, just ahead of Broeders-Bol.View image in fullscreenKeely Hodgkinson (right) had a much less eventful semi-final, winning ahead of Femke Broeders-Bol (left) – both qualified for the final.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/ReutersAsked whether she saw Werro fall, Hodgkinson said: “I heard the ‘oooh’ which is never a good sign. I don’t know what it looked like. You can’t worry about what happened to other people. I hope she’s OK and in the final for an exciting race.”She was clearly relieved with her time as she looked ahead to the race everyone is talking about. “Another 1:57 so I’m happy,” she said. “The excitement makes me excited. I can’t wait to step out there. I love a good challenge, I think it brings out the best in me. So yeah, hopefully it will be a really good race, a clean race, no one falling over tomorrow. No wind please. I’m going to talk to the Etsy witch, make sure there’s no wind.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBroeders-Bol should certainly not be discounted, given how comfortable she looked throughout as she finished just behind Hodgkinson.Neither Hodgkinson nor Werro will want the final to be slow given that Broeders-Bol’s personal best for 400m is 49.17sec – an indoor world record. That is significantly quicker than Werro’s personal best, 50.80, and Hodgkinson’s 51.14.The Dutch athlete isn’t shying away from talking up her chances either: “One of the reasons I went to the 800 is because I love to race, and tomorrow’s final is the ultimate race.”Asked whether it suits her that people are talking about Hodgkinson and Werro, rather than her, the four-time Olympic and world gold medallist started to smile.“Yeah, it’s different and quite nice,” she said. “I’ve always said being the favourite is a privilege because you know you’re very strong on paper. But I feel I’ve never slept so well, and have never been this relaxed. So I think it brings its advantages as well.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsKeely HodgkinsonAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Taiwan says it was hit by ‘abnormal’ AI-assisted cyber-attack  | Hacking | The Guardian
description: Taiwan’s statement comes a day after reports that suspected China-linked hackers had carried out a first-of-a-kind breach
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Taiwan’s statement comes a day after reports that suspected China-linked hackers had carried out a first-of-a-kind breach
Content: Taiwan did not say who was behind the AI cyber-attacks, but it has in recent years complained about China’s pressure on the democratically governed island through acts of ‘hybrid warfare’.Photograph: Sean Pavone/AlamyView image in fullscreenTaiwan did not say who was behind the AI cyber-attacks, but it has in recent years complained about China’s pressure on the democratically governed island through acts of ‘hybrid warfare’.Photograph: Sean Pavone/AlamyHackingTaiwan says it was hit by ‘abnormal’ AI-assisted cyber-attackTaiwan’s statement comes a day after reports that suspected China-linked hackers had carried out a first-of-a-kind breachGuardian staff with agenciesThu 13 Aug 2026 01.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaiwan says it detected AI-assisted cyber-attacks on government agencies that came from overseas last month, a new kind of threat that has been reported as “first-of-a-kind breach”.The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MDA) said its cybersecurity monitoring units ‌detected the “abnormal attack” targeting government agencies, which began on 20 July. The National Institute of Cyber Security issued a series of warning alerts while it investigated.The Financial TimesquotedDream – an Israeli AI company that detected the intrusion – as saying the attackers used open-source AI agents to build an autonomous hacking tool that behaved like a coordinated cyber team, describing it as a first-of-a-kind breach.‘A statement of freedom’: T-shirt slogan goes viral and book sales rocket in Taiwan after Hong Kong raidsRead moreDream was reported as saying that the tool compromised “at least 85 government user accounts, extracting more than 2,500 personnel records before expanding the attack to Taiwan’s nuclear safety agency and at least seven energy companies”.Taiwan has in recent years complained about what it sees as China’s “hybrid warfare” – from daily military drills near the island to disinformation campaigns and cyber-attacks – as Beijingramps up military and political pressure⁠on the democratically governed island to force Taipei to accept its claims of sovereignty.Though Taiwanese officials did not direct accusations atChina, the FT on Wednesday reported that China-linked hackers were suspected. Dream did not attribute the attack to a specific group, but said the use of Simplified Chinese in internal communications linked to the hack meant there was a high probability the operator was connected to China, the FT reported.Chinese cyber-attacks on Taiwan’s key infrastructure, from hospitals to banks, rose 6% in 2025 from the previous year to an average of 2.63m attacks a ⁠day, the island’s National Security Bureau said in January, adding some hacks were synchronised with military drills in “hybrid threats” to paralyse the island.The investigation into the AI-assisted attack said it showed clear characteristics of an “overseas source”, with hackers employing a hybrid approach that combined manual operations with AI agent-assisted attacks, such as Open Claw, the MDA said.“The relevant attack sources, methods, and scope of impact have all been fully investigated, and the affected units have successively completed their handling,” the ministry added.In response to this new type of threat, the government has established protective guidelines and strengthened system monitoring to block attacks early, it said.The statement did not mention China, and China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request ‌for comment on the attack.Taiwan’s MDA and Chinese authorities did not comment on the earlier FT report.‘A statement of freedom’: T-shirt slogan goes viral and book sales rocket in Taiwan after Hong Kong raidsRead moreThe threat of AI-assisted hacking campaigns has ​been growing for years but ramped up dramatically ​over the past few months after top AI labs ​released models, such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which can rapidly conduct reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities, and take advantage of them.Cris Thomas, a ​researcher who works as a ‌security advocate at the code ​security company Semgrep, said the ​spy campaign was an illustration of just how quickly AI-assisted hackers could hit their mark.Thomas cautioned against exaggerating the power of AI agents, however.“There’s still a human in there somewhere. Somebody had to choose who to attack, had to establish an objective and give it a directive,” he said. “It’s not totally 100% autonomous. There was a capable operator in charge that did that.”Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsHackingAI (artificial intelligence)CyberwarTaiwanChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Do I really need air conditioning in the UK? The best portable aircon tested – plus the pros, cons and alternatives | Summer | The Guardian
description: As hotter summers become the norm, home aircon can feel increasingly tempting. We put six units to the test for cooling power, noise and energy use – and explain what you need to know before buying
Author: Caramel Quin
Headline: As hotter summers become the norm, home aircon can feel increasingly tempting. We put six units to the test for cooling power, noise and energy use – and explain what you need to know before buying
Content: Cool dog? A portable unit can make hot, restless nights more manageable.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCool dog? A portable unit can make hot, restless nights more manageable.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianThe FilterSummerDo I really need air conditioning in the UK? The best portable aircon tested – plus the pros, cons and alternativesAs hotter summers become the norm, home aircon can feel increasingly tempting. We put six units to the test for cooling power, noise and energy use – and explain what you need to know before buyingHow to sleep in a heatwaveCan air conditioning be green?Caramel QuinThu 13 Aug 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Tell people you’re testing air conditioning, and the truth soon comes out: far more people have aircon than you’d ever imagine. It’s a guilty secret, the home improvement equivalent of Botox or weight loss jabs – everyone notices the results, but nobody admits to the method. Most portable aircons are in bedrooms, hidden away from visitors, so they’re easy to keep secret. And while friends with aircon don’t suddenly look younger or slimmer, they do look suspiciously well rested during a heatwave, while you’ve spent the night tossing and turning.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.So if you’re using an aircon unit, why have it in the bedroom? Warm air rises, so upstairs bedrooms can be the hottest by the end of the day, making for restless nights. And if your bedroom is in a loft conversion, it’s even worse: the roof absorbs the sun’s heat all day before radiating it back into the room after dark.Most UK homes are built to retain heat, not shed it. Cooling an entire home is difficult and expensive, but a single aircon unit can make at least one room – and a good night’s sleep – more achievable.So, should you get aircon? And if you do, should you feel guilty about it? Yes and no. It depends on how you power it, whether the machine is built to last, and whether you really need it.We are in aclimate crisis. This year’s hot summer hasn’t been a blip. In fact, extreme heat and flooding will worsen in the coming years. We got into this mess by burning fossil fuels, and we continue to do so, so the carbon footprint of your cooling matters. You could be making the problem worse by opting to have air conditioning. Unless you’re on a renewable tariff – or even better, producing itself yourself with solar panels – electricity use accelerates climate breakdown. (If you are looking to move to a renewable tariff, it’s worthresearching those that invest most in renewables.)Before you buy, read the “What you need to know” section at the bottom of this page on the global warming potential (GWP) of refrigerants. These are used in air-conditioning units, as well as fridges, freezers, heat pumps and other appliances that move heat. Some refrigerants have a global warming impact hundreds, or even thousands, of times greater than the same amount of CO2 if they escape into the atmosphere.We were facing our fifth heatwave of the year at the time of writing, and unsurprisingly, portable air conditioning units had been in high demand. None of the options I’ve recommended is currently in stock, with the first restock due in late November, and many more expected in March 2027. If you want a good-quality, well-recommended unit that’s built to last, bear that in mind. So take your time: these units are big investments built to last, and there’s lots to consider.How can I avoid using air conditioning?View image in fullscreenFan favourite: moving air across your skin helps sweat evaporate, making hot days more bearable.Photograph: Westend61/GettyFansThere are cheaper (and greener) alternatives to air conditioning, includingfansandevaporative air coolers, both of which I’ve tested for the Filter. Fans don’t actually lower a room’s temperature; they simply move air across your skin, helping sweat evaporate and making you feel cooler, like a breeze on a hot day.If you decide to go with a fan, buy a good one (my favourite,the Lume, is now on preorder for delivery from 31 August). Cheap models are often noisy, with much of that noise being wasted energy. A well-engineered fan is noticeably quieter and more effective.As you might have already discovered, fans and air coolers often sell out during hot weather, especially the good ones. If you find a model you like on preorder, it’s usually worth reserving it. Sadly, we’re likely to see more heatwaves.Air coolersEvaporative air coolerswork by drawing warm air through water-soaked pads. As the water evaporates, it absorbs heat, cooling the air by a degree or two, before it’s blown back into the room. The result isn’t the fridge-like chill of an air conditioner, but a gentler cooling effect – like a sea breeze on a hot day. The trade-off is that the fans built into evaporative coolers are often less powerful, so you don’t get the strong blast of air that you get from a standard fan.Importantly, evaporative coolers (sometimes known as swamp coolers) humidify your air, so aren’t a good option if you have damp and mould problems. They’re designed to be used with doors open and fresh air circulating. Many of the ones I recommend are now out of stock, but my favourite portable option, theMorphy Richards Flexi Freeze, was available at the time of writing.Keeping cool without electricityThere are natural ways to cool your home, too. The problem is that most houses in the UK have been designed to retain heat, not cope with prolonged hot weather.In countries where super-hot summers are the norm, homes are often built with high-thermal-mass walls, which warm up and cool down slowly, and external shutters that block the sun from entering through windows.We’ve written in depth aboutalternative ways to keep your home cool this summer. Closing and covering windows can keep out hot air and block solar heat by day – then opening them in the evening lets cooler air into your home, flushing out not just warm air but also the heat stored in your walls.If your home has windows on opposite sides, open both in the evening so cool air can blow through. If you live on more than one level, open windows upstairs and downstairs in the evening. Warm air will rise out of the top windows and will be replaced by cooler air that’s drawn in at the lower level.The case for air conditioningView image in fullscreenShutter speed: blocking out the sun by day can help keep indoor temperatures down before you turn to aircon.Photograph: John Keeble/GettyThere are valid reasons to own air conditioning, even during a climate crisis. Older people, young children and those with health conditions are more vulnerable to extreme heat, and some homes are simply much harder to keep cool.Like any appliance, an air conditioner has two main sources of carbon emissions: the CO2 generated from manufacturing and disposing of it (known as “embodied carbon” ) and the CO2 generated to power it over its lifetime.To reduce its overall impact, buy a unit that’s built to last, from a trusted brand with a long warranty, rather than the cheapest model you can find. A longer-lasting unit spreads its embodied carbon over many more years. Buying secondhand also reduces the impact, extending the life of an existing unit.But the biggest difference you can make is how you power your air conditioning. If you’re on a 100% renewable electricity tariff, then running it shouldn’t require burning fossil fuels (again, it pays todo your research here). Better still, if you have solar panels and a home battery, you can run aircon using electricity you’ve generated yourself. It’s a significant investment, but one that’s becoming increasingly attractive as fuel prices rise and solar panels and batteries get cheaper.Be aware that if you’re on a standard electricity tariff, the mix of fuels used to power your home will depend on the time of day. Around the middle of the day, electricity is typically supplied by a higher share of renewables. When demand peaks, typically in the early evening, gas-fired power plants are more likely to be brought online to meet it.So, if you can, run your aircon outside these evening peak hours. Use shutters, curtains, open windows and other natural cooling methods first, then use air conditioning for a short time before bed to take the edge off.I’ve tested portable air conditioners here, but for a full rundown on the types available, see the “What you need to know” section at the end of this article.Why you should trust meI’m a veteran, award-winning consumer tech journalist with decades of experience testing gadgets. I’m also a menopausal woman in her 50s, who honestly can’t recall the last time she felt cold – which may explain the appeal of wild swimming at this age. Oh, and I have a degree in engineering. Between the three, I’m well qualified to put these portable air conditioners through their paces, both from a scientific and personal perspective.How I testedView image in fullscreenTesting conditions: most units were put to work in the same room, with the exhaust hose vented through a casement window.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianUnsurprisingly, air-conditioning units have been hard to come by this summer, with many sold out, and review samples also in short supply. I focused on units that are going to be restocked and tested six, with details of stock levels and replenishment dates included, where available.Where possible, I tested units in the same 14 sq metre room with average ceiling height, and with doors and double-glazed windows closed, so it was the warmest room in the house. I opened a casement window for the hose.The only exception was the Midea PortaSplit. Its unusual design pairs an indoor unit with a rather heavy outdoor unit that remains permanently connected by refrigerant lines, so you can’t separate the two. As I couldn’t lift the outdoor unit through a window, I tested it in a larger 37 sq metre room with a sliding door – which was the only suitable space available.To test performance, I measured each unit’s power consumption at maximum draw with a plug-in energy meter, although since air conditioners cycle on and off, they don’t use that level of power all the time. The highest settings’ noise levels were recorded using a sound meter app from one metre away, and I measured each unit’s size.I also monitored room temperature with a thermometer placed on the opposite side of the room. This measured how much each unit cooled the whole room, rather than the cold air coming from the vent.Finally, I judged each air conditioner on how effective the cooling felt, how annoying I found the noise and how easy the controls were to use. I also considered the design, how easily each unit could be stored over winter and, of course, its price. Note that all models come with remote controls and on castors.All of the aircon units that weren’t collected by the manufacturers after testing were donated to charity. Some went toFurnishing Futures, a charity that creates fully furnished homes for women and children who have survived domestic abuse. And some went toLowri Housein Hackney, London, which provides safe, short-term accommodation for homeless patients leaving hospital, with support from the homeless and inclusion health charityPathway.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe best portable air conditioning units in 2026View image in fullscreenCool contenders: six portable aircon units were assessed for cooling, noise and energy use.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianBest portable air conditioner overall:Meaco MC10000MeacoMC10000£459.99£459.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveSuperb coolingWhat we don’t loveRemote is basic and there’s no appView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£459.99 at Aircon CentreCurrently out of stock; stock due 27 NovemberThis 10,000 BTU air conditioner is from the popular MeacoCool (MC) range. There are alsoProandCHmodelsthat offer a companion app and heating.It’s A-rated for energy efficiency and designed for a medium room. The controls and display sit on the top at an angle, so you can see them from a distance. This is welcome, as the remote control is pretty basic, and there’s no companion app.It uses R290 (propane) refrigerant, which has a low global warming potential of 3.3 (for more information on this, see the “What you need to know” section at the end of the page).Why we love itOn test, this was simply the best and fastest at cooling. It brought the temperature down by 3C in 15 minutes and 6C in two hours.The design is simple. For example, you have to manually open the louvres (the angled grilles on the front) and point them where you want the cold air directed. By directing them downwards, it created a cooling breeze on the floor and on my legs, which I found made everything feel cool.It also has a fan and dehumidifier. The sleep mode dimmed the display but didn’t immediately make it quieter, instead gradually increasing the target temperature by a couple of degrees throughout the night.It’s a shame that …the remote doesn’t have a display.Dimensions:32 x 32 x 74cm (WDH)Weight:26kgBTU:10,000Room size:medium (up to 28m²)Warranty:three yearsMeasured power use on top setting:890WPeak noise level on test:60dBMeacoMC10000£459.99£459.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveSuperb coolingWhat we don’t loveRemote is basic and there’s no appBest portable aircon unit for large rooms:Dimplex Eco IQDimplexEco IQ£599.99£599.99 at DimplexWhat we loveGood cooling, app and voice controlWhat we don’t loveLoud and the remote is basicView image in fullscreenCaramel Quin testing air conditioners: DimplexPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£599.99 at DimplexCurrently out of stockThe Dimplex Eco IQ has a really handy app featuring controls such as a 24-hour timer. It uses R290 (propane) refrigerant, which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.Why we love itThe unit looks classy, and is pretty compact considering it’s powerful enough for a large room. It offers 12,000 BTU, plus wifi and app control. This means you can control it from your Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant smart speaker if you want to control your aircon by voice.The cooling is impressive. It cooled the room by 1.5C in 15 minutes and 5C in two hours.I found the Dimplex a bit loud, though. It may measure the same number of decibels as others, but it has a fairly deep hum and a slight rattle, like the noise you hear from a fridge. This makes sense because, like a fridge, it uses a compressor and a refrigerant. The noise measured 60dB at its loudest (similar to a conversation – so you’ll definitely hear it, but you can learn to ignore it), and this went down to 55dB on sleep mode. However, I found the noise worth it for the cooling on a hot day.It’s a shame that …it’s loud. The remote control is also basic, to the point of looking a little cheap. It lacks a display, which is a shame because the unit’s display and controls are on top and so can’t be seen from across the room. You can always use the app, though.Dimensions:29 x 34 x 70cm (WDH)Weight:23.8kgBTU:12,000Room size:large (up to 35m²)Warranty:one year, extended to two if registered within 28 daysMeasured power use on top setting:1,400WPeak noise level on test:60dBDimplexEco IQ£599.99£599.99 at DimplexWhat we loveGood cooling, app and voice controlWhat we don’t loveLoud and the remote is basicBest split portable air conditioner:Midea PortaSplitMideaPortaSplit£1,099.99£1,099.99 at JoyBuyWhat we loveQuiet; energy efficient; great for suitable spacesWhat we don’t loveBulky; positioning limited because of the pipesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£1,099.99 at JoyBuyCurrentlyout of stockAnd now for something completely different. This “portable split” air conditioner has an indoor and outdoor unit, connected with refrigerant pipes. The pipes are 2.5 metres long and have a 6 x 2.7cm cross-section, instead of the usual 15cm diameter air hose.The units can’t be detached from each other because the pipes are full of refrigerant (R32, global warming potential 675), so it’s suitable only if you’re able to put the outdoor unit outside and close the door to leave a 2.7cm gap. Alternatively, you can mount the outdoor unit outside permanently if you’re able to accommodate space for the pipes. I found it easiest to bring it back inside when not in use: it stores neatly on top of the indoor unit. It also comes with a kit for sealing out hot air and a window lock, consisting of two fittings to stick on to the frame with Velcro to connect them, which keeps your window gap narrow.It’s large and heavy: you wouldn’t carry it up and down stairs, although it wheels around OK. If you’d struggle to get the 32.5kg indoor unit and 9.9kg outdoor unit into place, you may find JoyBuy’s £35 installation service good value; they’ll unpack it and bring it to the right room in your home. They’ll even mount it on the no-drill-required brackets if you have a suitable window.Why we love itIt’s much quieter than a “monobloc” one-piece portable aircon unit and could be a permanent fix for renters in modern flats. If you can bring it up to your flat in a lift and have a balcony on which to put the outdoor unit, you’re winning. And it offers year-round service: it’s an efficient A++-rated air conditioner and also an A+-rated heater.And despite its bulk, it’s good-looking. Controls are intuitive, and there are three displays: one on top with the controls, one on the front showing the target temperature, and one on the remote control. You can also control it via the app and add Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant voice control.It cooled the room during testing, and the dog approved of its cooling prowess, but comparing figures would be like comparing apples and oranges: the room I tested it in was considerably larger.If the Midea suits your home – a back door or a balcony really – it’s a good option.It’s a shame that …it’s only suitable for homes that can accommodate its pipes.Dimensions:indoor unit, 52 x 34 x 65cm (WDH); outdoor unit, 50 x 26 x 44cm (WDH)Weight:indoor unit, 32.5kg; outdoor unit, 9.9kgBTU:12,000Room size:large (up to 35m²)Warranty:two yearsMeasured power use on top setting:680WPeak noise level on test:40dBMideaPortaSplit£1,099.99£1,099.99 at JoyBuyWhat we loveQuiet; energy efficient; great for suitable spacesWhat we don’t loveBulky; positioning limited because of the pipesBest value air conditioner:Devola DVAC09CCBDevolaDVAC09CCB£439.99£439.99 at DevolaWhat we loveGood value for cooling a medium-sized roomWhat we don’t loveThere’s no display on the front, so use the appView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£439.99 at DevolaCurrently out of stock; stockexpected 27NovemberThis 9,000 BTU air conditioner is a good all-rounder for medium-sized rooms. It’s also a fan and dehumidifier, and Devola also offersa version with heating.It comes in black orwhite. I tested the black (known as the DVAC09CB; the white is DVAC09CW), and found the matching hose and accessories were a nice touch. It uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.The remote is simple, without a display, and the unit’s controls and display are on top, so you can’t see them from the other side of the room. The app paired easily, however, and it meant I could clearly see and control the mode and target temperature. You can also use the app to schedule and to pair with Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant for voice control.Why we love itThe unit looks good and is lightweight enough to lift. And the cooling feels powerful for its size. It reduced the room temperature only a little in the first 15 minutes, but it had dropped by 2C after an hour and 3C after two hours.I didn’t find the noise too annoying, either. The sound is reminiscent of a fan with the added deeper hum of a compressor: I could get used to it. The sleep button had no immediate impact on noise, simply dimming the display, but it gradually reduces cooling through the night to save energy.It’s a shame that …there’s no display on the front.Dimensions:35 x 35 x 70cm (WDH)Weight:24kgBTU:9,000Room size:medium (up to 28m²)Warranty:two yearsMeasured power use on top setting:895WPeak noise level on test:55dBDevolaDVAC09CCB£439.99£439.99 at DevolaWhat we loveGood value for cooling a medium-sized roomWhat we don’t loveThere’s no display on the front, so use the appThe best of the restMeaco MC12000RPROMeacoMC12000RPRO£549.99£549.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveWell-featured; powerful enough for large roomsWhat we don’t loveI found the noise annoyingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£549.99 from Aircon CentreCurrently out of stock, stock due 27 NovemberBest for:high-end air conThe 12,000 BTU capacity makes this powerful enough for large rooms, and it’s a well-featured unit too. The front display shows you the target temperature, and the remote control features a display. You can also pair it with an app for more functionality.It was immediately cooling, but performance was so-so: the temperature dropped 1C within 15 minutes and 3.5C after two hours. As with many others here, it uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s loud. It measured 60dB, like several others, but I found its deep hum annoying and had to turn up the TV.Dimensions:47 x 35 x 76cm (WDH);weight:29.5kg;BTU:12,000;room size:large (up to 35m²);warranty:three years;measured power use on top setting:1,255W;peak noise level on test:60dBMeacoMC12000RPRO£549.99£549.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveWell-featured; powerful enough for large roomsWhat we don’t loveI found the noise annoyingDreo 318SDreo318S£399.99£399.99 at DreoWhat we loveA good budget model for small roomsWhat we don’t loveThe hose was shorter than mostView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£399.99 at DreoCurrently out of stockBest for:small roomsThis has the lowest cooling capacity (7,500 BTU) on test, so it’s suitable only for small rooms up to 14 sq metre. The 1.5m hose was too short to reach my high window, too (meaning I had to test all of the monobloc air conditioners on top of a desk, to be sure of a fair test, even though most come with 1.8m hoses).It’s small but has decent features, including a front display, companion app and voice control via Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant, and the remote control features a display. Cooling was impressive considering its size: the temperature dropped 1.5C within 15 minutes and 3.5C after two hours. I liked the flat, magnetic area on top for storing the remote control, too.Sound is a deep hum, although it’s a bit quieter on sleep mode. As with others here, it uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.It didn’t make the final cut because …for only a little more, you can buy the Meaco MC10000, which offers much better cooling.Dimensions:39 x 36 x 63cm (WDH);weight:22.5kg;BTU:7,500;room size:small (up to 14m²);warranty:two years;measured power use on top setting:755W;peak noise level on test:55dBDreo318S£399.99£399.99 at DreoWhat we loveA good budget model for small roomsWhat we don’t loveThe hose was shorter than mostWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenDog days: portable aircon can cool a single room when other ways of beating the heat aren’t enough.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianWhat types of airconditioning are there?Here I’ve tested portable air conditioners. These are freestanding units with an exhaust hose that carries hot air through an open window. They’re designed to cool a single room and can be packed away at the end of summer. They need to be positioned close to an opening window and a power socket.Most are “monobloc” all-in-one designs that sit on castors and are portable, in that they can be wheeled from one room to another. However, they’re not light, so moving them between floors is another matter entirely.Another option is a “split” air-conditioning unit, which is a permanently installed system with two separate units. The indoor unit is usually mounted high on a wall and blows cool air into the room. The other unit sits outside the home (on a roof or hanging off the wall), with pipes and electrical cables connecting the two. These systems tend to be more expensive but much quieter.This test also features a portable split air conditioner, which is a hybrid between a portable aircon unit and a fixed split system. This, too, has two units, but the outdoor one is more compact, and the pipe is thin and more flexible, making it easier to move around. It works well on the ground floor, where you can safely put the external compressor unit outside on the ground, which also makes it quieter. Using it upstairs would require the use of brackets outside, which makes it rather less portable.Air conditioners use the same tech as air-sourceheat pumps. By compressing and expanding a refrigerant, they move heat from one place to another. In cooling mode, they pump heat out of your home; in heating mode, they bring heat in. If you’re installing a permanent split system, go for a reversible model so you can use it to cool your home in the summer and heat it in winter.I haven’t carried out a group test of split aircon units because they require professional installation, but I have tested theBosch Climate 3000i 3.5kW(from £2,420) fromBoxt. It cools a room quickly and also works as a heater, air purifier and dehumidifier, doing four jobs without taking up any floor space.How much does air conditioning cost to use?For each aircon unit here, I’ve measured its power use on the top setting, in watts (W). Electricity costs are in kilowatt hours (kWh). If, for example, you were using a 900W aircon for an hour, it would use 900Wh. Divide by 1,000 to convert it to kilowatt hours: 0.9kWh.The energy price cap for 1 July to 30 September 2026 is 26.11p a kWh. So that’s the price to use 1kWh of energy. Multiply 26.11p by 0.9kWh, and you’ll discover it costs 23p an hour to run a 900W portable aircon unit. It’s not a fortune if you use it sparingly, but fans are much cheaper to run: thewinner of my fans testcost less than a penny an hour.What is a BTU rating, and which one do I need?An air conditioner’s British Thermal Unit (BTU) rating indicates its cooling capacity. The higher the BTU rating, the larger the room it can cool. There areonline BTU calculatorswhere you can input your room measurements to find out the BTU you need. Above, I’ve given a maximum floor space for the models reviewed, assuming an average ceiling height of 2.5 metres.An undersized air conditioner will struggle, meaning it’s more likely to be on constantly and at higher risk of breakdown, so it’s important not to buy a unit that’s underpowered for your space. On the other hand, getting a more powerful unit than you need means it will be more expensive and larger than necessary. Make sure to measure your room and get a unit with the right BTU or only slightly more than you need on paper. For example, if you’re not sure which room it will be used in, buy a unit that suits your largest bedroom.What’s a window kit?When you poke the flexible hose out of the window to remove hot air, you’ll want to seal the rest of the window. How you do this depends on the type of window. I have hinged, casement windows, so I used sticky-backed Velcro to make a line around the window opening and then attached a fabric cover, with zips to open a hole to poke the hose through. Most air conditioners come with two window kits: the other is an adjustable solid cover for sash and other sliding windows.Howlong a warranty do I need?All the units on test have two- or three-year warranties. I’m a big fan of long product lifespans, as the “embodied carbon” used in your unit’s manufacture and shipping also matters, alongside the electricity it uses to cool you. The longer you can get your unit to last, the better. To give yours its best chance of a long life, clean or replace the air filters regularly, dry it out on the fan-only mode before winter storage, and store upright.What is GWP?Global warming potential (GWP)is a measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps in the atmosphere over time, relative to carbon dioxide – CO2 has a GWP of 1. This matters if the refrigerant leaks or is disposed of unsafely. Propane, used in many of these models, has a low GWP of 3.3 and is climate-friendly compared with refrigerants with a GWP measured in hundreds or thousands.What to do with your old air conditionerIf your old aircon works, try to find it a good home on a local swap site or street WhatsApp. If it’s not working, check your council website orRecycle Your Electricals. Electrical items don’t belong in general waste and, like fridges, air conditioners contain a refrigerant that needs to be removed by a specialist. If it’s allowed to leak into the atmosphere, it contributes to global warming as a greenhouse gas (which is where its GWP, above, comes in).For more, readreaders’ top tips for beating the heat this summerand our roundup of thebest folding fansCaramel Quin is a journalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plain language. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. Caramel is an engineering graduate who has won awards for communicating hi-tech subjects to normal people. When she’s not testing gadgets, she’s feeding pets (16 beasts at the time of writing) or pottering at the allotmentExplore more on these topicsSummerThe FilterHomesGadgetsInteriorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Are teens on e-motorbikes the ‘new Hells Angels’? Not so fast, boomers | California | The Guardian
description: Experts say better regulation is needed but that bad press about ‘motorized menaces’ puts the ebike revolution at risk
Author: Ryan Fonseca
Headline: Experts say better regulation is needed but that bad press about ‘motorized menaces’ puts the ebike revolution at risk
Content: A large group of mostly illegal dirt bikes and powerful ebikes take over downtown Los Angeles, on 25 October 2025.Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA large group of mostly illegal dirt bikes and powerful ebikes take over downtown Los Angeles, on 25 October 2025.Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesCaliforniaAre teens on e-motorbikes the ‘new Hells Angels’? Not so fast, boomersExperts say better regulation is needed but that bad press about ‘motorized menaces’ puts the wider ebike revolution at riskRyan Fonsecain Los AngelesThu 13 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeware, Americans: there’s a battery-powered threat cruising down beach paths, rolling up hiking trails and zipping along the streets of our cities.By now, you’ve probably seen footage on social media of teens racing along streets, popping wheelies and weaving around car traffic with reckless abandon. The Los Angeles Times recently dubbed them the “new Hells Angels”. Other news outlets have referred to them as “motorized menaces” terrorizing communities. Sounds scary.In reality, these aren’t members of afederally designated violent criminal organization– they’re young adults riding electric two-wheeled vehicles: e-motorcycles, e-scooters and e-mopedsthat have often been illegally built or modifiedto reach higher speeds than legal and regulated electric bicycles.The proliferation of these vehicles is especially noticeable in fair-weatherCalifornia, where mostly male riders have made headlines for dangerous antics and fatal crashes.In May, Todd Spitzer, the Orange county district attorney, launched a specialized unit targeting “juveniles and adults, including parents who knowingly allow their children to ride illegal E-Motorcycles”.That followed charges brought against parents earlier this year in the aftermath of crashes, including one in which a teen on an e-motorcyclefatally struck a pedestrian. In another case, a father was charged formodifying his 12-year-old son’s e-motorcycle to reach 60mph. The boy suffered serious injuries after he ran a red light and was hit by a motorist.The media attention and government crackdowns extend beyond the Golden state. In New Jersey, the state legislaturepassed a lawrequiring registration, a license and, in some cases, insurance for anyone to ride an ebike. Similar laws are already on the books in a few other states, and comparable legislation has been proposed in others, including California and New York.Look beyond some of the more hyperbolic headlines and you’ll see a familiar story about young people doing what they’ve always done: making dumb, dangerous decisions as they feel out the freedom of movement that grows with age.View image in fullscreenElectric bicycles in Manhattan on 5 August in New York City.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesThat generational constant is happening as local and state authorities play catch-up with cheap, speedy vehicles that have flourished through mostly unchecked online retail sales. They are often marketed as ebikes, despite exceeding speed and power rules set for actual ebikes. Critics argue this makes it difficult for consumers to know the difference.In this regulatory wild west, legal ebikes are caught in the crossfire. Experts, advocates and retailers say many officials are opting for scattershot over precise targeting to rein in illegal vehicles and invest in more education and infrastructure, putting the broader ebike revolution at risk.How e-moto’s ‘legal gray area’ threatens ebike boomThe US and dozens of other nations experienced a surge in electric bike sales during the pandemic, as millions of people craved open space and movement in response to stay-at-home orders. People found an alternative travel mode for local errands, school drop-offs and work commutes, leaving behind the hassles that come with driving.As components and batteries became cheaper to manufacture, new kinds of two-wheeled vehicles started to enter the market, many from China and often labeled as ebikes. Many of these vehicles had frames much more akin to motorcycles and dirt bikes than traditional bicycles. Another key difference: e-motos can go much faster, allowing riders tohit the same speeds as carsthat many riders are too young to drive.Ebikes are classified under federal law with specifics about their battery power – no more than 750 watts – plus rules about operable pedals to power the motor, and top speeds of 20mph for throttle bikes and 28mph with pedal assist only.It’s these mis-marketed, cheaply made “junk” vehicles that have given real ebikes a bad rap, said Kendra Ramsey, director of theCalifornia Bicycle Coalition. Her organization advocates for policies that promote the benefits of riding bikes, including ebikes, and protect riders on the road.“It is clear what an ebike is, but it’s not clear what it isn’t,” Ramsey said.View image in fullscreenPeople ride ebikes in Hermosa Beach, California. Legal ebikes are classified under federal law with specifics about battery power.Photograph: Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesBiking advocates point to existing rules for actual ebikes and argue the majority of riders are not thrill-seeking speedsters but commuters who have tapped into ebikes’ convenience and low environmental impact as a replacement for local car trips.Dillon Fitch-Polse, co-director of theBicyclingPlusresearch collaborative at the University of California, Davis, is concerned that authorities are responding to this “legal gray area” by adding bureaucratic barriers that will deter people of all ages from riding ebikes.“That’s too bad, because either [riders are] going to do it illegally or they’re going to lose out on the freedom that an ebike can provide,” he said.A better solution, Fitch-Polse said, would be to prohibit retailers from advertising these illegal bikes in the first place. There’s abipartisan effort in California’s state legislatureto do just that, which Ramsey’s organization is co-sponsoring.Rush to meet demand of unregulated vehicles leaves ‘big information gap’The e-moto trend is also putting shops that sell legal ebikes in a bind, said retailer Brett Thurber. He and his wife own the New Wheel, with locations in San Francisco, Oakland and nearby Larkspur.Thurber said kids and parents call his shops frequently or stop by in person seeking to buy e-motorcycles, which community-based businesses like his don’t sell. He uses those opportunities to educate people on the hazards of unregulated vehicles and preach the legal ebike gospel.Though he’s made some converts, Thurber is sure many callers hang up and buy the e-moto they wanted online. As a longtime bike rider, he gets the appeal.“Kids want freedom. They want something that’s cool,” Thurber said. “They like doing things that the adults kind of frown on and wag their fingers at.”E-moto retailers have marketed that freedom with cheap, illegal vehicles just a few clicks away on Amazon, Walmart and other online platforms. A quick Amazon search revealed how easily consumers can purchase an e-moto, even if they’re seeking a street-legal ebike.Typing “ebikes for teens” into Amazon’s search bar yielded dozens of vehicles that lack pedals and exceed the battery power of regulated ebikes.The first sponsored result advertised a 2,000W dirt-bike style “Electric Bike for Adults [and] Teens”. The product description read: “Whether you’re climbing mountain trails or speeding through city streets, this ebike for adult [sic] delivers thrilling acceleration and reliable climbing power.”Other listings contained similar mixed messaging. One “off road motorcycle” featured videos of young riders speeding and popping wheelies on public streets, which is illegal on this type of bike that is supposed to be registered in California as anoff-highway vehicle.“Safety is a top priority and we require ebikes sold in our store to meet applicable safety standards and Amazon policies. We are looking into the products in question,” a spokesperson for Amazon said via email when asked about those listings.Amazon had previously announced it would stop selling electric vehicles in California that don’t comply with state laws. Some e-motos advertised on their platform now include a notice that “this item cannot be shipped to your selected address due to local laws or Amazon policy”, before advising would-be buyers to change the shipping address.View image in fullscreenA 2,000W ‘ebike’ available on Amazon.Photograph: AmazonRamsey said that lack of market regulation leaves a “big information gap” for parents, the majority of whom might not knowingly put their children in danger.“A lot of adults are not in a good position to teach their kids good bicycling skills because they don’t ride bicycles themselves,” she said.Some states and cities are beginning to crack down on these online markets. In April, Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, issued a consumer alert for “too fast, too furious” electric vehicles.“Sometimes, what looks like an ebike or is marketed as an ebike is not a bike at all,” Bonta said. “Bike riders and parents: if your or your teen’s electric two-wheeled vehicle goes too fast, it might be a motorcycle or a moped – not an ebike.”Earlier this month, New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani,sent cease-and-desist letters to 42 retailerswho sell illegal two-wheeled electric vehicles that don’t meet the city’s legal requirements for ebikes or scooters.Media coverage ignores deadliest threat: carsUnsurprisingly, as more people hop on both legal and illegal electric vehicles, more people are being hurt or killed. Researchers at UC San Diego analyzed California collision data from law enforcement agencies and found that ebike injuries increased “exponentially” from 2018 to 2024 and were “associated with a higher severity of injuries compared with traditional bicycles”.Researchers noted that far more people on non-electric bikes were injured in crashes during the study period – more than 14 times as many compared with ebike riders. And the data is murky because e-motos “may be visually mistaken for ebikes and not be accurately identified by reporting agencies”.But recent media coverage and public discourse about ebikes tend to miss a car-sized blindspot: the majority of crashes that kill ebike riders involve automobiles,according to federal data.If you think it’s bad when someone operates a 50lb ebike recklessly, wait until you learn about how people drive around in 4,000lb cars, trucks and SUVs.Ebike proponents worry the critical coverage of ebikes and e-motos could further obscure the fact that US roads aredeadlier than nearly every other comparatively wealthy nation. And that’s driven by reckless behaviour of people behind the wheels ofincreasingly larger motor vehicles.Recent data compiled by theUS Consumer Product Safety Commissionshow 19 pedestrians were killed across the US in collisions with ebike riders in the eight years from 2017 to 2024. That’s roughly the average number ofpedestrians killed by motoristsevery single day of 2024.“It’s really sad to me that we have normalized so much traffic violence in society,” Fitch-Polse said. He argued public discourse and government officials take the easy route by pointing the finger at teenagers on trendy vehicles rather than reckoning with the systemic issues that make streets so dangerous in the first place.For Thurber, the mounting toll of kids being hurt and killed while riding bikes represents “a societal failure”. He said authorities should address that not by stifling the autonomy that more kids and young adults have embraced through biking, but by redesigning streets to better protect them and other vulnerable road users from people behind the wheel of an automobile.“My worry is that here … the tendency is to just put kids back in cars and have them be chauffeured around by their parents,” he said.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaEbikesCyclingWest CoastfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Schools across the US banned phones. Teens are demanding more offline support | US news | The Guardian
description: More students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments
Author: Claire Wang
Headline: More students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments
Content: Students outside Stuyvesant high school in New York, New York.Photograph: Bing Guan/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStudents outside Stuyvesant high school in New York, New York.Photograph: Bing Guan/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBuilding powerUS newsSchools across the US banned phones. Teens are demanding more offline supportMore students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environmentsBuilding power is supported byAbout this contentClaire WangThu 13 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs students across the country return to school this month, many will be confronting a new reality: classrooms without smartphones.Educators and parents have long fronted the fight against the debilitating influence technology can wield. Yet, many young people say they have been left out of important conversations around school phone policies, which are now in effect inat least 39 statesand Washington DC.Student organizers told the Guardian they support screen-time bans in schools, but such policies are often haphazardly enforced and don’t address the root causes of screen addiction, such as intense social pressure and feelings of isolation. In response, more students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments.Olivia Howard, a rising junior inNew Yorkstate, recalled receiving her first iPad when she was in kindergarten. For digital natives like herself, she said, quitting their devices cold turkey was never going to be easy.“We were the first generation to grow up on technology,” she said. “If legislators are implementing these phone bans, we need to take into account: what are the substitutes? Most kids my age have a relationship with technology, so there has to be other alternatives to replace it.”‘Harm extends beyond the classroom’InCalifornia, a new state law that took effect on 1 July requires school districts to develop policies that restrict phone use on campus. Elise Choi, a junior at the Orange County School of the Arts, said locking up devices is a step in the right direction but may not, on its own, be especially effective, since “kids will always find a way around regulations”.As a K-12 policy co-chief with GENUp, a youth-led education advocacy group, Choi spent most of the year authoring and building a coalition for a state bill that would mandate district-wide digital wellness education, which teaches students how social media and AI affect their mental health.“It’s not a matter of how long we’re on our devices but what it’s doing to us when we’re on it,” she said. “In general, the harm really extends beyond the classroom.”Teens often stay up late scrolling on social media and texting, Choi said, which can cause insomnia and affect their ability to focus at school. Add to that the constant pressure to seek validation by garnering more “likes” or followers.I’m an expert on adolescence: here’s why a smartphone ban isn’t the answer, and what we should do insteadRead more“Our entire social lives are happening online,” Choi said. “Digital wellness education is about giving students the understanding and skills to actually make better choices, set limits and understand the impact that it’s having on our health.”Other students are proactively shaping phone bans at their schools. Liv Kong, a rising senior at Legacy Magnet Academy in Tustin, California, led a student advisory group that conducted surveys and rolled out three pilot phone policies to determine which one best suited students and faculty.The idea for student-led pilots was formed a year ago, Kong said, after the school implemented a bell-to-bell ban without student input, which sparked a huge backlash. The students eventually chose a policy of banning phones in class but not during breaks.“Growing up, I’ve seen that imbalance of power between the people who make decisions and the people those decisions affect,” Kong said. “Our mission was to make sure there’s student body representation in those decisions.”Vihaan Bhardwaj, a rising senior at Mount Everest Academy and GENUp K-12 policy co-chief, said that when the San Diego school district banned phone use in classrooms last year, many students were apprehensive and confused about the intention behind the policy. In response, a committee with students from each school has been meeting regularly with top education officials to discuss how they can better communicate screen time mandates to students “in a way that feels supportive and not punitive”, he said.“Young people are on the ground to make sure policies are implemented in the right ways,” Bhardwaj said. “As we’ve been able to talk to them, we’ve been able to make more students aware that these policies are there to help them, not to restrict their freedom or rights.”Bhardwaj, 17, said he decided to join GenUP and the broader movement to ban phones from schools after an acne flare in middle school sent him spiraling.“Social media made me feel like I was doing everything wrong – eating wrong, using the wrong products – making my experience with such a normal part of teenage life so dramatic, so life or death,” he said. “[It] took a lot of my energy.”Building ‘real-world connections’After New York enacted a statewide bell-to-bell anti-screen policy last year, the non-profit #HalfTheStory formed Teen Tech Council, a youth-led initiative that allows students to apply for mini-grants and launch tech-free initiatives on campus. Over the past year, the campaign has supported 50 schools and reached 17,000 students across the state.Two teens in a rural school, noticing that phone use spiked after the art program was cut, placed rolling “crafts carts” around campus where students could use art supplies during and after school. At another school, a teen used the mini-grant to organize a phone-free scavenger hunt where students used disposable cameras to complete challenges.‘I don’t think my brain should have gone through that’: five young people on their experience of smartphones as teensRead moreCayden Boahene, a recent graduate from Democracy Prep Endurance high school in the Bronx, used a portion of a $4,500 grant to host a Wellness Day event during finals week, where nearly 100 students shot hoops, played board games and formed new friendships without phones.“I saw most of the students didn’t concentrate in class because of phones,” he said. “Some don’t connect with others and just connect through phones. I wanted to create an event to build real-world connections.”Howard, who goes to Valley Stream North high school in Long Island, said social media fueled an urge to compare with others in a way that felt detrimental to her mental health.“I thought everyone’s life was so perfect, so why is my life not like this?” she said, adding that the pressure intensified in high school as test scores and college prospects dominated conversations.Since the phone ban went into effect, Howard said, the school had become livelier, with one professor observing that he had never heard so much noise and conversation in the hallways. But for more introverted students, she said, the suddenly raucous atmosphere was overwhelming. Instead of phones, some just turned to Chromebooks during lunch.Over the past year, Howard and a group of students at Valley Stream have been working with school administrators to develop initiatives that would help students interact in a phone-free environment. This fall, she said, the school will be opening up a so-called “detox room”, furnished with books, stress toys and a sound machine, where students can “regulate their emotions” and relax.Howard also urged teachers to create more opportunities for in-person connection in the classroom, including more group assignments.“If someone’s super shy, that’s going to make them practice talking with other people,” she said.Explore more on these topicsUS newsBuilding powerUS educationSmartphonesMobile phonesCaliforniaNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I spent 18 months testing the best video doorbells – here are my favourites | Technology | The Guardian
description: Whether you want to improve your home’s security or simply know who’s at the door, the latest generation of smart doorbells will help put your mind at ease
Author: Andy Shaw
Headline: Whether you want to improve your home’s security or simply know who’s at the door, the latest generation of smart doorbells will help put your mind at ease
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterTechnologyReviewI spent 18 months testing the best video doorbells – here are my favouritesWhether you want to improve your home’s security or simply know who’s at the door, the latest generation of smart doorbells will help put your mind at easeThe best robot vacuums, testedAndy ShawThu 13 Aug 2026 05.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Doorbells have evolved. Today, they watch us as we approach, let the people inside the home know we’re coming sooner than our finger can hit the button, and give them a good look at our faces before they open the door. They’re essentially security cameras with a chime function.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.If you haven’t already installed one of these handy tools, there’s a huge array available. Choosing the best video doorbell can be a bewildering task, with various factors to consider, including how much of your doorstep you want to see and whether you’re prepared to pay for a subscription. To help make the decision a little bit easier, I tested 11 popular video doorbells to find the best.At a glanceBest video doorbell overallRingBattery Doorbell Pro£219.99 at AmazonBest budget video doorbellBlinkBattery Doorbell 2K+£69.99 at AmazonBest for Google Home usersGoogleNest Doorbell (battery)£129 at ToolstationBest subscription-free video doorbellEufyVideo doorbell E340£139.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust meI’ve been testing products, including everything fromvacuum cleanersand robotlawnmowersto computers and games, for various publications for more than three decades. I’ve also owned a video doorbell for several years, so I am well aware of their strengths and weaknesses. It gives me a good understanding of what I’m likely to be looking for in the next one I buy.How I testedView image in fullscreen‘I’ve mounted 11 doorbells to various rigged-up contraptions over the past 18 months or so.’Photograph: Andy ShawThe only way to test a doorbell is to stick it next to your front door and see how well it works. To this end, I’ve mounted 11 doorbells to various rigged-up contraptions over the past 18 months or so. With these, I can compare several doorbells at once, seeing how they all react to the comings and goings of my doorstep. Delivery drivers were rightly suspicious of the number of buttons and cameras that appeared as new models were reviewed, and struggled to work out whether it was them or the doorbells that were being tested.I’m not sure whether my neighbours noticed them all or spotted the number of times I lapped my drive at various times of day and night to test the movement sensors. If they did, they were too polite to mention it.I compare the doorbells by measuring how close I can get to the door before the motion detection is triggered, how much video is recorded and how useful that footage is. I time how long it takes for notifications to reach the doorbells’ apps on a smartphone and how long it takes for the doorbell to send an alert or ring a chime (if included) when its button is pressed. I also test the apps, examine the prices and consider the additional cost of subscriptions.All the doorbells that didn’t need to be returned to the brands after testing are being donated to theBritish Heart Foundation.The best video doorbells in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: RichLegg/GettyBest video doorbell overall:Ring Battery Doorbell ProRingBattery Doorbell Profrom£219.99£219.99 at Argos£219.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat footage day and night; clever pre-roll videoWhat we don’t loveExpensive; limited without a subscriptionView image in fullscreen£219.99 at Argos£219.99 at AmazonWhen this article was first published, it included an older version of Amazon’s Ring Doorbell Pro, which has since been discontinued. I wasn’t overly impressed with it for a variety of reasons, but Ring has pulled out all the stops with this newer version, addressing most of its weaknesses and leapfrogging its rivals with a host of useful features.Why we love itMost importantly, the video and sound quality are excellent. Ring still uses a slightly odd fish-eye lens, which provides a lot of area coverage but makes things look small at a distance and distorted up close. With 4K recording, however, it offers an unparalleled ability to zoom into footage from the app. It barely matters if someone looks small from a few metres away when you can zoom in on their face and still see a remarkable amount of detail.The picture quality is crystal clear in daylight and still excellent in low light, such as at dusk or when illuminated by a doorstep lamp. The night vision also works well when the ambient light is low enough for it to kick in.It’s also faster to respond than the previous model, alerting my phone within a couple of seconds when the doorbell is pressed or movement is detected. Ring does a particularly good job of tracking visitor movements by constantly storing a few seconds of video, which it can add to the beginning of the recording when motion is detected. It means you get to see people as they arrive, rather than seeing them only once they’re already on your doorstep.It’s a shame that …it doesn’t really work well without a subscription, which costs at least £4.99 per month.Subscription:Ring Solo, £4.99/mth or £49.99/yr (one device, 180-day storage); Ring Multi, £7.99/mth or £79.99/yr (all devices at one location, 180-day storage); Ring Pro, £15.99/mth or £159.99/yr (as Multi but adds video descriptions)RingBattery Doorbell Profrom£219.99£219.99 at Argos£219.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat footage day and night; clever pre-roll videoWhat we don’t loveExpensive; limited without a subscriptionFor more, read consumer technology editor Samuel Gibbs’Ring Video Doorbell Pro (wired) reviewBest budget video doorbell:Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+BlinkBattery Doorbell 2K+£69.99£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable, even with a subscriptionWhat we don’t loveLess sharp footage; slower motion detectionView image in fullscreen£69.99 at AmazonThe latest version of Blink’s Battery Doorbell has the lowest price of all the doorbells I’ve tested. Its resolution has been improved in this version from HD to 2K (although there’s also now anHD model that costs £10 less), but other elements have been downgraded. For example, the new Sync Module Core, which needs to be plugged into a nearby wall socket, doesn’t provide the option of local storage like its predecessor did, which means the £2.50/month Blink Basic subscription is now an essential add-on.Why we love itDespite this, the Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ remains excellent value for money. You can buy an annual subscription at a slight discount (£24.99/year) and still not have spent £100 in total.Considering it’s a cheaper model, I was impressed with the video footage. Daytime footage was clear, and with night vision enabled, it was good enough to clearly make out the faces of any visitors who wandered close to my front door.The motion detection doesn’t activate as quickly as its rivals, so the captured footage tends to show people already on your doorstep rather than making their approach. But the two-way communication was reasonably clear, and the app you use to control the doorbell is intuitive and simple to operate.It’s a shame that …on average, it took six seconds for motion detection notifications to reach my mobile devices, which is a little slow.Subscription:Blink basic, £2.50/mth or £24.99/yr (one device, 60-day storage); Blink basic AI, £5.49/mth or £54.99/yr (one device, 60-day storage, includes video descriptions); Blink plus, £8/mth or £80/yr (unlimited devices, 60-day storage); Blink plus AI, £14.99/mth or £149.99/yr (unlimited devices, 60-day storage, includes video descriptions)BlinkBattery Doorbell 2K+£69.99£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable, even with a subscriptionWhat we don’t loveLess sharp footage; slower motion detectionBest for Google Home users:Google Nest Doorbell (battery)GoogleNest Doorbell (battery)from£129£129 at Toolstation£136.97 at AmazonWhat we loveGood view angle; quick to send alerts to other devicesWhat we don’t love£80 subscription to store footage; no inbuilt chimeView image in fullscreen£129 at Toolstation£136.97 at AmazonDoorbells can be inundated with features, and their apps can be amazing. But if they don’t do a good job of letting you know when someone approaches your door and capturing a video of them, there really isn’t much point. The Nest Doorbell is excellent at this.Why we love itIn my tests, the Nest was a solid all-rounder. I found the viewing angle of its lens to be about perfect, not going so wide that people appear too small, but still capturing enough of the surrounding area to catch people skirting around its periphery. The video and audio were as consistently clear as those on any of the doorbells I tested, and they were decent in daylight and at night.The Nest would sometimes detect people right at the end of my drive (about 15m away), but proved consistent at capturing movement from about three metres away. There was a little delay between the button being pressed and notifications arriving on other Nest devices and smartphones, but it averaged a fairly reasonable five seconds. While not as fast as the doorbells with dedicated local chimes, which tend to go off almost immediately, this was among the fastest for sending alerts to smartphones and smart speakers.It’s a shame that …it doesn’t come with a chime. Instead, you need to buy a separateGoogle Home smart speaker, which costs £99.99 (or a last-gen Nest Mini if you can pick one up secondhand). If you have an existing Nest or Amazon Echo speaker, you can of course use that.
