title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra review: the top dog of folding Androids | Samsung | The Guardian
description: With great software and battery for two days, the pricey svelte folder strikes best balance between phone and tablet
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: With great software and battery for two days, the pricey svelte folder strikes best balance between phone and tablet
Content: The slim and light Fold 8 Ultra is a great phone that squeezes a quality tablet in your pocket.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe slim and light Fold 8 Ultra is a great phone that squeezes a quality tablet in your pocket.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSamsungReviewSamsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra review: the top dog of folding AndroidsWith great software and battery for two days, the pricey svelte folder strikes best balance between phone and tabletSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorThu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Samsung’s top folding phone for 2026 is its first to carry the “Ultra” moniker in its name, packing a much bigger battery and better cameras into the thin and light body of a book-style foldable.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra continues from where theexquisite Z Fold 7left off last year. With its svelte chocolate bar dimensions opening into a square tablet, the Ultra sits above the newpassport-shaped Z Fold 8as Samsung’s top model. Costing £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), it is a lot of money to pay for a phone, regardless of how many other devices it can theoretically replace in your pocket.The Ultra sticks with the tried and tested form of its many Z Fold predecessors, and is almost identical to the Fold 7 physically. Weighing 215g and being only 8.9mm thick when closed, it is about the same as a large normal slab phone. The tall and super-bright outside screen makes easy work of phone-type tasks such as messaging, calls and mapping.View image in fullscreenThe chocolate bar dimensions of the Ultra (right) provide plenty of space for messaging and other activities while being easier to use one-handed than the squat shape of the Fold 8 (left).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOpen up the Ultra like a book to reveal the 8in OLED tablet screen, which is notably crisper and brighter than previous models, with a new anti-reflective coating that makes it easy to see in direct sunlight.Browsing or reading books is particularly satisfying, while videos look great but have large letterboxing black bars top and bottom. The stereo speakers, when held in landscape, are good for watching TV without headphones.The crease is less visible where the display folds but is still noticeable when the screen is off or you run your finger over it, and the necessarily softer material picks up fingerprints easily and needs more care than a traditional hardened glass smartphone.View image in fullscreenReading books, comics and websites on the tablet screen is a joy on the go.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSpecificationsMain screen:8in QXGA+ 120Hz (422ppi) Amoled flexible displayCover screen:6.5in FHD+ 120Hz (422ppi) AmoledProcessor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for GalaxyRAM:12 or 16GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:One UI 9 based onAndroid17Camera:200+50+10MP rear with 3x telephoto; 10MP+10MP selfie camerasConnectivity:5G, dual sim, esim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, GNSSWater resistance:IP48 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)Dimensions folded:158.4 x 72.8 x 8.9mmDimensions unfolded:158.4 x 143.2 x 4.1mmWeight:215gTwo-day battery life and plenty of power for multitaskingView image in fullscreenThe Ultra fully charges in 60 minutes and hits 70% in half an hour using a 45W or greater USB-C power adaptor (not included). It also supports 20W wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Ultra has two meaningful upgrades on the inside. The latestQualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5chip has plenty of power for multitasking and demanding tasks, while a 13.6% larger capacity battery powers the phone through about two days of use. That is with the screens used for more than four hours each across a mix of wifi and 5G for browsing, messaging, taking notes, work and shooting photos, matching some of the longest-lasting folders available.Gaming and more intensive tasks hit the battery harder, but most people will only need to charge the Ultra every other day.One UI 9 (Android 17)View image in fullscreenThe tablet display is big enough to allow two apps to be run at full phone size when side by side for easy multitasking.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Ultra runs the same One UI 9 software built on the latest Android 17 as theFold 8. It is the best available for folding screens, allowing you to do more with the form while remaining a polished, customisable and refined experience.The Ultra can run up to three apps in a split-screen grid at once, plus more as floating windows, which can be handy for messaging while watching videos. Flex mode pushes the app or video to the top half of the screen when partly folded like a tiny laptop. You can have separate home screens for the phone and tablet displays, and choose whether or not to continue using apps on the outside when you shut the phone.TheNow Barworks great for putting live scores, music controls and other ongoing tasks on the bottom of the lock screen or in the status bar. The Ultra also has some of the better AI tools available, including Google’s Gemini and a proactive suggestion tool calledNow Nudgefromthe S26, which has been expanded for One UI 9.The Ultra will receive Android and security updates until 31 July 2033.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app can be used open or closed and has plenty of modes to get creative, including the downloadable Expert RAW for manual control.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Ultra has five cameras: a 10-megapixel selfie camera in each screen that is great for video calls; and three cameras on the back.The main 200MP rear camera is little changed from last year’s model and remains the best of the bunch, capable of shooting fantastic photos across a range of lighting conditions. By default it captures photos at 12MP but can shoot at 50MP or the full 200MP with a quick tap of button. It also manages a very good 2x crop zoom for a bit of magnification.The new 50MP ultra-wide camera is a big improvement on previous models, capturing brighter, more detailed photos, particularly in lower light settings. It also handles macrophotography well, producing excellent, highly detailed closeup shots.The 10MP 3x telephoto camera is the weakest of the bunch. It can shoot good photos with a bit of work, but it falls far short of modern rivals on zoom and quality, particularly with indoor lighting. Digital zoom takes over for further magnification up to 30x, which starts to fall apart beyond 10x.The cameras shoot great video, too, with a range of modes available including the impressive horizontal lock stabilisation featurefrom the S26 Ultra.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe rear cameras protrude prominently from the back of the phone causing it to wobble when in use on a desk or table.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe battery has an expected lifespan of at least 1,200 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone isgenerally repairable. Inside screenrepairs cost about £600. Samsung offers aself-repair programme, as well as Care+accidental damage insurancethat reduces the cost of repairs to £50.The Fold 8 is made from 14.4% recycled materials by weight. Samsung offerstrade-inandrecycling schemesfor old devices, and publishesenvironmental impact in its reports.PriceThe Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs from£1,899(€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999).For comparison, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 costs£1,699, theS26 Ultracosts£1,279, theHonor Magic V6costs£1,999.99and theGoogle Pixel 10 Pro Foldcosts£1,299.VerdictThe Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the best folding phone available. It is not a radical upgrade on last year’s excellent Z Fold 7 and does not really deserve the “Ultra” branding, but the longer, two-day battery life is very welcome.The form factor is great: easy to use as a regular phone when closed, plus an 8in internal screen that is brighter, crisper and much easier to use outdoors than before. The square tablet screen is great for multitasking, browsing and apps while being big enough to make watching video a good experience despite needing large letterboxing black bars.The triple camera on the back is generally capable and does not feel like a large downgrade from normal flagship phones, even if the 3x telephoto camera is a bit weak. The Ultra has the top Android processor from Qualcomm with plenty of performance for anything you would want to do.While you can get similar performance and battery life with better cameras and a less visible crease from some rivals, the Fold Ultra’s excellent, adaptable software is simply better and will be kept up to date until at least 31 July 2033.Samsung has given wealthy buyers a choice of shape for its book-style foldable phones this year, but while the squatter Fold 8 seems better for video on paper, the Fold 8 Ultra is the one to get.Pros:super thin and light, just like a regular phone when closed, great tablet screen, powerful multitasking with top performance, two-day battery life, water resistance, good set of cameras.Cons:extremely expensive, no dust resistance, more fragile than a regular device and costly to repair, weak zoom camera compared with the very best normal phones, not a big upgrade on last year’s Z Fold 7.View image in fullscreenThe Fold 8 Ultra is the most complete folding phone from Samsung yet, but comes at a very high cost.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsSamsungSmartphonesMobile phonesTablet computersAndroidreviewsShareReuse this content

title: AOC’s public egg-freezing shouldn’t feel radical. But in today’s US, it does | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The congresswoman’s decision is an assertion of women’s freedom and dignity at a time when our status is rapidly eroding
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The congresswoman’s decision is an assertion of women’s freedom and dignity at a time when our status is rapidly eroding
Content: ‘The principle that women can and should pursue ambitions other than marriage and motherhood turns out to be much more endangered than I thought it was.’Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The principle that women can and should pursue ambitions other than marriage and motherhood turns out to be much more endangered than I thought it was.’Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesOpinionAlexandria Ocasio-CortezAOC’s public egg-freezing shouldn’t feel radical. But in today’s US, it doesMoira DoneganThe congresswoman’s decision is an assertion of women’s freedom and dignity at a time when our status is rapidly erodingThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTShare“Don’t be weird about this,” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive star and rumored 2028 presidential contender, said on herlive video broadcastas she raised her shirt to angle the syringe into her abdomen. Then, with resignation, “even though I know all of you will be.”The New York Democrat is 36 years old, and this week she revealed that she is beginning the process of freezing her eggs during Congress’s August recess. In the video, Ocasio-Cortez said that she was seeking to destigmatize the realities of women’s lives as they navigate the conflicting demands of professional aspiration and family building; she explained to viewers the process of the hormonal injections she was administering to herself, showing them the drugs and injector she was using arrayed on a paper towel, beside a disinfecting towelette. The procedure, Ocasio-Cortez explained, was not covered by her insurance, and she would be paying “100% out of pocket”. She had been saving to afford it for some time. “This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life,” she said, going on to assert her hope that transparency about such questions will destigmatize women’s reproductive lives and promote their dignity.It’s a bold move from a likely presidential contender. The decision to go public with her egg-freezing distinguishes Ocasio-Cortez as the rare Democrat willing to articulate an alternative vision of gender politics in an era when the Trump administration and its allies have rapidly eroded women’s civil rights protections, reproductive rights and workforce access, but whenmany mainstream Democratshave eschewed a robust defense of women’s 20th-century gains in favor ofcoveting white male votesand making overtures to the manosphere. Still, more than a political statement of values, the move may also serve as an early confrontation with what may be among the future-candidate AOC’s thorniest electoral vulnerabilities: her sex.‘Bold and ethical’: doctors on AOC’s egg-freezing journey - and Maga’s criticisms of itRead moreBy now, it is hardly controversial to say that the status of women has rapidly eroded over the past decade. The culture has turned against women’s freedom and dignity. In 2016, Donald Trump was elected just weeks after the nation heard him proudly declare that hegrabbed women“by the pussy”, defeating the first electorally viable female presidential candidate in a huge symbolic defeat for women’s advancement that has still not been reckoned with. In 2022, the national right to an abortion was killed off by the supreme court in the Dobbs case, decimating women’s dignity still further and materially harming their health and economic prosperity. The rise of the manosphere has initiated adolescent boys and grown men alike into a vulgar, domineering style of public misogynist contempt; a rash of so-called “wellness” influencers have encouraged women to abandon their reliable hormonal birth control in deference to scientifically dubious superstitions; tradwives have told girls and women to abandon workforce participation, education, ambition, financial independence and basic self-respect in favor of a gauzy, aproned life of baking a lot and thinking very little. Meanwhile, the rise of AI and deepfake technology means that now any woman or girl whose face appears in public must subject herself to the possibility, and frequently the reality, of being humiliated and degraded withdigital pornography of her likeness, as a punishment for being female.Policy, too, has turned against women’s historic gains. The Trump administration’s dismantling of theDepartment of Educationmeans that there is now very little in the way of enforcement of Title IX, the law that was supposed to secure women’s equal right to education. The administration hasweaponized the Equal Employment Opportunity Commissionin an effort to combat fictitious discrimination against white men, turning the organization away from its mission of fighting the kind of discrimination that keeps women out of the workforce. Officials have threatened to cut educational funding for students inwomen-dominated fields, and they havedecimated Title X, turning the program meant to help low-income women meet their reproductive health and family planning needs into one that encourages childbearing instead. Programs meant tocombat teen pregnancy– a wildly successful investment in young girls’ gifts and potential – have been cut. Birth control hasbeen burned. There has been dispiritingly little pushback: shockingly few prominent political figures seem willing to mount a meaningful defense of the rights and dignity of women and girls.In this context, AOC’s earnest willingness to draw attention to the status of women, and to argue for herself – and, implicitly, for others – as valuable for their intellects and gifts, and not merely for their reproductive capacities, is notable in itself. In her video, Ocasio-Cortez noted that she would be undergoing the treatment while continuing to work, including before an appearance on ABC’s This Week this past Sunday. “I want you all to see that,”she said. “And because women can do anything, and I think it’s badass that I’m going to be giving myself shots in the green room [as I] get my glam on.”On the show, she was blunt about the political moment motivating her disclosure. “In this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country and normalize them,” Ocasio-Cortez said.Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez should run for president | Bhaskar SunkaraRead moreRadical feminism this is not. Ocasio-Cortez’s assertions of women’s worthiness and capacity for public life, and her celebration of her own reproductive choices and pledge to help make such freedom possible for others, would have been considered tepid, even banal, a decade ago, during the “girlboss” era, when women’s reproductive freedom and workplace access were more culturally accepted and less directly threatened by policy. Back then, I would have rolled my eyes at such a display; now, I could weep with gratitude. The principle that women can and should pursue ambitions other than marriage and motherhood turns out to be much more endangered than I thought it was then; the example of a prominent woman doing so turns out to be more precious.But AOC’s egg-freezing saga, coming as 2028 speculation mounts, raises another question: how voters will respond to a female candidate of childbearing age. Historically, female politicians of AOC’s national profile and political ambition have largely been post-menopausal, and already mothers. Ocasio-Cortez’s youth and beauty have at times been a political asset – it’s hard to imagine any female politician achieving her level of national prominence while looking like, say, JD Vance – but it has also presented her with unique obstacles and humiliations, and prompted contempt for her on the part of her opponents that at times is so virulent and obsessive that it seems downright Freudian. As the first in her cohort of millennial progressives, and an early innovator in vertical video engagement with her constituents, AOC has long been willing to buck conventional wisdom about what a successful candidate should do or say in public. As she mulls a presidential run, she now has to contend with something else that no other candidate has ever done successfully before: running as a woman.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAlexandria Ocasio-CortezOpinionWomenPregnancyGenderFeminismTrump administrationReproductive rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Mark Zuckerberg says the future of AI is for everyone. But who owns it?  | Raffi Krikorian | The Guardian
description: It’s a nice sentiment, but all AI users should ask three questions about their preferred choice of AI platform
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It’s a nice sentiment, but all AI users should ask three questions about their preferred choice of AI platform
Content: Mark Zuckerberg published an essay, The Future Is for Everybody, on Monday.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg published an essay, The Future Is for Everybody, on Monday.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Mark Zuckerberg says the future of AI is for everyone. But who owns it?Raffi KrikorianIt’s a nice sentiment, but all AI users should ask three questions about their preferred choice of AI platformThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 10.03 EDTShareOn Monday, Mark Zuckerberg published a 6,500-word essay,The Future Is for Everyone.The essay came with something even rarer: a new Meta open-weight model. An open-weight AI model is the kind of AI with which you download the entire thing, and it works on your own computer (with or without the internet) and nobody can switch it off except for you. Almost every mainstream AI tool you use, whether it be Gemini, ChatGPT or Claude, is one you rent access to. Meta’s is one that you can download and actually own. I downloaded it before I finished the essay. So can you.This major move by the world’s largest tech heavyweight comes amid a summer heavy with AI news, full of nations at war. Washington against Beijing; tech founder against tech founder. But beneath those conflicts is a deeper contest between two kinds of power: a government that can order technology offline in an instant, and a company that can simply close your account. Neither is necessarily villainous. But the rest of us are not merely the audience in this fight; we are the prize. And the terms are already being written: intelligence on lease, a future we pay for but never quite own.Before you sign a lease, you generally wonder three things. Can I be thrown out? When I go, what goes with me? And if the landlord loses interest, who keeps the place standing? Ask the same three questions of any technology that says it belongs to everyone.If the markets reject OpenAI and Anthropic, the US should nationalize them | Bruce Schneier and Nathan E SandersRead moreStart with eviction. In 2009, Amazon reached into people’s Kindles overnight and deleted a book that everyone who bought it thought they owned. Nineteen Eighty-Four. On 12 June of this year, the US government did the same thing to AI: three days after the American lab Anthropic launched its most capable model, an order from Washington forced it offline for everyone, everywhere. Within days of Anthropic’s release, I tried two Chinese open-weight models, Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2. I could download them. I could run them myself – and nobody could reach into my server and delete them. On several of my tasks, they performed nearly as well. As such, the deciding question on open or closed models is no longer capability; it is who has the power to switch it off.The second question is one Zuckerberg’s essay never asks: can you take it with you? The essay does make a real privacy commitment. It introduces a fully private mode, sealed the way WhatsApp is, where even Meta can’t reach. The landlord will be locked out by architecture, and not simply by a promise. But read carefully. The agent he describes will hold your health, stories of your children and years of your thoughts – all in a diary kept in someone else’s house. Ask again: can you take it with you?double quotation markEveryone using AI should have three demands – and none of them is ‘pick a better company to trust’And the third question: when the landlord loses interest, who keeps the place standing? Zuckerberg says Chinese models are leading on open-source AI because American labs face heavier data rules. That’s not quite the full story. Chinese labs open their models because opennessistheir business model. American labs, on the other hand, keep theirs closed because openness would undercut them. Meta was the exception – until it paused its open strategy last year. But then something remarkable happened: absolutely nothing. Everyone who had downloaded Meta’s models kept them, and just kept building. Companies can change their minds, but they cannot undownload a model from somebody else’s machine. The files people had saved kept the ecosystem alive, not the company’s goodwill.We’ve seen this pattern before. Decades ago, one company gave a free browser to billions – and that act almost closed the web. Internet Explorer was “for everyone” too. What saved the open web was not a better company stepping in, but software built to work for the use, rather than whoever made it.Mozillaexists because of this fight. And this current battle over AI is the sequel.So everyone using AI should have three demands – and none of them is “pick a better company to trust”.Hold.Washington already gets this – when Washington itself is the tenant. Its own security posture warns against AI that an outside company could easily switch off. Britain, Canada and Germany already spend significant money on sovereign computing. Extend these principles to civilian life, and critical services like hospitals and government agencies should be required to hold legally usable copies of capable open-weight models, along with the tools and computing capacity to run them. All should face rigorous security and safety testing, whether they come from China, the US or anywhere else. Test the capability, don’t ban the method.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTake.Demand of agents what we just won from models: portability. The memory a machine has of you should be exportable to a rival. The diary should not be trapped in the house. This is the fight that will define the decade.Build.Openness shouldn’t depend on one company’s willingness to keep sharing. We need to pool the nuts-and-bolts of open-source infrastructure – the testing labs, the harnesses that run the models and the standards – so that the open ecosystem has what the web has today: a foundation that no single company can switch off.Zuckerberg’s title is right: the future should be for everyone. Open models don’t eliminate dependency; they give us what digital infrastructure rarely provides – a real, practical way to walk away.Raffi Krikorian is the CTO of MozillaExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionMark ZuckerbergMozillaComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: AOC and Mamdani wanted to defund the police. Their backtracking puts organizers at risk | Derecka Purnell | The Guardian
description: Progressive and democratic socialist politicians are recanting pandemic-era statements on police and prison abolition
Author: Derecka Purnell
Headline: Progressive and democratic socialist politicians are recanting pandemic-era statements on police and prison abolition
Content: ‘What time is it when politicians from AOC to Donald Trump suggest progressive and left organizers are “woke” and “crazy”?’Composite: CQ-Roll Call, Chicago Tribune, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘What time is it when politicians from AOC to Donald Trump suggest progressive and left organizers are “woke” and “crazy”?’Composite: CQ-Roll Call, Chicago Tribune, Getty ImagesOpinionUS policingAOC and Mamdani wanted to defund the police. Their backtracking puts organizers at riskDerecka PurnellProgressive and democratic socialist politicians are recanting pandemic-era statements on police and prison abolitionThu 13 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 09.10 EDTShareThe north may not remember, but 9 August this year marked the 12th anniversary of the police killing of Michael Brown Jr in Ferguson, Missouri. That day, the US representativeAlexandria Ocasio-Cortezreassured an ABC news anchor that she, like other progressive politicians and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates, had “moved away” from statements they made during the pandemic, particularly on police and prison abolition. Questioned further, sheexplained:“I have a local city councilman that has this saying: ‘Woke 1 was crazy’… especially during Covid, I think that the doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place. And I actually think that the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful. I think that when we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime in bringing crime down. And I think that we all share in the goals of having as low a crime rate as possible. I think that, you know, during lockdown, of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today. And I’m grateful that these candidates have the opportunity to present who they are to their electorate and what they’re campaigning on in this moment.”A few days later, on Wednesday,Zohran Mamdani, the progressive New York mayor, who has previously stated that his pandemic-era tweets supporting the defund movement were “out of step” with where he is now,chimed inon Ocasio-Cortez’s comments, saying: “Sometimes what you believe in can change. I know there are some for whom they still believe in that. I’ve made very clear that I do not believe in defunding the police and that to me, delivering critical public safety also looks like working with our police department alongside many other partners.”The New York City councilman to whom Ocasio-Cortez was referring, Chi Ossé, was actuallyinspired by the abolitionmovement to run for office. But earlier this week, he wasquick to proudly claimcoinage of the term “woke 1”, which has been used by people who seek to minimize statements they made in the aftermath of George Floyd’s murder by police in May 2020.In one sense, these politicians are absolutely correct. If “woke 1” represents a political baptism in shallow waters, then I have met many who were swept up in an emotional online conversion toward the radical, romantic rhetoric of “defund the police”. I know the power of the feeling of being connected to an idea that can offer relief and salvation. Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani and Ossé appeared at an altar of abolition during a global movement that condemned policing. It was a vibe. Sure, they may have even been earnest at the time. But as the abolitionist Mariame Kaba has said about centuries of organizing: abolition is not about your feelings or how you identify. It’s what you do.During the pandemic, I was a couple of years off from an ongoing campaign to close a jail and about to enter a campaign to prevent another one from opening. I wrote my book, Becoming Abolitionists, in that time partially because of how quickly some conversions happened – through charismatic check-marked profiles and inspirational protests, rather than through an organization or collective. Many people were just beginning to understandhowabolition was connected to other movements, including those against capitalism, imperialism, racism and ableism. I wanted to focus on centuries of abolitionist resistance that gave rise to contemporary abolitionist demands. “Defund” wasn’t simply a new idea about removing dollars from a budget (though we’d take it!) and leaving everything in society the same. Rather, it was and is a personal and political commitment and strategy to eliminate carceral, communal, colonial, capitalist and climate-based violence while building the people, practices and institutions to help us thrive.This fact is what makes Ocasio-Cortez’s comments additionally troublesome. Even by her own logic, “crime” is largely a product of exploitative, unequal social relations, such aseconomic inequality, and democratic socialism would produce more equal social relationships and reduce crime. So if democratic socialism is effective, then why keep funding theNew York police department at $11bn? And why dismiss taking money away as “rhetoric”?double quotation markThe police were not created for public safety. They were created to keep property owners and slaveowners safeBecause: the police were not created for public safety. They were created to keep property owners andslaveowners safe. The abolitionist geographer Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes in Geographies of Global Change that “the best estimate for crime as a driving force of prison expansion shows it to account for little more than 10 percent of the increase. Rather, it is a greater propensity to lock people up, as opposed to people’s greater propensity to do old or new illegal things, that accounts for about 90 percent of US prison and jail growth since 1980.” The rhetoric of public safety obscures this history and protects the institution as a heavily unionized, violent jobs program. This does not mean the police never show up when someone needs help, or that people become cops because they only want to hurt others. What it does mean is that historically, cities arewilling to rely on the povertythat capitalism creates to fill its carceral ranks withpeople lookingto enter the middle class.Seeing progressive politicians move away from their earlier feelings poses a question about what they’re moving toward. Ossé and AOC did not introduce any “woke 1” legislation or resolutions that they now have to retract. Mamdani actually attempted the opposite: the racial justice working group of DSA, among others, successfullypressured him to reverse his commitmentto add almost 600 more officers and $70m to the NYPD, against his campaign promise to maintain the headcount of the force. He was positioning this movewhileboasting historic lowsfor crime in the city. So unlike the students, artists, congregants and organizers I met and know, the politicians prioritized political office over political homes. Because these figures represent more than their political ideas, I understand. But the dismissal is the problem. The ideas rooted in the defund movement that got them the spotlight were not polling well by the time their volunteers were canvassing for their political campaigns. As a result, they dismissed those ideas as something to grow and learn from, not to publicly explore and explain.By contrast, for example, upon receiving pushback from the “defund” framing, activists in North Carolina chose “refund Raleigh” instead as an organizing campaign strategy to explain abolition to the community, develop a public services investment strategy and secure policies that decouple public safety and police. Even decades before abolition entered a mainstream branding debate, Wilson Gilmore said that she and others organizing through Californians United for a Responsible Budget chose a “deliberately bland name” to attract community members to the campaign. Still, other organizers chose more explicit “defund” campaign names as clear sites of struggle, sacrificing public palatability for political clarity.These efforts are equally important: people, politicians and corporations weaponized the ambiguity of “Black lives matter” toward everything, including more police funding and hires. So whether explicit in naming “defund” or not, abolitionist organizers across the country have been spearheading electoral campaigns, mutual aid efforts, disaster recovery, anti-immigrant detention networks, stopping jails and more. It is not always successful and apparent, but the commitment remains because the struggle continues.Right now, DSA members like AOC, Ossé and Mamdani feel refreshing because electoral politics have been captured for so long by Democrats and Republicans. And the state has done such a horribly impressive job at exhausting, shackling, killing and exiling actual revolutionaries that politicians who repeat the slightest radical rhetoric can start tofeellike revolutionaries. What remains, though, is that the very movements producing that rhetoric, from abolition to Free Palestine, also produced the possibilities of their elections. And downplaying those movements puts organizers who continue this work at risk, especially right now.What time is it when politicians across the political spectrum, from AOC and Ossé toMarco RubioandDonald Trump, suggest that progressive and left organizers are “woke” and “crazy”? It is the time when those who have not yet realized that the demonization of people, organizations and ideas about justice – regardless of where they come from – leads to targeting, surveillance, deportation, imprisonment and death.If leaders of DSA, an organization of which I am also a member, want to continue to grow as an electoral political home for people who believe these ideas are not only possible, but also worth pursuing, they must know that they are subject to the same lessons they are teaching establishment Democrats right now: do not laugh off the political demands of those who put you in office. For all of what their constituents, canvassers and staffers did as part of a fight on our behalf, is it worth treating years-long radical, Black and multiracial pursuits of freedom as mere pandemic pandemonium? No, it’s not. But more than what we are called by any of them is what we continue to call ourselves. Our own histories, convictions and clarity, not politicians, lead the way.Explore more on these topicsUS policingOpinionUS prisonsUS politicsRaceAlexandria Ocasio-CortezcommentShareReuse this content

title: Lost jobs, inequality, rogue agents: why are we accepting oligarchs’ AI agenda? | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: The dangers of AI become clearer every day. Why are we still acting as if we have no choice about our future?
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: The dangers of AI become clearer every day. Why are we still acting as if we have no choice about our future?
Content: ‘Lost jobs. Lost wages. Widening inequality. Datacenters using up water and electricity and polluting the climate.’Photograph: Brandon Dill/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Lost jobs. Lost wages. Widening inequality. Datacenters using up water and electricity and polluting the climate.’Photograph: Brandon Dill/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Lost jobs, inequality, rogue agents: why are we accepting oligarchs’ AI agenda?Robert ReichThe dangers of AI become clearer every day. Why are we still acting as if we have no choice about our future?Supported byAbout this contentThu 13 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTShareRather than producing jobs, the US economy actually lost 23,000 jobs in July, according toBureau of Labor Statisticsdata released on Friday. In addition, May and June’s job numbers were revised downward, showing a combined 103,000 fewer jobs than previously reported.As if this weren’t bad enough, wage growth has also slowed. Average hourly earnings rose by just 0.1% from June.This isn’t just a single month’s slow wage growth, either. Average hourly earnings increased just 3.2% over the pastyear– the lowest annual growth rate in five years.What’s going on? It’s too early to tell. But evidence is mounting that artificial intelligence is playing a role.New research by economists at Morgan Stanleyshowsthat the rate of unemployment is half a percentage point higher than it would otherwise be in occupations significantly exposed toAI, which they put at about30%of all employment. The effect is even more dramatic among younger people.Workers in these exposed occupations are also finding it more difficult to transition from unemployment back into employment than workers in less exposed occupations, leading to longer spells of joblessness.And according toresearchby the economists Sania Edlich and Apollo Global Management’s Torsten Slok, wage growth in jobs exposed to AI has contracted by 6.7% since 2023. This slowdown in wage growth has already resulted in at least $28bn inlossesfor 5.8 million affected workers.Billionaires are trying to lull us into AI complacency. Don’t let them | Steven GreenhouseRead moreThese findings still don’t explain the startling loss of jobs in July or the downward revisions for May and June. There are probably many factors at play. But they suggest that employers may be anticipating they’ll need fewer workers in the future – and won’t need to pay them all that much in order to attract them.It doesn’t matter that AI may create more jobs over the long term. As John Maynard Keynes once noted, over the long term we’re all dead.More thanhalfof Americans surveyed by Reuters/Ipsos in June said they were worried AI will put someone in the household out of work.Edlich and Slok write: “The critical policy question is not whether AI will reshape the labor market more broadly, but how quickly, and whether workers will have the support they need when it does.”As a former secretary of labor who’s kept his eyes focused on the Trump regime, I can assure you workerswon’thave the support they need any time soon.Even if AI begins to generate the productivity bonanza its advocates predict – but that it hasn’t yet – there’s no reason to assume US workers will see any of the benefits in their paychecks. If you hadn’t noticed, wages have been stuck even as the stock market has roared.To the contrary, all signs point to vast riches for a few major AI investors and executives, while most Americans are left behind.Wealth inequality is already at record levels, and wealth at the top is quickly morphing into political power.AI is already breeding a vast wave of campaign money. The pro-AI Super Pac Leading the Future, backed by executives at OpenAI and Palantir,had amassed more than $140mas of April, while Public First Action,backed by Anthropic,isn’t far behind.As the great jurist Louis Brandeis is reputed to have said: “America has a choice. We can have great wealth in the hands of a few. Or we can have a democracy. But we can’t have both.”AI is pushing us further toward the first option.Meanwhile, there’s the planet to consider.Amazon is now investing in a natural-gas power plant linked to a Pecos county, Texas, datacenter. The site could become the country’slargest single source of climate pollution, the New York Times reported. According to regulatory records reviewed by the Times, the plant will be allowed to release 33m tonnes of carbon dioxide a year.So much forAmazon’s promiseto reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040 as part of its Climate Pledge. You can bet other giants in the AI race will be turning to natural gas, too.Oh, and I haven’t even mentioned the Frankenstein in the room. A few weeks ago, OpenAIadmittedthat two of its artificial intelligence models had gone rogue and hacked into another company.How soon before AI models escape all their cages?Just last week, scientists published a study documenting how they used AI tocreate new kinds of viruses, raising the frightening possibility that the technology could be used to invent dangerous pathogens.Lost jobs. Lost wages. Widening inequality. Datacenters using up water and electricity and polluting the climate. Vastly more money polluting our politics. Models escaping their cages and hacking into everything, possibly threatening human life on this planet.Can we pause for a moment and talk about what’s really happening here?As the sociologist Tressie McMillan Cottom says, AI has merged regressive politics with unchecked economic power under the guise of technological innovation. Far too much money is giving a small group of unelected people extraordinary power to determine our future in ways that are likely to remake – and could possibly destroy – our lives.We’re watching all of this roll out as if we have no choice, as if it’s inevitable, as if AI is just something we’re going to have to adapt to.But why shouldwehave to adapt toit, whenitis the product of people like Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Mark Zuckerberg and Dario Amodei?If the markets reject OpenAI and Anthropic, the US should nationalize them | Bruce Schneier and Nathan E SandersRead moreWhy shouldwebe confined to being spectators at their enormously dangerous game? Why shouldwehave to accept all these hugely negative, potentially life-threatening consequences?The fact is, we don’t.Communities across the US are organizing against datacenters near them. Maga supporters and progressives are joining together to say “no” to the noise, higher electricity bills and water shortages.Well, then, why can’t we stop the whole thing? Why can’t we decide that, to the vast majority of us, the incalculable costs and risks of AI aren’t worth the potential benefits?Critics argue that stopping or even pausing AI in the United States would risk American industry falling behind competitors overseas.But if the costs and risks exceed known benefits, why not let China or any other competitor try AI out first? Why shouldwebe the canary in this extraordinarily dangerous coalmine?Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSuper PacsOpenAIAnthropicAmazonTexasUS unemployment and employment statisticscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Jason Arday affair must not spell the end for diversity. Here’s how – and why – we should defend it | Joseph Harker | The Guardian
description: The scandal has given succour to the same old rightwing attacks on D&I, but companies that do it properly raise standards rather than lowering them, says Joseph Harker, the Guardian’s senior editor, diversity and development
Author: Joseph Harker
Headline: The scandal has given succour to the same old rightwing attacks on D&I, but companies that do it properly raise standards rather than lowering them, says Joseph Harker, the Guardian’s senior editor, diversity and development
Content: Jason Arday faced allegations of plagiarism over his PhD thesis.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday faced allegations of plagiarism over his PhD thesis.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianOpinionDEI policiesThe Jason Arday affair must not spell the end for diversity. Here’s how – and why – we should defend itJoseph HarkerThe scandal has given succour to the same old rightwing attacks on D&I, but companies that do it properly raise standards rather than lowering themThu 13 Aug 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.40 EDTShareThis has not been a good fortnight for the concept of diversity and inclusion. The fallout from theJason Arday affairhas been an all-out attack, by the rightwing media and political classes, on institutional efforts to reduce inequality.Arday was the Black academic who, in a fanfare of publicity, had been appointed a professor at Cambridge University in 2023. At the time, British institutions were still struggling to address the widespread issues of systemic racism thrown up by themurder of George Floydthree years earlier.Last month Arday faced allegations of plagiarism over his PhD thesis, and amid massive scrutiny he resigned last week. Cambridge University has now announced anindependent inquiryinto its appointment procedures, but many academics already believe that Arday was given the job more for his remarkable backstory than for his academic ability. Arday was, they felt, not at the level you would expect for a professorial chair at such an elite institution. But he was the man who said he couldn’t talk till he was 11, and couldn’t read till he was 18; who had run 30 marathons in 35 days, the last third of them with a leg fracture. What an amazing story. Arday gathered headlines and media appearances. He became a walking advert for how an institution withsuch a poor record on diversityhad progressed so far. Or had it?I’ve been promoting diversity and inclusion for more than 25 years, and one of the stock responses I often hear is: “I’d love our organisation to be more diverse, but we don’t want to lower standards.” It trips off the tongue so smoothly, always accompanied by an apologetic faux-empathetic shrug.Yet the response completely misunderstands what diversity and inclusion is about. If it meant lowering standards I’d never waste my time pushing it. Who could possibly believe in making their organisation worse? D&I is not about making a moral point that you believe in equality (though you should); it’s not about performing an act of charity because you feel sorry for poor, excluded minorities (though you might); it’s not even about a business case in the expectation of making more money (though you also might).The point of D&I is that you bring people into your organisation with different life experiences and perspectives; you value them and listen to them (that’s why it’s called “inclusion”); and the outcome is that you make more informed decisions, so that your organisation better serves its customers. This may or may not translate into profits, but it definitely makes you better, and able to spot changing trends and changing patterns of behaviour more quickly.Opening up your hiring to more diverse communities leads to more competition and thereforehigherstandards.This is also why it’s important to make the distinction between positive action and positive discrimination.Positive action is inclusive and offers training or short-term experiences to underrepresented groups, helping to level the playing field before they apply for permanent jobs. Positive discrimination (commonly referred to as quotas), excludes people from job applications, reduces the numbers who are able to apply, and therefore lowers standards.Positive discrimination has always been illegal in the UK; its US equivalent, “affirmative action” was legal but provoked a huge backlash and is nowin effect outlawed. Positive discrimination also leads to minorities in any organisation having doubt cast on their position, that somehow they’re second rate, the “diversity hire”.The backlash over the Arday appointment has cast this shadow once again over a whole swathe of Black academics. Many of them are nowfurious at what Cambridgedid. If the university had wanted to open the door for a Black professor, there are dozens of academics at the right level. The difference is that they wouldn’t have been such a PR hit. The message they’ve taken from Cambridge is that, if you’re Black, you only get a top job if you have a superhuman backstory. Level playing field? Really?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf Cambridge really were an inclusive institution it wouldn’t have been looking for the “quick fix” that the Arday appointment gave it: a superficial symbol that everything here is OK. Instead it would have been examining its recruitment processes, the retention and promotion rates of its minority academics, to see where the problems were and what could be done. Cambridge would ask: how can we identify true potential and what kind of support can we offer people from underrepresented groups to ensure they thrive in the institution? (This applies just as much to women, working-class people and those with disabilities.)The past 18 months, since Donald Trump regained the US presidency, have seen huge political efforts to turn the clock back on equality and racial justice. Many companies have stood firm; but some have caved in and ditched their policies. The difference is that some understand why diversity and inclusion matters, and some don’t: there isample evidencethat diverse organisations perform better.So what should be the lesson for progressives who believe in equality? If, after the past few weeks’ headlines, any institution feels under renewed pressure to ditch its diversity policies, the correct response is: “But we don’t want to lower our standards.”Joseph Harker is the Guardian’s senior editor, diversity and developmentDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsDEI policiesOpinionJason ArdayRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human history | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: It is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage too, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: It is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage too, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: A theatre in Mariupol, Ukraine, destroyed by Russian bombing, 25 April 2022.Photograph: Alexander Ermochenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenA theatre in Mariupol, Ukraine, destroyed by Russian bombing, 25 April 2022.Photograph: Alexander Ermochenko/ReutersOpinionHeritageUkrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human historySimon JenkinsIt is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage tooThu 13 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.13 EDTShareWars may not take summer holidays, but they do sometimes see exhaustion. As drones race back and forth acrossUkraineand the strait of Hormuz, a grim stalemate seems to have invaded the earth beneath. Aerial bombardment knows limited resistance and even less victory or defeat. Ukraine, Russia, Israel, Iran and their allies seem able to defy diplomacy and drop bombs on each other for ever.At which point the outside world can merely count some of the costs. Vladimir Putin’s known desire to eliminate Ukraine’s historical identity has led to its cultural devastation. Two weeks agoUnesco reportedthe destruction or dereliction of 545 of its historic buildings, including 156 religious sites and 43 museums. The attempted eradication of what Putin himself claims to be an intrinsic part of Russia’s own history is sickening.Russia’s bombing of Kyiv’s Pechersk Lavra complex andthe Dormition cathedral, coupled with shattering the magnificent St Sophia cathedral, are comparable to Ukraine bombing the Kremlin. So, too, is the attack on a cathedral and a museum in Odesa, andthe destructionof a theatre in Mariupol. These are defining monuments of Ukraine’s past. Yet their dereliction has received little publicity in the west.Meanwhile in Iran the beautiful city of Isfahan might surely have been spared Donald Trump’s egotistic bomb-fest. Not so.A Reuters surveyin June found the historic Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Jameh mosque and the governor’s palace partially destroyed. In Tehran, the Persian royal palace of Golestan has beenbadly damaged. Unesco reports of an attack on an 1,800-year-old fortress that embraced a prehistoric settlement reputedly 63,000 years old.The most savage consequence of the collapse of order in the Middle East is the reported damage or destruction of over 80% of the buildings in Gaza. The ancient city of Gaza itself is now largely rubble. Bombed by Israel are the medievalGreat Omari mosqueand the church of St Porphyrius, dating from the fifth century and one of Christianity’s most ancient sites.Gaza’s archives have been destroyed. The Omari mosque’s library and the adjacent cultural centre, whose thousands of ancient documents had survived the Crusades, havereportedly been lost. The Al Qarara museum wasbombed from the airand then bulldozed to the ground. A people’s entire past has been deliberately eradicated.As for Israel’s war on Lebanon, it culminated in June in what appeared to be the gratuitousbombing of the ancient port of Tyre. This included an attack on the site of the Roman hippodrome. The 1,000-year-old fortress of Beaufort was also damaged. The past is clearly without privilege.Aerial wars are unlike ground ones. Soldiers with guns have targets. So, we are constantly told, do modern missiles, but that does not explain the USbombing of an Iranian girls’ schoolin February. The reality is that bombers are casual because they are near invulnerable, while their victims appear small and anonymous. Bombers do not conquer territory or secure surrender. They are manifestations of leadership machismo.In the allied invasion of Italy in 1943-45, individual British and American officers were known to take steps to protect its monuments from destruction. As a result Italy’s ancient cities survived to a degree that Germany’s did not. In the aftermath, sincere efforts were made to evolve rules of war, including respect for cultural and historic monuments. War was still seen as a contest of professionals, not of cultures.The result was The Hague Conventionof 1954and the Convention for the Protection of Cultural Propertyin 1972. But recent years, in which we’ve seen a collapse of global governance, have left The Hague convention a paper tiger, like that other supposed discipline, the UN’s International Court of Justice. Victory today appears to lie in destroying an enemy’s identity and morale as much as in killing its people. When the Islamic State ruined much of the Iraqi city of Mosulin 2014, it set about eliminating all traces of its past. Trump’s threat to Iran, that “a whole civilisation will die tonight”, showed an equally primitive approach to conflict. It hardly warned his bombers to spare the mosques of Isfahan.Of international bodies,Unescois active in keeping a record of the fate of cultural heritage worldwide, but a record is just a record. Its listing of Russia’s and Israel’s devastation of their hated foes is like watching a historic tragedy unfold in real time. We might almost prefer it to happen behind our backs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne thing the outside world can do is help those seeking to help themselves. Thus theWorld Monuments Fund’s Crisis Response Programis invaluable. It sends aid, advice and materials to war zones, almost before the bombs have stopped falling. It was present in Mosul and its Ukraine Response Fund has many projects (26 of which are completed) helping to protect and stabilise bombed buildings, one day perhaps to restore them.As the west continues to meddle in foreign wars, perhaps this is the least that some of us can do. One of humanity’s deepest obligations is to its past. That past knows no national boundaries.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
