title: I’d rather drink eel-infested lake water than put my hand up for Alone Australia – which is what makes it such great TV | Emily Mulligan | The Guardian
description: Alone Australia is my idea of torture, but there is something charming about the contestants that put their hands up for this madness
Author: Emily Mulligan
Headline: Alone Australia is my idea of torture, but there is something charming about the contestants that put their hands up for this madness
Content: The cast of Alone Australia. Emily Milligan writes of the SBS show: ‘It seems very difficult, very cold and very uncomfortable. Kill me quickly rather than any of that.’Photograph: SBSView image in fullscreenThe cast of Alone Australia. Emily Milligan writes of the SBS show: ‘It seems very difficult, very cold and very uncomfortable. Kill me quickly rather than any of that.’Photograph: SBSOpinionTelevisionI’d rather drink eel-infested lake water than put my hand up for Alone Australia – which is what makes it such great TVEmily MulliganAlone Australia is my idea of torture, but there is something charming about the contestants that put their hands up for this madnessThu 13 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 20.04 EDTShareIdon’t enjoy watching innocent people suffer, but one exception is the show Alone Australia. Victims put their hands up to be left on a remote and desolate beach, hoping not to freeze to death, and if they’re lucky they may catch an eel and eat it raw. Needless to say this is my idea of torture. In my view, the $250,000 prize means nothing in the face of not having a warm shower with an elaborate selection of nice-smelling oils for more than one day.The contestants are left utterly alone with a lot of camera equipment and film themselves building shelters, fishing or losing the plot entirely.Bluey to be available in an Australian Indigenous language for the first timeRead moreMost of the contestants have a horrible time and, while I enjoy having a large variety of breakdowns available for my viewing pleasure on free-to-air TV, it’s often hard to watch. Recently a contestantwalked away from his camp in the Arctic and couldn’t be found for hours, which doesn’t bear thinking about. I hope he’s somewhere warm with plumbing now!One element of the show that I can’t help but appreciate is how wholesome some of the breakdowns can be. Several contestants clearly ache for their partner or sit cold and alone (aside from the eels) contemplating why on earth they are away from their families with their short time allotted on this Earth. It’s infrequent that folks pick up the phone to tap out because of the rain, wet socks or giving themselves food poisoning after attempting some gathering without the aid of ChatGPT. Instead, you see a thought start to percolate in their heads, swirl around and grow to a roar until they pick up the walkie-talkie and tap out.It’s in the name, but the “alone” part seems to be even harder for most contestants than the physically surviving in unbearable conditions with a few fish hooks and a flint part.As a self-confessed wouldn’t-leave-the-airport-lounge spectator of Alone, it does draw into stark relief how odd it is for the folks who put their hands up for this. Folks who can fashion a spear, aren’t repulsed by eels, who can make fire, are comfortable sleeping outdoors on ferns and can single handedly construct a shelter. These skills, while technically essential to our very survival, are now utterly fringe behaviours. It’s quite strange to want to kill, skin and eat a possum. The distance between all of us needing to be closely connected to nature, to the food we eat, the shelter we enjoy, couldn’t seem more distant from this humble writer’s point of view.It seems very difficult, very cold and very uncomfortable. Kill me quickly rather than any of that.I once saw a contestant on Alone bring her saucepan to a lake and take a long, deep, unfiltered drink of raw water. Is this how our ancestors lived? If so, would they want us doing so on TV when we have since invented zip taps? What crimes would our ancestors have committed for a memory foam mattress?I suppose there is nothing more natural than wanting to source your own food or build your own shelter. We’ve ended up in a world where bananas are wrapped in plastic and there’s casual excess wherever we look, with tropical fruits rotting in fridges out of season after being shipped across the world. This isn’t right. Foraging, now that seems like the ticket. What could be more natural, or time-consuming.Ground Up review – Sam Pang stars in ABC’s easily digestible AFL office comedyRead moreFor millennia we eked a living out of the land and now the utter basics are a distant memory and several YouTube videos away from most of us. Utterly basic knowledge about what plants are supposed to grow where we live needs to be explained to us by the kindly people on Gardening Australia.It’s illustrative that watching people going out bush, digging up worms for bait to hopefully catch a fish a week – this is entertainment. Like the astronauts beaming back to Earth the strange and unfamiliar life on a space station. This is how it feels watching folks boil and eat palm fronds or make themselves eat foul fungus, making optimistic calculations about how many calories could be contained in the glutenous muck.But there is something charming about the everyday people that put their hands up for this madness. Their familiar accents, their reasons for volunteering, usually to make their family proud, to pay for something important or prove something to themselves. I’m glad they’re filming it, because I’d sooner drink the eel-ridden raw lake water than put my hand up myself.Emily Mulligan is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsTelevisionOpinionSBSAustralian mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: I protested against Pauline Hanson 28 years ago – now my teenager is doing the same thing | Philippa Chandler | The Guardian
description: In 1998, when I was in year 11, my friends and I wagged school to protest against the One Nation leader. Now my daughter has joined the school walkout
Author: Philippa Chandler
Headline: In 1998, when I was in year 11, my friends and I wagged school to protest against the One Nation leader. Now my daughter has joined the school walkout
Content: ‘I just hope the teens had a safe experience and that my future grandkids don’t have to protest against Pauline Hanson too,’ Philippa Chandler writes.Photograph: Lisa Maree Williams/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I just hope the teens had a safe experience and that my future grandkids don’t have to protest against Pauline Hanson too,’ Philippa Chandler writes.Photograph: Lisa Maree Williams/Getty ImagesOpinionPauline HansonI protested against Pauline Hanson 28 years ago – now my teenager is doing the same thingPhilippa ChandlerIn 1998, when I was in year 11, my friends and I wagged school to protest against the One Nation leader. Now my daughter has joined the school walkoutGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 13 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 20.16 EDTShareAt lunchtime on Thursday, my daughter left school, caught a bus and train into Melbourne’s CBD with her friends, andscreamed her lungs out about Pauline Hanson.I gave her permission. I could hardly say no, considering I did the same thing 28 years ago.In 1998, I was in year 11 at Bunbury senior high school in Western Australia. Hanson was visiting our town, so I wagged school with my friends Steve, Kate and Andrea and joined a small protest outside the venue where she was speaking.Students shun calls to stay in school as anti-Hanson protesters gather across AustraliaRead moreWe had little first-hand experience of cultural diversity but we were outraged by her mean-spiritedness. Hanson had recently made a statement about being “the mother of the nation” (or something like that) so we chanted: “You are not our mother!” Even as white kids in a relatively monocultural regional town, we did not want to be represented by her.A photo of us made the local newspaper. The owners of the ice-cream shop where Steve and I worked were unimpressed to see two of their junior staff gain notoriety.The problem is that Hanson seems to thrive on attention, so perhaps a better strategy is to ignore her. Could my friends and I have unwittingly contributed to her rise?View image in fullscreenOur protest made it on to the cover of the local newspaper in 1998This afternoon, my teen’s school principal sent an email to parents reminding us that “schools play an important role in helping students understand constructive ways of sharing their views and having a voice on issues they feel strongly about”. I assume this was a response to a large number of teens attending the protest.The school does a wonderful job.But how exactly are young people supposed to raise their voice beyond school? They can’t share their opinions at the ballot box and, at 15, my daughter is banned from social media so can’t even express herself online.In the 1990s, social media was a distant prospect. Triple J had only recently expanded to regional WA and I had little concept of youth subcultures let alone youth politics.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBack then, we didn’t have memes but we used to mimic her famous question “please explain” and took delight in the satirist Pauline Pantsdown. I am shocked her career has had longevity.Protesting against Hanson was the first of many anti-racism protests I have participated in. Once I became a mother, I took my daughter along with me and we participated in Black Lives Matter and various Indigenous rights rallies.My daughter is now old enough to attend without me. As she has grown-up in a multicultural suburb, racism is a tangible issue that directly impacts her friends, neighbours and family.I just hope the teens had a safe experience and that my future grandkids don’t have to protest againstPauline Hansontoo.Philippa Chandler is a freelance journalist and academic who lives in MelbourneExplore more on these topicsPauline HansonOpinionOne NationAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain’s scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would help | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: This summer’s extreme weather and wars in Iran and Ukraine have made our need for food stockpiles more pressing than ever, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: This summer’s extreme weather and wars in Iran and Ukraine have made our need for food stockpiles more pressing than ever, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: A car driving between dried-out farm fields, Lullingstone, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA car driving between dried-out farm fields, Lullingstone, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Brook Mitchell/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionFood securityBritain’s scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would helpGeorge MonbiotThis summer’s extreme weather and wars in Iran and Ukraine have made our need for food stockpiles more pressing than everThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTShareWhen a business makes long-term plans, they call it prudence. When a government makes long-term plans, they call it communism. Any sustained state intervention attracts the prefix “Soviet-style”, and triggers vicious attacks across the billionaire media. So governments have developed a bias against long-term thinking. This may explain why we no longer maintain strategic food reserves.In Britain, wheresoils have parched, market analysts warn that we’re facing themost severe food security crisisin decades. In normal years, crop failures at home don’t threaten our security, thanks to global trade. This is one of the reasons why hunger and famines arerarer and less deadlythan they used to be. But this is not a normal year, because the problem is now global.Similar impacts are hittingfarmers across Europeand in the US, whose wheat production this year isforecast to be lowerthan at any point since 1971. Until a few weeks ago, harvest forecasts in Canada were excellent, now itsspring wheat is also shrivellingin hot and dry conditions.Ukraine has had a good growing season, but exportforecasts have been cutas a result of Russia’s attacks on its ports. At the same time, crucial global pinch-points for food and farming supplies are tightening: Donald Trump’s aimless war with Iran has caused majorreductions in shippingthrough the strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Suez canal. These have become essential trade routes for fertiliser and, more recently, food, thanks to the Middle East’s emergence as amajor re-export hub.One impact of these disruptions has been todivert more shippingthrough the Panama canal. But the canal is now afflicted by drought, which has led torestrictions on ships’ draught(depth under water). The global circulation on which our food security depends no longer looks reliable.Country diary: This is how bad the heatwave has got for us arable farmers – I’m going on holiday | Colin ChappellRead moreIt’s not just that these impacts can immediately restrict the availability of food, even in wealthy importers such as the UK (poorer nations in the global south are, of course, hit much harder). It’s that they also land on a global food structure that has becomesystemically fragile. It is now highlyexposed to the riskof cascading collapse that nearly brought down the financial system in 2008. In fact, it suffers fromvery similar dysfunctions. The government knows this, because a report by its own security adviserswarns that our food supplyis “at strategic risk of catastrophic failure” by 2030. It responded bysuppressing the report.As with all potential system failures, it’s impossible to say where the tipping point may be. But what we can say is that if such an event occurs, the impacts would be beyond contemplation. It could be the most deadly global crisis in modern history.A world in which governments hold strategic stockpiles has a better chance of weathering either a temporary shortfall or a systemic failure. If food reserves were big enough, they would buy us enough time to rebuild the system. In their absence, if the food system collapses, so does society.The UK once held strategic food reserves, albeit very limited. But in the late 1970s and early 1980s, our governments decided they were no longer necessary, as private retailers would maintain sufficient stocks. As the National Preparedness Commissionpoints out, this policy coincided with decisions by the big retailers to stop holding stocks and switch to a just-in-time system: goodbye warehouses, hello logistics. No subsequent government appears to have noticed that its food-security assumptions are based on conditions that no longer exist. Perhaps they looked away out of the fear of being labelled interventionist. Perhaps they fear criticism more than crisis.Today, as far as I can tell, the government’s sole food storage intervention is a single unpublicised paragraph on itsPrepare website. It instructs us to “Put together an emergency kit of items at home. This could include: Non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking … how much you need will vary based on your own circumstances.” Invaluable advice, I’m sure. That scarcely anyone has seen it, that many people have no space for an emergency food store and no money to buy it with is just bad luck. Perhaps we don’t deserve to survive.6:05Why the UK has a food security problem – videoI write as though I’m confident that the UK does not maintain stockpiles. For several years, I have been asking the environment department this simple question: does it or does it not hold them? The Conservatives were honest enough to say “no”. But since Labour took office, it has repeatedly failed to answer. When I asked again last week, it sent me a long disquisition on related subjects, but signally failed to answer the question. I then asked why it hadn’t answered, and received no reply to that either. I find this response more eloquent than a candid “no”. It tells me two things: “the answer’s still no” and “we know the policy is wrong”. Otherwise, it would be happy to tell me about it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government also told me: “The UK has a highly resilient food system, drawing on both strong domestic production and international trade and we do not expect the recent dry weather to have any impact on national food security.” This claim, which defies warnings from the security services, market analysts and the food trade itself goesbeyond complacency. It’s denial.As far as I can tell, since he became prime minister, Andy Burnham and his office have not said one word in public about the climate crisis.On Wednesday he chaired anemergency Cobra meetingto discuss the extreme heat, the drought and the wildfires. But, at the time of writing, there has yet to be a public statement about what has caused this crisis, and how we might cause less of it.Yet No 10 did find time last week to intervene on Westminster council’s plan tolimit vertical drinkingin Soho. Good to know it is laser-focused on the crucial matters of state.The government’s disregard and denial sustains our proud tradition of heroic failure, from the charge of the Light Brigade to Brexit. Food reserves are for losers. Prudence is for suckers. Somehow the words “British” and “invulnerable” have become muddled up.In good times, government stockpiles look like a waste of money and effort. But the role of governments is not to prepare for the good times. Governments exist to defend us from harm. And this isn’t possible without long-term plans.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsFood securityOpinionExtreme heatcommentShareReuse this content

title: Jason Arday is now the stick the right will use to beat back racial equality. Don’t let that happen | Afua Hirsch | The Guardian
description: The UK is far from equality in academia or society. You don’t need a Cambridge degree to see that Arday’s story is being used to stop any progress in its tracks, says journalist and academic Afua Hirsch
Author: Afua Hirsch
Headline: The UK is far from equality in academia or society. You don’t need a Cambridge degree to see that Arday’s story is being used to stop any progress in its tracks, says journalist and academic Afua Hirsch
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionJason ArdayJason Arday is now the stick the right will use to beat back racial equality. Don’t let that happenAfua HirschThe UK is far from equality in academia or society. You don’t need a Cambridge degree to see that Arday’s story is being used to stop any progress in its tracksThu 13 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.19 EDTShareIn 1987, a college at the University of Cambridge considered offering a prestigious position to a black man in what would be the first appointment of its kind. Not only did the man not have a degree, but he had left school at the age of 13, struggling with dyslexia and – at the time – unable to read or write. That he would later to go on to accumulate 20 honorary doctorates and become a professor of creative writing is only one way, and in my view not the best one, of measuring his talent.The man was the late, great poetBenjamin Zephaniah. And he had been nothing but transparent about his lack of credentials. In fact it was his background that made him eligible for this fellowship, which was designed to reach out to somebody in the community who didn’t have a degree, to give them the opportunity to have a connection with the university.Zephaniah had been privately offered the role but a formal offer had not yet been made when it was leaked to the rightwing press. The Sun and the Daily Mail newspapers enjoyed afeeding frenzyat the prospect of a black man – one with locs, no less – becoming a fellow at Cambridge.“Would you let this man near your daughter?” asked the Sun. “Just what are his qualities which have appealed to Trinity College?” the paper asked. Then, not bothering to hide its starkly racist views, it answered that there were none. No qualities, only problems, listed in order of severity: “He is black. He is a Rastafarian. He has tasted approved schools and Borstals.”The Sun offered no evidence whatsoever for the implication that Zephaniah was a rapist, as the headline suggested. Apparently none was needed – the audience already understood that a black man from Handsworth, Birmingham, who had “tasted Borstals” could not possibly be an appropriate or safe person to be associated with Cambridge University.In the years since Zephaniah did not receive the fellowship that should have been his due, Cambridge – like many elite universities – has been mired in actual scandals of rape, nepotism, plagiarism and more. Remember them? You probably don’t, because they barely made the news.For a period beginning in 2019, Trinity Hall, Cambridge, was embroiled in controversy after it emerged that not one but three people who worked at the college had beenaccused of sexual misconductby students. The ensuing outcryled the master to resign.In 2023, a professor from the same college was allowed to keep his job after having been found to haveplagiarised materialfrom a student essay.In 2015, a row broke out in which the renowned University of Leeds sociologist Zygmunt Bauman was accused ofmultiple instances of “self-plagiarism”. Colleagues claimed those allegations were motivated by another scholar’s “personal agenda” and said they were “tantamount to a form of intellectual violence wrapped in objective scholarship that plagues the academy”.Maybe it’s just my algorithm, but social media seems flooded with hot takes onJason Arday. I have worked with him – we were developing a project together at one point – and I have thought a lot about him in the years since.The fact is that many of Arday’s black peers in academic sociology have been voicing concerns about him for a while. He seemed, to them, to have come out of nowhere. His performance at high-profile academic events did not match the credentials that were being touted. I have had various conversations with sociology professors in which this has been the main topic of conversation, and their questions began to mount into a list. They did not voice them publicly because we all know that whatever the truth or the outcome, he would be unlikely to be treated fairly and we would all be damaged in the process. As for me, I was an interested observer to allegations the veracity of which I couldn’t personally verify. But hearing them from fellow black academics I respect was enough to put me on alert and raise a red flag for anyone who asked me whether publicly supporting him was a good idea.‘Old racist wine in a new bottle’: Black academics respond to Jason Arday affairRead moreSome of the people who did sign those letters are now feeling very angry that Arday did not protect them from what he must have known to be lies before they used their own reputations to defend his. Others are angry that he appears to be using his neurodivergence as an excuse for dishonesty, which of course it’s not.The media cannot conceal its excitement about his transgressions. Arday doesn’t need to be a fantasist to be the kind of man commentators would rather not see at a university like Cambridge – being black is enough. For them, the fact that he made stuff up is simply a massive bonus. Which explains why they have moved so quickly from identifying mistakes he has made to indulging in an orgy of delight at the prospect of smearing all black academics.Indeed, I seriously question whether Donald Trump received as much scrutiny for starting a war with Iran as Arday did for exaggerating hisathletic and academic credentials.Nor does the media care about protecting students, by the way. That is not an issue that sells newspapers, drives clicks or feeds the agendas of the rightwing billionaires who own most of our media.I have lost count of the number of emails, text messages, DMs and WhatsApps I received asking me to condemn the allegations against Arday. Not one of these messages asked me first if I know him, what my opinion about the allegations is or whether I actually agree with their assertion that they are baseless.It probably looks as if I support a lot of open letters and petitions, and I do. In recent months these have addressed unlawful deportations, the intimidation tactics of the far right, Labour’s imitation of the far right, the crackdown on free speech rights and protests for Gaza.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe due diligence involved in joining these causes includes checking the facts and legal basis of the petitions, and researching the backgrounds of individuals and organisations involved. I love that we show up for each other. I love that we take a stand. But knowing exactly what it is that we are supporting is essential.I have no idea what made Arday say things that are obviously fabricated. I hope he is OK, and I am unequivocal about condemning the media pile-on, which ranges from overt to dog-whistle racism, and which is completely disproportionate.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: The TelegraphWhat I do have to say aboutJason Ardayis really very simple. The overwhelmingly white dons and administrators at Cambridge chose one academic – unrecognised by many of his black peers in the field – and felt his was an appointment with which they could feel comfortable. This resembles a pattern we see elsewhere in public life, where the disproportionately few black people who are selected by white gatekeepers are sometimes chosen for reasons that seem to have little legitimacy among black peers.Black academics, and black people in general, have never and – it’s my confident prediction – will never demand the right to plagiarise, lie or fabricate our credentials. What we have been demanding is to be treated equally. To be appointed to the levels commensurate with our actual credentials, to have our work taken seriously by intellectual peers, and to be paid fairly and on equal terms for our labour. To not have opportunities taken away because of our race. To have our work, performance and legacy held to the same standards as everyone else’s.We are very far from anything resembling this. You don’t need a Cambridge degree to see how conveniently the Arday story is serving as a distraction while the media drags us even further in the wrong direction.I said people signed the petitions for Arday because we are overwhelmed by very legitimate, abundant instances of racism and the sometimes onerous task of doing the due diligence. The last takeaway from this sorry saga relates to this last point, and it’s important. I have heard people say that they assumed the allegations against Arday were baseless because Cambridge said so.We are too quick to look up to the institutions of the British establishment, and this makes us vulnerable. This is the same reason we accept OBEs, even as they insult our ancestry, and celebrate black “power” even when what that means is high status positions in companies, political parties or organisations that are harmful to our community.I’m not saying we can avoid these institutions – we are all navigating the same society. But we can be much smarter about how we interact with them, and whether we do so from a place of awe, or whether we do so from a place of strategy, with our eyes wide open.Afua Hirschis a writer, broadcaster and academic.
