title: I got married in the Vegas of Europe. It was the most romantic 20 minutes of my life | Jules Darmanin | The Guardian
description: Post-Brexit visa rules and faceless pen-pushers were keeping me and my partner apart. But love finds a way, writes French journalist Jules Darmanin
Author: Jules Darmanin
Headline: Post-Brexit visa rules and faceless pen-pushers were keeping me and my partner apart. But love finds a way, writes French journalist Jules Darmanin
Content: A newly married couple in the Nyhavn old town area of CopenhagenPhotograph: Jeppe Gustafsson/AlamyView image in fullscreenA newly married couple in the Nyhavn old town area of CopenhagenPhotograph: Jeppe Gustafsson/AlamyOpinionWeddingsI got married in the Vegas of Europe. It was the most romantic 20 minutes of my lifeJules DarmaninPost-Brexit visa rules and faceless pen-pushers were keeping me and my partner apart. But love finds a wayThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.33 EDTShareConsider your ideal wedding. You may picture religious pageantry, majestic domes and the auspicious light of the Divine beaming on a white dress. Maybe you see friends dancing on a pub’s veranda, cheering for you in front of a town hall, or anywhere really – the people you love are there, and it’s all that matters.What you are probablynotpicturing is a meet-up with Chris and Mitch, two complete strangers waiting for you and your future spouse by a nondescript fountain in the middle of Copenhagen. Judging by my soon-to-be-wife’s bewildered laugh throughout the entire 20 minutes of our wedding, this is not what she was picturing either. Should I add that neither of us is Danish, or lives inDenmark?My wife, who is attached to her privacy and thus will remain “my wife” for the purpose of this piece, is British-Polish, and made her life in the UK. I am French.Brexitmeans Brexit. To live happily ever after under the same London roof, we had to prove our commitment to the relevant authorities.Our immigration adviser – an odd but knowledgable fellow – was unsubtle about it. On a Zoom call about a year ago, he mimed a rifle being reloaded. To end ourlong-distance relationshipand build a life together, it was time for a shotgun wedding.But while love doesn’t wait, administrations around Europe like to take their sweet time. Marrying in Britain required a “fiance visa”, which would have allowed me to stay in the UK while waiting to get married, but not to work, making it financially unviable. Doing it in my home country would have required dealing with French bureaucracy – you can appreciate why we ruled that out. If only there was a simple way to marry abroad, we thought.A single Google search was enough to find an agency called Marry Abroad Simply.Despite the hundreds of five-star reviews praising “excellent communication”, “genuine kindness” and a “completely stress-free experience”, I couldn’t shake the feeling that getting wed with Marry Abroad Simply was a bit like going for a haircut to a salon named Best Haircuts. One would hope for a bit more mystique.But so be it – I dialled the WhatsApp number on the website and mumbled something to the effect of: “Hello, I’d like to marry my partner as soon as possible, please.” Instead of saying, “Sounds a bit dodgy, love”, a charming woman called Leanne laid out her fast-and-furious pitch.Plan A, she said, was Gibraltar, the easiest option when it comes to paperwork. However, the marriage certificate can take a few weeks to arrive in the post. Plan B was Denmark, but city halls were crowded, so we would need to pay extra for a quicker ceremony in the park. Finally, she added, “I can get you married in Georgia in a couple of weeks.”We opted for a compromise between speed and familiarity, and picked the “Copenhagen Express” package.Denmark, we found out in the process, is theVegas of Europe. Thanks to its lenient, multilingual administration, couples from around the world flock to the Scandinavian kingdom to elope. The trend startedmore than a decade ago, with Germans crossing the border to marry their partner from outside the Schengen area. It’s not a bad business: international couples bring about120m kroner (about £13.7m)to the economy every year.Leanne, who spoke to me after our blitz wedding, reckons her company helps 150 couples in Denmark every month. She often deals with cases more complex than ours, such as same-sex unions where one spouse comes from a country still denying them their rights. A former government document specialist, in 2013 she joined this industry specialising in quick, fuss-free wedding planning.Our own wedding attained summits of fusslessness you wouldn’t believe. The day before, our suitcases barely unpacked, we got to Copenhagen city hall, where the civil registrar desk also serves as a gift shop. We queued with other couples to prove our identity to the Danish government. Fake bouquets were displayed on a table next to a sign saying “Flowers (for rent) on your wedding day”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenFlowers for rent in Copenhagen city hall.Photograph: handoutWe passed on the offer and the next morning rushed to the flower shop at Copenhagen train station. The white and purple bouquet my partner chose would look splendid under the grey Danish sky. With our prêt-à-porter suit and dress, she was gorgeous and I was dapper enough. We were ready to walk down the aisle.After a 15-minute stroll through Copenhagen’s Latin Quarter, under the gaze of curious tourists and blase locals, we arrived at our venue: thegardens of the Royal Library. It’s a nice but unassuming park in the heart of the city. We had no guests, as you can imagine, and Marry Abroad Simply procured us Chris and Mitch.Chris and Mitch – bless them – were our professional and only witnesses. They introduced us to our officiant, a mild-mannered gentleman named Jesper. We then stood awkwardly in front of the building that housed centuries of Danish literature. Jesper gave a brief speech about how we, too, were writing the first page of our common book. Listening to the sniffs on the video Chris took of that moment, I believe he shed a tear. But Leanne since told me they could do several of these a day, so he may just have had a cold.We were so engrossed in the absurdity of the situation that we didn’t pay that much attention to Jesper’s speech. We said our vows, exchanged our rings, and kissed under the golf clap of onlookers. After some pictures, including a selfie with the gang, we crouched down on a bench to sign the papers. My wife and I were married.You might find this unromantic, but I couldn’t disagree more. Throughout our Danish escapade, we kept bumping into other couples roaming in and around city hall. We could often guess from their looks and their accents that they were there for reasons similar to us. They were lovers seeking to tear down the borders erected between them, to prove their most intimate devotion to faceless pen-pushers.That day was for us against the world. It was a day of boldness and belief in a bright future. To my readers longing for marriage, I say: forget bridesmaids, distant cousins and nervy photographers. What I wish for you is to marry abroad simply.Jules Darmanin is a French journalistExplore more on these topicsWeddingsOpinionEuropeMarriageDenmarkBrexitcommentShareReuse this content

title: The ABC has a tradition of mocking the powerful. Now, after the Rinehart furore, it risks creating a comedy no-go zone | Alan Sunderland | The Guardian
description: I didn’t think the Race Around the World segment was funny, but does the ABC really need to change its editorial policies to make sure violence and humour sleep in separate beds?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I didn’t think the Race Around the World segment was funny, but does the ABC really need to change its editorial policies to make sure violence and humour sleep in separate beds?
Content: ‘Violence is a very broad and vague concept, and if the ABC gets this one wrong it will be a pie in the face for all of us,’ writes Alan Sunderland.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Violence is a very broad and vague concept, and if the ABC gets this one wrong it will be a pie in the face for all of us,’ writes Alan Sunderland.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianOpinionAustralian Broadcasting CorporationThe ABC has a tradition of mocking the powerful. Now, after the Rinehart furore, it risks creating a comedy no-go zoneAlan SunderlandI didn’t think the Race Around the World segment was funny, but does the ABC really need to change its editorial policies to make sure violence and humour sleep in separate beds?Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 12 Aug 2026 22.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.29 EDTShareIgrew up on Bugs Bunny and Tom and Jerry. Most of my best-loved childhood TV friends were regularly shot at, beaten up, squashed under anvils or exploded in many and various ways. Many years later, I watched Basil Fawlty regularly attack Manuel, his hapless Spanish waiter, and of course the Three Stooges were little more than a relentless series of violent gags.Violence and humour may seem strange bedfellows, but they have been sleeping together for a very long time. So what are we to make about the latest round of outrage and handwringing overan ABC joke that clearly went too far?ABC changing editorial policy after Rinehart furore prompts fears of overreachRead moreI haven’t found too many people who thought that threatening cartoonish violence against Gina Rinehart was funny, and nor did I. The comment was criticised at the time on the program that aired it, the film-maker responsible for the comments has now apologised for a joke that went too far, and the ABC has joined in the apology and edited the segment to remove it completely, although not from our collective memory.Shouldn’t that be enough? Does the ABC really need to change its editorial policies to ensure that, from now on, violence and humour need to sleep in separate beds?Well of course it doesn’t. What’s more, it’s not actually going to.I don’t want to get too technical here, but the ABC has13 editorial policies– how’s that for a lucky number? One of them deals with harm and offence, and the ABC is not proposing to change a word of it. All the ABC intends to do is update its non-binding guidance for program makers on how to follow those unchanged policies.What will the updated guidance say? Well, based on recent comments by the ABC managing director, Hugh Marks, it is likely to advise that making jokes about violent acts against individuals is off the menu. Not funny. Not on our ABC. At least, that will be the ABC’s non-binding recommendation.Superficially, that seems like reasonable advice. Anyone who remembers US comedianKathy Griffinholding up a severed head that resembled Donald Trump, or even Alan Jones suggesting metaphorically that Julia Gillard should be put in a chaff bag and taken out to sea, knows that those remarks rarely fare well. Apologies are far more common outcomes than applause.ABC apologises to Gina Rinehart over controversial Race Around the World episodeRead moreBut at the same time, let’s take care. For every extreme example where violence, jokes and individuals don’t mix well, there are others where the humour is in the eye of the beholder. And if a piece of guidance, even if non-binding, creates a no-go zone for ABC comedy and entertainment programs, what kind of po-faced, anodyne world might we find ourselves in?It didn’t take me long to locate a brilliantoperatic parodyof the dismissal of the Whitlam government that aired on the ABC’s Gillies Report back in the 1980’s. Dodgy singing aside, it also showed Gough Whitlam collapsing on the steps of the Senate with multiple knives sticking from his back. Clearly an act of comic violence against a prominent individual. Hilarious even now, but will we see the likes of it again?From Norman Gunston and Aunty Jack to Black Comedy and Hard Quiz, the ABC has broadcast some fairly edgy things over the years, often targeting well-known Australians as the butt of their humour. Violence is a very broad and vague concept, and if the ABC gets this one wrong, it will be a pie in the face for all of us.Alan Sunderland is a former editorial director of the ABC and former news editor at SBSExplore more on these topicsAustralian Broadcasting CorporationOpinionAustralian mediaTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was fun to get pushed around’: Andrew Rannells on ‘razzle dazzle’, kissing co-stars and being a better friend to Lena Dunham | Movies | The Guardian
description: The star of Girls and The Book of Mormon talks about coming out, turning a showmance into a romance, and going toe to toe with the West Wing’s Allison Janney in new film Miss You Love You
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: The star of Girls and The Book of Mormon talks about coming out, turning a showmance into a romance, and going toe to toe with the West Wing’s Allison Janney in new film Miss You Love You
Content: ‘I’d rather do porn than Pokémon’ … Andrew Rannells.Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for SCADView image in fullscreen‘I’d rather do porn than Pokémon’ … Andrew Rannells.Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for SCADMoviesInterview‘It was fun to get pushed around’: Andrew Rannells on ‘razzle dazzle’, kissing co-stars and being a better friend to Lena DunhamRyan GilbeyThe star of Girls and The Book of Mormon talks about coming out, turning a showmance into a romance, and going toe to toe with the West Wing’s Allison Janney in new film Miss You Love YouThu 13 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImagine a cute, young, gay Jim Carrey with a withering line in put-downs: that is Andrew Rannells. Or rather, it was, back when he starred inLena Dunham’s HBO series Girlsas Elijah, the formerly closeted ex of her character, Hannah. Dunham had seen Rannells playing Elder Price, the zealous missionary spreading the good word in the original 2011 Broadway production of the bad-taste musicalThe Book of Mormon, for which he received a Tony nomination. Girls, in turn, spread the good word about him. To this day, fans still shout “Your dad is gay!” at him in the street, a call-back to the moment when Elijah tartly advises Hannah that she might want to fine-tune her gaydar.It is an older, gentler, salt-and-pepper-bearded Rannells who stars in the comedy-dramaMiss You, Love You. He plays Jamie, a personal assistant arriving in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to shepherd the spiky and recently widowed Diane (Allison Janney)through the initial weeks after her husband’s death from Parkinson’s. As it dawns on them that Diane’s son – Jamie’s employer – may not make it to his stepfather’s funeral, these strangers navigate their way through the grey area of their flung-together friendship.Initially, Jamie struggles to retain composure in the face of Diane’s gale-force disdain, as she picks and pecks at his every word. “I was just trying to keep up with what Allison was doing,” says Rannells, who is wearing a silvery-grey shirt and running a hand through his chestnut quiff. He knew Janney from starring together in thecomic thriller Another Simple Favor, but nothing prepared him for being harangued by her during the new film’s extended takes. “She is relentless. She goes and goes and goes. All her years on The West Wing really prepped her.”Watch the trailer for Miss You, Love You.Rannells is hardly low-energy himself. Whether in his impish US television appearances, collected in YouTube compilations with titles such as “andrew rannells being a little TOO ICONIC on talk shows”, or in his shopping-mall song-and-dance number as an incorrigible Juilliard graduate inRyan Murphy’s The Prom, he is all razzle-dazzle. “Yeah, I’m usually in that position,” he concedes. “It was fun this time to be on the other side of it and to feel what it’s like to get pushed around and bullied.”It is a few weeks before his 48th birthday and Rannells is speaking on a video call from the home in Los Angeles he shares with the actorTuc Watkinsand the latter’s twin teenage children. The room behind him is blurred, so it is impossible to identify the three paintings on the wall, but since Rannells put his stylish Manhattan apartment on the market last year for nearly $2.5m (£1.8m), Dogs Playing Poker is unlikely to be among them.He and Watkins met on the 2018 Broadway revival of the pre-Stonewall chamber-pieceThe Boys in the Band. Their first kiss was in character. “We would end each show making out on stage. Ten minutes of us rolling around while Jim Parsons was crying.” They hooked up but didn’t start dating until a year later, when the cast reconvened forMurphy’s Netflix version. “We turned a showmance into a relationship,” he says with a little twitch of the eyebrow.View image in fullscreenWithering put-downs … Rannells and Lena Dunham in Girls, 2017.Photograph: Apatow Productions/Kobal/ShutterstockGiven his success, it is natural to assume that Rannells’ performance as Jamie in Miss You, Love You was based on his own experience of having PAs. On the contrary, he says – he has never hired one. This may make him something of an outlier in Hollywood. “One of my closest friends has an assistant. At times, I’m closer to the assistant than I am to him.” Why has Rannells resisted? “Maybe it comes from years of working in theatre. I got in the habit of doing things for myself. To relinquish that control now would be, I think, hard for me.”Knowing when and how to ask for help is one of the lessons that Jamie must learn in the film. Rannells can sympathise. “You are raised in the midwest to take care of your own problems: don’t make waves, fix it, move on. Sometimes I do myself a disservice by not asking for what I need. I’m getting better at it. But I’ve certainly seen it abused. A lot of actors take advantage of people and I don’t want to be that person.”He grew up next door to a children’s theatre in Omaha, Nebraska, and took drama classes from a young age. Performing soon began to pay: from 13 to 31, he was a prolific voice actor in cartoons including Pokémon and Yu-Gi-Oh!. That spilled over into his burgeoning stage career: at 21, he toured the US in Pokémon Live!. “In retrospect, [I] would rather have done a snuff film or porn,” he said later.His big, gay New York life was under way by then. He came out to his parents shortly before leaving home to study drama at 19. “My family was mostly – what’s the best way to say this? – not shocked,” he wrote in Too Much Is Not Enough: A Memoir of Fumbling Toward Adulthood. That 2019 book also revealed, in a chapter entitled It’s Never the Priest YouWantto Kiss, that he had been sexually assaulted as a teenager by a Catholic priest.View image in fullscreenThe boys in the band …(from left)Zachary Quinto, Andrew Rannells, Matt Bomer and Jim Parsons at the 2018 Tony awards in New York.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Tony Awards Productions“My mum accepted my sexuality,” he says. “My dad said: ‘I don’t think you have to be this way, but I love you.’ I was like: ‘Eh, that’s not exactly what I wanted to hear, but whatever.’” A few months later, his father reached a different conclusion. “He said: ‘I realise you’ve always been this way and I’m sorry I said that.’” Hadn’t his dad introduced him to 1940s musicals from a young age? “Exactly! It was his fault.”Coming out was relatively plain sailing, but there was a crisis ahead. When Rannells was 22, he brought a date back to his apartment. In the bathroom later, he checked the phone messages he had been ignoring for the previous few hours and found that his family had been frantically trying to reach him. His father was in a coma; a few days later, he died.That night, with its intermingling of sex, intimacy and mortality, left an impression on Rannells. In 2017, he wrote about the awkwardness of being consoled in this devastating moment by a naked man he hardly knew: “After I hung up, he tried to hug me: ‘What happened?’ I wanted to shout: ‘Clearly nothing good! Put on some pants!’”That essay inspired him to write and direct How Do You Remember Me?, his half-hour contribution tothe Amazon series Modern Love. In the screen version, he highlights the disparity that exists between separate recollections of identical events. “I’m sure that guy has gone off and told that story, especially as I’ve become successful,” he says. “And I’m sure it’s mostly the same as mine – but also pretty different.”View image in fullscreenGale-force disdain … Rannells and Allison Janney in Miss You, Love You.Photograph: HBORannells had his own experience of seeing the familiar from a revealing new angle when he readDunham’s recent memoir, Famesick. Its tales of behind-the-scenes horrors on Girls include theallegedly hostile behaviour of Adam Driver, who Dunham claims berated her for forgetting her lines before hurling a chair at the wall next to her. “That book is a great example of seeing things differently,” Rannells says. “Girls was my first TV job and when I showed up on set I saw the fun, exciting part. At times, Lena would open up to me and I’d read things in the press that were untrue or unfair. But the book was hard to read as someone who is close to her now. I felt terrible that I wasn’t a better friend.”What could he have done? “Been more available. I let a lot of shit slide because so much was happening. I had a break-up, then a new relationship. I was doing The Book of Mormon eight times a week and working on Girls.” He left to shoot 22 episodes of Murphy’s 2012 gay-dads sitcom,The New Normal, before returning to Girls when The New Normal was cancelled. “Of course, there was another part of reading her book,” he says. “I was, like: ‘Why didn’t she talk about me more?’” Joking he might be, but there is a Reddit thread on that very topic. “I would like to say I started that thread, but I did not,” he says. The eyebrow twitches again. Did he or didn’t he? As ever with Rannells, you are left with a tantalising question mark.Miss You, Love You is on HBO Max in the UK and Ireland, the US and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsComedy filmsRyan MurphyComedyGirlsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Imelda Staunton: ‘Umbridge’s giggle needed to be short and sharp. So I just did a boom, boom’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor answers your questions on working with her dog, becoming a dame, Harry Potter, and making televisual history in The Singing Detective
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The actor answers your questions on working with her dog, becoming a dame, Harry Potter, and making televisual history in The Singing Detective
Content: Imelda Staunton … ‘Having my dog in the show was fantastic because she liked everything I did.’Photograph: Nick ThompsonView image in fullscreenImelda Staunton … ‘Having my dog in the show was fantastic because she liked everything I did.’Photograph: Nick ThompsonFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterviewImelda Staunton: ‘Umbridge’s giggle needed to be short and sharp. So I just did a boom, boom’As told toRich PelleyThe actor answers your questions on working with her dog, becoming a dame, Harry Potter, and making televisual history in The Singing DetectiveThu 13 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou andBill Nighywere comrades inPride, but play estranged spouses in & Sons. Was it more fun marching alongside him or giving him a piece of your mind?MrSOBaldrickIt’s fun doing anything with Bill Nighy!View image in fullscreenStaunton and Bill Nighy in & Sons.Photograph: Icon Film DistributionI once saw you atRHS Garden Wisley. Are you a keen gardener? What’s your favourite plant?HeyJudithBYes, I am a gardener. We love doing the garden. My favourite plant – this week – is the rose Munstead Wood, which has an incredible scent, and a deep, dark raspberry colour. It’s a rose we might be in danger of losing because of climate change. Roses need water, so I think we’re going to have to change our planting.View image in fullscreenWith her husband, Jim Carter, at the RHS Hampton Court flower show in 2022.Photograph: Karl Black/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.How’s your garden coping in the heatwave?irenehandalIt looks like Africa. We’re obeying the hosepipe ban, getting our steps in, and our weight work with watering cans, hour upon hour. Considering we live on a tiny island, you’d think they could just desalinate seawater for farmers, or for us to use on plants or gardens or whatever. However! Next question …You were in the year above me atLa Sainte Union Catholic School in Highgate,north London. I remember a girl with an amazing voice singingWouldn’t It Be Loverly as Eliza Doolittle in My Fair Lady, and I’ve always wondered: was it you?Anne210No, I don’t think it was me. But I did sing Blue Suede Shoes with my mate Angela Robinson – who I still know – with a guitar and a recorder. You can only imagine what that was like. However, we felt like pop stars, and we won the music festival, although there was no prize – apart from the kudos.View image in fullscreenStaunton as Mrs Kitty Warren with her daughter Bessie Carter as Vivie Warren in Mrs Warren’s Profession.Photograph: Johan PerssonWho was easiest to work with: your husband,Jim Carter, in Guys and Dolls; your daughter,Bessie, in Mrs Warren’s Profession; or yourdog, Molly, who played Chowsie in Gypsy at Chichester Festival theatrein2014?TopTrampThe dog, obviously. Because she was the easiest to carry. I carried the dog on stage. Try doing that with Jim Carter – not going to happen. And my daughter, who’s 5ft 9in, that’s not going to happen either. Having my dog in the show was fantastic because she liked everything I did, so that was quite useful. Did Molly have to audition? No, she knew someone in the show.My daughters know you first as the voice of their favourite books:Zog,The Smeds and the Smoosetc. Did all that stage and film discipline mean ittook only one or two takes in the booth?GH_ParisI think it was more to do with having done quite a lot of radio. I did a lot of Radio 4 plays in the early 80s, where all you’ve got is your voice. The microphone becomes the other character. That really laid the groundwork for all of the animation voices I’ve done in films and children’s books, including Julia Donaldson’s books. I love doing that because you can’t escape. You’ve only got the voice. It’s got to be so contained and the discipline comes from that, I think.Did gettingmade a dame in 2024feel like a bit of a demotion after playing the Queen?Dr_J_A_ZoidbergI’m still trying to cope with it.View image in fullscreenAs Dolores Umbridge in Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyHow did you come up with that chilling giggle forDolores Umbridge? Was your menacing performance based on any of your real teachers?Shannon_78676andDrMTobogganThankfully, it wasn’t based on any real-life teachers. I didn’t want it to be a silly giggle. I wanted it to be quite hard, but with a very high tone. I remember thinking I didn’t want it to take too long, so the laugh needed to be short and sharp. So I just did a boom, boom – two notes that didn’t take up too much time.What was it like working with the late, greatPete Postlethwaite, as he gradually turned into a rat in the2000 comedy Rat?maryfinnView image in fullscreenPete Postlewaite … ‘It was so good of him to come out of the fridge stark naked.’Photograph: Karen Robinson/The ObserverWell, the thing is – we never saw him turn into a rat. We saw him turn back into a human. Pete only did about three days on that film. It was so good of him to come over to Dublin and come out of the fridge stark naked. I don’t know why he came out of the fridge, but it was a pretty extraordinary effect. But that was him. Of course, I’d worked with Pete back in 1986 – we did a swashbuckling romp at the Royal Shakespeare Company, The Fair Maid of the West, with Sean Bean and Simon Russell Beale. Pete Postlethwaite was a genius. End of. Timing, heart and soul. I mean, he was just a genius, so it was a real joy that he came over and did three days on this mad little film.Which is harder on stage: delivering a page-long speech, or sitting silently with too much time to think about your next line?nivlek47Look, it’s always heaven when it’s someone else doing the work. It’s funny – when you start out in your career, you want all the big speeches. As it goes on, you start to think: “Oh, I’ve done that. Can someone else have a go?” So, at the moment, it’s quite nice. I loved doing George Bernard Shaw’s Mrs Warren’s Profession with my daughter last year, which has a lot of words. I was so relieved when it was her turn. I thought: “Off you go, you do it now.”When you were making The Singing Detective, did you feel you were making something extraordinary that would be remembered as part of televisual history?CaptainLibAbsolutely. You knew it was something completely off the wall, so unlike anything we’d ever seen on television before. I still remember the read-through: sitting in that room with Dennis Potter and the rest of the cast, not really knowing how we were going to put what was on the page on screen. That was Jon Amiel’s job as director, and Michael Gambon was sublime. Dennis Potter’s writing made me feel so inadequate. I thought: “How could I possibly be in this? How can I help bring this to life?” It was extraordinary. I’m sure Jon would agree it was one of his greatest pieces of work.View image in fullscreenAs Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown.Photograph: Alex Bailey/APYour parents came from County Mayo. Were you screaming at the TV whenMayo beat Kerryto win their firstGAA All-Ireland Senior FootballChampionshipin 75 years this July?ExileCuChulainnStrangely, in May this year, I was in Kerry for four weeks doing a film. I’d never been to that part of Kerry. It’s absolutely stunning. The people, the place, the scenery – everything was stunning. So my heart was completely in Kerry. Then a couple of months later, the football happened, so I’m afraid I was conflicted.You move between the West End and film/TV constantly. What does one give you that the other doesn’t?ethd58One is more knackering.I once saw you at RHS Chelsea opening a bottle of champagne with a sabre! Is this how you open it at home?dalyFoleyAlways.& Sons is in UK cinemas from 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewImelda StauntonBill NighyHarry PotterTelevisionScience fiction and fantasy filmsFilm adaptationsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I ran away to Paris to be a writer and ended up begging’: Bill Nighy on dashed dreams, golf emojis and playing a cranky novelist | Movies | The Guardian
description: As his new film & Sons hits the screen, the actor turned podcast agony uncle relives his ‘cliched’ ambitions, deplores working lunches – and yearns to do the splits like Prince
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: As his new film & Sons hits the screen, the actor turned podcast agony uncle relives his ‘cliched’ ambitions, deplores working lunches – and yearns to do the splits like Prince
Content: ‘I don’t do smiley emojis’ … Bill Nighy.Photograph: Charlie GrayView image in fullscreen‘I don’t do smiley emojis’ … Bill Nighy.Photograph: Charlie GrayMoviesInterview‘I ran away to Paris to be a writer and ended up begging’: Bill Nighy on dashed dreams, golf emojis and playing a cranky novelistRyan GilbeyAs his new film & Sons hits the screen, the actor turned podcast agony uncle relives his ‘cliched’ ambitions, deplores working lunches – and yearns to do the splits like PrinceThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 04.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdying patriarch summons his brood for a dramatic announcement. It may not be the most original starting point for a movie, but & Sons adds an eccentric twist – one that it would be unfair to reveal here but which nudges the material into the realm of science fiction. The father in question is a revered novelist who is as reclusive as JD Salinger and as whiskery and dishevelled as Catweazle. Dormant for decades, the fictional AN Dyer is first glimpsed in a horizontal position on the sofa, refusing to come to the telephone: “I don’t do phonecalls,” he grumbles.That is patently not true of the actor who plays him. “I spend a lot of time on the phone,”Bill Nighysays breezily. He is speaking to me from north-west London, where he has been nosing around bookshops. “I’m also an enthusiastic texter. I was always very quick on the old Nokia. Quite proud of myself, I was.” Where does he stand on emojis? “I used to be philosophically opposed. Most of them are a bit naff.” He then proceeds to list the exceptions. “I like the flamingo and the purple dahlia. I like the leaping shark. Sometimes I combine it with the leaping dolphin. Very occasionally, I like the golfer in mid-swing if I’m congratulating someone. I don’t do smiley faces.”double quotation markWhat one thing would make me turn down an acting job? TogasCommunicating over Zoom is a no-go, hence our phone conversation today. “It got to the point where every time I had a Zoom call, it made me unhappy. I’m old enough to be able to say, ‘Can I retire from Zoom?’” At 76, he has ruled out other undesirable experiences. “Food where you talk about work. That’s one. Particularly lunch. You have to sit there for so long and it just confuses the issue. Working lunches are absolutely out of the question now.” He has never been much of a partygoer either, and used to get what he calls “a thrill, or a kind of anti-thrill” from putting invitations, especially highly prized ones, straight in the bin. When I ask if there is any one thing that is likely to make him turn down an acting job, his answer is instant and unequivocal: “Togas.”View image in fullscreen‘No fireworks, no reaching for prizes’ … Imelda Staunton and Bill Nighy in & Sons.Photograph: Icon Film DistributionNo such garments in & Sons, which pits Nighy as Dyer against his vexed older offspring (played by Johnny Flynn and George MacKay) and the ex-wife (Imelda Staunton) who has never forgiven him for siring a son (Hamnet’s Noah Jupe) by another woman. The old man has been an abrasive and emotionally absent parent, but appears to believe his literary talent excuses that. Nighy has no time for such guff. “It’s like when footballers behave badly on the pitch and people say, ‘Temperament is part of his genius.’ Give me a break. That’s anathema to me. I don’t believe it in the least.”Dyer claims his goal as a father was to “do no harm”. Nighy himself has a daughter – the actor-director Mary Nighy – by his ex-partner, the actor Diana Quick, whom he was with for 27 years until 2008. Did he start out with a parenting philosophy? “Blimey, Ryan. It’s a long time ago.” Indeed: he has two grandchildren now. “But no. Not really. You make it up as you go along. You make mistakes, then correct them, and hopefully you arrive at something that works. My parents were not oppressive or unkind, and I didn’t want to be either.”Unkindness is fully part of Dyer’s repertoire in & Sons, along with rage and misanthropy – none of them qualities that Nighy is typically asked to play. “I’m not thought of in those terms,” he agrees. “Though of course, half my work is not in living memory. You get to the stage where everyone who watched it is dead.”View image in fullscreen‘I’ll never be Steve McQueen’ … Nighy as Davy Jones in Pirates Of The Caribbean: At World’s End.Photograph: Disney/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockStrangers still commend him on his performance as the unvarnished ex-rocker Billy Mack, who blithely admits that his new Christmas single is a “festering turd”, in Richard Curtis’s 2003 romcom Love Actually. Nighy has made his share of blockbusters, including two voyages with the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise, where he was hidden behind a beard of writhing, computer-generated tentacles. But it is the gentler figures, endearingly flawed, for which he is truly cherished, whether bracingly frank like Billy or sweetly diffident: the terminally ill, buttoned-up bureaucrat in Living, which earned the actor his only Oscar nomination to date; the husband who chickens out of cheating on his wife in Lawless Heart; or the Scrabble enthusiast searching for his missing son in Sometimes Always Never.Don’t count him out as a sex symbol either. One early success was The Men’s Room, the raunchy 1991 BBC series in which his explicit scenes as a libidinous academic earned the censure of the Broadcasting Standards Council. After playing Nighy’s wife in Notes on a Scandal, Cate Blanchett asked a journalist: “What thinking western woman do you know who wouldn’t want to embrace him?”If he is typecast today, it doesn’t faze him. “Maybe there are people out there who like it when I do the things I always do. Just like I always want Steve McQueen to do what he does.” What has Nighy learned from the minimalist star of The Great Escape? “That I’ll never be Steve McQueen,” he sighs. “You need a lot of confidence to do what he did. No fireworks, no reaching for prizes. It’s a kind of reckless restraint.” Prince is another hero. “Everything Prince did was attractive. Anyone who can do the splits and come back up on the backbeat … well, I’ll follow them anywhere.”It was writers who were the object of his youthful idolatry: Hemingway, Fitzgerald. There is a special poignancy, then, in seeing Nighy as a novelist in & Sons, since that is what he wanted to be for many years. Blame Mr Weir, the English teacher at his Catholic grammar school. “He told me, ‘You might want to try your hand at the novel.’ I must have been 14. I’m not claiming this as an early sign of my neglected genius. But it was like a bomb going off in my head.”View image in fullscreenOscar-nominated buttoned-up bureaucrat … Nighy in Living, 2022.Photograph: Album/AlamyAt 15, he got a job on The Field, the hunting and fishing magazine. What were his responsibilities? “I changed the roller towel in the ladies’ room. All the girls from the typing pool used to come in. Not because of my animal magnetism, I hasten to add, but because they knew they could make me blush. Those roller towels are quite tricky. I’d bugger it up and they’d start laughing.”Then there was the day he landed in trouble with the boss. “I’m from a small town – Caterham in Surrey – and I used to become very excited if I saw a Roller or a Bentley in the street. I got pulled up in front of the CEO because he’d driven past me and I’d started jumping up and down and waving. He said, ‘That’s not what I expect from an employee.’”Nighy’s next stop was Paris. “I am a walking, talking cliche,” he says. “I ran away to be a writer. Like a million others, I went straight to [the bookshop] Shakespeare & Company and hung about thinking I’d write killer sentences and find a girlfriend. Neither of which happened. I ended up begging on the Trocadéro.” He didn’t relinquish his literary dreams so much as let them wilt. “Someone suggested I go to drama school, and that became what I did. I thought I’d get around to writing eventually. I’m still thinking it. I’m just very good at procrastination.”He may not have a novel in the works but a kind of verbal memoir is unspooling, 25 minutes at a time, in the form of his podcast,Ill-Advised, in which he serves as a soothing agony uncle, meanderingly answering listeners’ queries about everything from fashion to avoiding social faux pas. Off-the-cuff being his preferred mode, he never sees the questions before recording. “I ramble on the spot but I find that I’ve thought about whatever the subject might be. I’ve already thought about trousers, for instance, because I’m a bit of a fetishist about lounge suits and shirt collars.”Ill-Advised, which is about to launch its third series, has more than 300,000 monthly listeners and was named 2026 Podcast of the Year by the Broadcasting Press Guild. That doesn’t stop Nighy being comically apologetic about it. “I triednotto have a podcast,” he assures me, giving the impression, as he usually does, that he has secured his tremendous career and the esteem of audiences, critics and contemporaries simply by the happy accident of stepping off the lift at the wrong floor. Perhaps he won’t ever be mistaken for Steve McQueen. His compliments about that actor, though, could plainly be applied to him, too. No fireworks, no reaching for prizes. A master of reckless restraint.& Sons is in cinemas from 21 August. The third series of Ill-Advised begins on 3 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmBill NighyPodcastsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: 116 Grams: A Play to Lose Weight review – a shocking satire of body policing | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Letícia Rodrigues takes on the titular challenge in this show about shame, rage and how female bodies are surveilled
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Letícia Rodrigues takes on the titular challenge in this show about shame, rage and how female bodies are surveilled
Content: Furious … Letícia Rodrigues in 116 Grams: A Play to Lose WeightView image in fullscreenFurious … Letícia Rodrigues in 116 Grams: A Play to Lose WeightEdinburgh festival 2026Review116 Grams: A Play to Lose Weight review – a shocking satire of body policingZoo Southside, EdinburghLetícia Rodrigues takes on the titular challenge in this show about shame, rage and how female bodies are surveilledArifa AkbarThu 13 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsmiling woman steps on to the weighing scales in front of the stage. She is glamorous with bobbed blond hair, gleaming nails and a trendy red trouser suit. She is exactly 84kg, she states. It is an opening gesture reminiscent of an old-school diet club like the one her mother first took her to at the age of eight.Letícia Rodrigues’s show is autobiographical, albeit dramatised through a character called Gorda who, like her, is Brazilian and has been deemed overweight for most of her life. So she is planning to lose the fat in each of her shows. The weigh-in will be followed by a weigh-out at the end of the hour. The goal is to be 116 grams thinner and so the show is also a training session, she says.She then whips off clothes, jogging, dancing, jumping up and down to the beat of Britney Spears whom Rodrigues wanted to look like as a girl, partly because she desired a career in song and dance, too.Directed by João Pedro Ribeiro and Rodrigues, this is a show that glints with satire and absurdism but is also ruled by dark forces: shame, trauma and rage at a world that has disallowed a girl to grow up loving her body. Rodrigues apparently wrote it after failed castings in Brazil due to body size. She is not body positive, she declares, as she sets about her maelstrom of exercise, which ranges from boxing with a plastic swan to juddering, expressive movement. For that she would have to love her body – and “I hate living in here”.Rodrigues’s show is hard to watch at times but it is also essential in an age when society and the media surveil female body-shape. Performed in Portuguese with English surtitles, the production is part of theSão Paulo Showcaseand chimes with other extreme-sport shows at the fringe this year, except it is clear that this one is ironic, and truly volcanic. It ends with a ballet sequence that is poignantly, sadly, beautiful. This does not seem like a reclamation of the body but a commentary on the kind of ones we see on stage – and who is deemed inappropriate to be there.As Far As We Know review – strange solo goes full pelt down the mean streetsRead moreThe songs of Spears are spliced with Swan Lake, and the show becomes less narrative and more experimental, which renders it abstract but also deepens its emotional power. Rodrigues performs it mostly naked: she is presenting the body that society wants shrunken or erased.Brave, incendiary and full of genuine shocks, this is exactly what a fringe show should be.At Zoo Southside, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreHealthDiets and dietingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: My Brilliant Career review – a joyous heroine lights up this rare and beautiful period drama | Television | The Guardian
description: Phillipa Northeast is brilliant as a young woman rebelling against society’s expectations in 1890s Australia. It is witty, intelligent and absolutely glorious to watch
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Phillipa Northeast is brilliant as a young woman rebelling against society’s expectations in 1890s Australia. It is witty, intelligent and absolutely glorious to watch
Content: Irrepressibly charming … Philippa Northeast, right, and Genevieve O’Reilly in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Ian Routledge/NetflixView image in fullscreenIrrepressibly charming … Philippa Northeast, right, and Genevieve O’Reilly in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Ian Routledge/NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewMy Brilliant Career review – a joyous heroine lights up this rare and beautiful period dramaPhillipa Northeast is brilliant as a young woman rebelling against society’s expectations in 1890s Australia. It is witty, intelligent and absolutely glorious to watchLucy ManganThu 13 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m hot headed, with a snub nose, and that’s why I prefer a direct gaze.”So speaks Sybylla, the charmingly irrepressible and irrepressibly charming heroine of My Brilliant Career, played utterly convincingly and with vim, vigour and joy by Philippa Northeast in the new adaptation of Miles Franklin’s 1901 Australian classic of the same name. Creator Liz Doran must have wept with happiness when they found an actor capable of bringing so much to an already glorious script – and who embodies the joie de vivre upon which so much of the plot, as everyone she meets becomes part of her orbit, depends.Sybylla is one of too many children for her hardworking mother and debt-ridden, irresponsible father to support. So she is sent from their impoverished farm in Possum Gully to stay with her maternal grandmother (Anna Chancellor), the aptly named Mrs Bossier. She is a successful horse breeder who lives in widowed splendour, with her other daughter Helen (Genevieve O’Reilly) miles away in a grand mansion. She has plenty of time on her hands to shape Sybylla into a proper model of womanhood and get her married off to a rich man who can take care of her and the rest of her family.Sybylla does not take kindly to the revelation of Granny’s plans. “I’m being gussied up! … Slowly turned on a spit of propriety!” she writes in horror to her sister Gertie back home. Sybylla had thought she was going to be at Caddagat House, see the wider world and fuel her ambition to become a writer. Knowing that husbands do not help this mission, she practises a cheerful kind of resistance against Mrs B while throwing herself into the rest of her new life. She makes friends with Nell (Sherry-Lee Watson), the talented horse trainer from an Indigenous family who dreams of becoming Caddagat’s foreman despite the handicap, in 1890s rural Australia, of both her background and her sex.Sybylla makes frenemies (but! He’s extremely attractive) with an English guest at the house, Frank (Jake Dunn), and becomes a mentee of sorts to their high society neighbour, the glamorously eccentric Augusta (Kate Mulvany, having a wild time). Augusta’s nephew Harry (Christopher Chung) is, like Frank, like all of us, drawn to this new, iconoclastic free spirit who has appeared in their midst – but the limits to Augusta’s bohemianism and other factors mean he is not as free in his turn as he might be to choose a wife.The Sybylla-Frank-Harry love triangle evolves slowly and convincingly as the three young people make their mistakes, are overheard saying things to each other that they shouldn’t and generally explore the different kinds of attraction that different people offer each other. But, refreshingly, it doesn’t become the dominant tale. Sybylla’s writing ambitions remain important, with Augusta urging her to try to get stories published in magazines as an alternative way of supporting herself and her family that would also allow her to retain her independence. The ramifications of her father’s incompetence increase. Bailiffs gradually strip the home of its few valuables and eventually another daughter must be sacrificed – this time to become a governess/maid of all work to a local family – to help manage his debts. The pressure on Sybylla to marry, and marry well, mounts as her friendships with Harry and Frank deepen in different ways. It is a rare and beautiful thing to watch people not flirt but connect by degrees.Mixed in with these parts most faithful to the novel are more modern elements. A male homosexual relationship, and the terrible fear and misery it brings in a time and place that finds it completely unacceptable, is movingly shown. Nell and her family – especially her sister’s secret relationship with the (white) neighbourhood policeman – demonstrate the forces of racism and colonialism at work. And sexism, if not outright misogyny, is in the air everyone breathes. From the need to get married for security (nicely thrown into relief by the freedom enjoyed by the various widows among the local folk), to Aunt Helen running the household and business for years only to be passed over without a word when it is deemed time for her brother to inherit everything, to Nell’s talents always being assumed to be simply the result of what her father taught her, no woman can escape its effects.Doran’s creation retains all the book’s sense of defiance but adds a welcome soupcon of more optimism too. It crackles with intelligence and wit, gives all of its characters room to breathe (although it may ultimately be Sybylla’s show, everyone has something meaningful to do and contribute, and the cast is all-round magnificent) and, without ever becoming superficial, never loses its lightness of touch. A joy. A brilliant, brilliant joy.My Brilliant Career is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon review – an engrossing story, if you can stomach it | Television | The Guardian
description: This documentary follows the shocking case of Neil Hopper, a top surgeon who had his own legs removed due to a fetish.
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: This documentary follows the shocking case of Neil Hopper, a top surgeon who had his own legs removed due to a fetish.
Content: Neil Hopper, the vascular surgeon, who faked sepsis and had both legs amputated.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenNeil Hopper, the vascular surgeon, who faked sepsis and had both legs amputated.Photograph: BBCTV reviewTelevisionReviewAn Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon review – an engrossing story, if you can stomach itThis documentary follows the shocking case of Neil Hopper, a top surgeon who had his own legs removed due to a fetish.Jack SealeThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo fetish or obsession is unique, and the internet can always connect you with others whose minds work the same way. It’s one of the great blessings and curses of the digital age, and central to An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon, a two-part documentary on which the “contains material some viewers may find disturbing” disclaimer is no exaggeration.We begin at the Royal Cornwall hospital, known locally as Treliske, in Truro, Cornwall. It used to have a man on its staff who was a minor medical superstar: Neil Hopper, a vascular surgeon, was well known for his clinical expertise and comforting bedside manner, particularly when advising on and performing amputations. He acquired full hero status in 2019, when he was diagnosed with sepsis and had both legs amputated below the knee but miraculously returned to work within six months, astonishing physiotherapists and other medical professionals with how well he adapted to disability.Documentary crews shadowed Hopper at work; he was welcomed on to the BBC Breakfast sofa to tell presenter Naga Munchetty his inspiring tale. Patients facing amputation were desperate for a consultation. Life without legs almost seemed like an improvement for Hopper, not least because a £466,653 insurance payout got him a new car, high-grade prosthetic limbs and an accessible extension on his home.‘I felt sick that he was near my mum’: a top amputation surgeon had his own legs removed due to a fetish. Were his patients safe?Read moreHaving set all that up, the programme switches to London for the lurchingly horrific saga of Marius Gustavson. Before beingimprisoned for life in 2024on multiple counts of grievous bodily harm with intent, Gustavson made a very good living from running an illicit website called the Eunuch Maker, which sold its users videos of … well, of what the name of the site implies. Men volunteered – although some seemed to have been carefully groomed by Gustavson, and none could legally consent to what happened next in any case – to attend Gustavson’s basement flat, where they were filmed undergoing amateur medical procedures in a non-sterile environment. Many were taken away by ambulance, having sustained irreversible injury. The more gruesome the content, the more the torture-porn addicts in the Eunuch Maker community – which had more than 20,000 members – enjoyed it. A good few of the butchered men were fulfilling a long-held desire to lose a part of their own body. Some performed the procedure themselves.Hopper was one of the Eunuch Maker viewers, which is partly why he is also in prison, having committed the offence of possessing extreme pornography. We see some of the incriminating messages Hopper exchanged with Gustavson, where his polite articulacy and medical idioms – “penectomy” is the term he used for what was done in videos he watched “thousands of times” – clang against the horror of what he is discussing.That Hopper had a Eunuch Maker login doesn’t count as a revelation since it’s the obvious explanation for being in the same documentary as Gustavson. The other crime Hopper was found guilty of last year constitutes the twist in the narrative, which arrives at the halfway point and is fairly guessable in a “No … nooooo, surely not. NO!” sort of way, although the first episode rather mischievously misleads viewers in order to conceal it.From there we have an exploration of body integrity identity disorder, a rare condition in which the patient rejects a body part in much the same way someone with gender dysphoria has an insistent feeling that their assigned gender is incorrect. That warrants sympathy rather than revulsion, but then we face the awful possibility of Hopper’s professional decisions having been compromised. The latter suspicion has, it is a great relief to hear, been allayed by reviews of his work that found no evidence of malpractice.It is quite the story – equally repellent and engrossing – but how should it be told? Any documentary like this has to earn the right to demand an hour and a half of your time when it would take 10 minutes to read an article about the case. Here, it’s not clear that television wins. The two main characters are unavailable because they are in prison, although Hopper’s TV appearances and social media content, filmed before his arrest, sharpen the picture of the gentle, self-effacing man colleagues and patients thought they knew. One of Gustavson’s victims speaks compellingly, but “Michael” inevitably has his face and voice disguised. An awful lot of the details are ably filled in by veteran local news reporter Olivier Vergnault, who is in it so much he ought to invoice the producers for a presenter’s fee instead of a contributor’s.This perfectly well-made programme sets it all out, but if it feels like too much time to invest in such strong ick, you could always search for Hopper and Gustavson online instead. You can find anything there, as this show proves so grimly.An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon is on Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryFactual TVCrimePornographyNHSreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Billion-streamers, Beyoncé and heart-bruising beauty: Frank Ocean’s 20 best songs – ranked!  | Frank Ocean | The Guardian
description: It’s a decade since the Los Angeles musician released the seminal album Blonde. To lessen the pain of his hiatus, we count down the best of an artist who redefined R&B
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: It’s a decade since the Los Angeles musician released the seminal album Blonde. To lessen the pain of his hiatus, we count down the best of an artist who redefined R&B
Content: Eclectic and inventive … Frank Ocean.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenEclectic and inventive … Frank Ocean.Photograph: Publicity imageRankedFrank OceanBillion-streamers, Beyoncé and heart-bruising beauty: Frank Ocean’s 20 best songs – ranked!It’s a decade since the Los Angeles musician released the seminal album Blonde. To lessen the pain of his hiatus, we count down the best of an artist who redefined R&BAlexis PetridisThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Acura Integurl (2011)Frank Ocean’s pre-fame demos are hard to find – there’s a fan-made, 64-track compilation called The Lonny Breaux Collection floating around – but worth checking out, as evinced by this brief but potent piano ballad. Sweet but heartsore, it packs an emotional punch; it would have been a highlight of the mixtapeNostalgia, Ultra, had it made the cut.19. Higgs (2016)The stark penultimate track onOcean’s “visual album” Endless– just vocals and gently fingerpicked acoustic guitar – takes its name from the invisible energy of the Higgs field, which the lyrics seem to equate with love. It presents the emotion as mysterious and fleeting; Ocean’s voice is racked, the melody haunting.18. Dear April (2020)One of a string of singles Ocean put out between 2017 and 2020 – his last releases to date, although he obliquely mentioned a new album duringhis chaotic Coachella appearance in 2023. Dear April was billed as acoustic, but it’s built around jazzy electric guitar and synth washes – understated, but truly beautiful.17. American Wedding (2011)Several tracks on Nostalgia, Ultra featured Ocean singing over other people’s music, but American Wedding – based on the Eagles’ Hotel California – prompted legal action. It’s understandably a fan favourite: he may nick the tune, but Ocean replaces the original’s coked-out ennui with anguish that snags against the slickly familiar backing.View image in fullscreenPlaying Coachella in Indio, California, 2012.Photograph: C Flanigan/FilmMagic16. Slide on Me (2016)The visual aspect of Endless – in which Ocean assembled a flight of stairs – may have been wilfully boring, but the music that accompanied it boasted tension between its hazy, dreamlike quality and its raw, mixtape-like roughness. This is audible to spectacular effect on Slide on Me’s blend of bumping R&B, lo-fi ambience and vocals that sit somewhere between nonchalant and pained.15. Cayendo (2020)Another of Ocean’s one-off single releases, the bilingual Cayendo fitted its moment perfectly. Released at the height of the Covid pandemic, it sounded as if it had been recorded by someone locked in their bedroom. Its muffled, grumbling guitar and vocal – shifting from deep and effect-smothered into anguished and emotive – captured a mood of troubled introspection.14. Nikes (2016)The first taste of Ocean’s second album, Blonde, threw listeners a curveball – a spare, crestfallen song that referencesthe murder of Trayvon Martin, over half of which is sung by Ocean with his voice sped up to the point where it sounds nasal and cartoonish. Inexplicably, it works, musically and as a statement of leftfield intent.Listen to Biking.13. Biking (2017)Take your pick from either version of Biking. The A-side pulls Jay-Z andTyler, the Creatorinto Ocean’s strange sound-world – Jay-Z sounds as if he is rapping after being locked in a cupboard. The “solo” version lops off the lo-fi intro and features Ocean’s urgent vocal over an unhurried beat and languidly strummed acoustic guitar.12. Rushes (2016)Rushes seems to reflect on a relationship gone wrong: “First I was rushing for a wait / This time I’m waiting for a rush.” It makes fantastic use of Ocean’s chief vocal foil on Endless, Jazmine Sullivan, burying her powerful voice in the mix so it functions like another instrument, adding suitably heady uplift to the chorus.11. Bad Religion (2012)Bad Religion is effectively the sound of Ocean coming out, tormented by his love for another man and his closeted status. It would have been a bold move whatever it sounded like, but it’s also a fantastic song, deploying the dramatic sound of a church organ and delaying the arrival of the beat until its immense climax.10. White Ferrari (2016)White Ferrari is far from the usual driving anthem; rather, it evokes someone lost in thoughts and memories as they motor along. It’s daring – there is no chorus, the arrangement keeps changing – and beautifully done, from the fleeting interpolation of the Beatles’ Here There and Everywhere toJustin Vernon’s heart-stopping guest vocal.View image in fullscreenAt Bonnaroo festival in Manchester, Tennessee, 2014.Photograph: Josh Brasted/WireImage9. Pink Matter (2012)Should you require evidence of how different Ocean was, consider Pink Matter, a complex, thoughtful rumination on the female anatomy – presented as a dialogue with a sensei – that’s about as far from your standard male R&B star’s approach to the subject as you could get. Plus: a fantastic guest verse fromAndré 3000.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion8. Nights (2016)One offourbillion-streaming tracks from Blonde, Nights’ exploration of a mind working overtime in the small hours – picking through childhood memories, the pressures of fame, failing relationships – sounds amazing. It warps and changes with each passing thought: clanging alt-rock guitar; eerie synth ambience; heavy-metal arpeggios; warm, beat-forward R&B.Queer sounds: our writers on their favourite LGBTQ+ songsRead more7. Lost (2012)The topic of drug use hangs over Channel Orange (see also: Crack Rock). On Lost, Ocean deploys one of his sweetest, poppiest melodies to depict the relationship between two co-dependent dealers. Despite the narrator’s promise of a better life, it isn’t clear who is dragging whom further into coked-out oblivion.6. Ivy (2016)Partly inspired by the Strokes – you can hear their influence in the muted guitar chug that underpins the track – Ivy splits the difference between indie rock and R&B ballad so skilfully that it’s impossible to categorise as either. The lyrics deal with memories and regrets; the closing scream isn’t so much cathartic as chilling.5. Self Control (2016)More relationship drama – has a relationshipevergone smoothly in an Ocean song? – originally intended to be sung as a duet; the female voice was eventually replaced by Ocean’s own, sped up. A wonderfully subtle string arrangement and a chorus of multitracked backing vocals amp up the infectious mood of sadness mixed with resignation.View image in fullscreenOn stage at Parklife festival in Manchester, England, 2017.Photograph: Visionhaus/Corbis/Getty Images4. Chanel (2017)The best of Ocean’s string of one-off singles, Chanel delves straight into the topic of sexual fluidity and notions of masculinity: “My guy pretty like a girl / And he got fight stories to tell.” The production is stripped back – there are moments when the music is barely there – focusing attention on Ocean’s gripping vocal.3. Pink + White (2016)An all-star cast – production by Pharrell, a Jon Brion string arrangement, Beyoncé on backing vocals – but it’s all about the song nevertheless. The haunting earworm of the piano figure, the 60s soul mood, the ache in Ocean’s voice as he sings “you showed me love”: Pink + White makes misery sound worth wallowing in.Frank Ocean at Coachella review – a rollercoaster ending in disappointmentRead more2. Novacane (2011)Amid the delightfully scrappy eclecticism of Nostalgia, Ultra is Ocean’s first classic. The brilliantly original storytelling – a dental student who dabbles in pornography and gets high on local anaesthetic – blends darkness and disquiet with flashes of wit, a fabulous, pulsing, slowly building production and a bright, pop-facing melody. It’s got the lot.1. Pyramids (2012)As statements of intent go, the first single from Channel Orange takes some beating. It’s nearly 10 shapeshifting minutes long, initially driven by a house rhythm and a riff that recalls Capella’s 90s Eurodance anthem U Got 2 Know. It changes completely midway through, first to an ambient interlude, then to spaced-out R&B, before concluding with a burst of rock guitar. (It also boasts an incomprehensible narrative about ancient Egypt and strippers.) Compelling and compulsive, it underlined that, rather than being an upstart kid fromthe Odd Future stable, Ocean was an artist whose musical ambition would have impressed his idol, Prince.Listen to the playlist. Note: five of the tracks in this article are not available to stream onSpotifyExplore more on these topicsFrank OceanRankedR&Bbest ofShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea Wolfe: The Dark review – existential reflection goes from whisper to gothic scream | Music | The Guardian
description: The genre-blending Californian artist casts off past toxic influences with a powerful set of tender, brooding and emotionally charged songs that wouldn’t feel out of place as festival anthems
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: The genre-blending Californian artist casts off past toxic influences with a powerful set of tender, brooding and emotionally charged songs that wouldn’t feel out of place as festival anthems
Content: ‘It’s not party music’ … Chelsea Wolfe.Photograph: Magdalena WosinskaView image in fullscreen‘It’s not party music’ … Chelsea Wolfe.Photograph: Magdalena WosinskaMusicReviewChelsea Wolfe: The Dark review – existential reflection goes from whisper to gothic scream(Loma Vista)The genre-blending Californian artist casts off past toxic influences with a powerful set of tender, brooding and emotionally charged songs that wouldn’t feel out of place as festival anthemsDave SimpsonThu 13 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Chelsea Wolfe wasinterviewed by the Guardian in 2015about her fourth album, Abyss, she revealed that her music had been informed by the bouts of sleep paralysis she’d suffered from since childhood. The condition – a transitional state between being awake and asleep – affects sufferers in different ways. Some wake up feeling paralysed, others see ghosts or demonic figures. For the California-born singer-songwriter, it meant “waking up, and you can move your body and your eyes are open, but there are figures and people from your dreams still present in your room”.View image in fullscreenChelsea Wolfe: The DarkNo surprise, then, that her music – a blend of drone, alt, folk, industrial and doom metal – had ended up so spookily unsettling. She appeared on album covers with pupil-less eyes, spoke in interviews about “following the path of witchcraft” and even covered Norwegian black metal act and convicted arsonist/murderer Burzum. She did have a sense of humour about it all, however, telling one interviewer, with a chuckle: “It’s not party music.” Since then, though, much has changed. Wolfe left Los Angeles for the mountains above the city – where she’s finally been able to enjoy a good night’s sleep. Sobriety since 2021 has also brought what she calls “a new clarity”. Both developments inform The Dark.The sublime opener Cold is again driven by lack of sleep, but for entirely different reasons as she taps into the insomnia that can result from a fracturing relationship. “Baby, when I’m next to you / Feels so cold / And it’s hard to sleep / And it’s hard to feel so alone,” she sings, dramatically ending up feeling as if she is “crying underwater / Screaming at the surface”. With its strummed folk beginning, brushed drums and layers of piano and acoustic guitars, the yearning gothic ballad is closer to, say, Annie Lennox than Ethel Cain and sets the scene for this much more accessible ninth album which channels her darker urges into something more universal.After 2024’s largely electronic, David Sitek-produced She Reaches Out to She Reaches Out to She, Wolfe felt as if she was continually returning to “a version of my old self”. So The Dark turns to Grammy-winning producer/co-writer Jennifer Decilveo, whose credits include Hozier and Miley Cyrus, and returns to a core of guitar, bass and drums (alongside longtime collaborator Ben Chisholm). Drone and doom metal has almost entirely made way for brooding bass lines, wailing guitars, dramatic dynamic shifts and subtle orchestrations. The dreamier, more gothic tracks recall Evanescence or, on Swallower, the Cure, while Wolfe’s haunting vocals literally span the spectrum from a whisper to a scream – or, on the driving, windswept Seethe, a blood-curdling howl. Her ethereal singing suggests, of all things, Cocteau Twins’ Elizabeth Fraser fronting the Sisters of Mercy.Chelsea Wolfe: The Dark (Live at Mono lake) – videoNow 42, the singer has talked about how The Dark has been driven by “letting go … being in my early 40s as a woman, growing older and wanting to be who I am now”. This process has involved letting go of old behaviours and toxic relationships as well as her old music, which has driven some emotionally powerful songs. In the beautifully sad I’m Not There, she tells someone: “It’s too late, we’re already strangers,” a sentiment which recalls Carole King’s It’s Too Late. In the slightly Lana Del Rey-ish Halo, she directly quotes Martha and the Vandellas – “Nowhere to run, nowhere to hide” – another unexpected reference point from an artist with Wolfe’s history.‘Techno in a monastery – are you ready?’ The Greek priest whose doom metal album is the year’s hippest recordRead moreWolfe subsequently disowned her more conventionally singer-songwriterly self-released 2006 debut Mistake In Parting as a “shitty breakup album”, but seems to be reacquainting with classic songcraft as well as allowing herself more warmth and introspection. The folky title track is a beautifully observed “love letter” to the comfort of the black (“Our love glows in darkness / In a world that feels so heartless”) which builds to a finale featuring Warpaint drummer Stella Mozgawa and former Nine Inch Nails bassist Justin Meldal-Johnsen.Death Is Not The End – not the Bob Dylan song – is a tender largely acoustic folk rumination on the afterlife. Wolfe gently whispers “I’ll see you again” as one might over a dearly departed’s coffin, before Nine Inch Nails guitarist Robin Finck lets fly with guttural, chilling noise. Dancer in the Sky is the closest Wolfe has come to an epic, anthemic love song, with an exquisite arrangement and a chorus made for people to sing along. In fact, a lot of these songs wouldn’t sound incongruous being performed before huge crowds holding phones or lighters in the air. Wolfe recently became the unlikely face of a perfume range (Ghosts, obviously) and is clearly edging towards to the mainstream, but after two decades at the culty coal face this powerful, mature collection should take her to a wider audience.This week Dave listened toShearwater and Laurie Anderson– You and Your DogThe Texans’ cascading clarinet, bass and cymbals make a beautiful backdrop for the art-pop legend’s moving reminisce about a beach walk and days long gone.The Dark is released on 21 August.
