title: Jordan Brookes: The Part of You That’s Always Screaming review – former fringe champ’s chewy croissant tale | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: This is a spiky, interrogative and surprisingly conventional set from an act who usually pushes standup to its limits
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: This is a spiky, interrogative and surprisingly conventional set from an act who usually pushes standup to its limits
Content: How are we affected by another’s gaze – or our own? …Jordan Brookes in The Part of You That's Always Screaming.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHow are we affected by another’s gaze – or our own? …Jordan Brookes in The Part of You That's Always Screaming.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewJordan Brookes: The Part of You That’s Always Screaming review – former fringe champ’s chewy croissant talePleasance Dome, EdinburghThis is a spiky, interrogative and surprisingly conventional set from an act who usually pushes standup to its limitsBrian LoganThu 13 Aug 2026 04.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 04.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can fall victim to your own high standards – and few comics have set higher standards than Jordan Brookes. A new show fromthe 2019 comedy award champis an event, at which half the fun is seeing how he’s monstered the form into some unforeseen new shape. If this year’s offering, The Part of You That’s Always Screaming, were delivered by any other comic, I’d be hailing it as one of the twistiest and deepest-thinking hours on the fringe. But it lacks Brookes’ usual ambition: its delivery is fairly conventional; things aren’t pushed as far as we expect.It’s all relative, mind you: this is still a set in which, at one unexpected moment, our comedian turns down the lights, turns up some disturbing industrial soundscape, and jerks threateningly across the stage. But then we act differently when we’re being watched – which is Brookes’ point here, in a show that worries intensely at the relationship between selfhood and being seen. It’s structured, deliciously, around an innocuous experience on a train, when Brookes snacking on a croissant becomes a performative act, awkwardly positioned as he is between the window and a window-gazing fellow passenger.Harriet Dyer: Easily Distra … review – how to sell a single shoe on eBay and other storiesRead moreHow are we affected by another’s gaze – or our own? Do you ever get tired of your own POV? What’s the worst thing cyber-hackers might see through your webcam? It’s always entertaining to trace the knotted thread of Brookes’ thinking, even as it spools away from the main subject, towards amusing standalone riffs on pickup artistry and (very droll, this) the idea of the super-strong mother who can lift a car to save her child.Really, I should be satisfied with the high quality of the comedy alone. But with Brookes, we’ve been trained to expect more, and I kept wondering when the opening routine, about the early film Train Pulling Into a Station, was going to get its stunt payoff, or what dramatic ending was in store for the croissant tale. These expectations were thwarted – but dial your expectations down merely to spiky and interrogative comedy, and they will be amply rewarded.AtPleasance Dome, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalJordan BrookesComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)FestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ham review – vegan take on Hamlet delivers meaty rebuke to carnivores | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Vengeance for a slaughtered pig is the starting point for a riotous parody that suggests the meat industry poses an existential threat to human survival
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Vengeance for a slaughtered pig is the starting point for a riotous parody that suggests the meat industry poses an existential threat to human survival
Content: Comeuppance for the sausage queen … Mary Higgins, left, and Ell Potter in Ham.Photograph: Jonny RuffView image in fullscreenComeuppance for the sausage queen … Mary Higgins, left, and Ell Potter in Ham.Photograph: Jonny RuffEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHam review – vegan take on Hamlet delivers meaty rebuke to carnivoresSummerhall, EdinburghVengeance for a slaughtered pig is the starting point for a riotous parody that suggests the meat industry poses an existential threat to human survivalKate WyverThu 13 Aug 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThat’s my next hotdog ruined. Shakespeare’s “too solid flesh” is squeezed into a sausage-shaped form in Mary Higgins and Ell Potter’s inventively guilt-trippy new show. Leaping wildly fromHamlet, this outrageous, confrontational performance-activism layers hooting comedy with world-ending dread as Mary (a vegan) attempts to persuade Potter (nicknamed “the sausage queen” by their dad) to change their meat-eating ways.Transposing Hamlet’s existential questions to the future survival of humanity via the meat industry’s impact on the planet, Higgins takes on the role of our stubborn, sauntering prince, seeking vengeance for the ghost of a poor, slaughtered, strangely seductive pig. Suave and silly, Potter is both ghost and Gertrude, the latter reading madness into the truth only her son is brave enough to face.Easy laughs are won through winking Shakespearean parody, but the further off-piste the show goes, the more Ham swerves what we already know and ignore, and jolts us into looking anew. Through naked dancing, a pet funeral, and a dom/sub relationship with a meat-eating member of the audience, this anarchic duo directs our avoidant gaze to our own impact on the planet. Though Higgins is on higher moral ground, Potter’s role is essential, with their effusive love of food stopping this from being purely haranguing – both for them and us – and twirling it into a genuine personal dilemma.Spin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundryRead moreThis isn’t about the murders of animals, Higgins says, but the suicide of the human race. (It’s also a bit about the murders of animals; they’re not afraid to show brutal, scarring images.) Inescapably a little preachy, the show is also riotously funny – until the very end when footage of recent forest fires blazes behind the performers. The clips start across the ocean and get closer: to Europe; the UK; Arthur’s Seat. It’s no longer a question of what might, or might not be.At Summerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Culture)TheatreFoodEdinburgh festivalFestivalsImmersive theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: As Far As We Know review – strange solo goes full pelt down the mean streets | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With increasing speed, Sam Ward tells the story of a woman who finds holes in her garden – but is it just a shaggy dog story?
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: With increasing speed, Sam Ward tells the story of a woman who finds holes in her garden – but is it just a shaggy dog story?
Content: Speed reader … Sam Ward in As Far As We Know.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenSpeed reader … Sam Ward in As Far As We Know.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAs Far As We Know review – strange solo goes full pelt down the mean streetsSummerhall, EdinburghWith increasing speed, Sam Ward tells the story of a woman who finds holes in her garden – but is it just a shaggy dog story?Mark FisherThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnd there is a man sitting at a desk, welcoming us to the theatre and opening a folder. And the folder contains a sheaf of paper that the man proceeds to read. And the more the man reads, the faster he goes. And the man hits such a speed we realise why he did not learn this script: it would be too prodigious a feat of memory.And as if to emphasise the pace, the man is soon accompanied by a percussive score byCarmel Smickersgill, which has a jazz freedom as well as a sense of urgency and is rather good. And as the story rattles out, so Han Sayles’s lighting design closes in on the man, who is the writer Sam Ward in this solo show by his companyYESYESNONOand he seems to be going faster still.And the story he tells is of a woman who discovers holes appearing in her garden and they are emitting a sound she cannot quite recognise. And as she tries to figure out the reason they are proliferating, she finds herself in a bank where there are next to no employees and even less money.Ten Ways to Die Happy review – gameshow invites you to don a robe and treasure timeRead moreAnd she is taken under the wing of a private detective straight out ofRaymond Chandlerwho only adds to her sense of disorientation, as do all the other strange events: the cave and the rooftop forest and the enigmatic messages telling her to look for the horizon.And as it plays out, you wonder whether this is a dreamlike odyssey with some insight to share – about what: uncertainty, alienation, the futile search for meaning? – or just a shaggy dog story that, for all the cool polish of its staging, goes around the houses for its own uncertain ends.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalFestivalsSummerhallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mrs Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library review – interrogating Hannah Arendt | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: An encounter in a police cell with a Nazi officer could have been the end of the political theorist, but Jenny Lyn Bader’s play has little feel for the dramatic
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: An encounter in a police cell with a Nazi officer could have been the end of the political theorist, but Jenny Lyn Bader’s play has little feel for the dramatic
Content: Playing it innocent … Brett Temple and Ella Kaille in Mrs Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library.Photograph: Valerie TerranovaView image in fullscreenPlaying it innocent … Brett Temple and Ella Kaille in Mrs Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library.Photograph: Valerie TerranovaEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMrs Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library review – interrogating Hannah ArendtTraverse theatre, EdinburghAn encounter in a police cell with a Nazi officer could have been the end of the political theorist, but Jenny Lyn Bader’s play has little feel for the dramaticMark FisherThu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 00.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Mrs Stern of the title is the married name ofHannah Arendt, the political theorist much remembered for her “banality of evil” insight. Jenny Lyn Bader sets her play not, as you might expect, in the Prussian state library, but in a police cell where Arendt has been hauled in for questioning not long after the Reichstag fire.The Nazi apparatus has extended its remit to political crimes and she, what with her bookish ways, errant husband and associations with Jewish intellectuals, has come under scrutiny.The suspicion is that rather than pursuing esoteric concerns, such as her doctoral dissertation on Love and Saint Augustine, she has been illegally researching antisemitism and farming out evidence to Zionist associates elsewhere in Europe. She plays it airy and innocent – her eyes might have strayed on to the occasional newspaper article when she was searching for a recipe – while her interrogator, an officer newly transferred from prosecuting conventional crimes, tries ineffectually to find cracks in her defence.At a time before the full horror of Hitler’s programme has come into place, it is still possible to expose contradictions in state policy: they come close to agreeing that Zionists and Nazis share common ground in the belief in a Jewish state, and only hasty backtracking gets them out of that one. In the meantime, the interrogator finds much to admire in Arendt’s worldview and, counter to Gestapo protocol, does his best to help her.View image in fullscreenHesitant … Ella Kaille and Brett Temple in Mrs Stern Wanders the Prussian State Library.Photograph: Valerie TerranovaGiven Arendt went on to flee Germany and make her name internationally, publishingThe Origins of Totalitarianismin 1951, the encounter marks a significant turning point that might easily have been the end of her. Sadly, the play has little feel for the dramatic. Rather, it is an old-fashioned back-and-forth between an evasive Arendt and an intrigued interrogator that fights shy of confrontation. It could transfer seamlessly to radio.Prophets review – a mysterious tale of faith at the end of the worldRead moreWorse, for a show that has already had a run in New York, Ari Laura Kreith’s production for Luna Stage is strangely stilted. Arms crossed and clutching a coffee cup, Ella Kaille is physically locked up as Hannah, while Brett Temple looks uncomfortably out of place as her toothless inquisitor. It makes for a hesitant, untheatrical performance.At Traverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreHannah ArendtNazismSecond world warreviewsShareReuse this content

title: RSC postpones Othello while leading actor Sharon D Clarke has cancer treatment | Sharon D Clarke | The Guardian
description: Radical reimagining of Shakespeare play was due to run at Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon from 13 February to 3 April 2027
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Radical reimagining of Shakespeare play was due to run at Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon from 13 February to 3 April 2027
Content: Clarke, a three-time Olivier winner, said she had been overwhelmed by the ‘tidal wave of love’.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClarke, a three-time Olivier winner, said she had been overwhelmed by the ‘tidal wave of love’.Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The GuardianSharon D ClarkeRSC postpones Othello while leading actor Sharon D Clarke has cancer treatmentRadical reimagining of Shakespeare play was due to run at Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon from 13 February to 3 April 2027Nadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentThu 13 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheRoyal Shakespeare Companyhas announced that it will postpone its radical production of Othello starring Sharon D Clarke, while the Olivier-winning actor undergoes treatment for cancer.The production, directed by Monique Touko, was scheduled to run from 13 February to 3 April 2027 at the Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon. Clarke, 60, is best known for her role as Lola Griffin in the BBC medical drama Holby City, as well as for her theatrical performances in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom and Caroline, or Change.In a statement on Thursday, Clarke said: “I would like to thank all the beautiful people at the RSC for their understanding, love, support and healing energy. Othello will be my north star as I undergo treatment.”She added that she, her family and wife – the writer and director Susie McKenna – had been “overwhelmed, humbled and buoyed by the tidal wave of love that we have received and are so blessed to have an army of strength and support to hold us up. Love and thanks to my beautiful people.”The RSC said anyone with tickets to see Clarke in Othello would be automatically refunded and a replacement production period would be announced at a later date.Touko, whose recent work has included Marie & Rosetta at @sohoplace and Jaja’s African Hair Braiding at the Lyric Hammersmith, said: “On behalf of the entire creative team, we send Sharon all the love for her ongoing treatment and recovery.“As a director, I have been incredibly blessed to collaborate with Sharon on this major reframing of Shakespeare’s tragedy, which reimagines Shakespeare’s Othello through the lens of misogynoir. Sharon is the ultimate collaborator. Her generosity and passion for this project continues to astound me and I look forward to us coming back together when the time is right to share this production with the world.”The RSC described the show as “set in a climate-threatened future in which a Black lesbian holds a seat of power”.It said it “re-imagines Shakespeare’s 400-year-old story through the lens of misogynoir, as an unsanctioned marriage perilously crosses boundaries of race, sex and status, allowing jealousy, suspicion and malign intent to close in.”The RSC’s co-artistic directors, Daniel Evans and Tamara Harvey, said Clarke’s casting as Othello was integral to Touko’s adaptation, “which is why we have taken the difficult decision to postpone, to give Sharon the time and space she needs to undertake treatment”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey added: “Sharon is, in every sense of the word, a warrior, and we know she will meet this challenge with the unwavering strength and indomitable spirit that she brings to so many aspects of her life and work. We look forward to revisiting this thrilling collaboration in the future and, on behalf of everyone at the RSC, we send Sharon our love and strength for a full recovery.”A three-time Olivier winner, Clarke has worked consistently on stage and screen since her first TV role in 1986’s The Singing Detective. Most recently, she starred as Lady Bracknell opposite Ncuti Gatwa in the National Theatre’s production of The Importance of Being Earnest.Explore more on these topicsSharon D ClarkeRoyal Shakespeare CompanyTheatrenewsShareReuse this content

description: A sensitive documentary looking at the complicated case of Rhianan Rudd. Plus: David Olusoga’s back with A House Through Time. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A sensitive documentary looking at the complicated case of Rhianan Rudd. Plus: David Olusoga’s back with A House Through Time. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Rhianan Rudd in The Schoolgirl Terrorist?Photograph: Rhianan RuddView image in fullscreenRhianan Rudd in The Schoolgirl Terrorist?Photograph: Rhianan RuddTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the tragic story of Britain’s ‘schoolgirl terrorist’A sensitive documentary looking at the complicated case of Rhianan Rudd. Plus: David Olusoga’s back with A House Through Time. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah J Davies,Phil Harrison,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellThu 13 Aug 2026 03.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Schoolgirl Terrorist?10pm, Channel 4What makes a teenage girl threaten to bomb a synagogue? In 2020, Rhianan Rudd, then 15, became the youngest girl to be charged with terror offences in the UK.She took her own lifetwo years later, five months after the charges were dropped. This sensitive documentary hears from her family to learn more about her vulnerable background, mental health issues and how she was groomed online by a neo-Nazi during lockdown – she even used a bobby pin to scratch a swastika on her head. Was her case handled correctly?Hollie RichardsonThe Big Deal With Steph McGovern8pm, BBC TwoThis new reality series set in the art world has an unmistakable whiff of an Alan Partridge Dictaphone idea, fused with Flog It!-esque daytime DNA and a dash of The Apprentice-style wheeler-dealing. First up, our amateur art dealers must sell graduates’ works.Hannah J DaviesA House Through Time9pm, BBC TwoDavid Olusoga’s social history series has reached a sixth season for very good reason: the single residence format remains a brilliant way of illuminating wider history via relatable personal histories. This time, he’s in Edinburgh, exploring a beautiful townhouse that has sheltered everyone from sculptors to spies.Phil HarrisonBetter Date Than Never9pm, BBC ThreeView image in fullscreenFingers crossed ….  Kento and date Rebecca at a cosplay ball on Better Date Than Never.Photograph: BBC/Northern PicturesThe return of a heartwarming show following new daters and, first up, 68-year-old farmer Dianne is back for a second stab at love. Elsewhere, 28-year-old Kento is looking for a fellow fan of anime, cats and anything to do with Japan – so sushi is the ideal dinner date with Maddie. Fingers crossed!HRThe Coen Brothers Story9pm, BBC FourIn 2000, documentarian Sarah Aspinall interviewed Joel and Ethan Coen. Now, she looks back at the experience and how they have since conquered Hollywood, speaking to their star collaborators, including Tilda Swinton, Jeff Bridges and George Clooney (“They really enjoy just making me the dumb shit in all their movies … and I love it”).HRPossession9pm, Sky AtlanticAs it reaches the halfway point, this supernatural thriller exploring Jamaica’s colonial past is building up an unsettling head of steam. After a weird encounter at the Hope Hill plantation, Gugu Mbatha-Raw’s conflicted lawyer Claudia is beginning to suspect her posh client Oliver (Jonny Lee Miller) may not be quite himself.Graeme VirtueFilm choiceView image in fullscreenShot in the palette of a telenovela … Ana Celeste Montalvo as Alejandra in A Child of My Own.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/NetflixA Child of My Own (Maite Alberdi, 2026), NetflixMaite Alberdi’s documentarystarts as a straightforward ripped-from-the-headlines dramatisation of a secret adoption, shot in the vibrant palette of a telenovela. Mexican hospital worker Alejandra has just had her third miscarriage when she meets Mayra, who doesn’t want the baby she is due to give birth to. Mayra agrees to hand her newborn over to Alejandra, who meanwhile will pretend to be going through her own pregnancy. It’s when their plan goes wrong that the film pulls the rug out from under the viewer. As other voices enter the frame, is the narrative we have been consuming true at all?Simon WardellLive sportSuper League rugby: Leeds Rhinos v Leigh Leopards, 7.30pm, Sky Sports Main EventAt Headingley Stadium.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mine by Adam Ouston review – novel told in a single sentence is a hallucinatory reading experience | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Ouston’s second novel follows a poet who is trapped in an abandoned mine in Tasmania while searching for inspiration for his ‘last great work’
Author: Catriona Menzies-Pike
Headline: Ouston’s second novel follows a poet who is trapped in an abandoned mine in Tasmania while searching for inspiration for his ‘last great work’
Content: Adam Ouston, author of Mine, which is ‘at once strenuous and exhilarating’.Composite: Rémi Chauvin/Transit LoungeView image in fullscreenAdam Ouston, author of Mine, which is ‘at once strenuous and exhilarating’.Composite: Rémi Chauvin/Transit LoungeAustralian book reviewsFictionReviewMine by Adam Ouston review – novel told in a single sentence is a hallucinatory reading experienceOuston’s second novel follows a poet who is trapped in an abandoned mine in Tasmania while searching for inspiration for his ‘last great work’Supported byAbout this contentCatriona Menzies-PikeThu 13 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 20.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ideal way to approach Mine, Adam Ouston’s second novel, might be to read it out loud in one exhausting sitting, to let its cadences roll and accumulate. This is a novel that consists of one long sentence, and thousands of clauses, digressions, conjunctions, modifications and clarifications. There is nowhere for the reader to rest.To read Mine out loud would leave one short of breath, parched, uncomfortable, delirious – and thus in sync with its central character, a poet, activist and teacher who has tumbled to the bottom of an abandoned mine shaft in western Tasmania, and now lies in the dark.This novel-in-a-sentence begins and ends with a howl, an urgent, pre-linguistic frequency that is “at once consoling and terrifying”. The poet is concerned with running out of air to breathe; claustrophobia, carbon monoxide poisoning, clean air rhetoric, and Tasmania’s ferocious winds and rains number among the many preoccupations of the novel’s roving consciousness.The poet has fallen into the mine while researching ghost towns, the subject of his last great work, “a reckoning of place that had gathered slowly within him over seven decades and into an eighth, a lifetime of writing and thinking and erasing and starting over”.He thinks of this undertaking as a “hauntology”, a reckoning with the revenant. Both the poet and the novel are concerned with lost futures, and particularly the aftermath of the rapacious exploitation of Tasmania’s mineral wealth; the novel reaches for “the secret, invisible story beneath the story, history without history, transporting, dreamlike”. The title of the novel carries the colonial prerogative to declare ownership over land and resources: “speak name own, mine”.It’s possible to conceive of Mine as a hallucinatory work of both environmental and social history. To do so requires the reader to hold the thread of narrative tightly as the novel winds through a maze of projections, identifications, repetitions and recursions. For this is not a linear history; “the darkness had prompted a fossilisation of his [the poet’s] inner timepiece”. Meanings accrete gradually. And yet narrative coordinates do emerge: an elegy for one of the poet’s friends, an account of Mawson’s expedition to Antarctica, a memoir of the poet’s journey on an icebreaker, a visit to the ghost town of Chester. The culmination of Mine is a bravura narration of the 1912 North Mount Lyell mine disaster, in which 42 men lost their lives, an intense demonstration of Ouston’s skill as a writer that brings together the major themes and figures of the book.I was unable to read Mine in one effortful spasm of breath and attention, just as I am not able to suspend time when I read other contemporary maximalist works whose narrators cannot or will not rest. These include Daniel Kraus’s Angel Down (2025), which won the Pulitzer prize for fiction in May; Lucy Ellmann’s Ducks, Newburyport (2019); Herscht 07769 (2024) by Laszlo Krasznahorkai; and Zone (2014) by MathiasEnard – all of which take the length of a novel to work through a sentence. Jon Fosse’s Septology extends a single sentence oversevenvolumes. But as useful as it is to locate this novel in an evolving tradition of transnational modernism, Mine is unequivocally a work about Tasmania, its brutal histories and its maddening ecology.This kind of writing is risky. Sections of Mine do buckle under conceptual overload and anxious multidirectional allusions. And yet what is the point of an experimental practice that is unwilling to take risks, or a maximalist novel that hesitates to cram in more ideas? Rather than guiding us along the well-tended and signposted duckboards of the realist novel, Mine requires us to cut our own track.The novel often recalls the “Age of Exploration Tracks”, that time when “cutting parties, armed with saws, axes, scrub-hooks, picks, and mattocks, carved and blazed access trails through the unrelenting rain and eucalypt forests, which itself was like boring through rock, a day’s toil to clear five metres”. This is not a bad description of what it’s like to read Mine, at once strenuous and exhilarating.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReaders for this kind of fiction tend to be self-selecting, and Ouston has already attracted a horde of admirers; his debut, Waypoints (2022), was longlisted for the 2023 Miles Franklin award. Mine is altogether a more accomplished work, not least because its formal radicalism is matched by the feral political energy of the activist-poet at its heart. The vitality of this expression of contemporary Australian modernism is grounded by the jeremiad against the exploitation of labour and the environment in Tasmania; as the poet reflects, “‘it was staggering what some people did and allowed to be done to something so precious”.Mine by Adam Oustonis out now (Transit Lounge, $34.99)Explore more on these topicsFictionAustralian book reviewsAustralian booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Universality by Natasha Brown audiobook review – a sparkling multi-voiced satire | Books | The Guardian
description: A magazine article about stolen gold sparks a culture war between a cast of politically polarised characters
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: A magazine article about stolen gold sparks a culture war between a cast of politically polarised characters
Content: Striking gold in Universality.Photograph: BA E Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenStriking gold in Universality.Photograph: BA E Inc./AlamyAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewUniversality by Natasha Brown audiobook review – a sparkling multi-voiced satireA magazine article about stolen gold sparks a culture war between a cast of politically polarised charactersFiona SturgesThu 13 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstinging dissection of wealth, class and the media, Natasha Brown’s satire begins with a man named Jake gazing at a gold bar he has found at a farm in West Yorkshire. Outside, an illegal rave is taking place which will end in three hospitalisations and property damage. Pondering what to do with the ingot that he has just used to bludgeon a stranger, Jake decides to do a runner.The story of the stolen gold is told by a journalist, Hannah, in a magazine article named A Fool’s Gold, replicated in full here, which she claims exposes “the fraying fabric of British society, worn thin by late capitalism’s relentless abrasion”. Her piece, which goes viral, features Richard Spencer, an arrogant, philandering banker and the owner of the farm, whose reputation is left in tatters; a contrarian rightwing newspaper columnist named Miriam Leonard, known as Lenny; and a group of radical anarchist squatters who call themselves The Universalists.Universality goes on to dissect the fallout from the article via the varying perspectives of its protagonists, all of which makes it ideal for the multi-voice audio treatment: Norma Butikofer narrates Hannah’s article while Hannah herself, a burnt-out literary journalist who stumbles on a scoop, is voiced by Anushka Chakravarti. Clare Corbett reads Lenny, antihero of the culture wars, and Daniel Weyman reads from the viewpoint of the self-pitying Richard, who calls Hannah’s actions “a cruel confidence trick”. Though we come to understand that each of the characters has an axe to grind; which of them, if any, can we trust?Further listeningThe Calamity ClubKathryn Stockett,Penguin Audio, 28hr 45minMeg, a young orphan deemed “unadoptable”, has her fortunes changed when she meets Birdie, the new bookkeeper at her orphanage. title: The End of Tom Six review – Human Centipede director delivers one last freaky flick | Movies | The Guardian
description: Now living with multiple sclerosis, Six rants about the masturbation film distributors won’t touch and the money mystery behind his horror hit
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Now living with multiple sclerosis, Six rants about the masturbation film distributors won’t touch and the money mystery behind his horror hit
Content: Disguised as Hunter S Thompson? … The End of Tom Six.Photograph: courtesy of Tom SixView image in fullscreenDisguised as Hunter S Thompson? … The End of Tom Six.Photograph: courtesy of Tom SixMoviesReviewThe End of Tom Six review – Human Centipede director delivers one last freaky flickNow living with multiple sclerosis, Six rants about the masturbation film distributors won’t touch and the money mystery behind his horror hitPeter BradshawThu 13 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 04.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifteen years ago, Dutch film-maker Tom Six succeeded where almost everybody fails – particularly in the world of horror. He actually shocked people. No self-respecting sophisticate admits to being shocked, of course, and no horror connoisseur will admit to being really and truly horrified. But Six really did freak audiences out with his extreme exploitation nightmare The Human Centipede, the first of a trilogy. It was a grenade in the faces of prim conformists, and also those badass horror fans who thought they’d seen it all.The “human centipede” of the title is created by a sadistic surgeon who imprisons three young people in a basement and sews them together mouth-to-anus as a vivisectional experiment. Six himself had been a director on theoriginal Dutch TV show Big Brotherthat started the global franchise, and it was easy to see how his movie masterwork was intended as a satire on consumerist voyeurism and cruelty. Or maybe it just sprang from the same dark creative place that gave birth to the TV phenomenon of the age.Either way, I remember tottering out of the screening theatre after watching it and whimpering to the critic and novelist Anthony Quinn that cinema was over now and that we should all go back to making our own entertainment like basket-weaving or singing around the piano. I concededthe first Human Centipede’s demonic punk inspiration, lost patiencewith the sequel, but foundthe third filmunexpectedly funny. So what happened to Tom Six after that?The answer comes in this chaotic, heavy-handed, self-indulgent, occasionally funny, zero-budget documentary, shot entirely in Six’s Amsterdam apartment – a lo-fi rant that he is uploading online on a pay-what-you-want basis. However huge The Human Centipede was, a massive talking point and punchline on numberless US TV comedies and talkshows, it didn’t make the director rich. As with the 70s adult movie Deep Throat, there is a mystery here about where exactly the profits went. Six went straight back to work on acomparably crazy and offensive feature called The Onania Club(tagline: “come and see, see and come”) about a group of bored American women who are addicted to other people’s pain. As he shrewdly says, it was “all safely metaphorical”, so that the horror had the status of satire.But Covid had upset the industry and timid distributors refused to touch it, despite rave reviews from luminaries including John Waters. And to make matters worse, Six found outhe had multiple sclerosis, which has now confined him to his apartment almost continuously, except for painful walks outside to get decaffeinated coffee, which is all he can digest (“like a hooker that only wants to cuddle”).Human Centipede director Tom Six reveals multiple sclerosis diagnosis in ‘final film’Read moreSix addresses the camera wearing hat and sunglasses, as if he is disguised as Hunter S Thompson, and he is comically (or not comically) surrounded by a ragtag circus of unlikely people that comprise his crew, including his vampily dressed, cocktail-quaffing partner Marci (Maartje Willems), and a small child doing the editing. There is a frowning “censor Nazi” (Servaes Nelissen) in full uniform, who is always whingeing about the proceedings being offensive – which is the cue for a great deal of rather tiresome comedy about woke attitudes. Six contrasts this tyrant with his grandfather, a heroic fighter in the Dutch anti-Nazi resistance in the second world war. (Strangely, he doesn’t talk about Big Brother.)And yet, despite all its very laboured non-PC humour, this film does have a relevant story to tell: about the terrible end awaiting all those who embark on risk-taking careers in indie film-making that end in failure. This slapdash aria of complaint has something in common with the rackety defiance of German exploitation maestro Uwe Boll who, grumpily out of step with liberal squeamishness, appeared inRadu Jude’s Do Not Expect Too Much of the End of the Worldand directed thecontroversial revenge thriller Citizen Vigilante. Six deserves his chapter in indie-cinema history, arguably alongside Sam Fuller and Roger Corman. And someone should release The Onania Club, or at least put it on at a festival. Can the UK’sFrightfestoblige?The End of Tom Six is on YouTube from 15 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsThe Human Centipede 3 (Final Sequence)Multiple sclerosisHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hellcat review – woman imprisoned in camper van in nasty survival horror | Movies | The Guardian
description: A woman wakes up in a trailer as it speeds along in this effective and icky thriller, though you do end up wondering when you (and she) will ever get out
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: A woman wakes up in a trailer as it speeds along in this effective and icky thriller, though you do end up wondering when you (and she) will ever get out
Content: What would you do? … Dakota Gorman as Lena in HellcatView image in fullscreenWhat would you do? … Dakota Gorman as Lena in HellcatMoviesReviewHellcat review – woman imprisoned in camper van in nasty survival horrorA woman wakes up in a trailer as it speeds along in this effective and icky thriller, though you do end up wondering when you (and she) will ever get outCatherine BrayThu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis survival thriller-horror starts in “what would you do?” mode, as a young woman wakes up in the back of a moving camper van with some sort of hideous wound on her arm. Well, what would you do? Lena (Dakota Gorman) approaches things fairly logically, first checking out her surroundings: under other circumstances the trailer would be quite charming, if slightly kitschy – floral curtains, varnished wooden panels, a “World’s Greatest Dad” mug and family photographs. Closer inspection reveals less homely details: conspiracy magazines and lurid novels, which in the presumed abduction scenario in which Lena finds herself, are hardly reassuring.When a disembodied voice begins to communicate with her, telling her that she has an hour to get to hospital before the veiny trails progressing from the wound on her arm reach her heart, she asks reasonable questions, which are met with cryptic replies and evasive half answers. The voice is emanating from the head of a taxidermised coyote type of beastie mounted on the wall, and it’s pretty clear this is the voice of the driver and apparent kidnapper. Naturally, the full situation is a little more layered than it initially seems.A big question for the viewer is whether the film will ever leave the confines of the trailer. A single-location film is a double-edged sword: it’s a high-wire act for the film-maker that, if written and performed well, can ably demonstrate their ability to master the essentials. Fail to sustain the audience’s interest, however, and you’re stuck without recourse to the bells and whistles that can help jolly things along. Hellcat does eventually leave the trailer, and probably needs to, after it reaches the end of the line in terms of ideas, even if it never repeats the tension of its opening sequence. But by this point we’re sufficiently invested in Lena that we want to know how it turns out – which is basically the point.Hellcat is on Shudder and AMC+ from 14 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hollywood encore: how ‘pro-shot’ Broadway shows became a major draw on the big screen | Broadway | The Guardian
description: Filmed versions of hit shows such as Hadestown, Hamilton and SIX have been transformed into cinematic events for those without hundreds to spend on tickets
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Filmed versions of hit shows such as Hadestown, Hamilton and SIX have been transformed into cinematic events for those without hundreds to spend on tickets
Content: A still from Hadestown: The Musical.Photograph: LD EntertainmentView image in fullscreenA still from Hadestown: The Musical.Photograph: LD EntertainmentBroadwayHollywood encore: how ‘pro-shot’ Broadway shows became a major draw on the big screenFilmed versions of hit shows such as Hadestown, Hamilton and SIX have been transformed into cinematic events for those without hundreds to spend on ticketsJesse HassengerThu 13 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s long been a source of frustration for theater fanatics: manyBroadwayshows, even those that don’t become years-long fixtures of the Great White Way, are professionally filmed, but often only for archival purposes, not public consumption. For years, those living outside of the greater New York City area unwilling to make an expensive trip of seeing a particular show were limited to the hierarchy of a touring company, a local production, or maybe, some years later for a particularly notable show, an airing of a filmed version on PBS. If all else fails, they could hope for an inevitably disappointing film version that failed to recapture the onstage magic. Starting in 2005, there were also occasional Fathom Events presentations of filmed stage shows, typically made available for one or two nights at a time, at premium prices (and looking more like ultra-big TV than polished cinema, at least at first).Analogue evil: why today’s horror film-makers are obsessed with obsolete techRead moreLately, though, so-called “pro-shot” movies – those filmed versions that used to pop up on public television’s American Playhouse or Great Performances series, as with the 1989 version of Into the Woods, aired two years after shooting but decades before Disney got around to making its Meryl Streep version – have been elbowing their way to the front of the line as a Broadway alternative. The highest-profile pro-shot so far has been Lin-Manuel Miranda’s smash Hamilton, intended to debut on the big screen but thrown to Disney+ during the pandemic-inspired yearlong break from wide theatrical releases. No surprise that the sudden ability to watch the original cast perform the most talked-about Broadway show in years from the comfort of the couch became an at-home event.It was a bit surprising, though, that five years later, Disney put Hamilton in movie theaters anyway – and that it cleaned up at the box office, despite or maybe because of how many fans already knew the show from a streaming service. By then, Hamilton was a pop-culture phenomenon featuring many now-familiar faces, inspiring fans attending at least one Manhattan theater to dress in costume for its opening night at the cinema (so, between Off-Broadway, Broadway, post-pandemic Broadway, and Disney+, at least its fifth opening night overall). Obviously that particular masterpiece draws particularly fanatical devotion.So it shocked some analysts when, last month, a pro-shot version of Hadestown, an acclaimed, Tony-winning and long-running but not exactly Andrew Lloyd Webber-scale musical, made over $10m in a wide North American cinema release, on par with Hamilton’s first weekend. Maybe some credit is due to the savvy timing of putting a musical that retells two major Greek myths in theaters simultaneously with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey; regardless, a five-days-only release was quickly extended, and while Hadestown (like Hamilton and other highly fan-driven events) dropped hard in subsequent weekends, it has collected over $20m so far. That’s actually a bit more than the 2025 Hamilton release; it also made more than the last Jackass movie, an Elvis Presley concert film, and recent wide-release movies starring Hugh Jackman, Jason Statham and Nate Bargatze.This week in the US, SIX The Musical Live! follows Hadestown into theaters, with a pro-shot version of the original West End production that takes a modernized look at the six wives of Henry VIII via a singing-contest framework. In October, movie star Rose Byrne will not be reprising her recent Broadway role in the revival of Fallen Angels for a film version; instead, the performance itself will be released directly to theaters. These aren’t coming from theater companies, either; Hadestown was a hit for the indie distributor Bleecker Street, while SIX is being put out by Focus/Universal. Suddenly your movie-ticketing app might start to look more like those “how many have you seen?” visual indices printed in the back of Broadway Playbills. Even shows that haven’t made it to theaters are getting splashier treatments: last summer, George Clooney’s Broadway debut in a stage version of his film Good Night, and Good Luck (casting him in a different, more central role than in the 2005 movie) aired live on CNN – a Broadway first – and eventually turned up on Netflix, where it’s currently streaming.Pro-shot Broadway shows at the cinema sit at the confluence of multiple observable post-pandemic cultural trends: as actually attending Broadway shows has become prohibitively expensive (especially for out-of-towners who may not have the flexibility to try various lotteries, day-of ticket sales, or just plain waiting out high demand), movie theaters have also become more flexible about what kind of material fills their auditoriums, and for how long. For years, most mainstream multiplexes booked movies in standard two-week blocks. Now Fathom Event-style limited revivals have become so popular that theaters and distributors have realized they don’t need to go through one particular company to show re-releases, big-ticket TV shows and you-are-there simulations of theatrical events. It’s a tribute to the flexibility of the movie theater as a public space – not least because hardcore theater fans probably know that pro-shots are more available at home than ever before, even beyond Hamilton. Naturally, there’s a streaming channel for that: BroadwayHD has livestreamed some productions, and has a library of titles, including some former hot tickets nonetheless unlikely to return in that particular form, like Hugh Jackman starring in Oklahoma!That was a production unlikely to be made into a “real” movie, and it’s hard to tell whether the accessibility of more Broadway shows will diminish the perceived appetite for full-on cinematic adaptations – or be seen as proof-of-concept that it need not take 20 years of audience-building to draw crowds to the multiplex. In fact, some of the longest-awaited movie versions – 2004’s The Phantom of the Opera, 2019’s Cats, even the less lengthy, but equally storied Rent, which came to screens with much of the original cast in 2005 – have been some of the least satisfying Broadway adaptations. On the other hand, the relatively swift commemoration of the Broadway blockbuster The Producers, with Tony darlings Nathan Lane and Matthew Broderick intact in the leads and joined by movie stars Will Ferrell and Uma Thurman, is one of the flop-sweatiest movie musicals ever made. A pro-shot probably would have more easily preserved the material’s reputation as an all-timer with the general public.Favoring the pro-shot does feel in line with certain 21st-century fandom trends, where some acolytes prioritize (or claim to prioritize, anyway) absolute fidelity over all else when it comes to seeing movies of their favorite books, comics or video games. It also might dilute the ephemeral magic of live theater, where part of the point is that sometimes-invisible interaction between performer and audience. The movie-theater experience of pro-shot theater, then, however makeshift, could be more important than a mere revenue stream. Maybe wider release of these records of original-cast productions – in addition to the greater good of preserving art that favored the rich and the lucky – will keep alive the notion that a lot of art does have that public component, and that a hard-to-get ticket isn’t the only way to access it.Explore more on these topicsBroadwayUS theaterMusicalsTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: James: Getting Away With It review – hippies, hardnuts and dreamers unite | Movies | The Guardian
description: Auto-hagiography it may be – most of the interviewees were in the band at some point – but this portrait of the seminal Manchester indie group is charming stuff
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Auto-hagiography it may be – most of the interviewees were in the band at some point – but this portrait of the seminal Manchester indie group is charming stuff
Content: Say Something or Sit Down … James in their heyday.View image in fullscreenSay Something or Sit Down … James in their heyday.MoviesReviewJames: Getting Away With It review – hippies, hardnuts and dreamers uniteAuto-hagiography it may be – most of the interviewees were in the band at some point – but this portrait of the seminal Manchester indie group is charming stuffLaurence PhelanThu 13 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time of their first flush of success – concomitant with the turn-of-the-90s Mancunian baggy scene, when indie discos thronged with people in big daisy petal T-shirts, and the anthemic Sit Down was only kept off the No 1 spot in the charts by Chesney Hawkes – James had already had as many ups, downs and near misses as most bands have in a lifetime.Subtitled Sects, Trance and Rock’n’Roll, this good-natured, funny and occasionally rousing documentary portrait details them all. It begins when their middle-class, boarding school-educated soon-to-be-singer Tim Booth meets cute with a bunch of working-class borderline hooligans in a band, after they sneak into the University of Manchester’s student union bar and swipe his drinks. Described by their manager as “a band that took all the wrong turns and made every mistake possible”, they turned down Factory Records’ offer to release a first album because they didn’t want to have a product number. They then turned down a support slot on the Smiths’ US tour because half the group had by then joined an esoteric meditation cult and the scheduling would have clashed with the bassist’s enlightenment.Later, the non-enlightened ones earned a reputation for being the party-hardiest reprobates on the 1997 Lollapalooza tour – the same year Korn, Snoop Dogg and the Prodigy were on the bill, no less. Mind you we only have their own word for it; Getting Away With It is a very insider account, to a fault, and other than sometime producer Brian Eno and lifelong superfan Chris Martin, virtually every interviewee in this documentary is or has been in James. The film is far more concerned with the internal dynamics of the band than their times or even their songs.James review – special band still filling arenas with anthems of warmth and humanityRead moreBut fair enough; the interpersonal dynamics are fascinating. They’re a mixture of hippies and hardnuts, dreamers and pragmatists, united by music. “We’re not alike but we share an ethos,” says one of them. And, quite deliberately it starts to seem, they have maintained a position on the brink of implosion, always dancing on the edge of chaos, generating drama to keep the sparks and the embers of their creativity glowing.James: Getting Away With It is in UK cinemas on 17 August for one night only.Explore more on these topicsFilmMusic documentaryDocumentary filmsIndiePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bruckner Symphony No 3 album review – Anima Eterna’s period instruments bring visceral drama | Classical music | The Guardian
description: There’s bone-crushing intensity in this striking recording of the original version of the Bruckner’s third. Pablo Heras-Casado teases out vital, almost operatic detail
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: There’s bone-crushing intensity in this striking recording of the original version of the Bruckner’s third. Pablo Heras-Casado teases out vital, almost operatic detail
Content: Measured but vital… conductor Pablo Heras-Casado.Photograph: Javier SalasView image in fullscreenMeasured but vital… conductor Pablo Heras-Casado.Photograph: Javier SalasClassical musicReviewBruckner Symphony No 3 album review – Anima Eterna’s period instruments bring visceral dramaAnima Eterna Brugge/Heras-Casado(Harmonia Mundi)There’s bone-crushing intensity in this striking recording of the original version of the Bruckner’s third. Pablo Heras-Casado teases out vital, almost operatic detailClive PagetThu 13 Aug 2026 11.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAccording to legend, in the summer of 1873 Anton Bruckner travelled to Bayreuth intending to dedicate one of a pair of scores to his hero, Wagner. Apparently, the two composers got legless and by the time Bruckner arrived back home, he could no longer remember which symphony the master preferred. In a flap, he put pen to paper: “Symphony in D Minor, where the trumpet begins the theme?” he fished. “Yes! Best wishes! Richard Wagner,” was the reply.View image in fullscreenAnton Bruckner: Symphony No 3 in D MinorPhotograph: Harmonia MundiWith its mighty peaks and faint reminiscences of the operas, the Wagnerian aesthetic looms large over the Third Symphony in D minor, especially in its more radical original version, presented here by period instrument specialistsAnima Eterna. Gut strings and original woodwind and brass are more pungent than their modern counterparts, but they sometimes struggle to summon the weight necessary for Bruckner. Not here. Pablo Heras-Casado conducts one of the most explosive and visceral accounts on record with his Belgian orchestra laying into the score with bone-crushing intensity.Compared with Roger Norrington, who opted for period instrument lite, and François-Xavier Roth’s foot-on-the-gas approach, Heras-Casado is more measured but no less vital. The results are almost operatic: his long-breathed Adagio comes across as an achingly lyrical aria; the furious Scherzo a frenetic micro-drama. The finale swings from rugged turmoil to broad good humour at the flick of a switch. Harmonia Mundi’s recording is strikingly immediate, revealing plenty of instrumental detail without stinting the music’s sonic amplitude.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
