title: We’re going to party like it’s 1629… the masques, the music and the mayhem of Banqueting House | Classical music | The Guardian
description: What music soundtracked 17th-century England? Ahead of a DJ set in Banqueting House, Georgia Mann looks at the wild, the experimental, the melancholic – and why a theorbo caused a security alert
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What music soundtracked 17th-century England? Ahead of a DJ set in Banqueting House, Georgia Mann looks at the wild, the experimental, the melancholic – and why a theorbo caused a security alert
Content: A scene from The Tempest at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, Stratford Upon Avon in 2016. Shakespeare’s play had its first recorded performance at the old Banqueting House in 1611.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from The Tempest at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, Stratford Upon Avon in 2016. Shakespeare’s play had its first recorded performance at the old Banqueting House in 1611.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianClassical musicWe’re going to party like it’s 1629… the masques, the music and the mayhem of Banqueting HouseWhat music soundtracked 17th-century England? Ahead of a DJ set in Banqueting House, Georgia Mann looks at the wild, the experimental, the melancholic – and why a theorbo caused a security alertGeorgia MannThu 13 Aug 2026 05.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 05.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing Charles is on the throne, there’s anxiety around the power-brokers of Whitehall, and an age of deep political division and conspiracy obsession is under way.That’s right, I’m referring to the middle years of the 17th century, a period I’m immersed in as I’m putting together a Jacobean-Carolean Classical DJ set, where the beats are to be dropped beneath one of the UK’s most awesome works of art: theRubens painted ceilingat the Banqueting House in Whitehall.After a period of restoration and conservation, the ceiling is on view again – and this weekend you’ll be able to feast your eyes on cherubim, goddesses and James I ascending to the celestial realm while listening to music that matches the visuals.double quotation markMasques were the 17th-century equivalent of a VIP ticket to Glastonbury, Glyndebourne and a Killing Kittens sex partyThe DJ set will see us segueing between music first performed in theBanqueting Housefour centuries ago, with lute songs and choral anthems employed as testament to the pioneering and introspective spirit of the age. This was an era in which amateur musicians had access, for the first time, to printed manuscripts; it was an era of heightened melancholy perfected by the Morrissey of his day, John Dowland; when the lute ushered in musical improvisation that John Coltrane and Jimi Hendrix would have relished. It was also an era of masques.Masqueswere the 17th-century equivalent of a VIP ticket to Glastonbury, Glyndebourne and a Killing Kittens sex party. Banqueting House’s architect, Inigo Jones, was also the set and costume designer of these masques, which encompassed opera, theatre, ballet and balland were always allegorical affairs, with mythological gods and goddesses parading around in outrageous costumes. These extravagant performances reinforced the divine right of the Stuart monarchy, and the audiencecourtiers, aristocracy dignitaries and diplomats – was seated according to status and rank. Masques also involved plenty of bad behaviour, with reports of performers in outrageous costume sometimes so hammered on stage that they vomited, and a chaotic tradition of the audience smashing up the refreshments table at the end of the show.View image in fullscreenOne of the last things Charles I saw on this earth: the Apotheosis of James I painted ceiling by  Rubens inside Banqueting House Royal Palace, Whitehall, London.Photograph: John Bingham/AlamyMusic was intrinsic to the power play at the Banqueting House, and much of it was wildly experimental. Jacobean music specialist and lutenist Elizabeth Kenny showcases some of the best of it on her album,The Masque of Moments. Masques would generally have featured three groups of instruments, she says: “A brass group, which often represented the underworld; a big band of violins, which accompanied the dancing that went on for hours; and a group in the middle made up of voices, lutes and viols. That group experimented with coloratura singing – cascades of notes – that would have blown people’s minds at the time.”The aristos were fully in on the action. Charles I’s wife, Henrietta Maria, danced the lead role in the masque Tempe Restored, in which she was lowered from the ceiling on a jewelled chariot. Strong Beyoncé energy. She was also rumoured to have been romantically involved with a star lutenist of the day, Jacques Gaultier – who obtained rock-star status for the way he played the treble lute, a tiny instrument that became a major element of the masques. (The lute section ranged from the teeny treble all the way through to a new-fangled beast of an instrument from Italy: the theorbo, a bass lute with an enormously long neck.) Importing musical ideas from Italy was de rigeur in the early 17th-century. Inigo Jones is said to be the person who brought the first theorbo to England. Apparently he was detained at the Jacobean version of customs because officials thought he had smuggled in a “popish machine” with which to assassinate the King.It was a lutenist, Robert Johnson, who composed music for the first ever performance of Shakespeare’s The Tempest at the Banqueting House in November 1611. Johnson wrote the song settings for Where the Bee Sucks and Full Fathom Five, music we still use today. Ruby Hughes performsFull Fathom Fiveon her recent album, Amidst the Shades; her pared back purity of tone perfectly captures the sense of an otherworldly, mournful spirit.Dowland was another contemporary of Shakespeare’s. He was a lutenist, composer, singer and master of melancholy, opting for cheery titles to his songs such as In Darkness Let Me Dwell and Flow My Tears. His greatest modern-day interpreter is the countertenor Iestyn Davies.“We have to really tune in to these songs,” Davies says. “We misunderstand this music as delicate and quiet, [but] it’s incredibly expressive. That’s why people like Sting get so hooked on it.” (Sting released an album of Dowland’s musicin 2006.) Listen to Davies singFlow My Tearsto experience what sadness meant in this era. “You need melancholy to cure your melancholy,” explains Davies of the belief at the time. “Songs were a way to access a deep sadness, and then get through it.”A year before Dowland’s death, Charles I ascended to the throne, an altogether different kingly creature to his father, James. Charles’s absolutist tendencies led to the schism with parliament, the civil war and, eventually, his death on the scaffold erected just outside the Banqueting House, where he was beheaded on 30 January 1649. Rubens’ epic painted ceiling was one of the last things Charles saw on this earth.Charles’s favourite composer was William Lawes, who fought and died for the king as a royalist soldier. Lawes’ Royal Consort Sets are written for viol consort, accompanied by a bass line of two plucked string instruments. They have a shadowy depth to them, flitting between dance forms of the day and a soulful solemnity that make for a poignant underscore to Charles’s final words: “I go from a corruptible to an incorruptible crown, where no disturbance can be.”View image in fullscreenPortrait of the composer John Dowland (1563-1626).Photograph: Album/AlamyLawes also wrote some exquisite sacred vocal music. The French early music ensemble Près de votre oreille (Close to your ear) recorded an album of it calledLighten Mine Eieslast year; the opening funeral elegy,Music, the Master of thy Art is Dead, is surely some of the most ethereally lovely music ever written about death.A new era at the Banqueting House dawned: that of the Lord Protector himself, Oliver Cromwell. I was surprised to discover that the man who led the Puritan government, which banned Christmas carols and shut down theatres, made the lavish environs of the Banqueting House his primary hall of audience in 1654.The Lord Protector was, in fact, a music lover who had his favourite organ from Magdalen College, Oxford, installed at his lavish apartments at Hampton Court, and employed various musicians to perform there. AsCromwell biographer Paul Layputs it, there’s a “spectrum of puritanism” and, ironically enough, Cromwell was at the milder end of it.And yet, thanks to the zealots, the theatres were shut and many musicians of the era found themselves forced to make a living playing in taverns and alehouses – the inspiration behind the hugely enjoyable Alehouse Sessions album by Norwegian early music ensemble Barokksolistene. It’s thought that these musical meetings during the Commonwealth era were the earliest public concerts in Britain.England’s republic was not destined to last anywhere near as long as Rubens’ ceiling, and the Interregnum officially ended on 29 May 1660. That same day, on his 30th birthday, Charles II made a triumphant return, processing through London and arriving at the Banqueting House to have his hand kissed by the gathered parliamentarians. This king had a taste for the theatre, and for actresses, and under the Merry Monarch the playhouses returned with ever more spectacular restoration entertainment.The 17th century closed with the destruction of almost all of the old palace at Whitehall in a massive fire. Banqueting House was left standing – but there were no more masquesthere – under the Georgians it became a chapel and under Victoria a military museum.As we prepare to return this music to the gloriously opulent space where it would have been heard 400 years ago, I’m reminded of lines from The Tempest, a play all about the power of theatre and the thin walls between fantasy and reality. Those ascendant Rubens paintings of a divinely ordained monarch will once again resound, as Prospero and Caliban’s island did, a place: “full of noises, Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight, and hurt not”.Classical DJ is at the Banqueting House, London, on 15 and 16 August.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicMonarchyOperafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Agent 64: Spies Never Die review – licence to kill time like the 90s never ended | Games | The Guardian
description: This GoldenEye 007-styled retro shooter is an agreeable set of straightahead shooting missions that hark back to a simpler time, with simpler controls
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This GoldenEye 007-styled retro shooter is an agreeable set of straightahead shooting missions that hark back to a simpler time, with simpler controls
Content: Polygon fighter … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Illustration: Replicant D6View image in fullscreenPolygon fighter … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Illustration: Replicant D6GamesReviewAgent 64: Spies Never Die review – licence to kill time like the 90s never endedPC; Replicant D6This GoldenEye 007-styled retro shooter is an agreeable set of straightahead shooting missions that hark back to a simpler time, with simpler controlsAlex SpencerThu 13 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith007 First Light, 2026 has already given us the best James Bond game in more than three decades, since the release of Rare’s N64 classic GoldenEye 007. But what about those players whose loyalties lie not with the super-spy himself but the particulars of that 90s interpretation of his adventures?Enter Agent 64: Spies Never Die. Made almost entirely by a single developer (who goes by the very cloak-and-dagger alias Replicant D6), its production values couldn’t be much further from the blockbuster First Light. There’s no voice acting, with all dialogue instead delivered via subtitles, while each location on your globe-trotting adventure is depicted by a repeating texture wallpapered over scenery so blocky you can count the individual polygons.View image in fullscreenFired up … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Illustration: Replicant D6In lieu of any high-budget flash, Agent 64’s big special effect is nostalgia. From the title onwards, this retro shooter is one long homage to GoldenEye, and to its un-Bonded successor, 2000’s Perfect Dark.Enemies have pinched facial features – a result of taking photographs of real people’s faces and wrapping them around diamond-shaped heads – and roll acrobatically from behind cover to take their next potshot, just as they used to. And yes, there’s a Big Head mode that swells those diamonds into enormous target-practice balloons.View image in fullscreenBrand new retro … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Illustration: Replicant D6Less explicably, Agent 64 retains the slightly strange control scheme of its inspirations, even though it doesn’t have to work around the (iconic but unwieldy) N64 pad that made it a necessity. You can pull a trigger for a zoomed-in precision aim, but somehow this is even fiddlier to steer with a modern analogue stick or mouse than it was back then. The first level features a pair of locks you must manually shoot; they remain the game’s toughest bosses.Better by far to just run and gun, letting the generous auto-aim do its thing. OK, the target your gun seeks out might not always be the one you expected, or wanted, but playing this way unlocks a hectic pace of action that – nostalgic warmth aside – is Agent 64’s greatest asset.It’s essential to the joys of split-screen deathmatch multiplayer, which generates the same kind of giggly fun that filled so many late 90s living rooms, especially once the match rules have been tweaked to allow only proximity mines or melee judo chops. (Youcanplay online, but this is so counter to the elbows-on-the-sofa appeal of the thing that I never actually attempt it.)Meanwhile, the story mode (which can be played solo or co-op with a partner) is so in hock to games of old that it ignores the subsequent 30 years of level-design knowhow. The number of dead ends and looping identical corridors can be infuriating, especially since dying means starting over from the beginning, but this is offset by the briskness of the missions. Each can be finished in less than five minutes, at which point the game will challenge you with a “par time” that often comes in undertwominutes.As you revisit these levels, trying to shave off vital seconds, their layouts begin to make much more sense. These are obstacle courses, really, where enemies aren’t so much a threat as they are something to be hurdled – or better yet, avoided. On top of this, Agent 64 piles hidden collectibles and challenge variants that recycle the levels in yet more ways, and their size makes them incredibly moreish.The fantasy on offer here isn’t really beingJames Bond. It’s being young again, with one illicitly acquired copy of GoldenEye to last you the summer and all the time in the world to pick the cartridge clean. For all its rough edges, that’s a mission Agent 64 pulls off with aplomb.Agent 64: Spies Never Die is out now, £19.64Explore more on these topicsGamesPCJames BondShooting gamesAdventure gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I wanted to capture the range of British culture at the time’: the photographer who documented late nights on the 90s London tube | Photography | The Guardian
description: In the 1990s, Mark McEvoy took portraits of punks, partiers and late-night lovers on the underground. His images show city life before smartphones – when people still had to rush to make the final train
Author: Luke Turner
Headline: In the 1990s, Mark McEvoy took portraits of punks, partiers and late-night lovers on the underground. His images show city life before smartphones – when people still had to rush to make the final train
Content: Crush hour … A couple on the Victoria line, 1993.Photograph: Mark McEvoyView image in fullscreenCrush hour … A couple on the Victoria line, 1993.Photograph: Mark McEvoyPhotography‘I wanted to capture the range of British culture at the time’: the photographer who documented late nights on the 90s London tubeIn the 1990s, Mark McEvoy took portraits of punks, partiers and late-night lovers on the underground. His images show city life before smartphones – when people still had to rush to make the final trainLuke TurnerThu 13 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark McEvoy’s tube photographs, taken inLondon Undergroundcarriages at around 11pm on Friday and Saturday nights from 1992 to 1995, capture moments that may seem superficially frivolous, but might be the most significant of our lives. These are the golden hours of the end of the week, where friendships are found and sealed; gabbled conversation rolls along with the sway of the carriages; and new lovers meet up en route for an encounter that may turn out to be a fleeting one-off, or in fact the beginnings of a lifelong companionship.All are swept along in the scramble to hop onboard the last tube – a panic that ended when all-night services began on some lines 10 years ago this month. The night tube arrived when my time of going out all weekend was fading, and gave me a slight feeling of missing out. Looking at photos of other people’s social lives can make one feel like that too; at the same time, it’s not hard to see ourselves in these tired, happy and thoughtful faces.These images feel so natural in part because McEvoy was not a voyeur but a participant in London’s mid-90s nightlife. Living in a shared flat in Camden Town, northLondon, he was part of the capital’s music scene, describing himself as “slightly hippy-ish, trendy, kind of casual, into funk, jazz and reggae”; he “smoked a lot of weed”. One night, travelling home from Brixton, he was struck by being surrounded by a very London mixture of people of different ages, races, sexualities and pop-cultural scenes – the tube carriage became a beautiful stage. “We’ve all been there,” he says of the underground train. “We can straight away relate to that space.”Thus inspired, he spent the next two years going underground around traditional pub closing time on Friday and Saturday nights. Most of the pictures were taken after McEvoy had asked his subjects for permission, and he found that usually they’d pose for a shot, then just carry on doing what they were doing before.The images are rooted in their time by the old wooden-floored rolling stock and tube seat patterns, and by the fashions of London’s subcultures: casuals, rockabillies, goths, and punks doing the punk thing and responding to requests for a photo by baring their arses. McEvoy documented the last years of the fiercely tribal nature of British youth culture before it was flattened out by the internet, as streaming homogenised music tastes.The lack of smartphones in these photos is striking. Yet the energy in them feels curiously universal, expressive of a particularly British shedding of reserve and the joy of closing time and just before, when a good night brings up the feeling that there’s always the potential for something more.Even today, with gen Z drinking far less than their predecessors, you still see similar scenes on the underground, although at 4am the train rattles along more quietly, carrying more wreckage. The life in the faces that McEvoy snapped three decades ago endures in a new generation, and even in those of us who are old enough to know better but still sometimes find ourselves rushing for the night tube. How can it not? It’s the eternal energy of London, written on skin and flesh; rage and laughter, smiles and tears.‘We’ve all been there, we can all relate’: Mark McEvoy on five of his night tube photographs(Main picture, above) “This couple were nuzzling up to each other, and when I asked if I could take a picture, they said yes straight away and started kissing. It was kind of a performance, but then it wasn’t. They thought: oh, this guy’s asked to take a picture; come on, let’s give him this. Or maybe they were about to kiss anyway.”View image in fullscreenSunglasses at night … An American Londoner on the Northern line, 1992.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“This passenger told me he’d just moved from the States. The big reason was because he got shot in the shoulder in gang crossfire. We started talking about the difference between America and England, and he said it was getting as bad here. I guess he was feeling the London tension.”View image in fullscreenMind the gap … A passenger seeming to pray on the Piccadilly line, 1994.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“The other side of my photography is capturing these moments. This is one of my favourite pictures in a way, because I obviously didn’t ask him to sit there, and he may or may not be praying. There were a few candid ones like that; people just crashed out, maybe having a rough time.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSubway sect … Punks larking about on the Northern line, circa 1990.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“I was very aware of all these different lives just passing each other, different backgrounds, ages, groups, tribes. I wanted to try to capture the variety of that: the wide range of British culture in that space at that moment.”View image in fullscreenTrain in vain … Revellers look for the party on New Year’s Eve, Jubilee line, 1994.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“These guys were running through the compartments. New Year’s Eve had just struck, so they thought: well, we’re not going to be able to make it up to Trafalgar Square, so let’s go crazy here.”View image in fullscreenUninvited guest … A lairy fellow traveller on the Northern line, 1993.Photograph: Mark McEvoy“He was drunk. As I stood up to get off, he said he wanted to be my assistant and followed me everywhere I went. He started talking to this Irish couple. I didn’t even know what they said, but within five seconds they started punching each other; it was mayhem. Then the train stopped. I just backed off the train very slowly and watched the doors close and the whole commotion disappear.”Mark McEvoy’s zineLondon Underground 1992-1995is out now. A selection of the tube series photos is planned for display at the London Transport Museum in spring 2027.Explore more on these topicsPhotographyArtLondonLondon UndergroundTransportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Living proof damaged landscapes can recover’: exploring a vast restored forest in southern Sweden | Sweden holidays | The Guardian
description: Söderåsen national park is one of Europe’s largest protected broadleaf woods, offering wild swimming, spectacular hiking trails and an inspiring story of regeneration
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Söderåsen national park is one of Europe’s largest protected broadleaf woods, offering wild swimming, spectacular hiking trails and an inspiring story of regeneration
Content: Sunrise over Söderåsen national park, Sweden.Photograph: Anders Tukler/AlamyView image in fullscreenSunrise over Söderåsen national park, Sweden.Photograph: Anders Tukler/AlamySweden holidays‘Living proof damaged landscapes can recover’: exploring a vast restored forest in southern SwedenSöderåsen national park is one of Europe’s largest protected broadleaf woods, offering wild swimming, spectacular hiking trails and an inspiring story of regenerationCoco Lone NealThu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the bus window, the ridge looks like a giant slumbering beast stretched deep green across the flat farmland. “It feels alive,” I say to the woman beside me. “Yes,” she answers. “It is where you would run for safety, don’t you think?”I am in southern Sweden to exploreSöderåsen national park, established in 2001 to protect more than 1,600 hectares (4,000 acres) of the larger Söderåsen ridgeline. Shaped over millennia by immense geological collisions, fractures, volcanic eruptions and ice ages, today it is one of northern Europe’s largest continuous protected broadleaf forests, and only 90 minutes by car from Copenhagen or, in my case, two hours bypublic transport.The little village of Röstånga at the gateway to the park is where travellers stop for supplies from the supermarket before disappearing into the forest on foot, bike or horseback, and people gather for food, live music and art.My room for the first night is inVilla Söderåsen, a grand timber-framed yellow and white guesthouse, which has stood at the park’s entrance since 1904. It was built for tourists arriving via the new railway in search of connection to nature. Sebastian and Åsa, the owners, want to continue that tradition. “We humans are as loud as elephants in the wood,” says Sebastian. “Sit quietly for half an hour and see what happens.”That evening, I eat with strangers at long wooden tables outside the hip restaurant and live music venueStationen. Music drifts out of open doors, adults chat around the fire, children run circles around us.View image in fullscreenPool of mystery … the ‘bottomless’ lake of Odensjön (Odin’s Eye).Photograph: Coco NealThe next morning, Åsa recommends I take a dip inOdensjön (Odin’s Lake). “Some say it is bottomless,” she says. It’s almost perfectly round, edged by steep beech-covered slopes, and fed by underground springs. Fifteen minutes into the forest and I am there.A woman making her way back to the village says: “There is a rock in the water, heated by the sun, sit there, let your body adjust.”Grasshoppers trill, spider silk trails from branches, noble chafer beetles glimmer like the aurora borealis, a dragonfly rests electric-blue on my now empty walking boots. I swim, the circle of blue sky rippling, and emerge ready for anything.A few years ago, scientists obtained a sediment core from the bottom of the lake, providing detailed information from the past 600 years of land-use history. This showed that in the 18th and 19th centuries the plateau was largely deforested. I would have been walking across a heath, repeatedly burned to improve grazing grounds. It is difficult to imagine as I move through endless layers of beech, mossy trunks, roots like octopus arms. Dead wood is left to rot, creating a rich habitat, that is the magic.Once I start searching, the signs of human history are everywhere too, from hollow ways to clearance cairns and dry-stone walls.Two hours of hiking later, I arrive at the second entrance to the park: Skäralid, a rift valley. The visitor centreNaturum, packed with information and playful exhibits, shares its premises withCafé Italia.Both look out onto a picturesque dam. A ranger explains that much of the initial conservation efforts since designation as a national park involved the felling of non-native Norway spruce and the planting of broadleaved trees in its stead.View image in fullscreenGreen idyll … several hiking trails weave through the woodlands of Söderåsen national park.Photograph: Nick Gregory/AlamyIn search of solitude, I choose the wilder three-hour Hjortsprångsrundan or Deer Leap circular, a trail named after a prehistoric hunting method where people drove game over a narrow cliff shelf. I pick my way along it, across heather and bilberry, to perch on the hard gneiss bedrock that blushes a startling mineral pink. A buzzard swoops down from the branch of a gnarled oak.The descent is like scrambling and slipping back through time into an entirely other world. Many of these slopes managed to escape the historical land clearances and thus are the closest to ancient woodland. But all around this area, ferns, lichen, fungi, seeds and spores are recolonising the land.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markThere’s a sudden crashing through the undergrowth. A young stag steps from a pocket of alder trees, pawing the groundThe scree slopes are dotted with springs pushed up from a subterranean lake and laced with streams that feed into the Skärån river. The scent in the bottom of the valley is heady, sweet and damp, bringing with it a keen awareness of how much is always happening just out of sight.I rest on a wooden walkway, pop a wild raspberry in my mouth and watch a slowworm the length of my forearm slither past. Then, a sudden crashing through undergrowth. Wolf? Wild boar? Moose? A young stag steps from a pocket of alder trees, pawing the ground. We look at one another. The sun drops, and as it does its light rises up the walls of the ravine.View image in fullscreenRooted … broadleaved woodland has replaced earlier spruce plantations.Photograph: Coco NealMy room for the second night is inSöderåsens Skafferi,avandrarhem, or wanderer’s home. The house glows like a lantern on the edge of the dark wood. The owner Elisabeth, who spent her childhood exploring Söderåsen on horseback, says the house was once the first nature school in Sweden.On my final morning I climb to Kopparhatten, the park’s highest viewpoint at 212 metres, and hold up a booklet with an image of a painting from 1840 of this same vista, almost bare of trees. “We used to holiday in the south,” a couple tell me. “But we’re searching for cooler climates now.” I wonder what stories they will bring home.Summer, all green infusion; autumn, rust and gold; winter, snow and stone; spring, wood anemones and paper-thin leaves. The national park feels like living proof that damaged landscapes can recover if nature, and humans, are given half a chance.Accommodationwas provided byVilla Söderåsen(doubles from1,095 Swedish Kronor,about £85,B&B). Coco also stayed atSöderåsens Skafferi(doubles fromaround £78).Söderåsen national parkhas multiple wild campsites with wind shelters and barbecue areas.For information on public transport access, visitskanetrafiken.seExplore more on these topicsSweden holidaysScandinavia holidaysEurope holidaysWalking holidaysRewildingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Berries with a hint of tarmac – what do we mean when we call a wine ‘fruity’?  | Wine | The Guardian
description: Bananas, peaches, strawberries – anything but ‘grapes’. What do all those volatile organic compounds really mean for your summer sipping?
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Bananas, peaches, strawberries – anything but ‘grapes’. What do all those volatile organic compounds really mean for your summer sipping?
Content: There’s no accounting for taste, so if you think you can taste felt-tip pens, then so be it.Photograph: fstop123/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThere’s no accounting for taste, so if you think you can taste felt-tip pens, then so be it.Photograph: fstop123/Getty ImagesWineBerries with a hint of tarmac – what do we mean when we call a wine ‘fruity’?Bananas, peaches, strawberries – anything but ‘grapes’. What do all those volatile organic compounds really mean for your summer sipping?Mina HollandThu 13 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.“Strawberries, cherries and an angel’s kiss in spring,”sang Nancy Sinatra. “Mysummer wineis really made from all these things …” Overlook the angel’s kiss and, if you’re a wine drinker, you might recognise some of those fruity tasting notes – strawberries and cherries, indeed, but also citrus, orchard, other stone fruits and the whole berry family. In fact, it’s common to liken a wine to almost any fruit – except grapes.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.A wine can have notes of almost anything – pencil shavings, tennis balls, cat pee – but fruit is the most obvious (clearly, wine is made from fruit) and universally recognised. If I told you I was getting, say, green apple and lime zest from a riesling, you would probably have a good sense of what that meant, and what you might be able to expect on tasting it yourself. If I described a petroleum aroma, that might sound a bit cryptic and much less appealing, unless you were familiar with this tasting note commonly found in riesling. In other words, a wine’s fruit profile is often leveraged as a marketing tool. What better example of this than the “strawberries and cream” of Provence rosé? It’s a tasting note that underpins our collective sense that rosé is a summer drop, perfect for sun-drenched days filled with watching tennis, ocean views and seasonal produce.But that probably sounds more cynical than I intended.Fruitnotes in wine are very much a real thing. When we talk about a wine having notes of tart cherry or candied orange, we’re describing what we find in its aroma – smell being, of course, a factor in how we taste. Wines contain aromatic compounds that are similar to or the same as those found in other fruits – for example, esters (made by yeasts during fermentation, bringing notes of banana, pear, pineapple), or compounds originating in grapes, including thiols (tropical fruit), norisoprenoids (dried fruit and honeyed notes) and terpenes (citrus and floral aromas).To deconstruct a wine in this way can feel pedantic – a wine is so much more than a collection of aromatic compounds, after all. Something of its magic lies in Sinatra’s ineffable “angel’s kiss in spring” – often, I find, this is the time or place in which you drink it, or the people with whom you do so – but today’s picks showcase some of the different fruit aromas you might find in grapes, styles and regions, from the apricots and orange blossom of the moscatel and torrontes blend from southern Chile to a simple, peachy Roussillon orange, to the damsons and dark cherries of a Georgian saperavi. Your summer wine really can have aromas of all these things.Six fruity little numbers to splash out onPipeño Blanco 2024, A Los Vinateros Bravos£20.90 Monty Wines, 12.5%. Apricot, peach and citrus peel in this skin-contact white made from aromatic, old bush vines in Chile.W/O Organic Nero d’Avola Rosato 2024£14.99Laithwaites, 12%. You’ll find all the summer berries in this volcanic and organic Sicilian rosé from Etna.Cote Mas Orange£10.25 Waitrose, 13%. Any orange notes in this orange wine are zesty and a little cooked; a peachy introduction to the genre.M&S Found Saperavi£12 Ocado, 13%. Saperavi means “dyed” – its skins bring deep colour and rich, grippy dark red fruit aromas. Great for a barbecue.Alain Grignon Reserve Carignan Vieilles Vignes2023/24£12.50, Majestic, 12.5%. A spicy, old vine carignan with lots of cherry and dried cranberry – a proper bargain crowdpleaser.Flavia Catarratto Zibibbo£33 Ocado, 12.5%. A delicious, tropical fruit bomb from Sicily – expect pineapple and grapefruit. I almost wanted a cocktail umbrella.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodFruitSummer food and drinkItalian food and drinkFrench food and drinkEastern European food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuits | Food | The Guardian
description: Combine these simple Italian baked treats with chilled fruit and thick cream for a playful summer pudding
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Combine these simple Italian baked treats with chilled fruit and thick cream for a playful summer pudding
Content: Rachel Roddy’s figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuits.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuits.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuitsCombine these simple Italian baked treats with chilled fruit and thick cream for a playful summer puddingRachel RoddyThu 13 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his exquisiteThe French Menu Cookbook, Richard Olney has clear ideas and strong opinions about everything, including dessert. He believed that rich desserts should follow only the simplest of meals, whereas with most menus (meaning all the sophisticated menus in his book), something light, airy and playful is best. His suggestions read like a summer fruit poem: peach melba, apple mousse with peaches, apricot fritters dusted with icing sugar, strawberries in sweetened orange juice, strawberries in beaujolais, strawberry mousse with raspberry puree, iced cherries and fresh almonds. One of his late summer/early autumn menus also suggests fresh figs with raspberry cream (figues à la crème framboise), which is both fun to make (the red puree streaking through the cream for a raspberry ripple) and to eat.An airy and playful pudding calls for an airy and playful biscuit. What better thanlingue di gatto,or cat tongues, so called because of their flat, elongated shape. Made from butter, sugar, flour, and egg whites,lingue di gattoare not complicated to make, but do require a piping bag, which can be mimicked by a zip-lock bag – just remember to scrape the mixture into the bag first, and only snip the end off when you are ready to pipe.This recipe is from Italian pastry chef Iginio Massari’s Non solo zucchero [Not Only Sugar] Volume 1, an invaluable step-by-step guide to short pastry, sponge cakes, butter masses, creams, cream puffs and meringues aimed at professional pastry chefs, but just as suitable (and revelatory) for enthusiastic but chaotic pastry cooks like me.There are various ways to serve this pudding. Olney suggests a large serving dish, which, considering his warning never to put tomato dishes on a red plate or those including spinach on a green one, shouldnotbe pink. Olney arranges the chilled fig slices first, then pours the raspberry cream over the top, which baffles me slightly, because the cream is so thick. An alternative is serving in individual bowls, saucers or glasses: a spoonful of the raspberry cream first, then topping it with a small pile of fruit (figs, the whole raspberries you’ve set aside, plus redcurrants and mint leaves). The cat tongue biscuits can be stuck in the cream like fairy wings, put on the side of the plate, or passed around the table on a separate plate so everyone can help themselves.Figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuitsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appServes84-6 ripe figs(pale green or dark purple)250g raspberries,washed250ml whipping cream1-2 tbspicing sugarA few redcurrantsA few mint leavesFor the biscuits50gsoft butter60gicing sugar3 egg whites(50g)60gplain flour, sifted30g flaked almondsPut the softened butter and icing sugar in a bowl, and use a spatula to mix them together. Fold in the egg whites, before adding the sifted flour and mixing again.Scrape the mixture into a pastry bag with a smooth 10mm nozzle (or a zip-lock bag you can snip the corner from). On a baking tray lined with baking paper, squeeze out lines that are 10cm long, ensuring you leave 4cm between each one. Top each one with three or four almonds, then bake at 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 for about eight minutes, until golden. Leave to cool a little before lifting on to a cooling rack.It is up to you whether you peel the figs before you slice each one into four; chill. Set aside half of the raspberries, then press the rest through a fine sieve for a smooth, bright-red puree. Whip the cream until stiff, then stir in the icing sugar to taste and the raspberry puree for a mottled effect.Divide the cream between four individual bowls or glasses, top with wedges of fig and a few raspberries, plus some redcurrants and mint leaves. Serve with the biscuits.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkDessertBiscuitsFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Escaping the ​heat​ and rediscovering the ​joy of ​cooking | Food | The Guardian
description: Parts of the UK are roasting but some of us are glad to turn the oven on. Bring on the​ ​curries and pasta pies
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Parts of the UK are roasting but some of us are glad to turn the oven on. Bring on the​ ​curries and pasta pies

Bring on the​ ​curries and pasta piesSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastFelicity CloakeThu 13 Aug 2026 07.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t wish to boast, but I’m typing this with a jumper on. Not because my flat has air-conditioning, but because it doesn’t – and the relentless heat of south-east England was having a seriously detrimental effect on my productivity and the health of my elderly dog (NB: the two are not mutually exclusive). So, witha second novel to write, I decided to rent a studio as far north, and as far west, as I could reasonably drive in a day. And, so far, I have no regrets. Driving through North Yorkshire, I had to put on a sweatshirt – the weather in the Pennines gave my car the first good wash it’s had in months – and now, in Scotland, the dog and I feast on hot porridge in the mornings. I’d genuinely forgotten what it’s like to be cold – and what it’s like to cook for pleasure.This newsletter isn’t just for those parts of the country enjoying, rather than suffering, the sunshine; yesterday it was raining and tonight the temperatures will drop to almost single digits. It’s also for anyone, wherever you are, who’s eaten enough cool, crunchy salads and chilled soups to last a lifetime, or at least until next summer. (You’re not alone: last month,Waitrose reported a spikein sales of cottage pie and robust South African red wine.)Much as I enjoy those things, I’m not craving winter food just yet; there will be time enough for that, and I’m keen to make the most of summer produce while we have it. I would have no issue turning on the oven for Yotam Ottolenghi’sMexican-inspired prawn-stuffed peppers, for example, or Sami Tamimi’sPalestinian versionwith freekeh, lamb and spicy tomato sauce. Unsurprisingly, I also have a soft spot for my ownProvençal-style stuffed courgettes.View image in fullscreenAn all-weather treat … berries with raw cream.Photograph: Matt Russell/The GuardianStaying with baked vegetables, now is the perfect time of year for an aubergine parmigiana –in her recipefor a slightly lighter take, Rachel Roddy recalls her partner informing her that his Sicilian grandmother always did any frying or baking early in the morning, so the hot work was finished for the day by 10am, an approach familiar to me from recent weeks of recipe testing in London. On the aubergine front, I’m afraid I couldn’t choose between highlighting Atul Kochhar’s Chettiar aubergine curry, Arto Der Haroutunian’s aubergine tagine and Anna Del Conte’s showstopping aubergine pasta pie inthis selection of recipesfrom 2013, so please have at them with my blessing.I must confess, however, that I brought tomatoes up to Scotland with me, which I’ve mostly been eating on toast (would that I had the right ingredients for Joe Woodhouse’s luxuriant take withcreme fraiche and mint). But if I happen upon any less worthy candidates, they’re going straight into Nigel Slater’ssausage, tomato and lentil bake gilded with chilli oil, or perhaps Jessica B Harris’fried green tomatoes, a dish that, I was strictly informed by a lady from Alabama a few years ago, needs no accompaniment.Although I suspect there must be great tomatoes available on the Scottish west coast, I know there to be fantastic berries and, thanks to the long, light days at this time of year, far better ones than most of those grown down south. You might fancy Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’sraspberry and almond streusel cake, or Anna Jones’sroast strawberries with lemon and black pepper, though, whatever the weather, I still prefer my berries raw with cream in afruit foolor anEton mess; the most complex I might get is Nigel’sloganberry cream with flapjack.When I find some really good ones, however, I’m more likely to eat them straight from the punnet. If you’re reading this somewhere hot, I very much suggest you do the same. Alternatively, take the day off cooking, and go and buy an ice lolly instead. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland’s best service station|I haven’t visited every service station in Scotland – in fact, I’ve visited very few of them, because I usually bring sandwiches – but having stopped at Cairn Lodge Services on the M74, I think it must be a strong contender for this crown. Newly refurbished by the same group asTebayandGloucesterservices, it boasts a farm shop and a cafe offering homemade food, canteen-style, on china plates. I had a bowl of courgette, pea and mint soup with an excellent cheese scone, and I will certainly be stopping there for breakfast on the way home. Why can’t we have more options such as this alongside the hamburgers?Great Taste awards results|The results of the Guild of Fine Food’s annual taste tests came out a couple of weeks ago, and it’s well worth having alook at the directoryto see what has scooped those coveted three stars. Having helped to judge the awards for the past decade or so, I can promise you that the process is as fair and as rigorous as possible, and a starred sticker is often all the sales pitch I need. My takeaway from my stint this year: Irish readers, if you’re not familiar with sour cream from Green Pastures, I’d suggest rectifying that. We ate it straight from the spoon with no embellishment.Best breakfast in Cornwall|I had the pleasure of spending a couple of nights in Penzance last month during the town’s literary festival, and thus of revisitingChapel House (boutique) B&B. The menu included, among other delights, fry-ups with both black and hog’s pudding (a creamy white pudding that deserves to be better known outside the West Country), and an amazingly light-green omelette with spinach, tarragon and cheese, cooked in plenty of butter. Wish I’d asked for the recipe now.
